pw-arch:0.title: Playwright architecture and test isolation
pw-arch:0.html:
Playwright drives the browser from outside through protocols: CDP for Chromium and its own patches for Firefox and WebKit. Tests run in a Node.js process and send commands to the browser, so several tabs, windows, domains and contexts are available in one test. Chromium, Firefox and WebKit are supported, as well as the languages TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Java and .NET.

The key hierarchy: Browser → BrowserContext → Page. A BrowserContext is an isolated "incognito session" with its own cookies, storage and cache, and creating one takes milliseconds. The test runner gives every test a new context by default, so tests don't share state with each other.

This is the main difference from Cypress: isolation is cheap, and parallelism is built in and free. Tests are distributed between workers, which are separate processes, each with its own browser.

pw-arch:1.title: What happens under the hood of the runner
pw-arch:1.html:
When I run npx playwright test, the main process collects the list of tests and then starts workers, which are separate Node.js processes. Each worker imports the test files itself, launches its own browser and runs the tests it was given. That is why module-level global variables are not shared between workers: each has its own copy.

An important detail that is often not known: after a test fails, the worker is destroyed, and a new one is started for the following tests. This guarantees that a "broken" state doesn't leak into other tests. The consequence: beforeAll and worker fixtures run again in the new worker. If an expensive test user is created in beforeAll, it will be created again after every failure.

Retries work the same way on new workers: a test that failed is restarted in a new process with a clean browser.

  • The main process: collects tests, distributes them, gathers results for the reporters.
  • A worker: its own browser (worker scope), its own fixtures.
  • A test: its own BrowserContext and Page (test scope).

Hence the rule: don't rely on the order of tests or on state in module variables. If test A wrote something to a variable, test B may run in another process and won't see it.

In an interview: The runner distributes tests between workers, which are separate processes, each with its own browser. After a test fails, the worker is restarted, so beforeAll may run several times. Because of this I don't keep shared state in module variables, and I get everything I need through fixtures.

pw-arch:2.title: Packages, browsers and channels
pw-arch:2.html:
There are two packages: playwright is a library for browser automation without a runner, and @playwright/test is a runner with fixtures, assertions, reporters and parallelism. For tests you take the second one, and the library is for scripts, scraping or integration with another runner.

Browsers are not taken from the system, but downloaded for a specific Playwright version: npx playwright install. On CI on Linux you add system dependencies: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium. After the package is updated, the browsers must be reinstalled, otherwise there is an error about a missing executable.

Besides the bundled Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, you can run branded browsers through channel:

projects: [
  { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  { name: 'google-chrome', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], channel: 'chrome' } },
  { name: 'edge', use: { ...devices['Desktop Edge'], channel: 'msedge' } },
],

WebKit in Playwright is not the real Safari, but the WebKit engine, close to it. It catches differences in rendering and behaviour well, but it doesn't replace a final check on a real iOS device. This is an honest answer that is valued in an interview.

In an interview: For tests I use @playwright/test, and I install browsers with npx playwright install --with-deps, because they are tied to the package version. If it is important for the business specifically to have Google Chrome or Edge, I add projects with channel. I also understand that WebKit is an approximation of Safari, not a full replacement for a real device.

pw-bcp:0.title: Built-in fixtures and manual creation
pw-bcp:0.html:
The runner provides the fixtures browser, context and page. browser has worker scope: one launched browser per worker. context and page have test scope: a new context and page for every test, which the runner itself closes after the test.

When you need more control, you create a context manually from the browser fixture:

test('guest sees the cookies banner', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({ locale: 'uk-UA' });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Cookies' })).toBeVisible();
  await context.close();
});

The runner doesn't close a manual context: that is my responsibility. If you forget context.close(), open pages will remain when a test fails, and video and HAR may not be written, because they are finalised exactly when the context is closed.

Context options are the same as the use section in the config: viewport, locale, timezoneId, storageState, permissions, extraHTTPHeaders, baseURL. The only difference is that through use they are applied to the built-in context fixture, and through newContext to my own context.

In an interview: browser lives at the worker level, while context and page are created for each test and closed automatically. If I need a separate context with different settings, I create it through browser.newContext() and close it myself, best of all in a fixture, so that the teardown runs even on a failure.

pw-bcp:1.title: Two users in one test
pw-bcp:1.html:
A classic task: check a chat or a money transfer between two people. Here you need two independent contexts, because tabs of one context share cookies, and the second user would simply "overwrite" the first one's session.

test('message reaches the recipient', async ({ browser }) => {
  const alice = await browser.newContext({ storageState: '.auth/alice.json' });
  const bob = await browser.newContext({ storageState: '.auth/bob.json' });
  const alicePage = await alice.newPage();
  const bobPage = await bob.newPage();

  await alicePage.goto('/chat/bob');
  await alicePage.getByRole('textbox').fill('Hello');
  await alicePage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click();

  await bobPage.goto('/chat/alice');
  await expect(bobPage.getByText('Hello')).toBeVisible();

  await alice.close();
  await bob.close();
});

Both contexts work in one browser, so this is cheap. A separate browser for the second user isn't needed.

The opposite situation is several pages in one context through context.newPage(). They share the session, and this suits checking synchronisation between tabs of one user, for example a logout in one tab must log out the other.

In an interview: For two users I create two contexts with different storageState, because a context is a separate session. Several pages of one context share cookies, so I use them only for single-user scenarios across several tabs.

pw-bcp:2.title: Page events as an extra check
pw-bcp:2.html:
A Page emits events you can subscribe to: console, pageerror, request, response, requestfailed, dialog, popup, download. This is useful not only for debugging, but also as an automatic quality check.

For example, unhandled JavaScript errors on a page often break functionality unnoticed by UI assertions. They can be collected and used to fail the test:

test('payment page has no JS errors', async ({ page }) => {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  page.on('pageerror', (err) => errors.push(err.message));
  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') errors.push(msg.text());
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  expect(errors).toEqual([]);
});

The difference: pageerror is an exception that nobody caught, while console with the type error is what the code itself printed through console.error. The latter is often noisy because of third-party scripts, so the list is usually filtered.

The requestfailed event helps catch requests that failed at the network level, for example blocked by CORS or a dropped connection. To avoid duplicating such code in every test, it is moved into an auto fixture.

In an interview: I subscribe to pageerror and console to catch JS errors that UI assertions don't see. To avoid copying this into every test, I make an auto fixture that checks after the test that there were no errors.

pw-loc:0.title: Locators, and Locator vs ElementHandle
pw-loc:0.html:
The recommended built-in locators are: getByRole, getByLabel, getByPlaceholder, getByText, getByAltText, getByTitle and getByTestId. The priority is getByRole with a name, because it reflects how the page is seen by a user and by assistive technologies. CSS and XPath through page.locator() are a fallback.

A Locator is lazy: when it is created it searches for nothing, and the search happens every time at the moment of an action or a check. So it survives re-rendering and doesn't give stale element errors. Before an action Playwright automatically waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable, enabled and able to receive events.

A Locator works in strict mode: if a selector finds several elements, the action throws an error, and you have to narrow it with filter, first, nth or a chain. An ElementHandle is a reference to a specific DOM node captured once, without auto-waiting and strict mode, so it is discouraged. It is rarely needed, for example to pass a node into evaluate.

pw-loc:1.title: getByRole in depth: options and precision
pw-loc:1.html:
getByRole searches by ARIA role and accessible name. It is important to know how name works: by default it is a case-insensitive substring search. So { name: 'Save' } will also find the "Save draft" button. For an exact match there is exact: true, and for a flexible one a regular expression.

page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save', exact: true });
page.getByRole('link', { name: /^Order #\d+$/ });
page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Cart', level: 1 });
page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'I agree', checked: true });
page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Menu', expanded: false });
page.getByRole('tab', { selected: true });

Additional options filter by state: checked, pressed, expanded, selected, disabled, level for headings. By default hidden elements are not taken into account; includeHidden: true changes that.

The accessible name comes from the element's text, aria-label, aria-labelledby or the associated label. If getByRole doesn't find a field, it is often a real accessibility bug: an input without a label wouldn't be read by a screen reader either. I report such cases to the developers instead of working around them with CSS.

To check the structure of a whole block, since version 1.49 there is toMatchAriaSnapshot: it compares the accessibility tree with a YAML template. This is handy for menus or forms where the composition and order of elements matter.

In an interview: In getByRole the name is searched as a case-insensitive substring by default, so for identical buttons I use exact: true or a regex. I also apply state options like checked or expanded. If a role isn't found, it is a signal of an accessibility problem.

pw-loc:2.title: Chains, filter, has, and, or
pw-loc:2.html:
Strict mode forces you to refine locators, and there are several tools for that.

A chain narrows the search area: page.getByTestId('cart').getByRole('button', { name: 'Remove' }). The inner locator is searched only inside the outer one.

filter keeps the elements that match a condition:

const row = page.getByRole('row')
  .filter({ hasText: 'INV-1042' })
  .filter({ has: page.getByRole('cell', { name: 'Paid' }) });
await row.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refund' }).click();

const activeItems = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasNot: page.getByText('Archive') });
const visibleToasts = page.getByRole('alert').filter({ visible: true });

The difference is important: a chain looks for a child element, while filter({ has }) returns the outer element itself that has such a descendant. That is, "find the row that has a Paid cell", not the cell itself. There are also hasText, hasNotText, hasNot and visible.

and intersects two locators for one element: page.getByRole('button').and(page.getByTitle('Subscribe')). or gives an alternative: "either a consent dialog or a Continue button", which is useful when an application may show one of two states.

first(), last(), nth() are the last resort. They are tied to the order in the DOM, so they break when the sort order changes. If I write nth, it is only when the order is part of the requirement.

In an interview: For tables I find a row through filter with hasText or has, and then the needed button inside the row. I use nth only when the order is important by the requirements. or helps when an application can legitimately show one of two states.

pw-loc:3.title: Test id, lists and the all() trap
pw-loc:3.html:
getByTestId searches for the data-testid attribute by default. If the project uses another one, for example data-qa, it is set in the config: use: { testIdAttribute: 'data-qa' }. I use a test id when there is no stable role or text: icons without a label, dynamic containers, multilingual texts.

To check a list, assertions on the whole locator are better than loops:

const items = page.getByRole('listitem');
await expect(items).toHaveCount(3);
await expect(items).toHaveText(['Bread', 'Milk', 'Cheese']);

toHaveText with an array checks the count and the order, and retries until the timeout.

The trap is locator.all(). It returns an array of locators for the elements that are in the DOM right now, and it doesn't wait. If the list is still loading, I get an empty array, and the loop simply checks nothing: the test is green, though nothing was tested. So before all() I first wait for the state, for example with toHaveCount.

await expect(items).toHaveCount(3);
for (const item of await items.all()) {
  await expect(item.getByRole('img')).toBeVisible();
}

Likewise count(), textContent() and allTextContents() return values at a single moment, without retries. They can be used for logic, but not for checks.

In an interview: For lists I use toHaveCount and toHaveText with an array, because they retry. all() doesn't wait for elements, so before it I always put an assertion on the count, otherwise the loop may walk through an empty array and give a falsely green test.

pw-wait:0.title: Web-first assertions
pw-wait:0.html:
Web-first assertions are expect with a locator: toBeVisible, toHaveText, toHaveValue, toHaveCount, toHaveURL and so on. They check a condition in a loop until it becomes true or the timeout expires, which is 5 seconds by default and is configured through expect.timeout. They are written with await before expect: await expect(locator).toHaveText('Done').

A bad practice is expect(await locator.textContent()).toBe('Done'): here the value is taken once, and two strings are compared without repeats. If the page hasn't updated yet, the test fails, and there is a temptation to add waitForTimeout. Likewise, instead of isVisible() with a check of the boolean value, use toBeVisible().

Additionally: expect.soft doesn't stop the test on a failure but collects all errors. expect.poll and expect(...).toPass() give retries for your own logic, for example for checks through an API. A negation check is written with not: await expect(locator).not.toBeVisible().

pw-wait:1.title: Actionability: what exactly is checked before an action
pw-wait:1.html:
The set of checks depends on the action. All actions wait for the element to be attached to the DOM, and beyond that the difference is as follows:

ActionWhat Playwright waits for
click, check, uncheck, setCheckedvisible, stable, receives events, enabled
hover, dragTovisible, stable, receives events
fill, clearvisible, enabled, editable
selectOptionvisible, enabled
screenshotvisible, stable

"Stable" means the element isn't animating for two frames in a row. "Receives events" means that at the click point there is exactly this element, not an overlay or a spinner. If an element is covered, Playwright waits and writes in the logs which element intercepts the click.

Two useful options. force: true turns off some of the checks: it is a workaround that may hide a real bug where a user also couldn't click. trial: true performs all the checks but doesn't do the action itself: this way you can wait for an element to be ready, for example before a hover menu.

Navigation has its own waits. page.goto waits for the load event by default. The option waitUntil: 'networkidle' is officially not recommended: on pages with polling or analytics it is unstable. After an action that changes the URL, better use await expect(page).toHaveURL(/orders/) or page.waitForURL.

In an interview: Before a click Playwright waits for the element to be visible, stable, enabled and not covered, and before fill it waits for the field to be editable. I use force: true very rarely, because it may hide a real bug with an overlay. Instead of networkidle I wait for a concrete result: a URL, an element or an API response.

pw-wait:2.title: expect.poll and toPass: retries for your own logic
pw-wait:2.html:
Web-first assertions retry only when a locator or a page is passed to expect. When you need to wait for something else, such as a status in the DB, an API response or a file, you use expect.poll or toPass.

expect.poll calls a function repeatedly and applies a matcher to the result:

await expect.poll(async () => {
  const res = await request.get(`/api/orders/${id}`);
  return (await res.json()).status;
}, { message: 'the order must become PAID', timeout: 30_000 }).toBe('PAID');

By default it takes the expect timeout (5 seconds), and the intervals grow: 100, 250, 500, 1000 ms. They can be set through intervals.

toPass retries a whole block of code with several actions and assertions until the block passes without errors:

await expect(async () => {
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Synced')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 1000 });
}).toPass({ timeout: 20_000, intervals: [1000, 2000] });

A tricky point: in toPass the default timeout is 0, meaning it doesn't take expect.timeout and retries until the test time runs out. So I set the timeout explicitly. Inside I also give the inner assertions short timeouts, otherwise one iteration would take 5 seconds.

In an interview: When I wait not for the UI but, for example, for asynchronous payment processing on the backend, I use expect.poll with a function that polls the API. If I need to repeat a whole sequence of actions, I take toPass and always give it a timeout, because by default it is limited only by the test timeout.

pw-wait:3.title: Soft assertions, messages and custom matchers
pw-wait:3.html:
expect.soft records an error but doesn't stop the test. The test will still be red, and the report will have all the failures together. This is handy for checking a form with many fields or a profile page: in one run you see all the discrepancies.

await expect.soft(page.getByLabel('Name')).toHaveValue('Rostyslav');
await expect.soft(page.getByLabel('Email')).toHaveValue('r@test.com');
await expect.soft(page.getByLabel('Phone')).toHaveValue('+380501112233');
expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();

The last line before the action is a practical trick: if the soft assertions have already failed, there is no point going further.

Soft shouldn't be put on preconditions. If a page didn't open, all the following checks will fail in a cascade and make the report noisy.

As the second argument of expect you can pass your own message: expect(locator, 'the pay button must be enabled').toBeEnabled(). It appears in the report and trace, and a failure reads without opening the code.

expect.configure creates a configured instance: const slowExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 15_000 }) or { soft: true }. And expect.extend lets you write custom matchers, for example toHaveValidIban, which return pass and message.

In an interview: I use expect.soft for independent checks of one page, to see all the discrepancies in one run, but not for preconditions. To important assertions I add my own message, so that a failure in the report is clear without the code.

pw-act:0.title: Actions on elements: what to use when
pw-act:0.html:
The main actions and nuances that are asked about in interviews:

  • fill clears the field and inserts the value at once. This is the standard for inputs.
  • pressSequentially types character by character with keyboard events. It is needed for fields with autocomplete or masks that react to every keypress. The old type is deprecated.
  • press('Enter') and combinations like press('ControlOrMeta+A'): a modifier that works on both Windows and macOS.
  • check and uncheck for checkboxes and radios: they verify that the state really changed. setChecked(bool) is convenient in parameterised tests.
  • selectOption for a native select: by value, label or an array for multiple. A custom dropdown made of divs doesn't work like that: there you click the option with getByRole('option').
  • hover, dblclick, click({ button: 'right' }), click({ modifiers: ['Shift'] }).
  • dragTo(target) for drag-and-drop. If the DnD library is non-standard, it is done manually through page.mouse.down, move, up.
await page.getByLabel('City').pressSequentially('Lvi', { delay: 100 });
await page.getByRole('option', { name: 'Lviv' }).click();
await page.getByLabel('Currency').selectOption({ label: 'UAH' });
await page.getByTestId('card-1').dragTo(page.getByTestId('column-done'));

For date fields fill expects the format the input accepts: for type="date" it is 2026-10-08, regardless of locale.

In an interview: For ordinary fields I use fill, and pressSequentially only when the field reacts to every keypress, like autocomplete. For a native select, selectOption, for custom dropdowns a click on option. check is better than click for checkboxes, because it verifies that the state changed.

pw-act:1.title: New tabs, popups and iframes
pw-act:1.html:
A new tab is a new Page in the same context. It has to be "caught" with an event, and the promise is created before the click, otherwise the event may arrive before I start listening:

const popupPromise = page.waitForEvent('popup');
await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Agreement' }).click();
const popup = await popupPromise;
await popup.waitForLoadState();
await expect(popup).toHaveURL(/contract/);

page.waitForEvent('popup') catches tabs opened from a specific page. context.waitForEvent('page') catches any new page in the context. A simplified option for tests where the tab doesn't matter is to remove target="_blank", but then the real behaviour isn't checked.

An iframe requires an explicit move into its document. There are two ways:

const card = page.frameLocator('#payment-iframe');
await card.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');

const frame = page.locator('#payment-iframe').contentFrame();
await frame.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

frameLocator and contentFrame() are lazy, like ordinary locators, and wait for the frame to appear. Cross-origin frames, for example a payment widget from another domain, work the same way, because Playwright drives the browser from outside.

Nested frames go as a chain: page.frameLocator('#outer').frameLocator('#inner').

In an interview: For a new tab I first create the waitForEvent('popup') promise, then click, then await the promise, otherwise you can miss the event. For an iframe I use frameLocator or contentFrame(), and cross-origin frames of payment systems work without workarounds.

pw-act:2.title: File uploads and downloads
pw-act:2.html:
Upload is done with setInputFiles on an input with type="file", even if it is hidden under a pretty button:

await page.getByLabel('Document').setInputFiles('fixtures/passport.pdf');
await page.getByLabel('Documents').setInputFiles(['a.pdf', 'b.pdf']);
await page.getByLabel('Document').setInputFiles({
  name: 'report.csv',
  mimeType: 'text/csv',
  buffer: Buffer.from('id,amount\n1,100'),
});
await page.getByLabel('Document').setInputFiles([]);

The buffer variant lets you generate the file right in the test, without storing it in the repository. An empty array clears the selection. If there is no input in the DOM and the dialog opens dynamically, you catch the filechooser event: page.waitForEvent('filechooser'), then fileChooser.setFiles(...).

A download is checked through the download event:

const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export CSV' }).click();
const download = await downloadPromise;
expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toBe('transactions.csv');
const filePath = test.info().outputPath(download.suggestedFilename());
await download.saveAs(filePath);

Then the file can be read through fs and its content checked: the number of rows, amounts, encoding. This is important in fintech, where reports for accounting are part of the requirements. Downloaded files are deleted when the context closes, so saveAs is needed if the file must be kept.

In an interview: For upload I use setInputFiles, often with a buffer to generate the file in the test. For download I catch the download event, save the file to the test's outputPath and check not only the name but also the content.

pw-act:3.title: alert, confirm and prompt dialogs
pw-act:3.html:
Playwright automatically dismisses native browser dialogs by default. That is, confirm will return false, and if a test expects a deletion after confirmation, it won't happen. To control a dialog, you subscribe to the event before the action:

page.once('dialog', async (dialog) => {
  expect(dialog.type()).toBe('confirm');
  expect(dialog.message()).toContain('Delete the account?');
  await dialog.accept();
});
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).click();
await expect(page.getByText('Account deleted')).toBeVisible();

For prompt you pass text to accept: dialog.accept('Reason'). To refuse, use dialog.dismiss().

A trap: if there is a dialog listener, Playwright no longer closes the dialog itself. If you forget accept or dismiss in the handler, the page hangs, because a native dialog blocks JavaScript execution. So I use page.once, not page.on, when a dialog is expected once, so the handler doesn't affect other steps.

A separate case is beforeunload, the "Leave the page?" dialog. In tests it appears on page.close({ runBeforeUnload: true }) and is handled the same way.

Custom modal windows made in HTML are not browser dialogs. For them there are ordinary locators: getByRole('dialog').

In an interview: Playwright dismisses native dialogs by default, so for confirm I register page.once('dialog') in advance and call accept. If there is a listener, the dialog must be closed in it, otherwise the page hangs.

pw-fix:0.title: Fixtures and scopes
pw-fix:0.html:
Fixtures in Playwright are a dependency injection mechanism: a test declares what it needs, for example { page, request }, and the runner prepares it. Custom fixtures are created with test.extend: the code before await use(value) is setup, and after it is teardown. Fixtures can depend on each other and are created only when a test has requested them.

There are two scopes: test (the default), where the fixture is created separately for each test, and worker, once per worker for all its tests. The scope is set with the third parameter: [async ({}, use) => {...}, { scope: 'worker' }]. Worker scope suits expensive things such as a DB connection or a test user.

There are several workers, so a worker fixture will be created in each of them; for unique data use workerInfo.workerIndex. The option auto: true runs a fixture without an explicit request, and option: true makes it a parameter set in the config. A typical pattern is fixtures with ready Page Objects, so a test gets loginPage right away.

pw-fix:1.title: Hooks, describe and conditional tests
pw-fix:1.html:
The structure of tests: test.describe groups tests, and the hooks beforeEach, afterEach, beforeAll, afterAll do preparation and cleanup. beforeEach has access to the same fixtures as the test, for example page. beforeAll has access only to worker fixtures, because it runs once per worker, not per test.

When to choose a hook and when a fixture? A hook is simpler for one file. A fixture is better when the logic is repeated in many files, when a guaranteed teardown is needed, and when it is important that preparation runs only for the tests that need it.

Controlling execution:

  • test.skip(condition, 'reason') skips on a condition, for example for a browser.
  • test.fixme(): the test is known to be broken, don't run it.
  • test.fail(): the test must fail; if it passes, that is an error. Useful for a known bug: as soon as it is fixed, the test will report it.
  • test.slow(): triple the timeout.
test('PDF export', async ({ page, browserName }) => {
  test.skip(browserName === 'webkit', 'Bug PAY-512 in WebKit');
  await page.goto('/reports');
});

test('quick search', { tag: ['@smoke', '@search'] }, async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');
});

Tags are set in the test details and filtered with --grep @smoke or --grep-invert @slow. Annotations annotation: { type: 'issue', description: 'PAY-512' } are visible in the HTML report.

In an interview: I use hooks for simple preparation in one file, and move repeated logic with teardown into fixtures. For known bugs I use test.fail with a link to the ticket, so the test itself reports when the bug is fixed. I mark the smoke suite with tags and run it with --grep.

pw-fix:2.title: test.step and the describe.configure modes
pw-fix:2.html:
test.step splits a test into named steps. In the report and trace you see not a flat list of clicks but "Login", "Add item", "Pay", and it is immediately clear at which business step it failed. A step can return a value:

test('purchase', async ({ page }) => {
  const orderId = await test.step('Place the order', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy' }).click();
    return page.getByTestId('order-id').innerText();
  });
  await test.step('Check the status', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByText(`Order ${orderId}`)).toBeVisible();
  });
});

Steps are conveniently wrapped in Page Object methods. The option { box: true } makes the error point to the step call in the test, not to a line inside the helper, which makes the report easier to read.

test.describe.configure sets the execution mode of a file or a block:

ModeBehaviour
defaultthe file's tests run sequentially in one worker, but a failure of one doesn't cancel the others
parallelthe block's tests are distributed between workers
serialsequentially; on a failure the rest are skipped, and on a retry the whole group is restarted

Through configure you can also set retries and timeout for a group. Serial is an exception for long dependent scenarios; almost always it is better to make tests independent by preparing data through the API.

In an interview: I wrap business stages in test.step so the report reads like a scenario. I use serial mode rarely, because on a retry it restarts the whole group; instead I make tests independent. I turn on parallel for files where tests don't share data.

pw-fix:3.title: Fixtures in depth: worker, auto, option, mergeTests
pw-fix:3.html:
A worker fixture with unique data for each worker:

type WorkerFixtures = { account: { email: string; password: string } };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  account: [async ({ playwright }, use, workerInfo) => {
    const api = await playwright.request.newContext({ baseURL: process.env.API_URL });
    const email = `qa+w${workerInfo.workerIndex}-${Date.now()}@test.com`;
    await api.post('/api/test/users', { data: { email, password: 'Secret123' } });
    await use({ email, password: 'Secret123' });
    await api.delete(`/api/test/users/${email}`);
    await api.dispose();
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

Note: the built-in fixtures request and page have test scope, so a worker fixture can't depend on them, and Playwright will throw an error. Here the worker fixture playwright is used, from which its own API context is created, and at the end it is closed with dispose().

An auto fixture runs for every test without an explicit request: [async ({ page }, use) => {...}, { auto: true }]. It fits collecting logs, checking JS errors, attaching artifacts.

An option fixture is a parameter with a default value that can be overridden in a config project or through test.use:

export const test = base.extend<{ currency: string }>({
  currency: ['UAH', { option: true }],
});

Built-in fixtures can be overridden: for example, a page that immediately opens the baseURL.

When there are many fixtures, they are split into modules and combined with mergeTests(dbTest, apiTest, uiTest), and custom matchers with mergeExpects. A fixture can also be given its own timeout, so that slow preparation doesn't eat up the test's time.

In an interview: For expensive preparation I make a worker fixture with workerIndex, so workers don't conflict over data. I use auto fixtures for cross-test checks and option fixtures for parameters that change between projects. I split a large set of fixtures into modules and combine them with mergeTests.

pw-net:0.title: Working with the network: page.route and mocks
pw-net:0.html:
page.route intercepts requests by a URL pattern or a regular expression. Then the request can be replaced with route.fulfill with your own status and body, passed on with route.continue with changed headers or body, or aborted with route.abort. The route must be declared before the action that triggers the request.

A common pattern is route.fetch(): get the real response, change part of the data and return it through fulfill. This lets you test boundary UI states without preparing data on the backend: an empty list, a 500 error, a very long text. For fully offline tests you can record traffic into a HAR and replay it with routeFromHAR.

To wait for a request use page.waitForResponse: the promise must be created before the action, and the await done after. context.route applies interception to all pages of the context. You shouldn't mock everything: some E2E tests must go to the real backend, otherwise integration bugs won't be visible.

pw-net:1.title: API testing in Playwright
pw-net:1.html:
For APIs there is the request fixture of type APIRequestContext, which sends HTTP requests without a browser: request.get, post, put, patch, delete. The baseURL and extraHTTPHeaders, such as a token, are set in the config. The response is checked through response.status(), response.json() and the assertion expect(response).toBeOK().

The API is used not only for separate API tests, but also for preparing data in E2E: create a user or an order through the API, and check through the UI only the needed flow. This makes tests faster and more stable. The API is also convenient for cleaning up data after a test in a fixture's teardown.

page.request and context.request share cookies with the browser context, so after a login through the UI requests already go authorised, and vice versa. For validating the response schema, zod or ajv is added. A separate context with different settings is created through playwright.request.newContext.

pw-net:2.title: Observe or replace: waitForResponse, waitForRequest, route
pw-net:2.html:
It is important here to distinguish two tasks. page.waitForResponse and page.waitForRequest only observe real traffic: the request goes to the backend, and I wait and check it. page.route intercepts the request and decides what to do with it.

Checking that the front end sent the right payload:

const reqPromise = page.waitForRequest((r) =>
  r.url().includes('/api/transfers') && r.method() === 'POST');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Transfer' }).click();
const req = await reqPromise;
expect(req.postDataJSON()).toMatchObject({ amount: 500, currency: 'UAH' });

With waitForResponse I wait for a specific request to finish and can get data from the response, for example the id of the created object.

Nuances of route:

  • The pattern is a glob (**/api/users*), a RegExp or a function of the URL. A glob with * doesn't cross /, while ** does.
  • If several handlers are registered for a URL, the last one fires. route.fallback() passes the request to the previous handler, and route.continue() sends it straight to the network.
  • page.unroute removes a handler. page.unrouteAll({ behavior: 'ignoreErrors' }) is useful at the end of a test when handlers are still running.
  • A Service Worker may intercept requests before Playwright, and then route doesn't see them. The solution is serviceWorkers: 'block' in the config.
In an interview: I use waitForResponse and waitForRequest to observe real traffic and check the payload, and route to replace a response. I know that the last registered handler fires, and that fallback passes the request on down the chain, while continue sends it straight to the network.

pw-net:3.title: HAR: recording and replaying traffic
pw-net:3.html:
A HAR is a file with a recording of HTTP traffic: requests, responses, headers, bodies. Playwright can both record it and replay it as a mock. This is useful when the backend is unstable, expensive or depends on third-party services, while you need to test the front end.

Recording and replay with one method:

test('catalogue from HAR', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeFromHAR('hars/catalog.har', {
    url: '**/api/**',
    update: process.env.UPDATE_HAR === '1',
    notFound: 'fallback',
  });
  await page.goto('/catalog');
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(12);
});

With update: true requests go to the real network, and the HAR is rewritten. Without it, responses are taken from the file. url limits which requests to mock: usually only the API, while static files load as they are. notFound: 'fallback' lets requests that aren't in the HAR through to the network; by default they are aborted.

Alternatives for recording: the context option recordHar: { path, urlFilter } or npx playwright codegen --save-har=file.har.

Risks worth mentioning: a HAR goes stale together with the API, so it must be updated regularly. Tokens and personal data end up in the file, so it must be checked before a commit. A request is matched by URL, method and body, so dynamic parameters, for example a timestamp in the query, may break the matching.

In an interview: I use HAR for stable front-end tests that don't depend on an unstable backend: I record traffic with routeFromHAR with update and then replay it. I limit it to the API only with the url option, update it regularly and check that no tokens end up in the file.

pw-net:4.title: APIRequestContext in depth
pw-net:4.html:
Besides the request fixture, you can create a separate API context with its own settings. This is needed for another service, another user, or in a worker fixture:

import { request, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const admin = await request.newContext({
  baseURL: 'https://api.test.bank',
  extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.ADMIN_TOKEN}` },
});
const res = await admin.post('/accounts', {
  data: { currency: 'UAH', type: 'savings' },
  params: { dryRun: 'false' },
});
await expect(res).toBeOK();
const { id } = await res.json();
await admin.dispose();

The body format is set by an option: data is JSON if an object is passed; form is application/x-www-form-urlencoded; multipart is multipart/form-data with files. Query parameters go through params.

By default request doesn't throw on 4xx or 5xx: the response is simply returned. This is convenient for negative tests where I expect 422. If I want any error to fail the call, there is the option failOnStatusCode: true. toBeOK() checks the range 200-299, and response.ok() returns the same result as a boolean.

APIRequestContext has its own cookies. After a login through the API you can save the state: await ctx.storageState({ path: '.auth/user.json' }), and use it in browser tests.

For purely API tests it is convenient to make a separate project without browser settings. The browser starts lazily, so if a test doesn't request page, it isn't launched.

In an interview: I create a separate API context with request.newContext with its own baseURL and token, and always call dispose. I remember that by default 4xx and 5xx don't throw, so I check the status explicitly. After a login through the API I can save storageState and use it in UI tests.

pw-auth:0.title: Authentication: storageState and a setup project
pw-auth:0.html:
StorageState is a JSON snapshot of a context's state: cookies and localStorage for each origin. Login is done once and the state is saved with page.context().storageState({ path: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' }), and tests pick up the file through use: { storageState }. The folder with state files is added to .gitignore, because live tokens are there.

The recommended way is a setup project: a separate project in the config with testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/, on which other projects depend through dependencies. Unlike globalSetup, a setup project is made of full tests: with fixtures, retries, a trace and display in the report. globalSetup remains for things without a browser, such as DB preparation or starting containers.

For several roles, separate state files are made (admin.json, user.json) and picked up through separate projects or test.use in a file. When one test needs two roles at once, two contexts are created through browser.newContext({ storageState }). SessionStorage is not saved in storageState: it is passed in manually through addInitScript.

pw-auth:1.title: Login through the API in a setup project
pw-auth:1.html:
A setup project doesn't have to log in through the UI. If the login form is already covered by separate tests, it is faster to get the session through the API:

// auth.setup.ts
import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';

setup('admin login', async ({ request }) => {
  const res = await request.post('/api/auth/login', {
    data: { email: process.env.ADMIN_EMAIL, password: process.env.ADMIN_PASSWORD },
  });
  await expect(res).toBeOK();
  await request.storageState({ path: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });
});

This works if the session is kept in cookies. If the application stores the token in localStorage, after an API login you need to open a page and write the token through page.evaluate, and then save page.context().storageState().

An important limitation of shared state: all workers use one user. If tests change the account's state (balance, settings, cart), they will start interfering with each other in parallel. Then you move to an account per worker: a worker fixture logs in a separate user with the index test.info().parallelIndex and saves the state to a file with that index.

One more nuance is the token's lifetime. If the session lives 15 minutes and a run takes 40, the tests at the end will start failing with 401. Then you either increase the TTL on the test environment, or log in again in a fixture.

In an interview: In a setup project I log in through the API and save storageState, because it is faster than the UI. If tests change account data, I use a separate user per worker through parallelIndex. I also take the session TTL into account relative to the run length.

pw-auth:2.title: Several roles and the logged-out state
pw-auth:2.html:
If a file tests only one role, test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' }) at the start of the file or describe is enough. If one test needs two roles at once, it is convenient to make fixtures that return ready pages:

type Roles = { adminPage: Page; clientPage: Page };

export const test = base.extend<Roles>({
  adminPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });
    await use(await ctx.newPage());
    await ctx.close();
  },
  clientPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/client.json' });
    await use(await ctx.newPage());
    await ctx.close();
  },
});

The test then looks like a scenario: a client submits a loan application, the administrator approves it, and the client sees the new status.

The opposite situation: storageState is configured globally, but you need a test for an unauthenticated user. Then the state is reset: test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } }).

SessionStorage doesn't end up in storageState. If the application keeps the session there, it is read in setup through page.evaluate and restored through context.addInitScript, which runs before the page's scripts.

Roles can also be separated into projects in the config: a project admin with one state file and a testMatch for admin tests, and a project client with another.

In an interview: For scenarios with two roles I make the fixtures adminPage and clientPage, each with its own context and storageState. For tests of an unauthenticated user I reset the state through an empty storageState. I restore SessionStorage through addInitScript.

pw-auth:3.title: globalSetup or a setup project: a comparison
pw-auth:3.html:
Both mechanisms perform preparation before the tests, but the difference is significant:

CapabilityglobalSetupsetup project
Visible in the HTML reportnoyes
Trace and screenshotsonly manuallyas in ordinary tests
The page, request fixturesnoyes
Retriesnoyes
Can run part of itnothrough dependencies

globalSetup is a function in a separate file that runs once before the whole run. It receives the config and can pass values to tests through process.env. If it returns a function, that becomes the teardown.

For a setup project the cleanup is done through the teardown property in the project: you give the name of the project that will run after all the dependent ones finish.

projects: [
  { name: 'setup', testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/, teardown: 'cleanup' },
  { name: 'cleanup', testMatch: /global\.teardown\.ts/ },
  { name: 'e2e', dependencies: ['setup'], use: { storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' } },
],

My choice: everything related to the browser and login goes into a setup project. I leave globalSetup for infrastructure: bringing up containers, running migrations, checking that the environment is available.

A nuance: if you run a test with a filter, for example npx playwright test checkout, the setup project still runs, because it is in dependencies. It can be skipped with the flag --no-deps when the state is already saved.

In an interview: A setup project is better for login, because it has a trace, retries, fixtures and shows up in the report, and cleanup is done through the teardown property. I leave globalSetup for infrastructure preparation without a browser.

pw-cfg:0.title: Configuration and projects
pw-cfg:0.html:
The main file is playwright.config.ts with defineConfig. At the top level you set testDir, timeout, retries, workers, fullyParallel, reporter and webServer for automatically starting the application before tests. The use section sets settings for all tests: baseURL, trace, screenshot, video, viewport, locale.

Projects are sets of tests with different settings: different browsers, mobile devices through devices['iPhone 13'], different roles or environments. Each project can override use, and have its own testMatch and dependencies. A specific project is run with the flag --project=chromium.

Typical values for CI: retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0, forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI, so that a forgotten test.only doesn't get into the pipeline. Also trace: 'on-first-retry' and screenshots only on failure. Environment variables are loaded through dotenv, and secrets come from CI.

pw-cfg:1.title: Parallelism, workers and sharding
pw-cfg:1.html:
Playwright runs tests in parallel in workers, which are separate processes. By default files run in parallel and tests inside a file sequentially; fullyParallel: true also parallelises tests within a file. The number of workers is set through workers, and on CI it is often reduced because of limited resources.

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' }) runs a block's tests sequentially, and if one fails, the rest are skipped: this is for dependent steps, but it is better to make tests independent. The parallel mode, conversely, parallelises tests in a particular file. For parallelism each test must work with its own data.

Sharding splits tests between several machines: npx playwright test --shard=1/4, in GitHub Actions through a matrix. Each shard produces its own report, so the blob reporter is used, the artifacts of all jobs are collected and merged with npx playwright merge-reports. The distribution goes by files, so files of uneven size give a skew between shards.

pw-cfg:2.title: Timeouts and the priority of settings
pw-cfg:2.html:
There are several timeouts, and they are often confused:

TimeoutDefaultWhere to set
Test (together with beforeEach and test fixtures)30 stimeout, test.setTimeout
The expect assertion5 sexpect.timeout
Action (click, fill)no limituse.actionTimeout
Navigationno limituse.navigationTimeout
The whole runno limitglobalTimeout

"No limit" means an action is in effect limited only by the test timeout. In practice I set actionTimeout to about 10-15 seconds: then a specific click will fail with a clear error, and not the whole test by timeout without details.

test.slow() triples a test's timeout, and test.setTimeout(60_000) sets a specific value. For a single assertion: toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 }).

Settings have a hierarchy, from general to specific:

  1. The config's top level and use.
  2. The use of a specific project.
  3. test.use in a file or describe.
  4. The options of a specific action or assertion.

A lower level overrides a higher one. test.use can't be called inside a test body, only at file or describe level, because it may require a new context.

globalTimeout is useful on CI: if something hangs, the run will stop instead of eating hours of the runner. maxFailures plays a similar role: stop the run after N failures when the environment is obviously down.

In an interview: By default a test has 30 seconds, an assertion 5, and actions and navigation have no separate limit. I set actionTimeout so a failure points to a specific action. On CI I add globalTimeout and maxFailures, so as not to burn resources when the environment is down.

pw-cfg:3.title: webServer and environment variables
pw-cfg:3.html:
The webServer option starts the application before the tests and waits until it responds:

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: [
    {
      command: 'npm run start:api',
      url: 'http://localhost:4000/health',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
      timeout: 120_000,
    },
    {
      command: 'npm run start:web',
      url: 'http://localhost:3000',
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    },
  ],
  use: { baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000' },
});

reuseExistingServer lets you use an already running server locally, while on CI it forces a fresh one to start. You can pass an array if you need to bring up a backend and a front end. After the run Playwright stops the processes itself.

For several environments (dev, stage) I keep .env.dev and .env.stage, load the needed one through dotenv at the start of the config by a variable, for example TEST_ENV, and take baseURL from it. Secrets don't sit in the repository: locally they are in .env, which is in .gitignore, and on CI in the pipeline's secrets.

baseURL lets you write page.goto('/login') and request.get('/api/users') with relative paths, so the same set of tests runs on any environment by changing one variable.

In an interview: I bring the application up before the tests through webServer with reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI. The environment is chosen by a variable from which the config takes baseURL, and secrets come from CI, not from the repository.

pw-cfg:4.title: CI: sharding, Docker and fast reruns
pw-cfg:4.html:
A typical pipeline in GitHub Actions with sharding:

jobs:
  e2e:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.55.0-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }} --reporter=blob
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-${{ strategy.job-index }}
          path: blob-report

A separate job after the shards downloads all the artifacts and runs npx playwright merge-reports --reporter=html ./all-blob-reports.

Details worth knowing:

  • fail-fast: false, so that a failure of one shard doesn't cancel the others.
  • The Docker image version must match the @playwright/test version, otherwise the browsers won't be found. The image provides identical fonts, which is critical for screenshot tests.
  • With fullyParallel: true sharding distributes individual tests, not files, so shards are balanced more evenly.
  • workers on CI are set from the runner's resources, for example '50%' or 1-2 on weak machines.

For faster work there are flags: --last-failed reruns only the tests that failed last time, and --only-changed runs tests from files changed relative to HEAD or a given branch (--only-changed=main). The first is handy locally after a failure, the second for quick feedback in a PR before the full run.

In an interview: On CI I run tests in the official Docker image of the same version, split them into shards through a matrix with fail-fast: false, and merge the blob reports with merge-reports. fullyParallel helps balance the shards more evenly.

pw-dbg:0.title: Diagnostics: trace viewer, reports, flaky tests
pw-dbg:0.html:
The trace viewer is the main debugging tool: a trace records every action, DOM snapshots before and after, the network, the console and the test's source code. On CI trace: 'on-first-retry' is usually set, so as not to spend resources on successful runs. A trace is opened with npx playwright show-trace or from the HTML report.

Locally for debugging there is UI mode (--ui) with time travel, the --debug mode with Playwright Inspector and page.pause(). Codegen (npx playwright codegen) records actions and suggests locators. Reports: the built-in HTML, list, JUnit for CI, as well as Allure.

To look for flakiness you use --repeat-each=10 and --retries, and in the HTML report such tests are marked as flaky. Typical causes: shared data between workers, no web-first assertions, waitForTimeout, animations, a slow CI environment. You treat the root cause: retries only mask the problem.

pw-dbg:1.title: Local debugging: the tools and when to use which
pw-dbg:1.html:
• npx playwright test --ui is UI mode. A list of tests, watch mode (rerun when a file changes), time travel through steps with DOM snapshots, network and console. My main tool when writing tests.
  • --debug or the variable PWDEBUG=1 is Playwright Inspector: step-by-step execution, the browser in headed mode, timeouts disabled. Convenient for stopping before a specific action.
  • await page.pause() is a breakpoint in code, which opens the Inspector right here.
  • --headed and launchOptions: { slowMo: 300 } let you see what is happening at a slowed-down pace.
  • The VS Code extension: running a single test, breakpoints, the Pick locator button, which shows the recommended locator for an element.

Codegen is more useful than it seems, not only for recording actions:

npx playwright codegen --device="iPhone 13" --lang=uk-UA https://app.test
npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json https://app.test/login
npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json https://app.test/dashboard

The first command opens the application with device emulation, the second saves the state after a manual login, the third opens it already logged in. I don't commit the generated code as is: I take the locators from it and rewrite the structure into a Page Object and fixtures.

This set doesn't work for debugging on CI, where the main thing is the trace.

In an interview: While writing tests I work in UI mode with watch mode, and to stop at a specific step I use page.pause() or --debug. I use codegen for quickly picking locators and saving login state, but I rewrite the code after it.

pw-dbg:2.title: Artifacts and reports
pw-dbg:2.html:
What to record is configured in use:

OptionUseful values
traceon-first-retry, retain-on-failure, on
screenshotonly-on-failure, on
videoretain-on-failure, on-first-retry

on-first-retry writes an artifact only on the first retry, so without retries it gives nothing. retain-on-failure always writes, but keeps only for tests that failed: this is more expensive in resources, but the artifact exists even without retries.

You can use several reporters at once:

reporter: process.env.CI
  ? [['blob'], ['junit', { outputFile: 'results/junit.xml' }], ['github']]
  : [['html', { open: 'on-failure' }], ['list']],

github adds error annotations right in the PR, JUnit is read by Jenkins or GitLab, and HTML is for people. For Allure you add allure-playwright.

Your own data is added to the report through testInfo.attach:

test('statement reconciliation', async ({ request }, testInfo) => {
  const res = await request.get('/api/statement');
  await testInfo.attach('statement', {
    body: await res.text(),
    contentType: 'application/json',
  });
});

This way API responses, backend logs and generated files appear in the report. When a test fails, the developer sees not only a screenshot but also the data the test worked with.

In an interview: On CI I set trace: 'on-first-retry' together with retries, screenshots only on failure, and several reporters: blob for shards, JUnit for CI and github for annotations in the PR. Extra data, such as API responses, I attach through testInfo.attach.

pw-dbg:3.title: How I systematically investigate a flaky test
pw-dbg:3.html:
A flaky test is not "just rerun it". My process:

  1. Reproduce. npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts --repeat-each=20. If it fails locally, good, there is something to debug.
  2. Check isolation. Run with --workers=1 and separately with --workers=4. If it fails only in parallel, the problem is shared data or an account between workers.
  3. Check the order. Run the test alone with -g "name". If it passes alone but fails in the suite, another test depends on it or leftover data.
  4. Compare the trace of a successful and a failed run. It often shows that on the failure the API responded slower, or a spinner still covered the button.
  5. Classify the cause: the test (no wait, a brittle locator), the data, the environment, or a real application bug, for example a race condition in the front end.

The last point is important: some flaky tests are real bugs that a user will also meet. If a double click creates two payments, it is not a test problem.

Until the cause is fixed, the test must not block the team. I mark it test.fixme with a link to a ticket or move it into a quarantine project with the tag @quarantine, which doesn't block the merge. But quarantine must have an owner and a deadline, otherwise it turns into a dumping ground.

A metric worth tracking is the share of flaky tests in runs. The HTML report marks a test as flaky if it passed only after a retry.

In an interview: I reproduce a flaky test with --repeat-each, check isolation by changing the number of workers, and compare the trace of a successful and a failed run. Then I classify the cause, because some flakiness is real race conditions in the application. Until it is fixed, the test goes into quarantine with a ticket and an owner.

pw-emu:0.title: Devices, viewport and media
pw-emu:0.html:
devices is a set of ready profiles: screen size, userAgent, deviceScaleFactor, isMobile, hasTouch and the default browser.

projects: [
  { name: 'mobile-safari', use: { ...devices['iPhone 13'] } },
  { name: 'mobile-chrome', use: { ...devices['Pixel 7'] } },
  { name: 'tablet', use: { ...devices['iPad Pro 11'], colorScheme: 'dark' } },
],

It is important to understand the limit: this is emulation in a desktop engine, not a real device. It checks responsive layout, the mobile menu and touch events through tap() well, but it doesn't catch bugs specific to mobile Safari or performance on a weak phone.

tap() needs hasTouch: true, otherwise there will be an error.

Other useful emulation options:

  • colorScheme: 'dark' or page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' }) for testing the dark theme.
  • reducedMotion: 'reduce' turns off animations if the application respects this setting; it also stabilises tests.
  • page.emulateMedia({ media: 'print' }) checks the printed version of a statement or a receipt.
  • offline: true or context.setOffline(true) in the middle of a test checks behaviour without a network.
  • javaScriptEnabled: false checks SSR pages.
  • viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 } and page.setViewportSize() for checking breakpoints.
In an interview: I cover mobile scenarios with projects using devices, understanding that it is emulation, not a real device. Separately I check the dark theme, offline through context.setOffline, and I turn off animations through reducedMotion.

pw-emu:1.title: Geolocation, permissions, locale and time zone
pw-emu:1.html:
For applications with maps, multilingual support or time zones, these settings matter:

test.use({
  locale: 'uk-UA',
  timezoneId: 'Europe/Kyiv',
  geolocation: { latitude: 49.8397, longitude: 24.0297 },
  permissions: ['geolocation'],
});

test('nearest branch in Lviv', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await page.goto('/branches');
  await expect(page.getByText('Lviv, Rynok Sq.')).toBeVisible();
  await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 50.4501, longitude: 30.5234 });
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Kyiv')).toBeVisible();
});

Geolocation won't work without a permission: the site will get a refusal. Permissions are granted through permissions in the config or context.grantPermissions(['clipboard-read'], { origin }), and reset with context.clearPermissions(). The set of supported permissions differs slightly between browsers.

locale affects navigator.language, the Accept-Language header and the formatting of numbers and dates through Intl. This lets you check that an amount is displayed as "1 000,50 ₴" and not as "1,000.50".

timezoneId changes the browser's time zone. Classic bugs caught this way: a transaction at 23:30 Kyiv time ends up in "tomorrow's" statement because the front end converts to UTC; or a date of birth shifts by a day. I run such tests with several zones, for example Kyiv and America/New_York, through projects or parameterisation.

In an interview: For localisation I set locale and timezoneId and check the formats of amounts and dates. For geolocation both geolocation and a permission in permissions are needed. Tests with time zones help catch date shifts at the day boundary.

pw-emu:2.title: Clock API: controlling time
pw-emu:2.html:
Since version 1.45 there is page.clock, which replaces Date, timers and requestAnimationFrame in the browser. This solves tasks that used to be painful: a session timer, an "offer valid for 10 minutes" banner, a status that changes at midnight.

The main methods:

  • clock.install({ time }) installs a fake clock with an initial time. Call it before goto, so the page loads with it already.
  • clock.fastForward('05:00') fast-forwards, and the timers that should have fired do fire; the string is in mm:ss or hh:mm:ss format, or a number of milliseconds.
  • clock.runFor(ms) runs time sequentially, executing each timer in turn.
  • clock.pauseAt(time) and clock.resume() stop time at a specific moment.
  • clock.setFixedTime(time): Date.now() always returns one value, while timers work as usual.
  • clock.setSystemTime(time) changes the current time without firing timers.
test('session expiry warning', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-10-08T10:00:00') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await page.clock.fastForward('14:00');
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Session is ending' })).toBeVisible();
  await page.clock.fastForward('01:00');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/login/);
});

Important: Clock controls time only in the browser. A session whose expiry is checked by the server won't end because of it: for the backend you need test endpoints or a short TTL on the test environment.

In an interview: For time-dependent logic I use page.clock: I set the time with install before navigation and fast-forward with fastForward. I understand it affects only the browser, so I check the server TTL separately.

pw-emu:3.title: Visual tests: toHaveScreenshot
pw-emu:3.html:
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('dashboard.png') compares a screenshot with a baseline. The first run creates the baseline and fails, and subsequent ones compare. Baselines are updated with npx playwright test --update-snapshots.

The assertion retries: it takes screenshots until two in a row match, and only then compares with the baseline. Animations are disabled by default, and the caret in fields is hidden.

Baselines are stored with a project and platform suffix, for example dashboard-chromium-linux.png. Fonts and rendering differ between macOS and Linux, so baselines are generated and checked in one environment, usually in the official Docker image, so that local and CI runs match.

Dynamic data is the main source of flakiness in visual tests. Tools against it:

await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('statement.png', {
  mask: [page.getByTestId('balance'), page.getByTestId('timestamp')],
  maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
  fullPage: true,
});
  • mask paints over the given elements.
  • maxDiffPixels and maxDiffPixelRatio allow a small difference; threshold (0.2 by default) is the sensitivity to the colour difference of a single pixel.
  • stylePath attaches CSS only for the duration of the screenshot, for example to hide a chat widget.
  • Fixed data through mocks and page.clock gives stable content.

A screenshot of a single component is expect(locator).toHaveScreenshot(), which is more stable than a whole page. For non-graphical data there is toMatchSnapshot.

In an interview: I write visual tests with toHaveScreenshot, generate baselines in Docker so there is no difference between macOS and Linux, and mask dynamic data with mask or stabilise it with mocks and page.clock. It is better to screenshot individual components than the whole page.

cy-0:0.title: What is Cypress and how does it differ from Selenium?
cy-0:0.html:
Cypress is a framework for end-to-end and component testing of web applications in JavaScript or TypeScript.

The main difference is where the test lives. Selenium drives the browser from outside through WebDriver: every command is a separate HTTP request to the driver. Cypress runs the test inside the browser, in the same tab as the application.

Hence the advantages: direct access to the DOM and window, automatic waits, time travel through steps in the Test Runner and a built-in network interceptor. Under the hood Cypress uses Mocha for test structure (describe, it, hooks), Chai for assertions and Sinon for cy.stub, cy.spy and cy.clock.

In an interview: Cypress is a framework for e2e and component testing in JavaScript. The main difference from Selenium is in the architecture: Selenium drives the browser from outside through WebDriver, where every command is a separate HTTP request, while Cypress runs tests right in the browser, next to the application. So it has direct access to the DOM, waits for elements itself, gives time travel for debugging and can intercept the network. Inside it is built on Mocha, Chai and Sinon.
And in Playwright:

Playwright also does without WebDriver, but works opposite to Cypress: it drives the browser from outside through one persistent connection and the browser's native protocol (CDP for Chromium, patched protocols for Firefox and WebKit). Tests can be written not only in JS/TS, but also in Python, Java and .NET.

cy-0:1.title: How is the Cypress architecture built under the hood?
cy-0:1.html:
Cypress consists of two parts that constantly communicate.

  • The Node process. It launches the browser, works as a proxy for all the page's HTTP traffic, runs cy.task (files, database), and takes screenshots and video.
  • The browser. The Cypress page contains two iframes: the spec iframe with your test code and the app iframe with the application. Since they are in one tab, the test sees the application's DOM directly, with no protocol in the middle.

Between the Node process and the browser there is a WebSocket. It is the proxy in Node that lets cy.intercept see and replace every request.

┌──────────── Browser (one tab) ──────────────────┐
│  spec iframe            │  app iframe           │
│  test + cy queue        │  application          │
│  direct DOM access ─────┼──►                    │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
               │ WebSocket + HTTP through the proxy
┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│  Cypress Node process                           │
│  proxy (cy.intercept) · cy.task · files · video │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
In an interview: Cypress works as two processes. The first is a Node process: it launches the browser, passes all network traffic through itself as a proxy and does everything the browser can't, such as working with files or a database through cy.task. The second is the browser itself, where two iframes live in one tab: my test in one and the application in the other. That is why the test has direct access to the DOM. Between Node and the browser there is a WebSocket, and it is the proxy that lets you intercept requests with cy.intercept.
And in Playwright:

Playwright has no iframe with the test next to the application. The test lives in Node, and the Playwright server sends commands to the browser through a protocol. So the test has no direct access to the DOM (only through page.evaluate), but it works without restrictions with several tabs, domains and contexts.

cy-0:2.title: How does cypress open differ from cypress run?
cy-0:2.html:
cypress open opens the interactive Test Runner: you pick a spec, see every command, can go back to any step (time travel), and the test reruns after a file is saved. This is the mode for writing and debugging.

cypress run runs tests without a UI, headless in Electron by default, with console output and screenshots on failure. This is the mode for CI.

npx cypress open                        # interactive
npx cypress run                         # headless, Electron
npx cypress run --browser chrome        # a specific browser
npx cypress run --spec "cypress/e2e/login.cy.ts"
npx cypress run --headed                # with a browser window
In an interview: Open is the interactive mode for development: I see every command, can go back to any step, and the test reruns on save. Run is a headless run for CI: without a UI, with console output and screenshots on failure. In run you can specify a browser, a specific spec, or run in headed mode.
And in Playwright:

The equivalent is npx playwright test, headless by default. Instead of the Test Runner there are --ui (UI mode with a timeline and DOM snapshots), --debug with the inspector, and --headed. Browsers are chosen with --project, not --browser.

cy-0:3.title: What do the project structure and the Cypress config look like?
cy-0:3.html:
Since version 10 the config lives in the file cypress.config.js or .ts. The old cypress.json is no longer used: if you mention it as current, it betrays outdated knowledge.

A typical structure: cypress/e2e for tests, cypress/fixtures for test data, cypress/support for custom commands and global settings.

// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com',
    specPattern: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
    defaultCommandTimeout: 6000,
    retries: { runMode: 2, openMode: 0 },
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      // cy.task, plugins, reports
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// cypress/
//   e2e/          tests *.cy.ts
//   fixtures/     JSON with test data
//   support/
//     e2e.ts      runs before every spec
//     commands.ts custom commands
In an interview: Starting from version ten the config is written in cypress.config.ts through defineConfig, with separate blocks for e2e and component testing. It sets baseUrl, the pattern for finding specs, timeouts, retries and setupNodeEvents for Node logic. Tests are in the e2e folder, test data in fixtures, and custom commands and global settings in support.
And in Playwright:

The config is playwright.config.ts. Instead of separate e2e and component blocks there are projects: different browsers, devices, a setup project for login. There is no support folder: shared logic lives in fixtures through test.extend.

cy-0:4.title: How do e2e tests differ from component testing in Cypress?
cy-0:4.html:
E2E opens the whole application through cy.visit and walks through a scenario like a user, with a real backend or network mocks.

Component testing mounts a single React, Vue or Angular component through cy.mount in a real browser, without the rest of the application. This is fast and isolated: convenient for checking states of a button, a form or a table with different props without bringing up the whole front end.

// component test
import { PriceTag } from './PriceTag';

it('shows the discount', () => {
  cy.mount(<PriceTag price={100} discount={20} />);
  cy.get('[data-cy=final-price]').should('have.text', '80');
});
In an interview: An E2E test opens the whole application and walks through a scenario like a user. Component testing mounts a single component with cy.mount in a real browser, without the rest of the application and without a backend. It is much faster and convenient for checking different states of a component, while e2e remains for the key end-to-end scenarios.
And in Playwright:

In Playwright component testing is still experimental (@playwright/experimental-ct-react and the like). For component tests Cypress is more mature right now.

cy-0:5.title: Cypress architecture and a comparison
cy-0:5.html:
Cypress runs tests inside the browser, in the same run loop as the application, and next to it a Node.js process works for tasks outside the browser. Selenium and Playwright drive the browser from outside: Selenium through WebDriver, Playwright through CDP and its own protocols. Because of this architecture Cypress has direct access to the DOM, window and the application's network requests.

Advantages: a convenient interactive runner with time-travel snapshots of every step, built-in retries and waits, an easy start, cy.intercept for the network, component testing. Limitations: only JavaScript/TypeScript, one tab, harder work with iframes and several domains, no Safari support (only an experimental WebKit).

Playwright is faster, has built-in parallelism without a paid service, multiple tabs and contexts, and languages besides JS. Parallelism in Cypress is possible, but usually through Cypress Cloud or third-party solutions such as sharding in CI.

cy-1:0.title: Why can't you write await cy.get() in Cypress?
cy-1:0.html:
Cypress commands return not a Promise but a Chainable object. Calling cy.get() executes nothing at that moment: it only puts a command in the queue.

When the test function finishes, Cypress itself runs the queue in order: each command waits for the previous one. So await here either does nothing or breaks the execution order. Values are obtained through .then() and checked with .should().

// ❌ doesn't work the way you expect
const text = await cy.get('h1').invoke('text');

// ✅ the value, through .then
cy.get('h1').invoke('text').then((text) => {
  expect(text).to.contain('Cart');
});

// ✅ the check, through should (with retries)
cy.get('h1').should('contain', 'Cart');
In an interview: Because Cypress commands return not a Promise but a chainable object. A cy.get call only puts the command in the queue, and Cypress itself runs that queue, sequentially, after the test body has finished. Await here either does nothing or breaks the order. I get values through then, and check through should, because should is also retried.
And in Playwright:

In Playwright it is the opposite: every action returns a real Promise, and await is mandatory. A typical mistake there is a forgotten await: the action isn't awaited, and the test becomes flaky. The ESLint rule no-floating-promises catches it.

const text = await page.locator('h1').textContent();
await expect(page.locator('h1')).toContainText('Cart');

cy-1:1.title: What is a subject and how do commands pass values along a chain?
cy-1:1.html:
Each command "yields" a result to the next one, and that is the subject. cy.get('li') yields a jQuery collection of elements, .its('length') yields a number, .invoke('text') a string.

There are commands that start a new chain (cy.get, cy.visit, cy.request), and commands that work with the previous one's subject (.find, .click, .should). Actions like .click() usually yield the same element onward.

cy.get('.cart-item')        // yields: all the cart elements
  .its('length')            // yields: a number
  .should('eq', 3);

cy.get('[data-cy=email]')
  .type('qa@test.com')      // yields: the same input
  .should('have.value', 'qa@test.com');
In an interview: A subject is the result that one command passes to the next one in the chain. For example, cy.get passes the found elements, its length passes a number, invoke text passes a string. Some commands start a new chain, like cy.get or cy.request, and others work with what came from the previous one, like find, click or should.
And in Playwright:

There is no subject chain. A locator is an ordinary object, it can be saved into a variable and narrowed (locator.locator()), and the value is returned by await.

cy-1:2.title: How do you keep a value between commands: variables, .then, aliases?
cy-1:2.html:
The statement const el = cy.get('h1') doesn't give an element: it is a Chainable. There are three correct ways:

  • .then(): you work with the value inside the callback.
  • An alias through .as('name'), then cy.get('@name'). For the DOM and for intercepts the alias looks up the current value again.
  • this.name: only in an ordinary function(), not in an arrow function, because an arrow has no this of its own.

Aliases are cleared between tests, so create them in beforeEach.

beforeEach(() => {
  cy.fixture('user.json').as('user');
});

it('login', function () {           // function, not an arrow
  cy.get('[data-cy=email]').type(this.user.email);
});

cy.get('[data-cy=total]').invoke('text').as('total');
cy.get('@total').should('match', /\d+/);
In an interview: An ordinary variable from cy.get is not an element but a chainable, so that doesn't work. I pass values either through then, or through an alias: I mark the result with as and then get it with cy.get and the at sign.
