You can also use this, but only in an ordinary function, because in an arrow function this is not the right one. Aliases are reset between tests, so I create them in beforeEach.
And in Playwright:

Aliases aren't needed: the value goes into an ordinary variable.

const total = await page.getByTestId('total').textContent();
const user = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('data/user.json', 'utf8'));

cy-1:3.title: How does .then() differ from .should() with a callback?
cy-1:3.html:
.should(cb) is retried: Cypress re-executes the preceding queries and the callback until all the assertions inside pass or the timeout expires. So you can't call other cy commands or cause side effects in it.

.then(cb) runs once. It is for getting a value and starting the following commands.

// ✅ retried until the condition becomes true
cy.get('.status').should(($el) => {
  expect($el.text().trim()).to.eq('Paid');
});

// ⚠️ runs once: if the status hasn't updated yet, it fails
cy.get('.status').then(($el) => {
  expect($el.text().trim()).to.eq('Paid');
});
In an interview: Should with a callback is retried: Cypress repeats the element search and the check until the assertion passes. So inside should you can't call other cy commands. Then runs exactly once, it is for getting a value and continuing the chain. If I check a state that changes over time, I choose should.
And in Playwright:

The equivalent of .should(cb) with retries is expect.poll() for a value or expect(async () => { ... }).toPass() for a block of assertions. A one-off check is expect(await locator.textContent()).toBe(...), like .then in Cypress.

cy-1:4.title: How do you combine Cypress with Promises and ordinary async code?
cy-1:4.html:
cy.wrap(promise) adds a Promise to the queue: Cypress waits for it to resolve and passes the value on. If the Promise rejects, the test fails.

For code that must run in Node (a database, files, token generation), cy.task is used: it returns a value or a Promise from the Node process into the test.

The main rule is not to mix: don't return a Promise from a test and don't await cy commands in one block.

const getToken = () => fetch('/api/token').then((r) => r.json());

cy.wrap(getToken()).its('token').then((token) => {
  cy.setCookie('auth', token);
});

cy.task('db:getUser', { email: 'qa@test.com' })
  .its('status')
  .should('eq', 'active');
In an interview: For a Promise there is cy.wrap: I wrap the Promise, Cypress waits for it in the queue and passes the value on. And code that must run in Node, such as database queries, I move into cy.task, which returns the result straight into the test. The main thing is not to mix the Cypress queue and await in one place, because the order of execution becomes unpredictable.
And in Playwright:

There is no mixing problem: Playwright is ordinary async/await, so Promise.all and any libraries work. An equivalent of cy.task isn't needed, because the test runs in Node anyway: you can go to the database directly from the test.

cy-1:5.title: The asynchrony of Cypress commands
cy-1:5.html:
Cypress commands don't run immediately: when called they are only added to a queue, and run sequentially later. They return not a promise but a chain object (chainable), so await cy.get(...) won't work as you expect. Mixing async/await with commands breaks the queue order.

Because of this you can't just assign a result to a variable: const text = cy.get('h1').text() won't give the text. To get a value you use .then(), which receives the result of the previous command. For reuse between steps there are aliases through .as() and cy.get('@alias').

Ordinary JS code outside commands runs immediately, before the commands in the queue, which is a frequent source of bugs. So conditional logic and calculations with values from the page are placed inside .then().

cy-2:0.title: What is retry-ability and what exactly is repeated?
cy-2:0.html:
Cypress divides commands into three groups, and they behave differently.

GroupExamplesBehaviour
Queriesget, find, contains, its, invoke, eq, filter, firstThey only read state, so it is safe to repeat them
Assertionsshould, andThey search for nothing, but they are what trigger the repeats
Actionsclick, type, check, selectThey change state, so they run once

How the retry loop works

When an assertion stands behind a query, Cypress finds the elements and checks the assertion, and if it didn't pass, after a few milliseconds it repeats both steps, the search and the check. It stops when the assertion passed or defaultCommandTimeout, 4 seconds, passed.

cy.get('[data-cy=cart-count]').should('have.text', '3');
// each moment: find the element → check the text → not 3? once more

Since Cypress 12 the whole chain of queries is repeated from the start, not only the last command. Before, Cypress could hold an old element that React or Vue had already re-rendered, and fail with the error "element is detached from the DOM". Now the element is looked up anew each time.

cy.get('[data-cy=order-list]')
  .find('[data-cy=order]')
  .first()
  .should('contain', 'Paid');
// on every attempt anew: get → find → first → should

Several assertions in a chain must pass at the same time, in one attempt:

cy.get('[data-cy=submit]')
  .should('be.visible')
  .and('not.be.disabled')
  .and('have.text', 'Pay');

Why actions aren't repeated

If click on "Pay" were retried while the page hadn't updated yet, Cypress would click a second time, and the order would be created twice. So an action runs exactly once.

But before that it waits for actionability, also up to 4 seconds. The element must be in the DOM, visible, not disabled (for type also not readonly), not animating and not covered by a modal or a loader. Before a click Cypress also scrolls the element into view. So "once" doesn't mean "blindly".

Traps you get caught on

1. .then kills retries. The callback in .then runs once.

// ❌ if the list is still loading, it fails at once
cy.get('li').then(($li) => {
  expect($li).to.have.length(3);
});

// ✅ retried
cy.get('li').should('have.length', 3);

// ✅ also retried: the callback inside should
cy.get('li').should(($li) => {
  expect($li).to.have.length(3);
});

2. An assertion right after an action. After .click() there is no query in the chain that can be restarted, so .should checks the same element that the click yielded. If the application re-rendered it, the test fails. It is more reliable to start a new chain.

// ⚠️ risky
cy.get('[data-cy=tab-stats]').click().should('have.class', 'active');

// ✅ reliable: a new chain with a query
cy.get('[data-cy=tab-stats]').click();
cy.get('[data-cy=tab-stats]').should('have.class', 'active');

3. .invoke with a side effect. It is a query, so during retries the method is called several times. For reading a value it is fine, for a function that changes something it is dangerous.

4. What isn't retried at all. cy.visit, cy.request, cy.task, cy.wait, .then have only their own timeouts, not a retry loop.

In an interview: In Cypress only queries are retried, the commands that read the DOM, like get, find or contains, together with the should that follows them. Since version twelve Cypress restarts the whole chain of queries on each attempt, so the element is looked up anew every time. Actions like click or type run once, because a repeated click could, for example, create an order twice. But before running they wait for the element to become visible, enabled, stable and not covered. Two practical things follow: I write checks with should, not then, because then isn't retried, and after an action I start a new chain with cy.get, so the assertion can look the element up again.
And in Playwright:

The mechanism is different: both actions and assertions wait. Before running, an action checks actionability and looks the element up by the locator each time, and expect(locator) is retried for up to 5 seconds. So Playwright has no split into queries and actions and no .then trap. But it has its own: expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true) checks the state once and isn't retried.

cy-2:1.title: Queries, actions and assertions: what is the difference?
cy-2:1.html:
TypeExamplesBehaviour
Queriesget, find, contains, its, invoke, eq, filterRepeated until the following assertion passes
Assertionsshould, andMake the preceding queries repeat
Actionsclick, type, check, selectWait for actionability, then run once
Othersvisit, request, wait, thenNot retried, have their own timeouts

The practical conclusion: put the assertion right after a query, not after an action. A chain .click().should(...) already checks the result of the click without clicking again.

In an interview: Queries are requests to the DOM: get, find, contains, its. They are repeated until the assertion after them passes. Assertions, should and and, are what trigger those repeats. Actions, click, type, select, wait for the element to become actionable but run once, because a repeated click could break the application's state.
And in Playwright:

There is no such split. Creating a locator does nothing, an action waits for the element to be ready, and the assertion expect(locator) is repeated. The only thing not retried is an assertion over an already obtained value: expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true).

cy-2:2.title: Why is cy.wait(3000) an antipattern and what to use instead?
cy-2:2.html:
A fixed pause is always a guess: if the application responded in half a second, the test wastes another two and a half for nothing; if it took four, the test fails. That is, the test is both slow and unstable.

Instead of a pause, wait for a concrete state: an assertion on an element or the completion of a specific request through an alias.

// ❌
cy.get('[data-cy=save]').click();
cy.wait(3000);

// ✅ wait for the state in the UI
cy.get('[data-cy=toast]').should('contain', 'Saved');

// ✅ wait for a specific request
cy.intercept('POST', '/api/profile').as('save');
cy.get('[data-cy=save]').click();
cy.wait('@save').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 200);
In an interview: Because it is a guessed number: if the application responded faster, the test waits for nothing, and if slower, the test fails. Instead I wait for a concrete state: either an assertion on an element, which is retried itself, or the completion of a specific request through an intercept with an alias and cy.wait on that alias.
And in Playwright:

The same rule: page.waitForTimeout() is an antipattern. Instead of it use a web-first assertion or page.waitForResponse().

cy-2:3.title: What timeouts does Cypress have and how do you override them?
cy-2:3.html:
TimeoutDefaultWhat it applies to
defaultCommandTimeout4 sQueries, assertions, actionability
requestTimeout5 sHow long cy.wait('@alias') waits for the request to be sent
responseTimeout30 sThe response to cy.request and to an intercepted request
pageLoadTimeout60 sPage load in cy.visit
taskTimeout60 scy.task

Increase a timeout locally, for a specific command, not globally, otherwise you hide the problem.

cy.get('[data-cy=report]', { timeout: 15000 }).should('be.visible');

describe('slow reports', { defaultCommandTimeout: 10000 }, () => {
  it('generates a PDF', () => { /* ... */ });
});
In an interview: The main one is defaultCommandTimeout, four seconds, for element search and assertions. For the network there is requestTimeout, five seconds for the request to be sent, and responseTimeout, thirty seconds for the response. There are also pageLoadTimeout for cy.visit and taskTimeout for cy.task. I override them locally: with the timeout option in a specific command or in a describe's config, not globally.
And in Playwright:
TimeoutDefault
The whole test (timeout)30 s
expect5 s
actionTimeoutno separate limit, bounded by the test
navigationTimeoutno separate limit, bounded by the test
globalTimeoutthe whole run

The key difference: Playwright has a timeout for the whole test, and Cypress doesn't have one by default.

cy-2:4.title: A test is flaky on CI. How do you look for the cause in Cypress?
cy-2:4.html:
Collect evidence. A screenshot on failure is taken automatically in cypress run. Video has been off by default since Cypress 13: turn on video: true for CI. Cypress Cloud has Test Replay with the DOM, network and console.

Reproduce. Run one spec many times, for example with a Cypress._.times loop or a plugin like cypress-burn, with the same resources as on CI.

Typical causes: cy.wait(ms) instead of waiting for a state; an action before the API response arrived; shared test data between tests; animations; dependence on test order; an intercept registered after the action.

Retries, retries: { runMode: 2, openMode: 0 }, are only a temporary bandage. Every test that passed on the second attempt must end with an investigation.

Cypress._.times(20, (i) => {
  it('checkout #' + i, () => {
    // the flaky test
  });
});
In an interview: First I collect evidence: a screenshot on failure, video (it has to be turned on explicitly, because it has been off since version thirteen), and Test Replay if there is Cloud. Then I reproduce it: I run the spec dozens of times in a loop. Next I check the typical causes: hard cy.wait calls, actions before the API response, shared data, animations, an intercept registered after the action. Retries in runMode help to survive until the release, but they don't cure anything, so I investigate each such test.
And in Playwright:

The main tool is Trace Viewer: trace: 'on-first-retry' gives a timeline with DOM snapshots, network and console without a paid service. Reproduction is --repeat-each=20, and checking for competition over data is --workers=1.

cy-2:5.title: Waiting and retry-ability
cy-2:5.html:
Cypress waits automatically: query commands like cy.get are repeated until the element is found or the timeout expires, 4 seconds by default (defaultCommandTimeout). Assertions through .should() are also retried together with the preceding query. Actions such as click and type wait for the element to become visible, not covered and not disabled.

Only the last query before an assertion is retried, and action commands like click are not repeated. So a chain should preferably be built so that the query and the check go together. A timeout can be overridden for a specific command through the timeout parameter.

cy.wait(5000) is bad, because it is a fixed pause: on a fast environment it needlessly slows the run down, and on a slow one it may still not be enough. The right way is to wait for a concrete condition: an element's visibility through should, or a network request through cy.intercept with an alias and cy.wait('@alias').

cy-3:0.title: How does cy.get() differ from .find() and cy.contains()?
cy-3:0.html:
• cy.get(selector) searches from the document root, even if it stands in a chain. The exception is inside .within().
  • .find(selector) searches only inside the previous subject.
  • cy.contains(text) searches for an element by text; you can specify a selector: cy.contains('button', 'Save'). In a chain it searches inside the subject.
cy.get('[data-cy=order]').find('[data-cy=price]');   // the price exactly within the order
cy.get('[data-cy=order]').get('[data-cy=price]');    // ⚠️ searches the whole page
cy.contains('button', 'Place order').click();
In an interview: cy.get always searches from the document root, even if it stands in a chain. Find searches only inside the previous element. And contains finds an element by text, and you can pass it a selector to narrow the search, for example a button with a particular text.
And in Playwright:

page.locator() searches across the page, locator.locator() inside another locator, and text with getByText(). An important difference is strict mode: if a locator for an action finds several elements, Playwright fails with an error at once.

cy-3:1.title: Which selectors does Cypress recommend and why?
cy-3:1.html:
The most stable ones are separate attributes for tests: data-cy, data-test, data-testid. They don't change when styles or markup are refactored.

Classes and ids for styling are brittle, and positional selectors like div:nth-child(3) are the worst. cy.contains is appropriate when the text is part of the requirement. For Playwright-style semantic locators there is the Testing Library plugin with cy.findByRole.

cy.get('[data-cy=submit]');                 // ✅
cy.contains('button', 'Sign in');           // ✅ if the text is a requirement
cy.get('.btn.btn-primary.mt-2');            // ⚠️ depends on styles
cy.get('form > div:nth-child(3) > button'); // ❌ breaks with the markup
In an interview: The best are separate attributes for tests, for example data-cy: they aren't touched when styles change. Contains by text is for when the text itself is the requirement. I don't use classes for styling or positional selectors, because they break with any change of markup. If you need semantic locators, there is the Testing Library plugin with findByRole.
And in Playwright:

Semantic locators are built in: getByRole, getByLabel, getByPlaceholder, getByTestId. The attribute for getByTestId is configured in the config through testIdAttribute, for example to data-cy.

cy-3:2.title: How do you narrow the search: within, eq, first, filter?
cy-3:2.html:
.within() limits all nested commands to one block, which is convenient for a table row or a product card. .eq(n), .first(), .last() take an element by index. .filter() keeps the elements that match a selector or a text through :contains().

Use indexes only when the order is part of the logic. Otherwise bind to the content.

cy.contains('[data-cy=row]', 'Order #1042').within(() => {
  cy.get('[data-cy=status]').should('have.text', 'Shipped');
  cy.get('[data-cy=cancel]').click();
});

cy.get('[data-cy=product]').filter(':contains("Thermos")').first().click();
In an interview: Within limits the search to one block: I find the right table row by text, and all the commands inside search only in it. Eq, first and last pick by index, but I use them only when the order really matters. Otherwise I narrow by content with contains or filter.
And in Playwright:

Instead of within there is locator composition, and instead of filter(':contains') there is filter({ hasText }).

const row = page.getByTestId('row').filter({ hasText: 'Order #1042' });
await expect(row.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Shipped');
await row.getByTestId('cancel').click();

cy-3:3.title: Why is { force: true } dangerous?
cy-3:3.html:
The option force: true turns off the actionability checks: Cypress no longer checks whether the element is visible, covered by a modal or disabled. The event simply fires at the element.

If force "fixed" a test, the test now passes despite a real problem: a user couldn't click, and the test is green. Justified use is rare, for example a hidden native input under a custom checkbox, and there must be a comment next to it saying why.

// ⚠️ only with an explanation
// the native input is hidden, the custom checkbox covers it
cy.get('input[type=checkbox]').check({ force: true });
In an interview: Force turns off the checks: whether the element is visible, not covered, enabled. If a test started passing only with force, most likely it is now hiding a real bug: a user couldn't click. I use it only in rare cases, for example for a hidden native checkbox, and always with a comment.
And in Playwright:

Playwright has the same { force: true }, and the risks are the same: it turns off the actionability checks.

cy-3:4.title: How do you work with iframes, new tabs, and file downloads and uploads?
cy-3:4.html:
• Iframe. There is no dedicated command. You take contentDocument.body and wrap it with cy.wrap, or use the cypress-iframe plugin. An iframe from another domain is not accessible because of the same-origin policy.
  • New tabs. Cypress works in only one. You remove target="_blank" and open the link in the same tab, or simply check the href attribute.
  • Upload. The built-in command .selectFile(), with drag-and-drop support.
  • Download. You check the file in the cypress/downloads folder with cy.readFile.
cy.get('iframe#payment')
  .its('0.contentDocument.body').should('not.be.empty')
  .then(cy.wrap)
  .find('[data-cy=card]').type('4242424242424242');

cy.get('[data-cy=docs-link]').invoke('removeAttr', 'target').click();

cy.get('input[type=file]').selectFile('cypress/fixtures/avatar.png');
cy.readFile('cypress/downloads/report.csv').should('contain', 'Total');
In an interview: For an iframe I take the contentDocument body and wrap it in cy.wrap, or I use the cypress-iframe plugin, but an iframe from another domain is not accessible. Cypress doesn't support new tabs, so I remove target blank or check the href. For uploading files there is the built-in selectFile, and a downloaded file I verify with readFile in the downloads folder.
And in Playwright:

Here Playwright is noticeably stronger. An iframe is page.frameLocator(), including from another domain. New tabs are context.waitForEvent('page'). Upload is setInputFiles(), download is page.waitForEvent('download').

await page.frameLocator('iframe#payment').getByTestId('card').fill('4242...');
const [tab] = await Promise.all([
  page.context().waitForEvent('page'),
  page.getByTestId('docs-link').click(),
]);

cy-3:5.title: Selectors and data-cy
cy-3:5.html:
The best Cypress practice is separate test attributes data-cy, data-test or data-testid. They don't change together with styles or text and clearly show developers that the element is used in tests. The selector looks like this: cy.get('[data-cy=submit]').

You should avoid CSS classes, especially generated ones, tags and positional selectors like div > span:nth-child(3). They break with any change of markup. An ID is fine if it is stable and not generated dynamically.

cy.contains works well when the text is part of what is being tested, but it is sensitive to changes in copy and localisation. For accessibility and stability, Testing Library for Cypress is often added, with search by role and name.

cy-4:0.title: What is cy.intercept and where exactly does the interception happen?
cy-4:0.html:
cy.intercept intercepts the HTTP requests the page makes. Interception happens not in the browser but in the Cypress Node process, through which all the traffic passes as through a proxy. So it also sees requests from third-party scripts.

Two modes: spy, only to observe and check the request and response; stub, to replace the response. cy.intercept doesn't intercept WebSocket messages, only HTTP.

cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products*').as('products');   // spy
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products*', { fixture: 'products.json' }); // stub
In an interview: Intercept intercepts the page's HTTP requests, and does it in the Cypress Node process, because all the traffic goes through its proxy. You can just observe a request and check it, or you can replace the response with a fixture or any data. It doesn't intercept WebSocket, only HTTP.
And in Playwright:

page.route() intercepts requests at the browser protocol level, not through a proxy. A route is bound to a page or a context. Unlike Cypress, WebSocket can also be intercepted and mocked through page.routeWebSocket().

cy-4:1.title: How do you wait for a request and check it through an alias?
cy-4:1.html:
You register an intercept, give it an alias with .as(), perform the action, and then cy.wait('@alias'). It yields an interception object with request and response, so you can check what exactly the front end sent and received.

cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders').as('createOrder');
cy.get('[data-cy=checkout]').click();

cy.wait('@createOrder').then(({ request, response }) => {
  expect(request.body.items).to.have.length(2);
  expect(response.statusCode).to.eq(201);
});
In an interview: I register an intercept with an alias, perform the action that triggers the request, and do cy.wait on that alias. It returns both the request and the response, so I check that the front end sent the right body and that the backend responded with the expected status.
And in Playwright:

There are no aliases: the wait for a request is created before the action and awaited after it.

const orderResp = page.waitForResponse('**/api/orders');
await page.getByTestId('checkout').click();
const resp = await orderResp;
expect(resp.status()).toBe(201);
expect(resp.request().postDataJSON().items).toHaveLength(2);

cy-4:2.title: How do you replace or change a server response?
cy-4:2.html:
A static stub goes as the third argument: a fixture, a body, a status, a delay. A dynamic one goes through the req handler: you can change the request before sending, respond completely with req.reply, or let the request through to the server and change the real response in req.continue.

// a server error
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/stats', { statusCode: 500, body: { error: 'boom' } });

// a slow network
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/stats', { fixture: 'stats.json', delay: 2000 });

// the real response, but with one field replaced
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/stats', (req) => {
  req.continue((res) => {
    res.body.total = 0;
  });
});
In an interview: For simple cases I pass the response as the third argument: a fixture, a status code, a delay. That is how I check how the UI behaves on a five hundred error or on a slow network. If I need to change a real response precisely, I write a handler: I let the request through to the server with req.continue and change one field in the response.
And in Playwright:

Replacing is route.fulfill(), passing through is route.continue(), aborting is route.abort(). Modifying a real response is route.fetch() and fulfill with a new body.

await page.route('**/api/stats', async (route) => {
  const response = await route.fetch();
  const json = await response.json();
  json.total = 0;
  await route.fulfill({ response, json });
});

cy-4:3.title: Why must an intercept be set before the action, and what happens if there are several on one URL?
cy-4:3.html:
An intercept fires only on requests that happened after it was registered. If you set it after cy.visit or a click, the request may slip through, and cy.wait will fail on timeout. A classic cause of flaky tests.

If several intercepts match one request, the one defined later fires first. Handlers can pass the request on, and the option times: 1 limits an intercept to one response, which is convenient for the scenario "an error first, then success". All intercepts are reset before every test.

cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user', { statusCode: 200, fixture: 'user.json' });
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user', { times: 1 }, { statusCode: 503 });
// the first request → 503 (defined later, fires first)
// the following requests → 200
In an interview: An intercept sees only the requests that happen after it is registered, so I always set it before visit or a click. Otherwise the request slips through and wait fails, which is a frequent cause of flakiness. If there are several intercepts on one URL, the last one defined fires first, and with times one I can build a scenario where an error comes first and then a success.
And in Playwright:

The rules are similar: a route must be registered before the action, the last registered handler fires first, a request can be passed on through route.fallback(), and the option { times: 1 } exists too.

cy-4:4.title: cy.intercept
cy-4:4.html:
cy.intercept intercepts the application's HTTP requests by method and URL pattern. It is used for waiting on requests, stubbing responses and checking what exactly the application sent. The interception must be declared before the action that triggers the request.

For waiting: cy.intercept('GET', '/api/users').as('getUsers'), then an action and cy.wait('@getUsers'). After that you can check the request or response body and the status code. For a stub you pass a static response or a fixture, for example cy.intercept('GET', '/api/users', { fixture: 'users.json' }).

You can simulate errors and a slow network: statusCode: 500, forceNetworkError: true, delay. You can also change a request or response on the fly through a callback. This lets you test the UI in isolation from an unstable backend.

cy-5:0.title: What is cy.request and how does it differ from cy.intercept?
cy-5:0.html:
cy.request sends an HTTP request itself, from the Cypress Node process, not from the page. So CORS doesn't block it, and cookies are sent and stored automatically. It is a tool for API tests and data preparation.

cy.intercept sends nothing: it intercepts the requests the application makes.

cy.requestcy.intercept
What it doesSends a requestIntercepts a page's request
From whereThe Node processThe Node process's proxy
What forAPI tests, login, data preparationMocks, checking the front end's requests
In an interview: cy.request sends an HTTP request itself, and does it from the Node process, so CORS doesn't get in its way. I use it for API tests, login and data preparation. cy.intercept sends nothing: it intercepts the requests the application makes, to replace or check them.
And in Playwright:

The equivalent of cy.request is the request fixture (APIRequestContext). The main difference: the browser doesn't start, so API tests are much faster and are parallelised by workers. page.request shares cookies with the page.

cy-5:1.title: How do you check the status, body and headers of a response?
cy-5:1.html:
cy.request yields a response object with status, body, headers and duration. Individual fields are conveniently obtained with .its(), and several checks in .then().

cy.request('GET', '/api/products/42').then((res) => {
  expect(res.status).to.eq(200);
  expect(res.headers['content-type']).to.include('application/json');
  expect(res.body).to.have.property('id', 42);
  expect(res.body.price).to.be.a('number').and.be.greaterThan(0);
  expect(res.duration).to.be.lessThan(1000);
});

cy.request('/api/products').its('body').should('have.length.greaterThan', 0);
In an interview: cy.request returns a response object with the status, body, headers and duration. One field I get with its, and several checks I do in then: the status, content-type, the presence and type of fields in the body, and if needed, that the response came faster than a certain threshold.
And in Playwright:
const res = await request.get('/api/products/42');
await expect(res).toBeOK();
expect(res.headers()['content-type']).toContain('application/json');
const body = await res.json();
expect(body).toMatchObject({ id: 42 });

cy-5:2.title: How do you test negative scenarios: 400, 401, 404?
cy-5:2.html:
By default cy.request fails on any 4xx or 5xx status. For negative tests you need the option failOnStatusCode: false, otherwise the test will fail before your check. This is one of the most frequent questions.

cy.request({
  method: 'POST',
  url: '/api/orders',
  body: { items: [] },
  failOnStatusCode: false,
}).then((res) => {
  expect(res.status).to.eq(400);
  expect(res.body.message).to.contain('items');
});

cy.request({ url: '/api/admin', failOnStatusCode: false })
  .its('status').should('eq', 401);
In an interview: By default cy.request fails on any four hundred or five hundred status. So for negative cases I add failOnStatusCode false and then check myself that the expected code came: four hundred for invalid data, four hundred and one without a token, four hundred and four for a nonexistent resource, and that the error message is meaningful.
And in Playwright:

The opposite behaviour: Playwright doesn't fail on 4xx and 5xx by default, and you check the status yourself. To make it fail, as in Cypress, there is the option failOnStatusCode: true.

cy-5:3.title: How do you build a CRUD chain in one test?
cy-5:3.html:
You create an entity, take the id from the response, read, update and delete it, and at the end check that it really disappeared. Each step passes data to the next one through .then().

it('product CRUD', () => {
  cy.request('POST', '/api/products', { name: 'Thermos', price: 500 })
    .then(({ status, body }) => {
      expect(status).to.eq(201);
      const id = body.id;

      cy.request('GET', '/api/products/' + id)
        .its('body.name').should('eq', 'Thermos');

      cy.request('PUT', '/api/products/' + id, { name: 'Thermos', price: 450 })
        .its('body.price').should('eq', 450);

      cy.request('DELETE', '/api/products/' + id)
        .its('status').should('eq', 204);

      cy.request({ url: '/api/products/' + id, failOnStatusCode: false })
        .its('status').should('eq', 404);
    });
});
In an interview: I create the entity with POST, take the id from the response and pass it on through then. Then I read with GET and check the data, update with PUT, delete with DELETE, and at the end make sure that GET returns four hundred and four. That way one test covers the resource's whole lifecycle and cleans up after itself.
And in Playwright:

The logic is the same, but with await and without nested callbacks: the chain reads from top to bottom, and the id goes into an ordinary variable.

cy-5:4.title: How do you organise authorisation in API tests?
cy-5:4.html:
You log in with a request, save the token and pass it in the Authorization header. To avoid repeating code, move it into a custom command. The login and password come from environment variables, not from the code.

// cypress/support/commands.ts
Cypress.Commands.add('apiLogin', () => {
  return cy.request('POST', '/api/auth/login', {
    email: Cypress.env('USER_EMAIL'),
    password: Cypress.env('USER_PASSWORD'),
  }).its('body.token');
});

// the test
cy.apiLogin().then((token) => {
  cy.request({
    url: '/api/orders',
    headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token },
  }).its('status').should('eq', 200);
});
In an interview: I log in with a request, get the token and pass it in the Authorization header. The logic is moved into the custom command apiLogin, to avoid duplication. I take the credentials from environment variables, so they don't end up in the repository.
And in Playwright:

It is convenient to create a separate context with a header and hand it out through a fixture.

const api = await playwright.request.newContext({
  baseURL: process.env.API_URL,
  extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token },
});

cy-5:5.title: How do you validate a response schema?
cy-5:5.html:
Checking individual fields doesn't catch the situation where the backend changed a type or removed a field you didn't check. JSON schema validation checks the whole structure: required fields, types, formats.

The simplest is to add the chai-json-schema plugin and keep the schemas in fixtures. An alternative is ajv through cy.task or your own command.

// cypress/support/e2e.ts
import chaiJsonSchema from 'chai-json-schema';
chai.use(chaiJsonSchema);

// the test
cy.fixture('schemas/product.json').then((schema) => {
  cy.request('/api/products/42').its('body')
    .should('be.jsonSchema', schema);
});

// fixtures/schemas/product.json
// { "type": "object",
//   "required": ["id", "name", "price"],
//   "properties": {
//     "id": { "type": "integer" },
//     "name": { "type": "string" },
//     "price": { "type": "number", "minimum": 0 } } }
In an interview: Checking individual fields misses changes you didn't foresee, for example when the backend changed a field's type. So I validate the whole response against a JSON schema: I add chai-json-schema, and I keep the schemas themselves in fixtures. That way the test fails immediately if the contract changed.
And in Playwright:

Chai plugins aren't needed: the test is in Node, so ajv is plugged in directly, and the result is checked with expect(validate(body)).toBe(true).

cy-5:6.title: How do you combine API and UI in one test?
cy-5:6.html:
Prepare data through the API, check through the UI, clean up through the API again. This is many times faster and more stable than creating everything with clicks, and it tests exactly what is needed.

The second technique is to check that the front end sent the right request: an action in the UI, an intercept with an alias, a check of the request body.

let productId;

beforeEach(() => {
  cy.request('POST', '/api/products', { name: 'Test product', price: 99 })
    .its('body.id').then((id) => { productId = id; });
});

afterEach(() => {
  cy.request('DELETE', '/api/products/' + productId);
});

it('the product is visible in the catalogue', () => {
  cy.visit('/catalog');
  cy.contains('[data-cy=product]', 'Test product').should('be.visible');
});
In an interview: I create the needed data through the API in beforeEach, the test itself checks only the UI, and in afterEach I clean the data up through the API again. This is much faster and more stable than creating everything with clicks. I used a similar approach on a Playwright project, where test objects were deleted through the API after every test.
And in Playwright:

The same, but through a fixture: creation before await use(), deletion after. Cleanup is guaranteed even if the test fails, and you simply add this fixture to the signature of the test that needs it.

cy-5:7.title: What limits does Cypress have for API testing and when should you take another tool?
cy-5:7.html:
• There is no built-in parallelism without Cypress Cloud or plugins.
  • WebSocket can't be tested directly.
  • It isn't suitable for load testing: for that use k6 or JMeter.
  • For API tests a browser is still started, so it is slower than pure HTTP clients. More convenient output is given by the cypress-plugin-api plugin.

A large set of pure API tests is more convenient to keep in Postman/Newman, Playwright request or Supertest. Cypress is justified when API tests mostly serve UI tests and the team wants one stack.

In an interview: Cypress is suitable for API tests, but has limits: without Cloud there is no parallelism, WebSocket can't be tested directly, load can't be checked with it, and even for API tests a browser is started. If there are many API tests and they are standalone, I would take Postman with Newman or Playwright request. Cypress is justified when the API mostly helps the UI tests and you want to keep one stack.
And in Playwright:

For APIs Playwright is more convenient: without a browser, in parallel through workers, with an HTML report. WebSocket can be listened to through page.on('websocket') or mocked through routeWebSocket. But load testing is likewise not its job.

cy-6:0.title: How does Cypress isolate tests from each other?
cy-6:0.html:
Since Cypress 12 testIsolation is on by default: before every test the page is cleared to about:blank, and cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage are erased for all domains.

The consequence: each test must prepare its own state itself, and you can't rely on the previous test having left the user logged in or a page open.

The difference from Playwright: there isolation is given by a new BrowserContext, while here the state is cleared in the same browser.

In an interview: Since version twelve Cypress clears the page, cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage before every test: this is testIsolation. So tests are independent, and each prepares its own state. Unlike Playwright, where each test gets a new context, Cypress clears the state in the same browser.
And in Playwright:

Isolation "out of the box" is different: each test gets a new BrowserContext, a separate profile like incognito. Nothing is erased, the context is simply created anew in milliseconds.

cy-6:1.title: What is cy.session and how do you avoid logging in in every test?
cy-6:1.html:
cy.session(id, setup) performs the login once, saves cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage, and in later tests restores them without logging in again. The option validate checks that the session is still valid, otherwise the login runs again. cacheAcrossSpecs: true shares the session between spec files.

It is better to do the login inside setup through the API, as it is faster.

Cypress.Commands.add('login', (role = 'user') => {
  cy.session(role, () => {
    cy.request('POST', '/api/auth/login', {
      email: Cypress.env(role + '_email'),
      password: Cypress.env(role + '_password'),
    }).its('body.token').then((token) => {
      window.localStorage.setItem('token', token);
    });
  }, {
    validate() {
      cy.request('/api/me').its('status').should('eq', 200);
    },
    cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
  });
});

beforeEach(() => {
  cy.login('admin');
  cy.visit('/dashboard');
});
In an interview: For this there is cy.session: it performs the login once, saves the cookies and storages, and in later tests simply restores them. Validate checks that the session is still alive, and if not, logs in again. I do the login itself inside through the API. A separate session id per role lets you switch between users quickly.
And in Playwright:

The equivalent is storageState: a setup project logs in, saves cookies and localStorage to JSON, and other projects pick up the file through dependencies. A separate file per role, and in one test you can have two contexts with different roles at once.

cy-6:2.title: How do you work with several domains through cy.origin?
cy-6:2.html:
A test is bound to one origin. When a scenario moves to another domain, for example login through an external provider or a payment page, the commands for it are written in a cy.origin block.

The block runs in the context of the other domain, so variables from outside don't get in there: they must be passed explicitly through args. Custom commands inside are also unavailable without separate registration.

const user = { email: 'qa@test.com', password: 'secret' };

cy.visit('/');
cy.get('[data-cy=sso-login]').click();

cy.origin('https://auth.provider.com', { args: user }, ({ email, password }) => {
  cy.get('#email').type(email);
  cy.get('#password').type(password, { log: false });
  cy.get('button[type=submit]').click();
});

cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
In an interview: For scenarios with another domain, such as an SSO login, there is cy.origin: the commands for the other domain are written inside that block. An important nuance is that variables from outside don't get in there, so I pass them explicitly through args. In practice I more often bypass the external login through the API and keep cy.origin for the single test that checks the flow itself.
And in Playwright:

There is no restriction: the test simply goes to another domain, and all commands work as usual. Several tabs and contexts within a test are also normal.

cy-6:3.title: Why is programmatic login better than login through the UI?
cy-6:3.html:
A UI login in every test is slow, and if the login form breaks, all tests fail even though they were checking something quite different. A programmatic login through the API plus cy.session is faster and more stable.

The UI login flow itself is checked by one separate test: for the form, validation and the redirect.

In an interview: If every test logs in through the form, it is slow, and a broken form fails the whole suite even though the tests check something else. So I log in through the API and cache the session with cy.session, and I verify the login form itself with one separate test.
And in Playwright:

The approach is the same: login through the API, the result is saved in storageState, and the UI login is checked by one separate test.

cy-6:4.title: Custom commands and cy.session
cy-6:4.html:
Custom commands are added with Cypress.Commands.add in the file cypress/support/commands.js. They encapsulate repeated actions: login, creating data through the API, filling in forms. In TypeScript their types are declared in the Chainable interface.

A UI login in every test is slow, so it is better to log in with an API request cy.request. Even better is to wrap this in cy.session, which caches cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage between tests. The session is identified by a key, for example the user's login, so each role has its own cache.

cy.session has a validate parameter, a function that checks the session is still valid; if not, the login runs again. The option cacheAcrossSpecs lets you reuse the session between files. This is the equivalent of storageState in Playwright.

cy-6:5.title: Tabs, iframes, cross-origin
cy-6:5.html:
Cypress works in one tab, so new tabs don't open. A typical solution is to remove the target="_blank" attribute with invoke('removeAttr', 'target') and open the link in the same tab. Or simply check the href attribute and go to it with cy.visit.

For an iframe there is no built-in command: you get contentDocument.body through .its() and wrap it in cy.wrap. This is often moved into a custom command, or the cypress-iframe plugin is used. A cross-origin iframe won't work like this without turning off browser security.

To move to another domain within a test, since version 12 there is cy.origin, inside which commands for the other domain run. A typical case is login through a third-party SSO provider. Variables are passed into cy.origin explicitly through args, because the callback runs in a different context.

cy-7:0.title: How do you create a custom command and type it in TypeScript?
cy-7:0.html:
Commands are registered in cypress/support/commands.ts through Cypress.Commands.add. For TypeScript to know about the new command, you extend the Chainable interface.

// cypress/support/commands.ts
Cypress.Commands.add('getByCy', (id: string) => {
  return cy.get('[data-cy=' + id + ']');
});

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      getByCy(id: string): Chainable<JQuery<HTMLElement>>;
      login(role?: string): Chainable<void>;
    }
  }
}

// the test
cy.getByCy('submit').click();
In an interview: I register custom commands in support through Cypress.Commands.add. For TypeScript to suggest and check them, I extend the global Chainable interface in the Cypress namespace. Typical examples are getByCy for data attributes and login.
And in Playwright:

There are no custom commands. Their role is played by fixtures through test.extend<MyFixtures>() (typed with a generic), helper functions and Page Object methods.

cy-7:1.title: Page Object or App Actions: which do you choose?
cy-7:1.html:
Page Object is classes with methods that wrap cy commands for a specific page. A test reads like a scenario, and the locators are in one place.

App Actions is an approach promoted by the Cypress team: instead of clicks through the UI, control the application's state directly, through the API or functions exposed on window. This is faster and more stable for preparing state.

In practice they are combined: Page Object for the actions the test verifies, the API for preparation.

export class StatisticsPage {
  private chart = '[data-cy=stats-chart]';
  private period = '[data-cy=period-select]';

  visit() {
    cy.visit('/statistics');
    return this;
  }

  selectPeriod(value: string) {
    cy.get(this.period).select(value);
    return this;
  }

  chartShould(...args: Parameters<Cypress.Chainable['should']>) {
    return cy.get(this.chart).should(...args);
  }
}

// the test
new StatisticsPage().visit().selectPeriod('30d').chartShould('be.visible');
In an interview: I use Page Object: classes with methods for each page, so the locators are collected in one place and a test reads like a scenario. The Cypress team also suggests App Actions: controlling the application's state directly, without the UI. I combine both: I prepare state through the API, and I use Page Object for the actions the test really verifies. That is exactly how my framework was built on the project for "Come Back Alive".
And in Playwright:

A Page Object with async methods, and pages are often passed into a test through fixtures, without new in every test. App Actions can be done through page.evaluate() or the API.

cy-7:2.title: What are fixtures in Cypress? Are they the same as in Playwright?
cy-7:2.html:
No, and it is easy to get confused here. In Cypress a fixture is simply a file with test data in the cypress/fixtures folder, loaded through cy.fixture() or used as a response in cy.intercept.

In Playwright a fixture is a dependency injection mechanism that prepares resources (a page, a context, a logged-in user) and cleans them up after the test. The closest equivalent in Cypress is hooks plus custom commands.

cy.fixture('users/admin.json').then((admin) => {
  cy.get('[data-cy=email]').type(admin.email);
});

cy.intercept('GET', '/api/stats', { fixture: 'stats-empty.json' });
In an interview: In Cypress a fixture is simply a file with test data, which I load through cy.fixture or use as a response in intercept. In Playwright it is something completely different: a dependency injection mechanism that prepares and cleans up resources. So if I am asked about fixtures, I clarify which tool is meant.
And in Playwright:

Here a fixture is a dependency injection mechanism with setup and teardown. Test data from JSON is simply imported or read through fs.

cy-7:3.title: How do you configure different environments and environment variables?
cy-7:3.html:
Variables are available through Cypress.env('NAME'). Sources: the file cypress.env.json (not committed), OS environment variables with the CYPRESS_ prefix, the --env flag, the env block in the config.

For several environments, in setupNodeEvents you read the environment name and set the matching baseUrl. On CI secrets are passed through the pipeline's secrets.

// CI: CYPRESS_USER_PASSWORD=*** npx cypress run --env envName=staging

// cypress.config.ts
setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
  const urls = {
    dev: 'https://dev.example.com',
    staging: 'https://staging.example.com',
  };
  config.baseUrl = urls[config.env.envName || 'dev'];
  return config;
}
In an interview: I read variables through Cypress.env. Locally they live in cypress.env.json, which isn't committed, and on CI they are passed as environment variables with the CYPRESS_ prefix from the pipeline's secrets. I pick the environment with the env flag, and in setupNodeEvents I set the right baseUrl.
And in Playwright:

Variables are ordinary process.env, often together with dotenv. Environments are set through use.baseURL or separate projects.

cy-7:4.title: What are cy.task and setupNodeEvents?
cy-7:4.html:
The test code runs in the browser, so it can't reach a database, the file system or Node libraries. cy.task passes the call to the Node process, where tasks are registered in setupNodeEvents.

A task must return a value or a Promise. If it returns nothing, you must return null, otherwise Cypress will give an error.

// cypress.config.ts
import { Client } from 'pg';

setupNodeEvents(on) {
  on('task', {
    async 'db:query'(sql) {
      const client = new Client({ connectionString: process.env.DB_URL });
      await client.connect();
      const res = await client.query(sql);
      await client.end();
      return res.rows;
    },
    log(message) {
      console.log(message);
      return null;
    },
  });
}

// the test
cy.task('db:query', "SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = 1042")
  .its('0.status').should('eq', 'paid');
In an interview: Since the test runs in the browser, it can't reach the database or files directly. For this there is cy.task: I register a task in setupNodeEvents, it runs in Node and returns the result into the test. For example, I check in PostgreSQL that an order got the right status. A task must return something, at least null.
And in Playwright:

An equivalent isn't needed: the test runs in Node anyway, so you import the PostgreSQL client straight into the test or a fixture.

cy-7:5.title: Fixtures in Cypress vs Playwright
cy-7:5.html:
In Cypress fixtures are static files with test data, usually JSON, in the cypress/fixtures folder. They are loaded through cy.fixture('user.json') or passed to cy.intercept as a response body. Essentially this is just a data store.

In Playwright fixtures are a dependency injection mechanism: functions that prepare the environment before a test and clean it up after. They have test and worker scopes, can depend on each other and are passed into a test as parameters. The built-in fixtures are page, context, browser, request.

The equivalent of Playwright fixtures in Cypress is the beforeEach and before hooks, custom commands and cy.session. This is a frequent point of confusion, so it is worth clarifying at once in which sense the term is used.

cy-7:6.title: Page Object vs App Actions
cy-7:6.html:
A Page Object is a class that encapsulates a page's selectors and actions, so the test works with methods like loginPage.login(user). It gives reuse and one place to change selectors. The downside in Cypress is an extra layer of abstraction over chainable commands and the temptation to do everything through the UI.

App Actions is an approach recommended by the Cypress team: the application's state is prepared directly through its internal functions, available through window, or through the API. For example, instead of clicks on a task creation form, the test calls an application function and immediately gets the needed state. This is faster and more stable, but requires access to the application's code.

In practice I would combine them: a Page Object or modules with functions for UI interactions, and data preparation through the API and custom commands. Through the UI we go only through what is actually being tested.

cy-8:0.title: How do you run Cypress in GitHub Actions?
cy-8:0.html:
The simplest is the official action cypress-io/github-action: it installs dependencies with a cache, starts the application if needed, waits for it and runs the tests. Artifacts with screenshots are uploaded on failure.

name: e2e
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  cypress:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cypress-io/github-action@v6
        with:
          browser: chrome
          start: npm start
          wait-on: 'http://localhost:3000'
        env:
          CYPRESS_USER_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.USER_PASSWORD }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: screenshots
          path: cypress/screenshots
In an interview: I use the official action cypress-io github-action: it installs dependencies with a cache, brings up the application, waits for it and runs the tests. Secrets are passed from the repository's secrets, and on failure screenshots are saved as artifacts. Tests run on every pull request.
And in Playwright:
- run: npm ci
- run: npx playwright install --with-deps
- run: npx playwright test
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: always()
  with:
    name: playwright-report
    path: playwright-report

There is also an official Docker image with browsers: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright.

cy-8:1.title: How do you parallelise Cypress tests?
cy-8:1.html:
On one machine Cypress doesn't run in parallel: one process, one browser, specs one after another. Parallelisation is only across several machines.

  • Cypress Cloud: cypress run --record --parallel distributes specs between machines taking duration into account. This is a paid service after a free limit.
  • For free: a matrix in CI plus the cypress-split plugin, which divides specs between runs.

The unit of distribution is a spec file, so large specs are better split up.

strategy:
  matrix:
    containers: [1, 2, 3, 4]
steps:
  - uses: cypress-io/github-action@v6
    env:
      SPLIT: 4
      SPLIT_INDEX: ${{ strategy.job-index }}
In an interview: On one machine Cypress runs specs sequentially, so parallelisation happens only across several machines. The official way is Cypress Cloud with the record and parallel flags, but it is paid. For free you can build a matrix in CI and split the specs with the cypress-split plugin. The unit of distribution is a spec file, so I keep specs small.
And in Playwright:

Parallelisation is free and built in: workers on one machine (half of the CPU cores by default) plus --shard=1/4 between machines and merge-reports for merging reports. The unit of distribution is a test, not a file.

cy-8:2.title: What reports, screenshots and videos does Cypress give you?
cy-8:2.html:
In cypress run a screenshot on failure is taken automatically. Video has been off by default since Cypress 13 and is turned on with video: true.

Reports: the built-in spec reporter in the console, mochawesome for HTML (with a separate report merge after the run), allure-cypress for Allure with history and trends, JUnit XML for CI.

// cypress.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  video: true,
  screenshotOnRunFailure: true,
  reporter: 'mochawesome',
  reporterOptions: {
    reportDir: 'cypress/reports',
    overwrite: false,
    html: false,
    json: true,
  },
});
In an interview: On a failure in run mode a screenshot is taken automatically, and video has to be turned on explicitly, because it has been off since version thirteen. For HTML reports I use mochawesome, and if I need history and trends, Allure through allure-cypress. For CI systems there is JUnit XML.
And in Playwright:

An HTML report with a built-in Trace Viewer comes out of the box. Screenshots, video and traces are configured in use: screenshot, video, trace. Allure goes through allure-playwright, JUnit through a built-in reporter.

cy-8:3.title: Flaky tests in Cypress and retries
cy-8:3.html:
The most frequent causes: fixed cy.wait instead of waiting for conditions, races with network requests, animations, tests depending on each other and on shared data. Also unstable selectors, an element re-rendering after it was found, and a slow CI environment.

The treatment: wait for requests through cy.intercept and aliases, build chains with assertions that are retried, isolate tests and create data through the API. Each test must start from a known state. For diagnostics: video, screenshots and Test Replay in Cypress Cloud.

Retries are configured in the config: retries: { runMode: 2, openMode: 0 }, where runMode is for cypress run on CI and openMode is for interactive mode. You can set retries for an individual test or a describe block too. But retries only mask the problem, so flaky tests must be tracked and the root cause fixed.

cy-9:0.title: What are the key differences between Cypress and Playwright?
cy-9:0.html:
CypressPlaywright
Where the test livesInside the browserOutside, through the browser protocol
AsynchronyA command queue, no awaitPromises, async/await
WaitingRetry of queries and should, 4 sAuto-waiting of actions, expect 5 s
IsolationState cleared in one browserA new BrowserContext per test
Tabs and domainsOne tab, cy.originAny number
ParallelismBetween machines, Cloud or a pluginWorkers built in, sharding
BrowsersChromium, Firefox, WebKit experimentalChromium, Firefox, WebKit
Networkcy.intercept through a proxypage.route through the protocol
DebuggingTime travel in the Test RunnerTrace Viewer, UI mode
LanguagesJavaScript, TypeScriptJS/TS, Python, Java, .NET
In an interview: The fundamental difference: Cypress runs inside the browser, and Playwright drives it from outside. Everything else follows from that. Cypress has a command queue instead of async/await, one tab, parallelism only across machines and network interception through a proxy. Playwright has ordinary promises, multiple tabs and domains, isolated contexts, built-in workers and supports several languages. On the other hand, Cypress has very convenient debugging with time travel.

cy-9:1.title: When would you choose Cypress over Playwright?
cy-9:1.html:
Cypress is appropriate when the application is single-page, with one domain and one tab, and the tests are written mostly by front-end developers for whom time travel and component testing in the same tool matter.

The deciding factor is more often the existing stack: if the project already has a large suite on Cypress and people who know it, there is no point rewriting. For a new project without such a legacy, today the default is usually Playwright.

In an interview: I would choose Cypress if the application is single-page, on one domain, and the tests are written together with front-end developers who find time travel and component tests convenient. Even more important is what already exists on the project: if there is a large Cypress suite and the team knows it, it isn't worth rewriting. And for a new project from scratch I would take Playwright.

cy-9:2.title: How would you migrate a project from Cypress to Playwright?
cy-9:2.html:
• Don't rewrite everything at once. New tests are written in Playwright, the old ones run in parallel in CI and are moved gradually, starting with the most critical and most flaky.
  • Migrate the architecture, not the syntax. A Page Object carries over almost directly, but the methods become async. Custom commands turn into fixtures or helpers. cy.session is replaced by storageState with a setup project.
  • Network: cy.intercept with an alias becomes page.route or page.waitForResponse.
  • Risks: two stacks in CI for a while, training the team, implicit dependencies between Cypress tests that become visible in a parallel run.
  • Success criterion: less flakiness, a faster run thanks to workers, coverage didn't drop.
// Cypress
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/stats').as('stats');
cy.get('[data-cy=period]').select('30d');
cy.wait('@stats');
cy.get('[data-cy=chart]').should('be.visible');

// Playwright
const stats = page.waitForResponse('**/api/stats');
await page.getByTestId('period').selectOption('30d');
await stats;
await expect(page.getByTestId('chart')).toBeVisible();
In an interview: I wouldn't rewrite everything at once. New tests are written in Playwright, the old ones live alongside in CI and are moved gradually, starting with the critical and most unstable ones. I migrate the architecture, not the lines: Page Objects almost directly, but with async, custom commands become fixtures, cy.session becomes storageState, an intercept with an alias becomes waitForResponse. The main risks are two stacks at once and hidden dependencies between tests that surface in a parallel run. I measure success by stability, run speed and the fact that coverage didn't drop.

cy-10:0.title: Does Cypress run tests in parallel and does it retry failed tests automatically?
cy-10:0.html:
Both statements are false.

Parallelism: on one machine Cypress runs specs sequentially: one process, one browser. In parallel only across several machines: through Cypress Cloud (--record --parallel) or for free through a CI matrix and a plugin like cypress-split.

Retries: off by default. They must be turned on explicitly in the config, usually only for CI.

// cypress.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  retries: { runMode: 2, openMode: 0 },
});
In an interview: No. On one machine Cypress runs specs sequentially, and parallelism exists only across several machines, through Cloud or by splitting specs in CI. And rerunning failed tests is off by default, I turn it on in the config for runMode, and I investigate every test that passed on a retry separately.
And in Playwright:

In Playwright both are built in: workers parallelise tests on one machine (half the cores by default), and --shard splits between machines. Retries are also off by default and set in the config (retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0), but the on-first-retry trace immediately shows why a test failed.

cy-10:1.title: How do you keep login and cookies between tests?
cy-10:1.html:
Cypress.Cookies.preserveOnce was removed in Cypress 12, and copying cookies by hand is a brittle workaround. The modern answer is cy.session: it caches cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage after login and restores them in later tests, and validate checks that the session is still valid.

More detail is in the question about cy.session in the "State, sessions, isolation" section.

In an interview: The modern way is cy.session. It performs the login once, caches cookies and storages, and restores them in later tests. Copying cookies by hand and the old preserveOnce are approaches from versions before twelve.
And in Playwright:

The equivalent is storageState: a setup project logs in and saves the state to JSON, and other projects pick up the file through dependencies.

cy-10:2.title: How do you make a pause (sleep) in Cypress?
cy-10:2.html:
Technically cy.wait(ms) really does pause, but the right answer in an interview is to explain why you shouldn't: a fixed pause makes the test both slow and unstable.

Instead: an assertion that is retried itself (should('be.visible')), or waiting for a specific request through cy.intercept and cy.wait('@alias'). Justified use of cy.wait(ms) is rare, for example checking a debounce, where the time itself is the requirement.

In an interview: Formally it is cy.wait with milliseconds, but I don't do that, because it is a guessed number: the test either waits for nothing or fails. I wait for a concrete state: an assertion on an element or the completion of a request through an intercept with an alias.
And in Playwright:

In Playwright the same antipattern is page.waitForTimeout(). Instead use web-first assertions and waitForResponse.

cy-10:3.title: How do you use XPath in Cypress?
cy-10:3.html:
There is no native XPath support, and the official plugin @cypress/xpath is no longer maintained by the Cypress team. You can still see it on old projects, but recommending it as a solution is a sign of outdated knowledge.

The tasks for which XPath is used are covered by built-in means: search by text with cy.contains, moving through the tree with .closest(), .parents(), .siblings(), .next(), semantic search with Testing Library and cy.findByRole.

// XPath: //td[text()='Order #1042']/parent::tr//button
cy.contains('td', 'Order #1042').closest('tr').find('button').click();
In an interview: Out of the box Cypress has no XPath, and the plugin for it is no longer maintained. In practice it isn't needed either: I search by text through contains, and go from an element to its parent or sibling through closest, parents or siblings.
And in Playwright:

Playwright supports XPath natively (page.locator('xpath=...'), and a string with // is recognised automatically), but recommends getByRole, getByText and getByTestId.

cy-10:4.title: How do you install Cypress correctly?
cy-10:4.html:
Locally in the project, as a dev dependency: npm install --save-dev cypress. Then the version is pinned in package.json and the lock file, it is the same for all developers and on CI, and it is run through npx cypress.

A global install gives different versions on different machines and breaks reproducibility. Only the Cypress binary is stored separately, in the system cache, and it is checked with npx cypress verify.

In an interview: Locally in the project as a dev dependency, so the version is pinned and the same for everyone and on CI. A global install gives a version mismatch between machines.
And in Playwright:

The same rule: npm i -D @playwright/test in the project, plus npx playwright install for the browsers.

cy-10:5.title: The element is hidden and the click doesn't go through. What do you do?
cy-10:5.html:
First understand why it is hidden. If it is covered by a modal, a loader or a cookie banner, the test has found a real problem, or has to close the obstacle first itself. If the element appears after an action, you need to wait for the state with should.

{ force: true } turns off the actionability checks, and the test may pass where a user couldn't click. It is justified only for deliberate cases such as a hidden native checkbox under a custom one, and with a comment.

In an interview: First I find out the cause: whether the element is covered, hasn't appeared yet, or it is a bug. Force turns off the checks, and a test can turn green where a user would be stuck, so I use it only in rare justified cases and with a comment.

cy-10:6.title: How does requestTimeout differ from responseTimeout?
cy-10:6.html:
requestTimeout (5 s) is how long cy.wait('@alias') waits for the application to send a request. If the request didn't go out within 5 seconds, the error is "No request ever occurred".

responseTimeout (30 s) is how long to wait for the response: to an intercepted request in cy.wait and to cy.request.

So these are two different stages: "did the request go out" and "did the response come". The diagnosis differs: the first timeout usually means the action in the UI didn't fire or the intercept was registered after it, and the second means a slow backend.

In an interview: They are two stages. requestTimeout is five seconds for the request to be sent at all, and if it runs out, the problem is usually in the test or the UI. responseTimeout is thirty seconds for the server's response, and that is already about the backend.

cy-10:7.title: How do you recognise an outdated answer about Cypress structure?
cy-10:7.html:
Outdated (before v10)Current
cypress.jsoncypress.config.js / .ts
cypress/integrationcypress/e2e, files *.cy.ts
testFilesspecPattern
cypress/plugins/index.jssetupNodeEvents in the config
cy.server(), cy.route()cy.intercept()
Cypress.Cookies.preserveOncecy.session()
Cypress DashboardCypress Cloud
Video is always recordedOff by default since v13

Any of the terms on the left in your answer signals that your experience ended before version 10.

In an interview: Since version ten the config is cypress.config, tests are in the e2e folder, instead of testFiles there is specPattern, and plugins moved into setupNodeEvents. The network is intercepted through intercept instead of the old server and route, and sessions are kept through cy.session.

cy-11:0.title: What hooks does Cypress have and how do they work?
cy-11:0.html:
Hooks come from Mocha: before runs once before all the tests of a block, beforeEach before every test, afterEach after each one, after once after all. Hooks in cypress/support/e2e.ts apply globally to all specs.

A tip from the Cypress team itself: it is better to do cleanup in beforeEach than in afterEach. If a test failed or you stopped it in the Test Runner, afterEach may not run, and the next test starts with a dirty state.

describe('Cart', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.request('DELETE', '/api/cart');   // a clean state BEFORE the test
    cy.login();
    cy.visit('/cart');
  });

  it('empty cart', () => {
    cy.contains('Your cart is empty').should('be.visible');
  });
});
In an interview: Hooks come from Mocha: before and after run once per block, beforeEach and afterEach for every test. I do state preparation and cleanup in beforeEach, because afterEach may not run if the test failed, and then the next one starts with a dirty state.
And in Playwright:

There are the same hooks (test.beforeEach, test.afterAll…), but preparation and cleanup are usually moved into fixtures: the code after await use() runs even when the test fails.

cy-11:1.title: What types of assertions does Cypress support?
cy-11:1.html:
• Chai BDD: expect(x).to.eq(), .to.include(), .to.have.length().
  • Chai TDD: assert.equal(), assert.isTrue().
  • Chai-jQuery: assertions of DOM state: be.visible, have.class, have.text, be.checked.
  • Sinon-Chai: for spies and stubs: be.called, calledWith.

Two styles of use: implicit through .should('have.text', 'X'), which is retried; explicit through expect inside .then, which runs once, while inside .should(cb) it is retried.

In an interview: Cypress uses Chai in the BDD and TDD styles, Chai-jQuery for checking DOM state and Sinon-Chai for stubs and spies. More important than the list is the difference between implicit assertions through should, which are retried, and explicit expect in then, which run once.

cy-11:2.title: How do you work with Shadow DOM?
cy-11:2.html:
By default cy.get doesn't go inside a shadow root. Two ways:

  • Locally: the command .shadow(), which moves into the element's shadow root.
  • Globally: includeShadowDom: true in the config, then all queries pass through shadow boundaries.
cy.get('payment-widget').shadow().find('[data-cy=pay]').click();

// or in cypress.config.ts
// e2e: { includeShadowDom: true }
In an interview: By default Cypress doesn't see the contents of a shadow root. Locally I go in with the shadow command, and if there are many components with Shadow DOM, I turn on includeShadowDom in the config.
And in Playwright:

In Playwright locators pass through open Shadow DOM by default: nothing needs to be turned on.

cy-11:3.title: How do you do hover and drag-and-drop?
cy-11:3.html:
Cypress has no native hover: .trigger('mouseover') fires a JS event, but not the CSS :hover state. If a menu is shown only through CSS, .invoke('show') or the cypress-real-events plugin, which generates real browser events, will help.

Drag-and-drop is a chain of events through .trigger. If a library works on the HTML5 drag API, dragstart, drop and dataTransfer are needed, and here a plugin is often used too.

cy.get('[data-cy=menu]').trigger('mouseover');

cy.get('[data-cy=card]')
  .trigger('mousedown', { button: 0 })
  .trigger('mousemove', { clientX: 400, clientY: 200 })
  .trigger('mouseup');
In an interview: Hover and drag-and-drop are done through trigger with the needed mouse events. But trigger fires only JS events, not the real CSS hover state, so for such cases I use the cypress-real-events plugin.
And in Playwright:

Built in and through real browser events: locator.hover() and locator.dragTo(target).

cy-11:4.title: How does cy.exec differ from cy.task?
cy-11:4.html:
Both commands run something outside the browser, in the Node process.

  • cy.exec('command') runs a shell command: a database seeding script, a migration, npm run. It returns the exit code, stdout and stderr.
  • cy.task('name') calls a Node function that you registered in setupNodeEvents: a DB query through a library, working with files, generating data. It returns any value.

The rule of choice: there is a ready script, use cy.exec; you need logic and returning data into the test, use cy.task.

cy.exec('npm run db:seed').its('exitCode').should('eq', 0);
cy.task('db:query', 'SELECT count(*) FROM pets').its('0.count').should('eq', '5');
In an interview: Both work in Node. cy.exec runs a shell command, for example a database seeding script, and returns the exit code and the output. cy.task calls a Node function that I registered in the config and returns data into the test, which is how I make database queries.
And in Playwright:

Equivalents aren't needed: the test is in Node anyway, so a shell command is run through child_process, and the DB is called directly.

cy-11:5.title: What Node events does Cypress have, for example after:run?
cy-11:5.html:
These are hooks of the whole run level, not of a test. They are registered in setupNodeEvents and run in Node:

  • before:run / after:run are before and after the whole cypress run; after:run receives the results.
  • before:spec / after:spec are around each spec file; after:spec is often used to delete videos of tests that passed.
  • before:browser:launch configures the browser: flags, extensions, window size.
  • after:screenshot processes or renames a screenshot.
setupNodeEvents(on) {
  on('after:run', (results) => {
    if ('totalFailed' in results) {
      console.log('Tests failed:', results.totalFailed);
    }
  });
}
In an interview: These are run-level events that I register in setupNodeEvents. After:run fires after the whole run and receives the results, which is handy for reports or notifications. After:spec fires after each file, and before:browser:launch lets you configure the browser.
And in Playwright:

The equivalents are globalSetup / globalTeardown in the config or a setup project; run results are in your own reporter through onEnd.

cy-11:6.title: How do you control the order in which specs run?
cy-11:6.html:
Through specPattern as an array of paths in the needed order, or through --spec in the CLI. But the right part of the answer is to explain that test dependence on order is itself a problem: such tests break with parallel splitting, rerunning a single test, or retries.

If a scenario needs data from a previous step, it is prepared through the API in beforeEach, not through another test.

specPattern: [
  'cypress/e2e/login.cy.ts',
  'cypress/e2e/checkout.cy.ts',
],
In an interview: Technically the order can be set with an array in specPattern. But I try to make tests independent of order, because such tests break with parallel runs and repeats. I create the needed data through the API before every test.
And in Playwright:

The same principles, but by default the order is even less predictable because of workers; for deliberately sequential scenarios there is test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' }).

cy-11:7.title: Which browsers and operating systems does Cypress support?
cy-11:7.html:
Browsers: the Chrome family (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, the built-in Electron), Firefox and WebKit (the Safari engine), the latter experimentally. The last three major versions are officially supported. Internet Explorer, Opera and the real Safari are not, and mobile browsers and native apps aren't either.

OS: Windows, macOS and Linux with current versions; Node.js, the supported LTS versions. Check the exact minimum versions in the documentation before an interview: they change with every major release.

In an interview: Cypress works with browsers of the Chrome family, including Edge and Electron, with Firefox and experimentally with WebKit. There is no real Safari, no mobile browsers and no native apps, which is one of the main limitations compared to Playwright or Appium.
And in Playwright:

Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit fully, plus mobile device emulation, but also without native mobile apps.

cy-11:8.title: How do you debug tests in Cypress?
cy-11:8.html:
• Time travel: in cypress open hover over a command in the Command Log and you will see a DOM snapshot at that moment.
  • cy.pause() stops execution; then you can step through commands.
  • .debug() stops in DevTools with the current subject (DevTools must be open).
  • cy.log() writes to the Command Log; cy.task('log', ...) to the CI terminal.
  • A click on a command in the Command Log prints details to the console: the subject, elements, the request and response.
  • On CI: screenshots, video (if turned on) and Test Replay in Cloud.
cy.get('[data-cy=total]').debug();
cy.pause();
cy.get('[data-cy=checkout]').click();
In an interview: Locally I use time travel in the Command Log, cy.pause to stop the test and go step by step, and debug to look at the subject in DevTools. A click on a command in the log shows all the details in the console. On CI I look at screenshots, video and the logs that I print through cy.task.
And in Playwright:

The equivalents: page.pause(), npx playwright test --debug with the inspector, UI mode (--ui) and Trace Viewer for CI.

cy-11:9.title: How do you work with URLs, navigation and browser history?
cy-11:9.html:
• cy.url() is the full URL as a string.
  • cy.location() is an object with pathname, search, hash; convenient for checking parts.
  • cy.go('back') / cy.go('forward') are the back and forward buttons.
  • cy.reload() reloads the page.

All of them are queries or commands with retries, so assertions on the URL wait for navigation themselves.

cy.location('pathname').should('eq', '/statistics');
cy.location('search').should('include', 'period=30d');
cy.go('back');
cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
In an interview: For URLs there are cy.url and cy.location, the second is more convenient because you can check the path or parameters separately. For history there is cy.go back and forward, and for refreshing cy.reload. Assertions on the URL are retried, so they wait for navigation themselves.
And in Playwright:

await expect(page).toHaveURL(/statistics/), page.goBack(), page.goForward(), page.reload().

ts-basics:0.title: Why TypeScript in a test framework
ts-basics:0.html:
