TypeScript is JavaScript plus a static type system. Types exist only at compile time: after transpilation to JS they are completely erased and check nothing at runtime. This is a key idea to state honestly in an interview: TS catches errors in code, but doesn't guarantee that an API response really has the shape you described.

What TS gives an automation engineer in practice:

  • Autocompletion for Page Objects, fixtures, API clients. A new engineer sees which methods exist and which arguments they take.
  • Safe refactoring. Renamed the accountId field in a model, and the compiler shows all the tests that broke.
  • Documentation in code. The type TransferRequest explains the contract better than a comment.
  • Early errors: a typo in a field name, undefined where a string is expected, a forgotten await.

Basic primitives: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, bigint, symbol. For arrays, string[] or Array<string>, for tuples [string, number].

const baseUrl: string = process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000';
const retries: number = 2;
const headers: Record<string, string> = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' };
const pair: [currency: string, amount: number] = ['UAH', 10050];

You don't need to annotate every variable explicitly: TS infers the type itself (type inference). I put annotations at the boundaries: function parameters, return values of public methods, data models.

In an interview: For me TypeScript is a tool that catches errors before tests run and makes the framework self-documenting. But types are erased at runtime, so I additionally validate API data with a schema, rather than just trusting the type.

ts-basics:1.title: any, unknown and never
ts-basics:1.html:
any turns off type checking. With a variable of type any you can do anything, and the compiler stays silent. Worse, any "infects" everything it touches: the result of anyValue.foo.bar is also any. In test code this is a typical source of errors that show up only at runtime.

unknown is a safe alternative. You can put anything into an unknown variable, but you can't use it without a check. First you must narrow the type: typeof, instanceof, a type guard or schema validation.

async function readBody(res: Response): Promise<unknown> {
  return res.json();
}

const body = await readBody(res);
// body.id; // error: 'body' is of type 'unknown'
if (typeof body === 'object' && body !== null && 'id' in body) {
  console.log(body.id); // now it is allowed
}

never is a type with no values. It is returned by a function that always throws or never finishes. The most useful application is an exhaustive check: if you forgot to handle a variant in a switch over a union type, the compiler shows an error.

type Status = 'PENDING' | 'COMPLETED' | 'FAILED';

function label(s: Status): string {
  switch (s) {
    case 'PENDING': return 'In progress';
    case 'COMPLETED': return 'Success';
    case 'FAILED': return 'Error';
    default: {
      const unreachable: never = s;
      throw new Error(`Unknown status: ${unreachable}`);
    }
  }
}

If you add the status REVERSED, the code stops compiling until you handle it.

In an interview: any turns off checks, so in our framework it is forbidden by an ESLint rule. For external data I use unknown and narrow the type with a check, and never for an exhaustive switch, so that a new status doesn't go unnoticed.

ts-basics:2.title: Literal types, as const and satisfies
ts-basics:2.html:
A literal type is a type with one specific value: 'GET', 200, true. A union of literals gives very precise contracts: type Currency = 'UAH' | 'USD' | 'EUR'. You can no longer pass 'usd' in lowercase.

When you write const method = 'GET', TS infers the literal type 'GET'. But for let or object properties the type is widened to string. To keep literals, as const is used: it makes all fields readonly and fixes the exact values.

const ENDPOINTS = {
  accounts: '/api/v1/accounts',
  transfers: '/api/v1/transfers',
} as const;

type Endpoint = typeof ENDPOINTS[keyof typeof ENDPOINTS];
// '/api/v1/accounts' | '/api/v1/transfers'

const CURRENCIES = ['UAH', 'USD', 'EUR'] as const;
type Currency = typeof CURRENCIES[number]; // 'UAH' | 'USD' | 'EUR'

The second technique is an array of values plus a type derived from it. That gives you one source of truth: the array can be used in parameterised tests and the type in signatures.

The satisfies operator (since TS 4.9) checks that a value conforms to a type, but doesn't "widen" it to that type. This is convenient for test data configs:

type UserRole = 'admin' | 'operator' | 'viewer';
const users = {
  admin: { login: 'admin@test.io', role: 'admin' },
  viewer: { login: 'viewer@test.io', role: 'viewer' },
} satisfies Record<string, { login: string; role: UserRole }>;

users.admin.login; // ok, the keys are known exactly

Instead of enum I more often take a union of literals: it doesn't generate runtime code and combines better with JSON from the API.

In an interview: I use a union of literals for statuses, currencies and HTTP methods, because it is a precise contract with no runtime code. as const fixes a config as immutable with exact types, and satisfies checks an object against a type without losing the specific keys.

ts-obj:0.title: interface or type
ts-obj:0.html:
Both ways describe the shape of an object, and for API models the difference is often unnoticeable.

interface Account {
  id: string;
  iban: string;
  balance: number; // in minor units
}

type Transfer = {
  from: string;
  to: string;
  amount: number;
};

The key differences:

  • type can describe anything: a union, a tuple, a primitive, a function, mapped and conditional types. interface describes only the shape of an object or a class.
  • interface supports declaration merging: two declarations with the same name merge. That is how library types are extended, for example adding a field to a global interface.
  • Inheritance: interface B extends A, and for types an intersection type B = A & { ... }. On a field conflict extends gives a clear error at once, while an intersection may silently produce never for the field.
  • Classes can implements both an interface and an object type.
interface ApiError { code: string; message: string }
interface ValidationError extends ApiError {
  fields: string[];
}

type Result = { ok: true; data: Account } | { ok: false; error: ApiError };

The practical rule I follow: interface for data models and class contracts (Page Object, clients), type for unions, utilities and everything more complex. The main thing is consistency in the project, not the "right" choice.

In an interview: For object models there is almost no difference. type is needed for unions, tuples and advanced types, while interface can do declaration merging and gives clearer errors with inheritance. In a project I stick to one convention.

ts-obj:1.title: Optional, undefined and null
ts-obj:1.html:
The ? sign makes a field optional: middleName?: string means the field may be absent entirely, or be undefined. This is not the same as middleName: string | undefined: in the second case the field is required, but may have the value undefined.

interface Customer {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  phone?: string;          // may be absent
  closedAt: string | null; // the field is always there, but may be null
}

For API testing this difference is fundamental. If the contract says closedAt is always present and may be null, and the backend started omitting the field, that is a contract regression. The type must reflect the real contract, not "what is more convenient".

Compiler options that strengthen the checks:

  • strictNullChecks (part of strict): without it null and undefined can be assigned to any type, and half of TS's benefit disappears.
  • exactOptionalPropertyTypes: forbids explicitly assigning undefined to a field with ? if undefined isn't stated in the type.
  • noUncheckedIndexedAccess: access by index arr[0] or record[key] gives T | undefined. Very useful, because rows[0].amount on an empty array is a classic test failure with an unclear error.

Working with optionals, I use optional chaining and nullish coalescing:

const phone = customer.phone ?? 'not specified';
const city = customer.address?.city;

A dangerous trick is the non-null assertion customer.phone!. It tells the compiler "trust me" and checks nothing at runtime. In tests an explicit check with expect(...).toBeDefined() or an assertion function is better.

In an interview: ? means the field may be absent, and | null means the field is there, but empty. For API contracts these are different things, and I reflect them exactly. I turn on strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess and avoid the ! operator.

ts-obj:2.title: readonly and immutability
ts-obj:2.html:
readonly forbids overwriting a field after the object is created. This is a compiler check; at runtime the object stays ordinary and mutable.

interface TestUser {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly email: string;
  balance: number;
}

const user: TestUser = { id: 'u1', email: 'a@test.io', balance: 0 };
// user.id = 'u2'; // compile error

For arrays there is readonly string[] or ReadonlyArray<string>: push, splice, sort and other methods that mutate the array are unavailable. The utility Readonly<T> makes all top-level fields readonly.

An important nuance is that readonly is shallow. Nested objects remain mutable:

const config: Readonly<{ api: { timeout: number } }> = { api: { timeout: 5000 } };
// config.api = {...}; // error
config.api.timeout = 1; // compiles!

For deep immutability you use as const on literals (it makes everything readonly at all levels) or write your own DeepReadonly type. A real runtime freeze is given by Object.freeze, but it is also shallow.

Where this is useful in automation:

  • Shared test data and configs. If one test mutates a shared object, another test fails depending on run order, a classic flaky. readonly catches such a mutation at compile time.
  • Constants of endpoints, roles, limits.
  • Parameters of helper functions: function sum(amounts: readonly number[]) guarantees that the helper won't sort the caller's array in place.
In an interview: readonly is protection at the compiler level, it is shallow and blocks nothing at runtime. I use it for shared test data and configs, so a test doesn't accidentally change an object that other tests depend on.

ts-narrow:0.title: Basic narrowing: typeof, instanceof, in, truthiness
ts-narrow:0.html:
Narrowing is when TS, after a check, understands that a variable has a narrower type. The compiler analyses the control flow: if, switch, an early return, throw.

function formatAmount(value: string | number): string {
  if (typeof value === 'number') {
    return value.toFixed(2); // here value: number
  }
  return value.trim(); // here value: string
}

The main tools:

  • typeof is for primitives: 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'undefined', 'object', 'function', 'bigint', 'symbol'. A trap: typeof null === 'object', so for objects I always add !== null.
  • instanceof is for classes: if (err instanceof Error). In catch the variable has type unknown (with useUnknownInCatchVariables, part of strict), so this is a common pattern.
  • in checks that a field exists: if ('errors' in body).
  • Truthiness is if (value). Careful: it filters out both 0 and an empty string. For a transfer amount 0 is a valid value that you can lose this way.
  • Equality: if (status === 'FAILED') narrows a union of literals.
try {
  await client.createTransfer(payload);
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof Error) {
    console.log(err.message);
  } else {
    console.log('Non-error thrown', err);
  }
}

Narrowing also works through an early exit: after if (!account) throw new Error('not found') the variable account is no longer undefined.

In an interview: Narrowing is when, after a typeof, instanceof, in check or a comparison, TS itself understands a more precise type. I remember the traps: typeof null gives 'object', and a truthy check filters out zero, which is critical for money.

ts-narrow:1.title: Discriminated unions
ts-narrow:1.html:
A discriminated union is a union of types with a common literal field (the discriminant). Checking this field narrows the whole object. This is the cleanest way to describe responses that come in different shapes.

type ApiResult<T> =
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: { code: string; message: string } };

function unwrap<T>(res: ApiResult<T>): T {
  if (res.status === 'error') {
    throw new Error(`${res.error.code}: ${res.error.message}`);
  }
  return res.data; // here res is the success branch
}

A classic fintech example is payment methods or events:

type Payment =
  | { kind: 'card'; pan: string; expiry: string }
  | { kind: 'iban'; iban: string }
  | { kind: 'wallet'; walletId: string };

function describe(p: Payment): string {
  switch (p.kind) {
    case 'card': return `Card *${p.pan.slice(-4)}`;
    case 'iban': return `IBAN ${p.iban}`;
    case 'wallet': return `Wallet ${p.walletId}`;
  }
}

If a function has a return type and the switch doesn't cover all the variants, under strict the compiler will say the function may return undefined. For explicitness I add a default branch with never.

Why this is better than one type with a pile of optional fields: with { pan?: string; iban?: string; walletId?: string } you can create a meaningless object with none of the fields or with all of them at once. A union makes impossible states unrepresentable.

In an interview: A discriminated union is a union with a common field such as status or kind, and checking that field narrows the whole object. I describe success or error responses and different payment types this way, so that invalid combinations of fields simply don't compile.

ts-narrow:2.title: User-defined type guards and assertion functions
ts-narrow:2.html:
When the built-in checks are not enough, you write your own type guard: a function with the return type value is T. If it returns true, TS narrows the variable to T.

interface Account { id: string; balance: number; currency: string }

function isAccount(value: unknown): value is Account {
  return (
    typeof value === 'object' && value !== null &&
    typeof (value as Account).id === 'string' &&
    typeof (value as Account).balance === 'number'
  );
}

const body: unknown = await res.json();
if (!isAccount(body)) throw new Error('Unexpected account shape');
body.balance; // Account

Important: the compiler doesn't verify that the guard's body is honest. If a guard returns true for a wrong object, you get a lying type. So complex checks are better generated from a schema.

An assertion function is a function with the signature asserts value is T. It returns nothing and throws an error if the condition isn't met. After the call the type is narrowed.

function assertDefined<T>(v: T, msg: string): asserts v is NonNullable<T> {
  if (v === undefined || v === null) throw new Error(msg);
}

const row = rows.find(r => r.txId === txId);
assertDefined(row, `Transaction ${txId} not found`);
row.amount; // without '?' and without '!'

In practice, for validating API responses I use a schema library, for example zod: schema.parse(body) checks data at runtime and returns a value with the right type, and the type is derived from the schema through z.infer. That way the type and the check don't drift apart.

In an interview: A type guard is a function with value is T, after which TS narrows the type, and an assertion function with asserts throws an error and narrows the type further down the code. The compiler doesn't check their logic, so for API responses I prefer validation with a schema from which the type is derived.

ts-gen:0.title: Why generics: a typed API client
ts-gen:0.html:
A generic is a type parameter. A function or class works with different types but keeps the link between input and output. Without generics you have to choose between duplicating code and any.

class ApiClient {
  constructor(private readonly baseUrl: string) {}

  async get<T>(path: string): Promise<T> {
    const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}${path}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`GET ${path} -> ${res.status}`);
    return (await res.json()) as T;
  }
}

const account = await client.get<Account>('/api/v1/accounts/42');
account.balance; // number, with autocompletion

It is important to be honest here: as T is an assertion, not a check. If the server returned a different object, the type will lie. So in a mature framework the generic takes a schema, and the type is derived from it:

import { z } from 'zod';

async function getParsed<S extends z.ZodTypeAny>(path: string, schema: S): Promise<z.infer<S>> {
  const res = await fetch(path);
  return schema.parse(await res.json());
}

Now T isn't passed by hand but is inferred from the argument. This is a general rule: the best generics are the ones TS infers itself from the parameters, not the ones you have to state in angle brackets.

Other typical places for generics in tests: ApiResult<T>, a paginated response Page<T>, a helper retry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T>, a test data factory build<T>(defaults: T, overrides?: Partial<T>): T.

In an interview: Generics let you write one method get<T> that returns the right type for any endpoint. But as T checks nothing, so I pass a schema into the client and derive the type from it, so the type and the real data don't drift apart.

ts-gen:1.title: Constraints, keyof and defaults
ts-gen:1.html:
The extends constraint says that a type parameter must have a certain shape. Without it nothing is known about T inside the function.

interface HasId { id: string }

function findById<T extends HasId>(items: readonly T[], id: string): T | undefined {
  return items.find(item => item.id === id);
}

The combination with keyof gives type-safe access to fields. A classic example is a helper that extracts a column from results:

function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(rows: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][] {
  return rows.map(r => r[key]);
}

const amounts = pluck(transactions, 'amount'); // number[]
// pluck(transactions, 'amout'); // error: a typo in the field name

T[K] is an indexed access type, the type of field K in object T. The returned type exactly matches the chosen field.

A type parameter can have a default value:

interface Page<T, Meta = { total: number }> {
  items: T[];
  meta: Meta;
}
type AccountsPage = Page<Account>;

Typical mistakes with generics:

  • A type parameter is used only once. function log<T>(x: T): void is no better than x: unknown. A generic makes sense when it links several places.
  • Stating the type by hand where it can be inferred.
  • Overly complex generics in test code. A test should read quickly, and complex typing belongs in the framework's library layer.
In an interview: With extends I constrain a type parameter, for example T extends HasId, and K extends keyof T gives safe access to fields without typos. If a type parameter appears only once, a generic isn't needed.

ts-gen:2.title: Generics in Playwright: fixtures
ts-gen:2.html:
In Playwright generics most often appear in fixtures. test.extend<T>() takes a type that describes the new fixtures, and after that they are typed in every test.

import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { LoginPage } from './pages/login-page';
import { ApiClient } from './api/api-client';

type Fixtures = {
  loginPage: LoginPage;
  api: ApiClient;
};

export const test = base.extend<Fixtures>({
  loginPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(new LoginPage(page));
  },
  api: async ({ request }, use) => {
    await use(new ApiClient(request));
  },
});

test('user sees balance', async ({ loginPage, api }) => {
  // loginPage: LoginPage, api: ApiClient
});

For worker-scoped fixtures there is a second parameter: base.extend<TestFixtures, WorkerFixtures>(). For example, a test account that is created once per worker.

Another place is typing project options. A fixture can be declared as an option with { option: true } and its value set in playwright.config.ts for different projects, for example different currencies or markets.

Generics are also useful in wait helpers:

async function pollUntil<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, done: (v: T) => boolean, timeoutMs = 10_000): Promise<T> {
  const start = Date.now();
  while (Date.now() - start < timeoutMs) {
    const value = await fn();
    if (done(value)) return value;
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));
  }
  throw new Error('pollUntil timeout');
}

Although in Playwright there is already expect.poll for this, and I use it first.

In an interview: In Playwright I type fixtures through test.extend<Fixtures>(), and then the Page Object and API client are typed in every test. For worker-level fixtures there is a second type parameter.

ts-util:0.title: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit
ts-util:0.html:
Utility types are built-in generic types that transform other types. They let you avoid duplicating models.

UtilityWhat it does
Partial<T>all fields become optional
Required<T>all fields become required
Readonly<T>all fields readonly (shallowly)
Pick<T, K>keeps only the listed keys
Omit<T, K>removes the listed keys

A typical use in automation is a test data factory. The base object is valid, and the test overrides only what matters for the scenario:

interface TransferRequest {
  fromAccount: string;
  toAccount: string;
  amount: number;
  currency: 'UAH' | 'USD';
  description: string;
}

function buildTransfer(overrides: Partial<TransferRequest> = {}): TransferRequest {
  return {
    fromAccount: 'UA213223130000026007233566001',
    toAccount: 'UA903052992990004149123456789',
    amount: 10_000,
    currency: 'UAH',
    description: 'autotest',
    ...overrides,
  };
}

const negative = buildTransfer({ amount: -1 });

Omit is handy for a creation body: the server generates id and createdAt, so the request is the model without them:

interface Account { id: string; iban: string; currency: string; createdAt: string }
type CreateAccountBody = Omit<Account, 'id' | 'createdAt'>;
type AccountSummary = Pick<Account, 'id' | 'iban'>;

A nuance: Omit doesn't check that the key exists. Omit<Account, 'idd'> compiles without errors. Pick does check keys.

In an interview: I use Partial in test data factories, so a test overrides only the needed fields, and Omit and Pick to derive a request type from a model without duplication. That way, when the model changes, all derived types update automatically.

ts-util:1.title: Record, Exclude, Extract, NonNullable
ts-util:1.html:
Record<K, V> is an object with keys K and values V. If K is a union of literals, TS requires all the keys. This is convenient for lookup tables that must be complete:

type Currency = 'UAH' | 'USD' | 'EUR';

const minorUnits: Record<Currency, number> = {
  UAH: 2,
  USD: 2,
  EUR: 2,
};
// add 'JPY' to Currency -> an error until you add the key

Exclude<T, U> removes from a union the variants that match U. Extract<T, U> does the opposite, keeping only them. NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined.

type TxStatus = 'PENDING' | 'COMPLETED' | 'FAILED' | 'REVERSED';
type FinalStatus = Exclude<TxStatus, 'PENDING'>;
// 'COMPLETED' | 'FAILED' | 'REVERSED'

type Event =
  | { type: 'deposit'; amount: number }
  | { type: 'withdrawal'; amount: number }
  | { type: 'blocked'; reason: string };
type MoneyEvent = Extract<Event, { amount: number }>;

type MaybeId = string | null | undefined;
type Id = NonNullable<MaybeId>; // string

A practical example: a helper that waits for a transaction's final status accepts only FinalStatus. Passing 'PENDING' as the expected final state won't work, and a meaningless test won't compile.

A trap with Record<string, V>: access map['anyKey'] has the type V, though the key may be absent. Here noUncheckedIndexedAccess or the type Partial<Record<string, V>> helps.

In an interview: Record over a union of keys guarantees that a map covers all the variants, for example all currencies. Exclude and Extract filter a union, and that is how I pick out, for example, only the final transaction statuses for a wait helper.

ts-util:2.title: ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited
ts-util:2.html:
These utilities derive types from functions. They are useful when a model isn't described explicitly or when you don't want to duplicate it.

  • ReturnType<typeof fn> is the type a function returns.
  • Parameters<typeof fn> is a tuple of parameter types.
  • Awaited<T> unwraps a Promise: Awaited<Promise<Account>> gives Account. It also works with nested promises.
async function createTestUser(role: 'admin' | 'viewer', balance = 0) {
  return { id: crypto.randomUUID(), role, balance, token: 'jwt...' };
}

type TestUser = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTestUser>>;
// { id: string; role: 'admin' | 'viewer'; balance: number; token: string }

type CreateArgs = Parameters<typeof createTestUser>;
// [role: 'admin' | 'viewer', balance?: number]

Where I use this:

  • The result type of a factory or a fixture without a separate interface.
  • A wrapper over a function that keeps its signature, for example step logging:
function withLog<F extends (...args: any[]) => Promise<unknown>>(name: string, fn: F) {
  return async (...args: Parameters<F>): Promise<Awaited<ReturnType<F>>> => {
    console.log(`[step] ${name}`, args);
    return (await fn(...args)) as Awaited<ReturnType<F>>;
  };
}

The any[] in the constraint here is a deliberate and accepted technique: it is needed so that any function fits the constraint.

A limitation: if the source of truth is an external contract (OpenAPI), it is better to generate types from it than to derive them from the implementation. Otherwise the type adjusts to a bug in the function.

In an interview: ReturnType and Parameters derive types from a function, and Awaited unwraps a promise, so Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>> gives the result type of an async function. I use this for factories and wrappers, but I take API contracts from OpenAPI, not from the implementation.

ts-class:0.title: Access modifiers and parameter properties
ts-class:0.html:
TS has three access modifiers:

  • public is the default, accessible from anywhere.
  • protected is accessible in the class and its subclasses.
  • private is only inside the class.

Important: these are compiler checks. At runtime a private field is an ordinary object property. Real privacy is given by JS private fields with #: #token is inaccessible from outside even at runtime.

export class LoginPage {
  private readonly emailInput: Locator;
  readonly submitButton: Locator;

  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {
    this.emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email');
    this.submitButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' });
  }

  async login(email: string, password: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
    await this.page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
    await this.submitButton.click();
  }
}

constructor(private readonly page: Page) is a parameter property: it declares the field and assigns it at the same time. It is convenient, but since TS 5.8 there is the option erasableSyntaxOnly, which forbids this syntax together with enum, because it generates JS code rather than simply being erased. It is relevant if TS is run directly through type stripping in Node. In an ordinary Playwright project parameter properties work.

readonly on a field means it can be assigned only at declaration or in the constructor.

How I decide what to make public in a Page Object: public are business-level actions (login, makeTransfer) and locators needed for expect in tests. Internal details are private.

In an interview: public, protected and private are checked only by the compiler, and for real privacy at runtime there are fields with #. In a Page Object I make business actions and locators for checks public, and hide page and helper methods.

ts-class:1.title: abstract, implements and inheritance in a Page Object
ts-class:1.html:
An abstract class can't be created directly. It sets shared logic and forces subclasses to implement abstract methods.

export abstract class BasePage {
  protected abstract readonly path: string;

  constructor(protected readonly page: Page) {}

  async open(): Promise<void> {
    await this.page.goto(this.path);
    await this.waitForLoaded();
  }

  protected abstract waitForLoaded(): Promise<void>;
}

export class AccountsPage extends BasePage {
  protected readonly path = '/accounts';

  protected async waitForLoaded(): Promise<void> {
    await expect(this.page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Accounts' })).toBeVisible();
  }
}

implements checks that a class conforms to an interface, but inherits nothing. This is useful for interchangeable implementations: for example PaymentsApi and PaymentsMock implement one interface.

interface PaymentsGateway {
  pay(amount: number, currency: string): Promise<{ txId: string }>;
}

class PaymentsApi implements PaymentsGateway {
  async pay(amount: number, currency: string) {
    return { txId: 'real-id' };
  }
}

An honest position on inheritance: deep Page Object hierarchies (BasePage, then AuthorizedPage, then DashboardPage) quickly become brittle. I prefer composition: a page consists of components (Header, TransferForm, Table), and shared things are passed through fixtures. One level of a base class is fine, three is already a signal to refactor.

static members belong to the class, not the instance. They suit factories or constants, but not state: static state is shared between tests in a worker and can cause flakiness.

In an interview: An abstract class gives shared logic and forces subclasses to implement the needed methods, while implements only checks the contract. In a Page Object I keep at most one level of inheritance and prefer composition from components.

ts-class:2.title: The this trap and arrow methods
ts-class:2.html:
In JS the value of this is determined by how a function is called, not where it is declared. If you pass a class method as a callback, this is lost.

class TokenStore {
  private token = '';
  set(value: string) { this.token = value; }
  get() { return this.token; }
}

const store = new TokenStore();
const getter = store.get;
// getter(); // TypeError at runtime: this === undefined

Classes in JS are always in strict mode, so this will be undefined, not the global object.

Solutions:

  • Pass an arrow: items.map(x => helper.format(x)).
  • Bind: store.get.bind(store).
  • Declare the method as an arrow property: get = () => this.token;. Such a function captures the instance's this. The downside is that it is created for each instance and doesn't live on the prototype.

TS helps partly: you can explicitly declare a this parameter in the signature (function f(this: Foo)), and then a wrong call won't compile. But for ordinary class methods the compiler doesn't catch the loss of this when passed as a callback.

Where I saw this in automation: passing a Page Object method into test.step or into a retry helper as retry(page.reload). I write retry(() => page.reload()), and there is no problem.

In an interview: this in JS depends on how a function was called, so a method passed as a callback loses its context. I pass an arrow wrapper function or use bind, and I pay attention to this in code review.

ts-async:0.title: Promise, async/await and a forgotten await
ts-async:0.html:
An async function always returns a Promise. await pauses the function until the promise finishes, and returns its value or throws an error.

A forgotten await is the most common mistake in TS automated tests. The consequences depend on the place:

test('transfer is created', async ({ page }) => {
  page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click(); // no await
  expect(page.getByText('Transfer successful')).toBeVisible(); // no await
});

Here the click may not have time to execute, and the web-first assertion returns a promise that nobody awaits. The test may pass green without checking anything, or fail with a strange error such as "Target page, context or browser has been closed", because the test has ended while the action is still in progress.

For an ordinary expect(value).toBe(x) await isn't needed: it is a synchronous check. It is needed for web-first assertions (toBeVisible, toHaveText), expect.poll and expect(...).resolves/rejects.

How I protect myself:

  • The ESLint rule @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises catches promises whose result isn't handled. It requires a type-aware linter configuration.
  • The rule @typescript-eslint/await-thenable catches await on a non-promise.
  • The return type Promise<void> in Page Object methods, so it is visible that a method is asynchronous.

One more trap: return without await inside try. If you write return client.get() in try, the promise's error won't get into this function's catch. return await in try is the right variant.

In an interview: A forgotten await is a classic cause of falsely green tests: the check returns a promise that nobody awaits. I turn on the no-floating-promises rule in the linter and remember that web-first assertions in Playwright always need await.

ts-async:1.title: Promise.all, allSettled, race, any
ts-async:1.html:
MethodWhen it finishesResult
Promise.allall succeed or the first erroran array of values or the first error
Promise.allSettledwhen all have finishedan array of fulfilled or rejected statuses
Promise.racethe first to finish in any waythe first one's value or error
Promise.anythe first successfula value or an AggregateError if all failed

Promise.all is for independent preparation steps that must all pass:

const [sender, receiver] = await Promise.all([
  api.createAccount({ currency: 'UAH', balance: 100_000 }),
  api.createAccount({ currency: 'UAH', balance: 0 }),
]);

A nuance: when one promise fails, the others are not cancelled, they keep running, and their result is just ignored. If that involves creating data, you may get "garbage" in the test environment.

Promise.allSettled is for when you need each result, for example for cleanup: delete all created entities and don't stop at the first error.

const results = await Promise.allSettled(createdIds.map(id => api.deleteAccount(id)));
const failed = results.filter(r => r.status === 'rejected');
if (failed.length) console.warn(`Cleanup failed for ${failed.length} items`);

A classic pattern in Playwright with Promise.all is waiting for an event that an action triggers:

const [response] = await Promise.all([
  page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/transfers') && r.request().method() === 'POST'),
  page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click(),
]);

The wait must be started before the action, otherwise the response may arrive before we start listening. The same can be written like this: first const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(...) without await, then the click, then await responsePromise.

In an interview: Promise.all fails on the first error and fits when you need all the results, allSettled waits for everything and gives the status of each, which is handy for cleanup. race takes the first to finish, any the first successful. In Playwright I subscribe to waitForResponse before the click through Promise.all or a saved promise.

ts-async:2.title: Sequential or parallel, and the forEach trap
ts-async:2.html:
await in a for...of loop runs operations sequentially. map plus Promise.all runs them in parallel.

// sequentially: 10 requests of 200 ms = ~2 s
for (const id of ids) {
  await api.deleteAccount(id);
}

// in parallel: ~200 ms
await Promise.all(ids.map(id => api.deleteAccount(id)));

Sequential is needed when steps depend on each other or the order matters: for example, a deposit, then a transfer, then a balance check. Or when the API has a rate limit. Parallel is for independent operations. For hundreds of requests I limit concurrency (processing in chunks or a library like p-limit), so as not to bring down the test environment.

The main trap is forEach with an async callback:

ids.forEach(async id => {
  await api.deleteAccount(id);
});
console.log('done'); // runs BEFORE the deletion

forEach ignores the returned promises. It doesn't wait for them, and errors inside become unhandled rejections. The test goes on, checks run on uncleaned data, and the error may pop up in another test. The same goes for filter, some, find: they don't understand async predicates, and a promise is always truthy.

// wrong: all the elements pass the filter
const active = accounts.filter(async a => (await api.getStatus(a.id)) === 'ACTIVE');

The right way is to first get all the statuses with Promise.all, and then filter synchronously.

reduce with async also works sequentially only if you explicitly await the accumulator, so I avoid it and write for...of.

In an interview: for...of with await runs requests one at a time, Promise.all with map in parallel, and the choice depends on whether there is a dependency between steps. forEach doesn't wait for async callbacks, so I never use it that way, only for...of or Promise.all.

ts-async:3.title: Error handling in asynchronous code
ts-async:3.html:
An error in an async function turns into a rejected promise. It is caught with try/catch around await or with .catch().

async function getBalance(accountId: string): Promise<number> {
  try {
    const res = await api.get(`/accounts/${accountId}`);
    return res.balance;
  } catch (err) {
    throw new Error(`Failed to get balance for ${accountId}`, { cause: err });
  }
}

The principles I follow in test code:

  • Don't swallow errors. catch (e) {} in a helper turns a failure into a falsely green test or an unclear failure further on.
  • Add context. An Error with the cause option (ES2022) keeps the original error and adds what exactly we were doing.
  • In catch the variable has type unknown, so I check err instanceof Error before touching message.
  • For negative tests, don't write try/catch by hand, use await expect(promise).rejects.toThrow(...). A manual try/catch without an expect in the success branch will miss the case where there was no error.
await expect(api.transfer({ amount: -100 })).rejects.toThrow(/amount/i);

In Playwright API tests request.post() doesn't throw on 4xx/5xx by default, but returns the response. The status must be checked explicitly: expect(res.status()).toBe(400) or expect(res).toBeOK(). There is the failOnStatusCode option, which makes it throw on non-2xx.

I use finally for guaranteed cleanup, but in Playwright it is better to rely on fixtures: the code after use() runs even if the test failed.

In an interview: I don't swallow errors in helpers and wrap them with context through cause. For negative scenarios I use expect(...).rejects, and in Playwright API tests I check the status explicitly, because request doesn't throw on 4xx by default.

ts-adv:0.title: keyof, typeof and indexed access
ts-adv:0.html:
keyof T gives a union of a type's keys. typeof value in a type position takes the type from a value. T[K] is the type of the field with key K. Together they let you derive types from one source of truth.

const ROUTES = {
  login: '/login',
  accounts: '/accounts',
  transfers: '/transfers/new',
} as const;

type RouteName = keyof typeof ROUTES;            // 'login' | 'accounts' | 'transfers'
type RoutePath = (typeof ROUTES)[RouteName];      // '/login' | '/accounts' | '/transfers/new'

async function goTo(page: Page, name: RouteName) {
  await page.goto(ROUTES[name]);
}

Now goTo(page, 'acounts') won't compile, and a new route is available automatically.

Indexed access also works with arrays: (typeof CURRENCIES)[number] gives a union of the tuple's elements. And with nested types: Account['owner']['address'].

The difference between the two typeof: in a JS expression typeof x === 'string' is a runtime operator that returns a string. In a type position type T = typeof x is a TS operator that takes the static type of a variable. The syntax is the same, the meaning is different.

A useful pattern for test data:

const testUsers = {
  admin: { email: 'admin@test.io', role: 'admin' },
  operator: { email: 'op@test.io', role: 'operator' },
} as const;

type TestUserKey = keyof typeof testUsers; // 'admin' | 'operator'
type Role = (typeof testUsers)[TestUserKey]['role'];

A fixture or helper takes TestUserKey, and typos in roles disappear.

In an interview: keyof typeof CONFIG gives a union of a constant object's keys, and T[K] the value's type. I type routes, roles and test users this way, so there is one object as the source of truth and no typos in strings.

ts-adv:1.title: Mapped types and conditional types
ts-adv:1.html:
A mapped type iterates over keys and builds a new type. That is how Partial, Readonly, Record are implemented.

type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };

// modifiers: -? removes optional, -readonly removes readonly
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };

Since TS 4.1 keys can be renamed with as:

type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => Promise<T[K]>;
};

interface Balance { available: number; blocked: number }
type BalanceApi = Getters<Balance>;
// { getAvailable: () => Promise<number>; getBlocked: () => Promise<number> }

A conditional type is an "if" at the type level: T extends U ? X : Y. Together with infer it lets you extract part of a type.

type ItemOf<T> = T extends readonly (infer I)[] ? I : never;
type Tx = ItemOf<Transaction[]>; // Transaction

type UnwrapResult<T> = T extends { status: 'success'; data: infer D } ? D : never;

An important property is distributivity. If T is a "naked" type parameter and a union is passed in, the condition is applied to each member separately. That is how Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T works. To turn off distributivity, the parameter is wrapped in a tuple: [T] extends [U].

Honestly about practice: in tests I write such types rarely. They are needed in the framework layer: a typed API client, factory generators. If a type is hard for a colleague to read, it is better to simplify it.

In an interview: A mapped type iterates over the keys of keyof T and builds a new type, and that is how Partial and Readonly are built. A conditional type is a type-level condition, and with infer you can extract, for example, an array's element type. In tests I use this moderately, mostly in the library layer.

ts-adv:2.title: Template literal types
ts-adv:2.html:
Template literal types build string types from a template, like template strings, only at the type level. When a union is substituted, a Cartesian product results.

type Method = 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';
type Version = 'v1' | 'v2';
type ApiPath = `/api/${Version}/${string}`;

type RouteKey = `${Method} ${ApiPath}`;
const key: RouteKey = 'POST /api/v1/transfers'; // ok
// const bad: RouteKey = 'POST /transfers';     // error

${string} means any string in that position, and ${number} a string that looks like a number.

Built-in utilities for string types: Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, Uncapitalize.

Practical examples in automation:

  • Test identifiers for a helper over getByTestId, to follow a naming convention (the TestId type below).
  • Event or metric keys (the TransferEvent type below).
  • Data format (the IsoDate type below): a rough restriction that catches obvious mistakes but doesn't fully validate a date. The string '1-2-3' would also pass.
type TestId = `${'btn' | 'input' | 'row'}-${string}`;
type TransferEvent = `transfer.${'created' | 'completed' | 'failed'}`;
type IsoDate = `${number}-${number}-${number}`;
type Env = 'dev' | 'stage';
type BaseUrl = `https://${Env}.bank.example`;

function urlFor(env: Env): BaseUrl {
  return `https://${env}.bank.example`;
}

A limitation: template literal types check only literals known at compile time. A string from .env or from an API response has the type string, and it still has to be validated at runtime.

In an interview: Template literal types set a string template at the type level, for example a method plus a path that starts with /api/. I use them for conventions: route keys, test ids, environment URLs. But I understand this is compile-time only, and I validate external data separately.

ts-mod:0.title: ES Modules and CommonJS
ts-mod:0.html:
Two module systems coexist in Node:

  • CommonJS: require() and module.exports. Historically the Node standard.
  • ES Modules: import and export. The language standard.

How Node decides which system: .mjs files are always ESM, .cjs always CommonJS, and .js depends on the "type" field in the nearest package.json ("module" or "commonjs", CommonJS by default).

In TS code we almost always write import/export syntax, and the compiler or runner turns it into the needed format. So confusion arises not in test code but in configuration: errors like "require is not defined in ES module scope" or "Cannot use import statement outside a module".

Useful things:

import type { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test'; // type only, erased
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export { LoginPage } from './login-page';      // re-export, a barrel file
export type { Account } from './models';

import type guarantees that the import will be completely removed at compile time. This matters with the verbatimModuleSyntax option, which requires type imports to be marked explicitly, and helps avoid runtime circular dependencies.

I prefer named exports over default: the name is fixed, and auto-import and refactoring work better.

Playwright transpiles TS test files itself, so a separate build step isn't needed. But it doesn't check types: a test with a type error will run. So on CI I add a separate step npx tsc --noEmit.

In an interview: Node has CommonJS with require and ES Modules with import, and for .js the choice is determined by the type field in package.json. Playwright transpiles TS itself, but doesn't check types, so on CI I have a separate tsc --noEmit step.

ts-mod:1.title: tsconfig for a test project
ts-mod:1.html:
tsconfig.json sets how the compiler checks and builds code. For a Playwright test project, a minimal sensible config:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": { "@pages/*": ["src/pages/*"], "@api/*": ["src/api/*"] }
  },
  "include": ["tests", "src", "playwright.config.ts"]
}

What the key options mean:

  • strict turns on a group of checks: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, useUnknownInCatchVariables and others. Without it TS gives little benefit.
  • target is which JS version to compile the syntax down to. For Node 20+ ES2022 fits.
  • module and moduleResolution are the module format and the rules for resolving imports. NodeNext matches Node's behaviour, Bundler is for code that goes through a bundler.
  • noEmit is type checking only, without generating JS. Playwright does the running.
  • skipLibCheck doesn't check the dependencies' .d.ts files, speeding up compilation.
  • paths are import aliases instead of ../../../pages. Playwright supports paths from tsconfig.
  • resolveJsonModule lets you import JSON with test data, typed.

Important: with module: NodeNext in an ESM project, relative imports require the .js extension in the path, even if the file is .ts. This often surprises newcomers.

In an interview: In a test project I always turn on strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess, set noEmit, because Playwright runs the tests, and configure paths for short imports. I run type checking separately on CI with tsc --noEmit.

ts-mod:2.title: Environment types, .d.ts and environment variables
ts-mod:2.html:
.d.ts files contain only type declarations, without code. They are used for JS libraries and for extending existing types.

A typical task is typing process.env. By default every variable has the type string | undefined, and that is right: the variable may be missing.

// src/env.ts
function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Missing env variable ${name}`);
  return value;
}

export const env = {
  baseUrl: required('BASE_URL'),
  apiToken: required('API_TOKEN'),
  timeoutMs: Number(process.env.TIMEOUT_MS ?? '30000'),
} as const;

I prefer such a module to a global extension of the ProcessEnv type through declaration merging. A type extension only tells the compiler "the variable exists", but doesn't check that at runtime. A module with a check fails immediately with a clear error, instead of in the middle of a test with undefined in a URL. Even better is to validate the variables with a schema.

The @types/... packages contain types for JS libraries, for example @types/node. The types option in tsconfig limits which global types are picked up automatically. If one repository has both Playwright and Jest, the global expect may conflict, and then separate tsconfigs are set up for different parts.

Another tool is project references and several tsconfigs: a base tsconfig.base.json and separate configs for e2e, API tests and utilities through extends.

In an interview: .d.ts are files with types only. I don't just type environment variables, I read them through a module with a check, so a test fails immediately with a clear error if a variable is missing. For different parts of the repository I use separate tsconfigs through extends.

ts-js:0.title: Floating-point numbers and money
ts-js:0.html:
number in JS is a 64-bit floating-point number (IEEE 754). Decimal fractions like 0.1 have no exact binary representation.

0.1 + 0.2;            // 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3;    // false
1.005 * 100;          // 100.49999999999999
(1.005).toFixed(2);   // '1.00', not '1.01'

toFixed rounds the binary value, not the decimal one you see in the code, so the result is sometimes unexpected. Besides, toFixed returns a string.

How to work with money correctly:

  1. Store amounts in minor units (cents) as integers: 10050 instead of 100.50. Integers up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1) are represented exactly.
  2. Know the number of minor units for the currency: most have 2, but JPY has 0, and some currencies have 3 (for example KWD).
  3. For fractional calculations (percentages, rates, fees) use a decimal library (decimal.js, big.js) with an explicit rounding mode. Banks often use banker's rounding (half-even), and the test must know exactly which rule is in the specification.
  4. For very large integers there is BigInt, but it doesn't mix with number in arithmetic.
const toMinor = (amount: string): number => Math.round(Number(amount) * 100);
// better through a library:
// new Decimal('100.505').toDecimalPlaces(2, Decimal.ROUND_HALF_EVEN)

In tests: I compare amounts in minor units with toBe, not fractional ones with toBe. If I need to compare fractional values, I use toBeCloseTo with a precision. For display I use Intl.NumberFormat, not manual concatenation.

In an interview: 0.1 + 0.2 in JS doesn't equal 0.3 because of the binary representation, and toFixed also rounds inaccurately. So I compare money in minor units as integers, and compute fees and rates with a decimal library with an explicit rounding rule from the specification.

ts-js:1.title: Converting strings to numbers
ts-js:1.html:
There are several ways to turn a string into a number, and they behave differently:

Number('42');       // 42
Number('');         // 0  - a trap!
Number(' ');        // 0
Number('12px');     // NaN
Number('1e3');      // 1000
Number(null);       // 0
Number(undefined);  // NaN

parseInt('12px', 10);  // 12 - takes the prefix
parseInt('1e3', 10);   // 1
parseFloat('1,5');     // 1 - a comma is not a separator
parseFloat('1 000.50');// 1

Key traps:

  • Number('') returns 0. An empty amount field in the UI will turn into zero, and a test may "successfully" check a zero amount.
  • parseInt and parseFloat silently discard everything after the first invalid character. The amount '1 250,50 UAH' from the UI becomes 1.
  • I always call parseInt with radix 10.
  • ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt) gives [1, NaN, NaN], because map passes the index as the second argument (the radix).
  • NaN !== NaN. The check is Number.isNaN(x), not x === NaN.

For amounts from the UI I write an explicit parser for the specific format: I remove spaces (including the non-breaking space that Intl.NumberFormat uses as a thousands separator), the currency, replace the comma with a dot, check with a regex and only then convert. Even better is to compare with the expected string formatted by the same Intl.NumberFormat with the right locale.

function parseUiAmount(text: string): number {
  const clean = text.replace(/[\s  ]/g, '').replace('UAH', '').replace(',', '.');
  if (!/^-?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$/.test(clean)) throw new Error(`Bad amount: ${text}`);
  return Math.round(Number(clean) * 100); // minor units
}

My principle for amounts from the UI: the parser must fail on an unexpected format, not return part of a number.

In an interview: Number('') gives zero, and parseInt silently truncates a string at the first invalid character, so for amounts from the UI I write a strict parser that fails on an unexpected format. I check NaN with Number.isNaN, and call parseInt only with radix 10.

ts-js:2.title: Comparison: == and ===, ||, ?? and ?.
ts-js:2.html:
== performs type coercion before comparing, === doesn't. The coercion rules are unintuitive:

'' == 0;               // true
'0' == false;          // true
null == undefined;     // true
null == 0;             // false
NaN == NaN;            // false
[1] == 1;              // true

I always use ===. The only common exception is x == null, which checks both null and undefined, but even there I prefer explicitness. The ESLint rule eqeqeq enforces this. TS partly catches meaningless comparisons of different types, but not all.

The || operator returns the right operand if the left is falsy. Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. So || for default values breaks valid zeros and empty strings:

const fee = response.fee || 500;     // fee = 0 becomes 500 - a bug
const fee2 = response.fee ?? 500;    // 0 stays 0
const timeout = Number(env.TIMEOUT) || 30_000; // here || deliberately catches NaN too

?? (nullish coalescing) substitutes a value only for null and undefined. For money, limits and counters this is a critical difference: a zero fee is a valid business case.

?. (optional chaining) stops evaluation and returns undefined if the left part is null or undefined: res.data?.items?.[0]?.amount. A trap in tests: excessive ?. masks a problem. If items must always be there, then expect(body.data?.items?.length).toBeFalsy() passes both for an empty array and for a missing field. So I first check the structure explicitly, and then the value.

In an interview: I always use ===, because == does a non-obvious type coercion. For default values I take ??, not ||, because || would replace a valid zero, such as a zero fee, with the default.

ts-js:3.title: Strings, dates, mutations and sorting
ts-js:3.html:
Strings. The operators < and > compare strings by UTF-16 codes: 'B' < 'a' is true, '10' < '9' is true, and Ukrainian letters like і, ї, є don't stand in their places of the alphabet. To check sorting in the UI I use a.localeCompare(b, 'uk') or Intl.Collator. For natural sorting of numbers in strings there is the option { numeric: true }.

Sorting. Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator sorts as strings and mutates the array in place:

[10, 1, 2].sort();               // [1, 10, 2]
[10, 1, 2].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 10]
const sorted = amounts.toSorted((a, b) => a - b); // ES2023, no mutation

Dates. Months in Date are numbered from zero: new Date(2026, 0, 15) is 15 January. A date-only string new Date('2026-01-15') is parsed as UTC, and a date with a time and no zone new Date('2026-01-15T10:00') as local time. getDate() returns the local day, and a test that works in Kyiv fails on CI in UTC near midnight. Overflow: 31 January plus setMonth(1) gives March. My rules: exchange dates in ISO 8601 with Z or an offset, fix TZ on CI and in playwright.config.ts through timezoneId, take a library (date-fns, Luxon) for calendar logic, and control time in tests through page.clock.

Mutations and copies. Objects and arrays are passed by reference. Spread { ...obj } and [...arr] make a shallow copy: nested objects are shared.

const base = { amount: 100, meta: { tags: ['a'] } };
const copy = { ...base };
copy.meta.tags.push('b'); // base changed too
const deep = structuredClone(base); // a deep copy, Node 17+

structuredClone doesn't copy functions (it throws) and loses a class's prototype. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) loses undefined, turns Date into a string and breaks on BigInt.

In an interview: sort() without a comparator sorts as strings and mutates the array, so I pass a comparator or use toSorted. Months in Date are zero-based, and I fix time zones on CI. Spread makes only a shallow copy, and for a deep one I take structuredClone.

mq-0:0.title: How do QA, QC and testing differ?
mq-0:0.html:
• Testing is checking the product: running it, finding defects, comparing with the expected result.
  • QC (Quality Control) is quality control of the finished product. Testing is its main part. The focus is on the product: find defects.
  • QA (Quality Assurance) is assuring the quality of the process so that defects don't appear: standards, requirement reviews, retrospectives, process improvements. The focus is on the process: prevent defects.

That is, testing ⊂ QC ⊂ QA.

In an interview: Testing is the search for defects in a product. QC is quality control of the product, and testing is its main part. QA is wider: it is work on the process so that defects don't appear at all, with requirement reviews, standards, process improvements. Testing is part of QC, and QC is part of QA.

mq-0:1.title: Name the 7 testing principles.
mq-0:1.html:
1. Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence.
  2. Exhaustive testing is impossible, so prioritisation and test design techniques are needed.
  3. Early testing saves time and money: a bug in requirements is cheaper than a bug in production.
  4. Defect clustering: most bugs are concentrated in a few modules.
  5. The pesticide paradox: the same tests stop finding new bugs over time, and they must be updated.
  6. Testing depends on context: banking and a landing page are tested differently.
  7. The absence-of-errors fallacy: a product with no bugs that users don't need is still a failure.
In an interview: Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence. Exhaustive testing is impossible, so we prioritise. Testing should happen as early as possible. Defects cluster in a few modules. The same tests stop finding bugs over time: the pesticide paradox. Testing depends on context. And a product with no bugs that users don't need is still a failure.

mq-0:2.title: How does verification differ from validation?
mq-0:2.html:
Verification is "are we building the product right?": conformance to the specification and requirements. Often static: review of requirements, design, code.

Validation is "are we building the right product?": does it solve the user's real problem. Usually dynamic: testing the working system, UAT.

In an interview: Verification answers whether we are building the product right, that is, whether it matches the specification. Validation answers whether we are building the right product, that is, whether it solves the user's problem. A product can fully match the requirements and still be unneeded.

mq-0:3.title: What are SDLC and STLC?
mq-0:3.html:
SDLC is the software development life cycle: requirements → design → development → testing → release → support. Models: Waterfall, the V-model, iterative, Agile.

STLC is the testing life cycle within the SDLC:

  1. Requirements analysis: what to test, what the risks are, questions for the PM.
  2. Planning: strategy, scope, resources, entry and exit criteria.
  3. Test design: test cases, checklists, test data.
  4. Environment setup.
  5. Test execution and defect reports.
  6. Closure: a report, metrics, lessons.
In an interview: SDLC is the life cycle of developing a product from requirements to support. STLC is the testing life cycle inside it: requirements analysis, planning, test design, environment setup, test execution and closure with a report. In a role where QA is responsible for the whole cycle, these are exactly the stages.

mq-0:4.title: What test levels are there?
mq-0:4.html:
• Unit: individual functions or classes, usually written by developers.
  • Integration: the interaction of modules or services: API, database, queues.
  • System: the whole system as one, against the requirements. This is QA's main work.
  • Acceptance: is the product ready for the business: UAT, alpha and beta.

A related idea is the testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, the fewest expensive e2e tests.

In an interview: The levels are unit, integration, system and acceptance testing. Unit is written by developers, integration checks the interaction of components, system checks the whole system against requirements, and acceptance checks readiness for the business. The testing pyramid says there should be more fast low-level tests than expensive end-to-end ones.

mq-0:5.title: How does static testing differ from dynamic testing?
mq-0:5.html:
Static is without running code: review of requirements, mockups, test cases, code, static analysis. It finds defects earliest and cheapest.

Dynamic is with running the program: everything we usually call testing.

The job description directly asks to "validate requirements and provide early feedback": this is static testing of requirements, and it is worth mentioning with an example.

In an interview: Static testing is without running the program: review of requirements, design, code. Dynamic is when we run the system and check its behaviour. Static is cheaper, because it finds problems before they are coded: for example, I find a contradiction in the requirements already at grooming.

mq-1:0.title: Functional and non-functional testing: what is the difference?
mq-1:0.html:
Functional is what the system does: logic, business rules, conformance to requirements.

Non-functional is how it does it: performance (load, stress), security, usability, accessibility, compatibility, reliability, localisation.

In an interview: Functional testing checks what the system does: does a transfer work, is the fee calculated correctly. Non-functional checks how it does it: speed, security, usability, browser compatibility.

mq-1:1.title: How do smoke, sanity and regression testing differ?
mq-1:1.html:
KindWhat it checksWhen
SmokeThe critical functions work, the build can be tested at allOn every new build
SanityA specific change or fix works, narrow and deepAfter a small fix
RegressionChanges didn't break what worked beforeBefore a release, after changes
In an interview: Smoke is a broad shallow check that the build is alive and the main functions work. Sanity is a narrow check of a specific change or fix. Regression is a check that new changes didn't break existing functionality, and it is the widest of the three.

mq-1:2.title: How does a retest differ from regression testing?
mq-1:2.html:
A retest is checking that a specific bug is fixed: we go through the same steps as in the bug report.

Regression is checking that a fix or a new feature didn't break anything else. A retest checks one place, regression checks everything around it.

In an interview: A retest is checking that a specific bug is fixed, by the steps from the report. Regression is checking that this fix or new feature broke nothing nearby. After a fix I do both: a retest of the bug itself and regression of the related functionality.

mq-1:3.title: What are black box, white box and grey box?
mq-1:3.html:
• Black box: we test against requirements without knowing the code. The main approach of manual QA.
  • White box: we test knowing the internal structure: branch and condition coverage. Usually developers.
  • Grey box: we partly know the internal structure: the database schema, the API, logs. For example, after an action in the UI we check the record in the DB or the request in DevTools.
In an interview: Black box is testing against requirements without knowing the code. White box is with full knowledge of the internal logic. Grey box is in between: I don't read the code, but I check the database, API requests and logs. That is how I work most often: an action in the UI, then checking the request in DevTools and the record in the database.

mq-1:4.title: What is exploratory testing and how do you do it in a structured way?
mq-1:4.html:
Exploratory testing is studying the product and designing and executing tests at the same time, without ready cases. It is strong where requirements are incomplete or you need to find the most important bugs quickly.

So that it isn't chaotic "clicking around", sessions with a charter are used: a goal ("explore refunds with partially paid orders"), a fixed time (60–90 min), notes, and a result of bugs, questions and ideas for new cases.

In an interview: Exploratory is when I study the product and design and execute tests at the same time. To keep it controlled, I work in sessions: I set a charter with a specific goal, limit the time and keep notes, and at the end I have bugs, questions for the team and ideas for new test cases.

mq-1:5.title: What are alpha, beta and UAT?
mq-1:5.html:
• Alpha: internal testing by the team or employees before release outside.
  • Beta: a limited group of real users in a real environment.
  • UAT: acceptance testing by the customer or the business: does the product meet business needs. QA often prepares the scenarios and supports the process.
In an interview: Alpha is internal testing before release outside. Beta is real users in a limited group. UAT is acceptance of the product by the business or the customer, and my role there is to prepare scenarios, the environment and data and to help sort out what they find.

mq-1:6.title: How does integration testing differ from end-to-end?
mq-1:6.html:
Integration is checking the interaction of two or three components: front end and API, a service and a database, our backend and a payment provider. It can use mocks for the other parts.

End-to-end is the full user path through the whole system: registration → top-up → transfer → statement, with real integrations.

In an interview: Integration checks the joint of several components, for example how our backend works with a payment provider. End-to-end is the whole user path through the system from start to finish. There are more integration tests and they point more precisely at the place of a problem, while e2e checks the most important scenarios as a whole.

mq-1:7.title: Exploratory testing
mq-1:7.html:
Exploratory testing is studying the product and designing and executing tests at the same time, where the next step is determined by the result of the previous one. It is not chaotic "clicking around": it has a goal, boundaries and recording of results. It is especially useful for new features, incomplete requirements and finding non-obvious bugs.

Session-based testing structures this process: a session has limited time, usually 60–120 minutes, and a specific charter. A charter is the mission of a session, for example "Explore order checkout with different payment methods to find validation problems". During the session notes are kept: what was checked, what bugs and questions were found.

After a session a debrief is held with the team lead or the team. Heuristics are used for ideas: boundary values, interrupting flows, changing the network, parallel actions, "tours" of the product.

mq-1:8.title: Functional, integration, system testing
mq-1:8.html:
Functional testing checks that the system does what the requirements describe, regardless of the internal implementation. For example, a product filter by price returns only products in the given range. It is a type of testing, not a level, and it is applied at all levels.

Integration testing checks the interaction between modules or services. For example, after an order is placed the orders service correctly passes data to the payment service and the notification service. Here we look for problems at the joints: data formats, API contracts, timeouts.

System testing checks the whole system as a whole in an environment as close to production as possible. For example, the full user path from registration to receiving an order confirmation email. This includes both functional and non-functional checks.

mq-1:9.title: Regression vs retest and the scope of regression
mq-1:9.html:
A retest is a repeated check of a specific fixed bug by the same steps. Regression is checking that changes haven't broken already working functionality. A retest is always tied to a bug, regression to changes in the code.

I determine the regression scope under limited time through risk analysis. First the areas touched by the changes and the adjacent modules they are integrated with. Then the critical business flows: login, payment, order checkout. Then the areas where bugs have historically been frequent.

A conversation with the developer about what exactly changed and an analysis of the git diff help. Everything stable and repeatable should preferably be covered by automated tests, and manual time spent on new and risky areas.

mq-1:10.title: UAT
mq-1:10.html:
User Acceptance Testing is the final level of testing, where the customer or end users check that the system meets their business needs. The question here is not "are there no bugs" but "does the product solve our problem". It is held after system testing in an environment close to production.

It is performed by business users, the PO or customer representatives, not by QA. QA's role is to prepare the environment and test data, help compose UAT scenarios and explain how to use the system. QA also records and traces the problems found and separates defects from change requests.

Varieties: alpha and beta testing, operational acceptance, contract acceptance. The result of UAT is a decision to accept the product, or a sign-off.

mq-1:11.title: Kinds of load testing and JMeter
mq-1:11.html:
Load testing checks the system's behaviour under the expected load, for example 1000 simultaneous users at peak hours. The goal is to make sure that response time and the number of errors are within the SLA. Stress testing loads the system beyond normal to find the breaking point and check how it recovers.

Spike testing is a sudden short-term jump in load, as during a sale or a mailing. There are also soak or endurance testing, a long load over hours to look for memory leaks, and scalability testing. Key metrics: response time (average and the percentiles p95, p99), throughput, error rate, CPU and memory usage.

In JMeter the basis is a Test Plan, in which a Thread Group sets the number of virtual users, the ramp-up and the number of iterations. A Sampler is the request itself, for example an HTTP Request. Assertions check the response: the status code, text or time. Listeners collect and show results, for example the Summary Report. Config Elements (CSV Data Set Config, HTTP Header Manager), Timers for pauses and running in non-GUI mode for real tests are also important.

mq-2:0.title: What are equivalence classes?
mq-2:0.html:
We split input data into groups where the system behaves the same, and take one value from each group, valid and invalid.

Example: a transfer amount of 1–10,000 UAH. Classes: less than 1 (invalid), 1–10,000 (valid), more than 10,000 (invalid), and also non-numeric values and an empty field.

In an interview: We split input data into groups where the system behaves the same, and test one representative from each, valid and invalid. For example, for an amount from one to ten thousand: a value in the range, below, above, text and an empty field. That reduces the number of tests without losing coverage.

mq-2:1.title: What is boundary value analysis?
mq-2:1.html:
Bugs most often live at the boundaries of ranges, so we test values at the boundary and next to it.

For 1–10,000: 0, 1, 2 and 9,999, 10,000, 10,001. For money, fractional boundaries also matter: 0.99, 1.00, 1.01 and 10,000.00 / 10,000.01.

In an interview: Errors are most often at the boundaries, so I test the boundary itself and the value next to it on both sides. For a range from one to ten thousand that is zero, one, two, and nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, ten thousand, ten thousand and one. For money I add fractional boundaries in cents.

mq-2:2.title: What is a decision table and when do you use it?
mq-2:2.html:
When the result depends on a combination of several conditions. Each column is a combination of conditions and the expected action.

Condition / rule1234
Sufficient fundsYesYesNoNo
Limit not exceededYesNoYesNo
ResultTransferRefusal: limitRefusal: fundsRefusal: funds

The table immediately shows missed combinations and questions for the requirements: which error to show when both conditions are not met?

In an interview: I use a decision table when the result depends on a combination of conditions. I write out all the combinations and the expected result for each. Besides test cases, this often gives questions for the requirements, for example which error to show when two conditions fail at once.

mq-2:3.title: What is state transition testing?
mq-2:3.html:
For objects that pass through states: an order, a payment, an account. We build a diagram of states and transitions and test the valid transitions, as well as the invalid ones: that the system doesn't allow them.

Payment:
  Created → Pending → Authorized → Captured → Settled
                    ↘ Declined
  Captured → Refunded

Invalid transitions for a test:
  Declined → Captured    (a declined payment can't be debited)
  Refunded → Refunded    (a double refund)
  Created  → Settled     (skipping steps)
In an interview: For entities with states, such as payments, orders and accounts, I draw a state diagram and check all the valid transitions. And most importantly the invalid ones: that a rejected payment can't be debited, and a refunded one can't be refunded a second time.

mq-2:4.title: What is pairwise testing?
mq-2:4.html:
When there are many parameters and checking all combinations is impossible. Most defects are caused by the interaction of two parameters, so it is enough to cover all pairs of values, not all combinations.

Example: 3 browsers × 3 OSes × 3 languages × 2 account types = 54 combinations; pairwise reduces it to ~9–12. They are generated with tools like PICT or online generators.

In an interview: Pairwise helps when there are too many parameters to try all combinations. Most bugs come from the interaction of two parameters, so I cover all pairs of values. For example, fifty-four combinations of browsers, OSes and languages shrink to about ten, and I generate them with a tool.

mq-2:5.title: What are error guessing and experience-based checklists?
mq-2:5.html:
Experience-based testing: where does it usually break? Empty fields, spaces at the start and end, very long strings, special characters and emoji, a double click, the Back button, refreshing the page in the middle of a process, losing the network, several tabs open at once.

This complements formal techniques, not replaces them.

In an interview: Error guessing is when from experience I know the typical places of breakage: empty fields, special characters, a double click, refreshing the page in the middle of a process, a dropped network. I use it together with formal techniques, not instead of them.

mq-2:6.title: Equivalence classes and boundary values: age 18–65
mq-2:6.html:
Equivalence classes split input data into groups where the system behaves the same, so one value from each class is enough. For the field "age 18–65" we have a valid class 18–65 and two invalid ones: less than 18 and more than 65. Representatives: 30, 10 and 80.

Boundary values check the boundaries, because that is where developers most often make mistakes. For the two-point approach I take 17, 18, 65, 66; for the three-point one 17, 18, 19, 64, 65, 66. Expected: 18 and 65 are accepted, 17 and 66 are not.

Additionally I check invalid data types: an empty field, 0, a negative number, a fractional 18.5, letters, spaces, special characters and a very long number. It is also worth clarifying with the analyst whether the boundaries are inclusive, because this is a frequent ambiguity in requirements.

mq-2:7.title: Decision table and state transition
mq-2:7.html:
A decision table is used when the result depends on a combination of several conditions. For example a discount: whether the user is VIP and whether the order amount is more than 1000 hryvnias. We build a table with all combinations of conditions and the expected actions, so missed or contradictory rules are visible.

For n binary conditions there will be 2 to the power n combinations, so the table is often reduced by merging rules where some condition doesn't affect the result. This technique is useful for business rules, tariffs, access rights.

State transition is applied when a system has states and transitions between them. An example is an order: New → Paid → Shipped → Delivered, with a possible transition to Cancelled. We test all the valid transitions and check that the invalid ones are forbidden, for example it is impossible to cancel an already delivered order.

mq-3:0.title: What is a test plan and what is in it?
mq-3:0.html:
A document that describes what, how, when and by whom we test. Typical sections:

  • Scope: what we test and what we do not test.
  • Approach: test levels and kinds, manual or automated.
  • Environments, test data, tools.
  • Entry and exit criteria (when we start, when it is ready for release).
  • Risks and the plan of action for them.
  • Roles, schedule, artefacts.

In Agile a test plan is often shorter and alive: a page in Confluence for a release or a feature.

In an interview: A test plan describes what we test and what we don't, with what approach, on which environments and with which data, the entry and exit criteria, risks and roles. In Agile I keep it short and alive, for example a page in Confluence per release.

mq-3:1.title: How does a test strategy differ from a test plan?
mq-3:1.html:
A strategy is the general approach to testing at the product or company level, and it changes rarely: which test levels, what we automate, which environments, standards, metrics.

A plan is the concrete application of the strategy to a project, a release or a feature: scope, schedule, people, risks.

In an interview: A strategy is the general approach to testing at the product level, and it rarely changes. A plan is the concrete application of the strategy to a release or a feature, with dates, people and scope.

mq-3:2.title: What does a good test case consist of?
mq-3:2.html:
• An ID and a clear title: what we check.
  • Preconditions: system state, user, data.
  • Steps: short, one action each.
  • The expected result: specific and verifiable.
  • Priority, link to a requirement, type (positive or negative).

The quality criterion: another tester will go through the case without questions and will assess the result the same way. One case, one check.

ID:        TC-PAY-014
Title:     A transfer that exactly exhausts the daily limit
