Preconditions: The user is logged in, the daily limit is 10,000 UAH,
            9,000 UAH has already been transferred today, the balance is 5,000 UAH
Steps:
  1. Open "Transfer to card"
  2. Enter a valid recipient card number
  3. Enter the amount 1,000.00
  4. Confirm the transfer
Expected:  The transfer succeeds; the remaining limit is 0.00;
           the balance is 4,000.00 minus the fee per the tariff
Priority:  High   Requirement: REQ-LIM-03
In an interview: A good test case has a clear title, preconditions, short steps and a specific expected result, plus a priority and a link to a requirement. My criterion: another tester must be able to go through it without questions and assess the result the same way.

mq-3:3.title: When test cases and when checklists?
mq-3:3.html:
A checklist is a list of checks without detailed steps. Quick to write and maintain, it fits an experienced team, smoke, exploratory, and stable simple parts.

A test case is a detailed scenario. It is needed for complex logic, new people on the team, regulatory requirements and scenarios that will later be automated.

In an interview: Checklists are faster, and I use them for smoke, exploratory sessions and stable simple parts. I write detailed test cases for complex business logic, for scenarios that will be automated, and where audit traceability is needed, as in fintech.

mq-3:4.title: What is a traceability matrix?
mq-3:4.html:
A table of links "requirement → test cases → results → defects". It shows whether every requirement is covered by tests, what broke and which requirements a change will affect.

In Jira this is often done with links between stories, test cases (Zephyr, Xray) and bugs.

In an interview: A traceability matrix links requirements to test cases, results and defects. It shows that every requirement is covered and helps assess the impact of changes. In Jira I do this with links between stories, cases in Zephyr and bugs.

mq-3:5.title: What should be in a test report?
mq-3:5.html:
• What was tested: scope, build, environment, period.
  • Results: passed, failed, blocked, not executed.
  • Open defects by severity, especially blockers and critical ones.
  • Risks and what wasn't tested and why.
  • A recommendation: ready for release or not, with conditions.

A report is written for the people who make decisions, so the main thing is the conclusion and the risks, not tables of numbers.

In an interview: In a report I show what was tested and on which build, the execution results, open defects by severity, risks and what wasn't tested. And always a clear recommendation on the release, because the report is read by the people who make decisions.

mq-3:6.title: How do you prepare test data?
mq-3:6.html:
• Cover the classes: valid, invalid, boundary, empty, special characters.
  • Have different types of users: new, with history, blocked, with different roles and tariffs.
  • Create data through the API or SQL, not manually through the UI: faster and reproducible.
  • Don't use real personal data, only anonymised or generated.
  • Document where it lives and how to restore it.
In an interview: I prepare data for equivalence classes and boundaries, with different types of users. I create it through the API or SQL, so it is fast and reproducible, and I never use real personal data, only generated or anonymised.

mq-3:7.title: Test case vs checklist
mq-3:7.html:
A test case is a detailed scenario: preconditions, steps, test data and the expected result for each step. A checklist is a short list of what to check, without a step-by-step description. A test case is reproducible by anyone, even a newcomer who doesn't know the product.

A checklist is quicker to write and maintain, but the result depends on the executor's experience. I choose test cases for critical functionality, complex business logic, regulatory requirements and as a basis for automation. Checklists are for smoke, stable parts of the product, exploratory sessions and when requirements change often.

In practice they are often combined: a checklist for broad coverage, test cases for key flows. The main criterion is the balance between the cost of documentation and the risk of missing a defect.

mq-3:8.title: A quality test case
mq-3:8.html:
The basic structure: ID, title, preconditions, steps, test data, expected result, priority and a link to a requirement. The title must be short and describe exactly what we check, for example "Login with a wrong password shows an error". Each test case checks one thing, so that when it fails it is immediately clear what broke.

Steps are atomic and concrete: not "enter data" but "enter the value test@mail.com in the Email field". The expected result is measurable and unambiguous, without words like "works correctly". A test case must be independent of others and not depend on the order of execution.

A good test case is also easy to maintain: without unnecessary UI details that change often. And it must be traceable to a requirement, so that coverage is visible.

mq-4:0.title: What should a good bug report contain?
mq-4:0.html:
• Title: what, where, under what condition. Not "transfer doesn't work" but "Transfer fails with 500 if the amount has 3 decimal places".
  • Environment: build, browser, OS, device, user.
  • Preconditions and steps to reproduce, minimal.
  • Actual and expected result.
  • Evidence: a screenshot, video, log, the request and response from DevTools.
  • Severity, priority, reproduction rate.
Title:        [Payments] Transfer returns 500 if the amount has 3 decimal places
Environment:  staging, build 2.14.3, Chrome 129, Windows 11
Preconditions: user qa_user_03, balance 5,000.00 UAH
Steps:
  1. Open "Transfer to card"
  2. Enter the amount 100.555
  3. Click "Continue"
Actual:       the error "Something went wrong"; POST /api/transfers → 500
Expected:     field validation "No more than 2 decimal places", the request is not sent
Reproducible: 5/5
Attachments:  video.mp4, HAR file, request/response
In an interview: A good report has a title that makes clear what is broken and under what condition, the environment, minimal steps, the actual and expected result and evidence: a screenshot, video, the request and response from DevTools. The goal is for the developer to reproduce the bug without a single question to me.

mq-4:1.title: How does severity differ from priority?
mq-4:1.html:
Severity is how strongly a defect affects the system. Determined by QA.

Priority is how urgently it must be fixed. Determined by the business or the PM.

High priorityLow priority
High severityPayments don't go throughA report used once a year crashes
Low severityA mistake in the bank's name on the home pageA pixel shifted in the footer
In an interview: Severity is the technical impact of a defect on the system, and QA determines it. Priority is how urgently to fix it, and that is the business's decision. They don't always coincide: a typo in the bank's name on the home page is low severity, but high priority, because it hits the reputation.

mq-4:2.title: What is the life cycle of a bug?
mq-4:2.html:
Typically: New → Assigned → In Progress → Fixed → Ready for QA → Verified → Closed.

Branches: Reopened (the retest failed), Rejected / Not a bug, Duplicate, Cannot reproduce, Deferred / Won't fix. The specific statuses depend on the Jira workflow on the project.

In an interview: A bug is created, assigned to a developer, fixed, returned to QA, I do a retest and close it. If the retest failed, I reopen it. There are also statuses like duplicate, cannot reproduce, not a bug or deferred. The exact workflow depends on the Jira settings on the project.

mq-4:3.title: What do you do if a bug doesn't reproduce?
mq-4:3.html:
1. Repeat under exactly the same conditions: environment, build, user, data, browser.
  2. Collect more data: logs, console, network, the time of the incident, the transaction ID.
  3. Look for conditions: a race (fast actions), cache, time zone, specific data, load.
  4. Ask the developer to check the server logs by time.
  5. If it still doesn't reproduce, document everything found and the frequency and defer it with monitoring, rather than just closing it.
In an interview: First I reproduce under exactly the same conditions: environment, build, user, data. I collect the logs, the network and the time of the incident, look for special conditions such as a race or a cache, and ask the developer to look at the server logs. If it doesn't reproduce, I document everything found and the frequency instead of just closing it.

mq-4:4.title: The developer says "it's not a bug". What do you do?
mq-4:4.html:
First check yourself: what do the requirement, the mockup, the agreement say? Maybe I misunderstood the expected behaviour.

If the requirement is unambiguous, show it and the evidence. If the requirement is ambiguous or silent, the question is not for me or the developer, but for the PM or the product owner: they decide how it must be. I record the outcome in the ticket.

The main thing is to argue about the product's behaviour, not about who is right.

In an interview: First I check myself against the requirement and the mockup. If the requirement is clear, I show it and the evidence. If it is ambiguous, the question goes to the PM, because the expected behaviour is defined by the product, not by me and the developer. I record the decision in the ticket so we don't come back to it a second time.

mq-4:5.title: The bug report and steps to reproduce
mq-4:5.html:
Structure: title, environment, preconditions, steps to reproduce, actual result, expected result, severity, priority and attachments. The title answers the question "what, where, under what conditions", for example "Cart: the total isn't updated after removing an item". The environment includes the browser, OS, build version, test environment and test account.

Steps must be numbered, minimal and sufficient for anyone to reproduce the bug the first time. Before writing it is worth reproducing the bug again and discarding extra steps. I always specify concrete test data and the reproduction rate if the bug is intermittent.

Attachments are a screenshot, video, console logs, a HAR file or an API response. One bug is one report, and before creating it I check whether there is a duplicate.

mq-4:6.title: Severity vs priority
mq-4:6.html:
Severity is how much a defect affects the system technically; QA determines it. Priority is how urgently it must be fixed from the business's point of view; usually determined by the PO or a manager. These parameters are independent of each other.

High severity, low priority: the application crashes if you enter 1000 characters in a rarely used settings field of an old version of a report. Low severity, high priority: a mistake in the company name or the logo on the home page before a release. High severity and high priority: users can't pay for an order.

Typical severity levels: blocker, critical, major, minor, trivial. Priority usually has the levels high, medium, low or P1–P4.

mq-5:0.title: What ceremonies are there in Scrum and what is QA's role in them?
mq-5:0.html:
• Planning: I estimate the testing scope and risks, so that testing fits in the sprint.
  • Grooming / Refinement: I ask questions about requirements, suggest acceptance criteria, look for edge cases.
  • Daily: status, blockers: no environment, a bug blocks testing.
  • Review / Demo: I show or help show the result.
  • Retrospective: what to improve in the quality process.
In an interview: At planning I estimate the testing scope and risks. At grooming I ask questions about requirements and suggest acceptance criteria, which is the most valuable ceremony for QA. At the daily I speak about blockers, at the demo I show the result, and at the retro I suggest process improvements.

mq-5:1.title: What are Definition of Ready and Definition of Done?
mq-5:1.html:
DoR is when a task is ready for work: there are clear requirements, acceptance criteria, mockups, an estimate, known dependencies.

DoD is when a task is considered finished: the code is in main, code review is passed, tests are written and passed, critical-level bugs are closed, documentation is updated.

QA influences both: not accepting a task into the sprint without acceptance criteria and not closing it without verification.

In an interview: Definition of Ready is the criteria for when a task can be taken into work: clear requirements, acceptance criteria, mockups. Definition of Done is when it is finished: the code is merged, tested, and there are no critical bugs. As QA I watch both: without acceptance criteria we don't take a task into the sprint, and without verification we don't close it.

mq-5:2.title: What is shift-left and how can QA give early feedback?
mq-5:2.html:
Shift-left is moving testing as early as possible in the process, because a defect in requirements is many times cheaper than a defect in production.

  • Review requirements and mockups before development starts.
  • Take part in grooming: edge cases, negative scenarios, contradictions.
  • Test cases before the feature is ready, so the developer sees what will be checked.
  • Testing the API when there is no UI yet.
In an interview: Shift-left is testing as early as possible. I review requirements and mockups before development, at grooming I ask about boundary and negative scenarios, I write test cases in advance so the developer sees what will be checked, and I test the API before the UI appears.

mq-5:3.title: How do you support a release and the post-release check?
mq-5:3.html:
Before the release: regression, checking the release notes, confirmation that all the release's tasks are tested, a go/no-go decision together with the team.

During and after: a smoke of the critical scenarios in production (without real transactions, or on test accounts), checking migrations and configurations, monitoring errors and logs in the first hours, readiness for rollback.

In an interview: Before a release I run regression and give a go or no-go recommendation. After the deploy I do a smoke of the critical scenarios in production on test accounts, check the logs and monitoring, and together with the team I know under which conditions we roll back.

mq-5:4.title: QA's role in Scrum ceremonies and the Definition of Done
mq-5:4.html:
At grooming and sprint planning QA analyses user stories from the point of view of testability, asks questions about edge cases and helps formulate acceptance criteria. QA also estimates the testing scope, so that the team's estimate includes it. This is where QA most effectively prevents defects, before any code is written.

At the daily QA briefly says what was tested and what is in progress, and voices blockers: an unstable environment, unclosed bugs, unclear requirements. At the sprint review QA can demonstrate functionality. At the retrospective QA suggests process improvements: for example, getting builds earlier or adding automated tests to the pipeline.

The Definition of Done is a team-wide checklist for when a task is considered fully finished. It usually includes: the code passed review, unit and automated tests are written and pass, manual testing against the acceptance criteria is done. Also: there are no open critical bugs, the documentation is updated, the changes are deployed to the test environment. Acceptance criteria are specific to a particular story, and the DoD is for all tasks.

mq-5:5.title: Cypress in Jenkins or GitLab CI
mq-5:5.html:
The basis is running npx cypress run in the pipeline with the needed parameters: browser, config, specs, environment variables. The most convenient is to use the official Docker image cypress/included or cypress/browsers, where browsers and dependencies are already installed. In GitLab CI this is a separate job in .gitlab-ci.yml, in Jenkins a stage in the Jenkinsfile.

Secrets (logins, tokens, environment URLs) are passed through CI/CD variables or Jenkins credentials, not stored in the repository. Caching node_modules and the Cypress binary speeds up runs. Parallelisation is done with several jobs, each running its part of the specs: manually, through parallel: in GitLab, or through Cypress Cloud with the parameters --record --parallel.

Artifacts: screenshots and video from the cypress/screenshots and cypress/videos folders are kept only on failure, so as not to take up space. For reports Mochawesome or Allure are used, and the JUnit reporter gives integration with the tests tab in GitLab or Jenkins. Notifications in Slack or Teams with the result and a link to the report are also set up.

mq-5:6.title: Which tests at which stage of the pipeline
mq-5:6.html:
The principle is fast feedback: the closer to the developer, the faster the tests must be. On every commit and merge request the linter, unit tests, API tests and an E2E smoke set run, a few minutes in total. A merge request can't be merged if this stage didn't pass: this is a quality gate.

After the merge into the main branch and the deploy to dev or stage a wider set runs: integration tests and critical E2E scenarios. The nightly run is a full E2E regression on several browsers, which may take long and doesn't block development. Heavy checks can also go there: visual regression, basic performance and security checks.

Before a release: full regression on staging, UAT and manual testing of new features. After the deploy to production: a short smoke to check that the main flows work. Unstable tests must not block the pipeline: they are isolated in quarantine and fixed separately.

mq-6:0.title: What is client-server architecture?
mq-6:0.html:
A client (a browser, a mobile app) sends requests, and the server processes them and returns responses. The server works with a database and other services.

For QA this means: a bug may be on the client (display, validation), on the server (logic, data) or at the junction (a wrong request, an unexpected response). DevTools helps quickly localise where exactly.

Browser ──HTTP request──► Server (API) ──► Database
        ◄─HTTP response─              ◄──
In an interview: The client sends a request, the server processes it, works with the database and returns a response. When I find a bug, the first thing I do is determine where it is: if the request is right and the response is wrong, it is the backend; if the response is right but shown wrongly, it is the front end.

mq-6:1.title: What are the main HTTP methods and status codes?
mq-6:1.html:
Methods: GET to retrieve, POST to create, PUT to replace completely, PATCH to change partially, DELETE to remove.

GroupExamples
2xx success200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xx redirection301, 302, 304 Not Modified
4xx client error400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422, 429 Too Many Requests
5xx server error500, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout

A frequent question: 401 is not authenticated (who are you?), 403 is authenticated but has no rights.

In an interview: GET retrieves, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes partially, DELETE removes. Codes: the two hundreds are success, the three hundreds redirection, the four hundreds a client error, the five hundreds a server one. An important difference: four hundred and one means the system doesn't know who you are, and four hundred and three means it knows but doesn't give you rights.

mq-6:2.title: How do cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage differ?
mq-6:2.html:
CookieslocalStoragesessionStorage
Sent to the serverYes, with every requestNoNo
LifetimeUntil expires or the end of the sessionUntil deletedWhile the tab is open
Size~4 KB~5–10 MB~5 MB
Visible between tabsYesYesNo

For security a cookie with a token must be HttpOnly (inaccessible from JS), Secure (HTTPS only) and with SameSite.

In an interview: Cookies are sent to the server with every request and are limited to a few kilobytes. LocalStorage lives in the browser until it is cleared, and sessionStorage only while the tab is open. For security I check that the session cookie has the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags.

mq-6:3.title: How do you use DevTools in testing?
mq-6:3.html:
• Network: requests and responses, statuses, duration, payload; a HAR file for a bug report.
  • Console: JS errors and warnings.
  • Elements: the DOM, styles, checking that a field is really disabled and not just grey.
  • Application: cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage.
  • Device toolbar: responsiveness and mobile sizes.
  • Network throttling: a slow network and offline.
In an interview: In DevTools I look at the Network tab: requests, statuses and response bodies, and I save a HAR for a bug report. Console for JS errors, Application for cookies and storages, the device toolbar for responsiveness, and throttling to check behaviour on a slow network.

mq-6:4.title: How do you approach cross-browser and responsive testing?
mq-6:4.html:
First determine the matrix from analytics: which browsers, OSes and devices clients really use. Then prioritise: the most popular get full testing, the rest a smoke of critical scenarios.

Check: layout at breakpoints, behaviour of form elements, date and number formats, the virtual keyboard on mobile, screen orientation. Tools: emulation in DevTools, real devices, cloud farms such as BrowserStack.

In an interview: I build a matrix of browsers and devices based on analytics, not everything at once. The most popular configurations I test fully, and the rest with smoke. I check the layout at breakpoints, forms, date and number formats, and I always check part of it on real devices, because emulation doesn't show everything.

mq-6:5.title: What happens when you enter a URL
mq-6:5.html:
First the browser parses the URL and looks for the domain's IP address through DNS: the browser cache, the OS cache, the ISP's resolver, and then the root, TLD and authoritative servers. Then a TCP connection is established through a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. For HTTPS a TLS handshake follows: the server sends a certificate, the browser verifies it, and the parties agree on encryption keys.

Then the browser sends an HTTP request with a method, headers and cookies. The request may pass through a CDN, a load balancer and a reverse proxy before it reaches the application server. The server processes the request, goes to the DB or other services and returns a response with a status code, headers and HTML.

The browser parses the HTML and builds the DOM, loads CSS, JS and images in parallel and builds the CSSOM. Then come layout, paint and composite, and the page is displayed. JavaScript runs and may make additional API requests and change the DOM.

mq-6:6.title: A front-end or back-end bug through DevTools
mq-6:6.html:
The main tool is the Network tab: I find the request related to the action and look at the request and response. If the front end sent wrong data (wrong fields, format, a missing parameter), it is a front-end bug. If the request is right and the backend returned an error or wrong data, it is a backend bug.

If the backend returned correct data and the UI shows something else, the bug is on the front end: in display, handling or state. If the request wasn't sent at all, I look at the Console tab for JS errors. I also check status codes: 5xx usually points to the backend, and a 4xx needs analysis of which of them is wrong, per the API contract.

Additionally: the Application tab for cookies, localStorage and tokens, Elements for the DOM and styles, Performance for speed. You can repeat a request through Copy as cURL in Postman to isolate the backend from the UI. In a bug report I attach the request, the response and a HAR file.

mq-6:7.title: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage
mq-6:7.html:
Cookies are small data up to 4 KB that the browser automatically sends with every request to the matching domain. They can be set both by the server through the Set-Cookie header and by JS. They have an expiry and security attributes: HttpOnly (inaccessible to JS, protection from XSS), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (protection from CSRF).

localStorage holds about 5–10 MB of data, doesn't send it to the server automatically and stores it with no expiry until it is deleted. sessionStorage has a similar size, but lives only within one tab and is cleared when it closes. Both are accessible only through JavaScript and are tied to the origin.

For testing: I check that sensitive data, such as session tokens, is stored in HttpOnly cookies and not in localStorage. I also check behaviour after logout, closing the tab, in incognito mode and in a new tab. In DevTools this is visible on the Application tab.

mq-6:8.title: The DOM, layout and responsiveness
mq-6:8.html:
The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree-shaped representation of the HTML document in the browser's memory, which JavaScript can manipulate. Each tag becomes a node, and changing the DOM changes what the user sees. Locators in automated tests work with the DOM.

I check the layout against the Figma mockup: spacing, fonts, colours, sizes, alignment. Typical problems: text spilling out of its block, overlapping elements, long words that break the layout, missing hover, focus and disabled states. For analysis I use the Elements tab in DevTools and extensions like PerfectPixel.

I test responsiveness through Device Mode in DevTools at different breakpoints, for example 320, 768, 1024 and 1440 pixels, and on real devices. I also check screen orientation, zooming, cross-browser behaviour and working from the keyboard. For visual regression you can use screenshot tests: Percy or Applitools.

mq-6:9.title: JavaScript basics
mq-6:9.html:
== compares with type coercion, so '5' == 5 gives true, and null == undefined is also true. === compares without coercion, taking the type into account, so '5' === 5 gives false. In practice I always use === to avoid non-obvious bugs.

var has function scope and hoisting with the value undefined, so it is hardly used now. let and const have block scope; let can be reassigned, const can't. But const for an object or array doesn't make it immutable: the contents can be changed, only the reference can't be reassigned.

JS is single-threaded, and asynchrony is implemented through the event loop: synchronous code runs on the call stack, and callbacks wait in queues. Microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (setTimeout). A promise has the states pending, fulfilled and rejected; async/await is syntactic sugar over promises, and errors are caught with try/catch.

mq-7:0.title: What is a REST API and what do you check in API testing?
mq-7:0.html:
REST is an architectural style: resources by URL, standard HTTP methods, a response usually in JSON, and the server keeps no state between requests.

What I check:

  • The status code and the response body: fields, types, values.
  • Headers: Content-Type, caching, CORS.
  • Negative cases: invalid data, missing fields, wrong types, 401/403/404.
  • Business logic: the data really changed in the system (GET after POST, a check in the DB).
  • Response time.
In an interview: REST is an approach where resources have their own addresses and actions are performed with standard HTTP methods. I check status codes, the structure and values of the response, headers, negative cases with invalid data and without authorisation, and that the change really happened, through a following GET or in the database.

mq-7:1.title: How do you work in Postman?
mq-7:1.html:
• Collections: requests grouped by functionality.
  • Environments: variables for dev, staging, prod: {{baseUrl}}, {{token}}.
  • Pre-request scripts: get a token, generate data.
  • Tests: assertions on status and body, saving values into variables for following requests.
  • Collection Runner / Newman: running a whole collection, Newman from the CLI in CI.
// the Tests tab in Postman
pm.test("Status 201", () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));

const body = pm.response.json();
pm.test("Amount saved", () => pm.expect(body.amount).to.eql(100.50));

pm.environment.set("transferId", body.id);   // for the next request
In an interview: In Postman I gather requests into collections, move addresses and tokens into environment variables, get a token in pre-request scripts, and in the Tests tab I write checks and save values, for example an ID, for the following requests. A collection can be run through the Runner or Newman in CI.

mq-7:2.title: What is Swagger and how do you use it?
mq-7:2.html:
Swagger (OpenAPI) is an API specification: endpoints, parameters, request and response schemas, error codes. Swagger UI lets you send requests right from the browser.

As QA I use it as a source of API requirements, for a quick check of an endpoint, and for finding discrepancies between the documentation and real behaviour, which are bugs too. The specification can be imported into Postman.

In an interview: Swagger is API documentation in the OpenAPI format with the ability to send requests from the browser. I use it as API requirements, for quick checks, and I look for discrepancies between the documentation and real behaviour. I also import the specification into Postman, so I don't have to create requests by hand.

mq-7:3.title: What is idempotency and why test it?
mq-7:3.html:
An operation is idempotent if a repeated call gives the same result as the first. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not: two POSTs create two records.

I test: resending the same request (a double click, a retry after a timeout), and the system must not create a duplicate.

In an interview: An idempotent operation gives the same result on repeat. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, and POST isn't. I check that a repeated request, for example after a double click or a retry after a timeout, doesn't create a duplicate.

mq-7:4.title: How do you test authentication and authorisation in an API?
mq-7:4.html:
• A request without a token → 401.
  • With an expired or forged token → 401.
  • With a valid token but without rights (an ordinary user on an admin endpoint) → 403.
  • Access to other people's data: user A requests user B's resource by ID → 403 or 404. This is an IDOR vulnerability, one of the most frequent.
  • A token after logout no longer works.
In an interview: I check requests without a token and with an expired token, which must give four hundred and one, and with a token without the needed rights, four hundred and three. Most important is whether a user can get someone else's data by substituting another ID: that is an IDOR vulnerability. And that the token stops working after logout.

mq-8:0.title: What basic SQL queries should QA know?
mq-8:0.html:
SELECT with filtering, sorting and limiting, aggregate functions and grouping.

-- the user's last 10 transactions
SELECT id, amount, currency, status, created_at
FROM transactions
WHERE user_id = 1042
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- the number and total of transactions by status
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01'
GROUP BY status
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0;
In an interview: I confidently use SELECT with filtering through WHERE, sorting and LIMIT, as well as the aggregate functions COUNT and SUM with GROUP BY. HAVING is for filtering already grouped results, unlike WHERE, which filters rows before grouping.

mq-8:1.title: What kinds of JOIN are there?
mq-8:1.html:
• INNER JOIN: only rows that have a match in both tables.
  • LEFT JOIN: all rows of the left table, from the right only if there is a match, otherwise NULL.
  • RIGHT JOIN: the opposite.
  • FULL JOIN: all rows of both tables.

A LEFT JOIN with a NULL check is a convenient way to find "orphans": records without related data.

-- transactions without an audit log entry (and each must have one)
SELECT t.id, t.amount
FROM transactions t
LEFT JOIN audit_log a ON a.transaction_id = t.id
WHERE a.id IS NULL;
In an interview: INNER JOIN returns only rows with a match in both tables, LEFT JOIN all rows of the left one, and from the right only if present. I often use LEFT JOIN with a NULL check to find records that lack required related data, for example transactions without an audit log entry.

mq-8:2.title: How do you use SQL to verify data?
mq-8:2.html:
• After an action in the UI or API: check that a record appeared with the right values.
  • Find duplicates.
  • Check integrity: there are no records without related data.
  • Prepare test data or find a user in the needed state.

On shared environments, only SELECT, unless there is explicit permission to change data.

-- duplicate payments with the same idempotency key
SELECT idempotency_key, COUNT(*)
FROM payments
GROUP BY idempotency_key
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
In an interview: After an action in the UI or API I check in the database that the record was created with the right values. I also look for duplicates and records without required relations, and I find users in the needed state for tests. On shared environments I only read, unless I have permission to change data.

mq-9:0.title: What should you check in calculations with money?
mq-9:0.html:
• Precision: money can't be calculated in float: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3. The right way is decimal or integer minor units (cents).
  • Rounding: which rule (up, to nearest, banker's to even) and at which step. Different steps give different sums.
  • Currency minor units: the hryvnia and the dollar have 2 places, the yen 0, the Bahraini dinar 3.
  • Splitting: 100 UAH among three is 33.33 + 33.33 + 33.34, and the sum must add up.
  • Display: thousands and decimal separators, the currency sign, negative amounts.
In an interview: I check that money is calculated without float, because that is where errors like zero point one plus zero point two not equalling zero point three come from. I clarify the rounding rule and the step where it happens, the number of decimal places for each currency, and that when splitting, the sum adds up to the cent.

mq-9:1.title: What states does a payment have and what do you test in them?
mq-9:1.html:
Typically: created → processing → authorised (funds blocked) → debited → settled, with branches "declined", "cancelled", "refunded", "partially refunded".

What to test:

  • Every valid transition and the prohibition of invalid ones (refunding a declined payment).
  • The balance in each state: available and blocked.
  • Provider timeout: the payment doesn't disappear and isn't duplicated, and the state is clarified later.
  • A partial refund: the sum of refunds doesn't exceed the payment amount.
  • Notifications to the user in each state.
In an interview: A payment goes through states from creation to settlement, with branches of decline, cancellation and refund. I test all the valid transitions and the prohibition of invalid ones, the balance at each stage, behaviour on a provider timeout, and that the sum of partial refunds doesn't exceed the payment amount.

mq-9:2.title: What are the typical risks in payment scenarios?
mq-9:2.html:
• Double debit: a double click, a retry, the Back button.
  • Races: two parallel transfers from a balance that is enough for only one.
  • A dropped connection after sending but before the response: which state does the user see?
  • Limits: daily, monthly, per operation; what happens at the day boundary.
  • Time zones: is "today" for the limit by server time or the user's? What about an operation at 23:59?
  • Currencies: is the rate fixed at the moment of creation or of debit?
In an interview: The main risks are double debit, races in parallel transfers, a dropped connection in the middle of an operation, limits at the day boundary, time zones and the moment of fixing the currency rate. A double click and two tabs with the same transfer I check in every payment scenario.

mq-9:3.title: What is reconciliation and how do you test it?
mq-9:3.html:
Reconciliation is comparing our system's data with the data of a bank or payment provider: every operation with us has a matching one at the provider, with the same amount and status.

I test: a full match; an operation exists with us but not at the provider, and vice versa; a difference in amount or status; duplicates in the provider's file. I check that discrepancies end up in a report or a queue for manual review, and don't get lost.

In an interview: Reconciliation compares our operations with the bank's or provider's data. I test not only a full match, but also discrepancies: an operation exists in only one system, different amounts or statuses, duplicates. The main thing is that every discrepancy ends up in a report for review and doesn't disappear.

mq-9:4.title: What should you know about security and compliance in fintech?
mq-9:4.html:
• PCI DSS is the standard for card data: the full number is masked (only the last 4 digits are visible), CVV isn't stored anywhere, including logs.
  • GDPR: personal data: minimisation, the right to deletion, consent.
  • KYC / AML: verifying the customer's identity and combating money laundering: restrictions before verification, suspicious operations.
  • Audit: every financial operation and settings change has a record of who, what, when.
  • SCA / 3-D Secure: confirming a payment with a code or in the bank's app.

As QA I check this at the behaviour level: that the card number is masked in the UI, API responses and logs, and that an unverified user runs into limits.

In an interview: I know the basic requirements: PCI DSS, where the card number is masked and CVV isn't stored anywhere, even in logs; GDPR for personal data; KYC and AML for customer checks; audit of all financial actions; payment confirmation through 3-D Secure. As QA I check this at the behaviour level: in the UI, in API responses and in logs.

mq-10:0.title: How do you choose quality metrics for a project?
mq-10:0.html:
Not from a list of "popular metrics", but from a goal. A convenient framework is GQM (Goal → Question → Metric):

  1. Goal: "reduce the number of defects that reach production".
  2. Questions: how many defects do we miss? At which stage should we have caught them? Which modules are the most problematic?
  3. Metrics: defect leakage, the distribution of production bugs by module and by the stage where they could have been found.

Rules: every metric has an owner and an action it triggers; there are few metrics (3–5 key ones); we look at the trend, not a single value.

In an interview: I start with the goal, not the metric, following the Goal-Question-Metric approach. For example, the goal is fewer bugs in production, the question is how many we miss and where we should have caught them, and the metrics are defect leakage and the distribution of production bugs by module. I keep three to five key metrics, each of which leads to a concrete action, and I look at trends, not individual numbers.

mq-10:1.title: What are defect leakage, DRE and defect density and how do you calculate them?
mq-10:1.html:
MetricFormulaWhat it shows
Defect leakageproduction bugs ÷ (bugs before release + production bugs) × 100%What share of defects we miss
DRE (Defect Removal Efficiency)bugs before release ÷ (bugs before release + production bugs) × 100%Catching efficiency: 100% − leakage
Defect densitynumber of defects ÷ size (module, KLOC, story points)Which parts are the most problematic

Example: in a release 45 bugs were found before production and 5 after. Leakage = 5 ÷ 50 = 10%, DRE = 90%.

A nuance worth saying: count only significant defects (for example Major and above) and over a fixed window after the release, otherwise minor things distort the picture.

In an interview: Defect leakage is the share of defects we missed into production out of all those found. DRE is the opposite, the share found before release. For example, forty-five bugs before release and five after is ten percent leakage and ninety DRE. Defect density shows which modules are the most problematic. I count only significant defects and over a fixed window after release, so that minor things don't distort the picture.

mq-10:2.title: How does requirements coverage differ from code coverage? Is 100% needed?
mq-10:2.html:
Requirements coverage is what share of requirements or acceptance criteria have tests, and how many of them passed. It is calculated through a traceability matrix or links in Jira/Zephyr.

Code coverage is what share of lines or branches is executed by tests. Measured by tools, mostly for unit tests.

100% is not the goal. High code coverage doesn't guarantee quality checks (a test may execute a line and verify nothing), and 100% of requirements may mean superficial cases. More important is risk coverage: critical scenarios covered deeply, secondary ones sufficiently.

In an interview: Requirements coverage shows what share of requirements has tests, and code coverage what share of the code is executed by tests. A hundred percent isn't a goal for me: a test may execute a line and verify nothing. I aim at risk coverage: critical scenarios must be covered deeply, and secondary ones sufficiently.

mq-10:3.title: Which process metrics do you track?
mq-10:3.html:
• Defect fix time by severity: do we meet the agreed deadlines.
  • Reopen rate: the share of bugs that get reopened: a signal about the quality of fixes or retesting.
  • Rejected rate: the share of bugs rejected as "not a bug" or a duplicate: a signal about the quality of reports or requirements.
  • Test execution progress: executed, passed, blocked as of the current release moment.
  • Time in the "Ready for QA" status: whether testing is becoming a bottleneck.

Each of them is a reason for a conversation at the retro, not an evaluation of people.

In an interview: I look at defect fix time by severity, reopen rate, how many bugs get reopened, rejected rate, how many are rejected as not a bug or a duplicate, test execution progress and how many tasks are waiting for QA. A high rejected rate, for example, hints that the problem is in the requirements or in my reports, and that is a topic for the retro.

mq-10:4.title: Which metrics do you use for automation?
mq-10:4.html:
• Automation coverage: the share of regression cases that are automated, especially critical ones.
  • Flaky rate: the share of tests that sometimes fail and sometimes pass with no code changes. The goal is close to zero, because flakiness destroys trust in the whole suite.
  • Run time and its trend: whether feedback on a PR is slowing down.
  • Pass rate on main: stability.
  • Defects found by automated tests: whether automation really catches regressions.
  • ROI: how many hours of manual regression are replaced minus maintenance costs.
In an interview: For automation I track the share of automated regression, flaky rate, run time, the pass rate on the main branch and how many regressions the automated tests actually caught. Flaky rate is the most important for me: if the team stops trusting red tests, automation loses its point.

mq-10:5.title: Which metrics are harmful and why?
mq-10:5.html:
Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

  • The number of bugs found as a KPI → minor bugs get split into several, conflicts with developers, and nobody works on preventing defects.
  • The number of test cases or automated tests written → many small and duplicated cases.
  • "Zero bugs in production" as QA's personal goal → fear of releases and excess bureaucracy.
  • Metrics for comparing people → distorted data.

Metrics must show the state of the system and the process, not evaluate individual people.

In an interview: I am careful with metrics like the number of bugs found or cases written as a KPI. By Goodhart's law, when a measure becomes a target, people optimise the number rather than the quality: bugs get split, cases get duplicated. Metrics must show the state of the product and the process, not evaluate people.

mq-10:6.title: How do you build a quality dashboard for different stakeholders?
mq-10:6.html:
Different people need different answers:

  • Business / PM: is the release ready, open blockers and critical issues, risks, the trend of production incidents.
  • The team: sprint testing progress, bugs by status, flaky tests, time in "Ready for QA".
  • Management: trends over a quarter: leakage, fix time, release stability.

Technically: JQL filters in Jira and gadgets on the dashboard, Zephyr or Xray reports, Allure for automated tests; for more complex needs, Grafana or BI tools.

-- open critical bugs of the current release
project = PAY AND issuetype = Bug AND fixVersion = "2.15"
  AND priority in (Highest, High) AND statusCategory != Done

-- production bugs for the last 30 days (for leakage)
project = PAY AND issuetype = Bug AND labels = production
  AND created >= -30d ORDER BY priority DESC
In an interview: I build a dashboard for the audience. The PM needs an answer on whether the release is ready and what the blockers are, the team needs sprint progress and bug statuses, management needs quarterly trends. Technically these are JQL filters and gadgets in Jira, Zephyr reports and Allure for automated tests.

mq-10:7.title: How do you prove quality improved? What are DORA metrics?
mq-10:7.html:
You need a baseline (the state before changes), a trend over several releases and a link to a change in the process. One number proves nothing.

DORA metrics are four delivery performance metrics that assess both speed and stability:

  • Deployment frequency: how often we release.
  • Lead time for changes: from commit to production.
  • Change failure rate: the share of releases that caused an incident or a rollback. The closest to QA.
  • Time to restore: how long recovery after an incident takes.

A strong answer: quality improved if change failure rate and leakage fall, while release frequency doesn't, that is, we didn't buy stability at the price of speed.

In an interview: I record a baseline and show a trend over several releases, tied to a specific process change. DORA metrics suit this well: deployment frequency, time from commit to production, the share of failed releases and recovery time. Real improvement is when the share of failed releases falls and release frequency doesn't.

mq-11:0.title: What is Docker and why does QA need it?
mq-11:0.html:
Docker packages an application together with all its dependencies into a container that runs the same on any machine. Containers are lighter than virtual machines: they share the host OS kernel, so they start in seconds.

For QA this means:

  • A reproducible test environment: the end of "it works for me".
  • Bringing up the application with a database, cache and mocks locally with one command.
  • A clean database for every run.
  • The same environment for automated tests locally and on CI.
  • Reproducing a bug on a specific version of a service.
In an interview: Docker packages an application with all its dependencies into a container that works the same on any machine. For me as QA it is a reproducible environment: with one command I bring up the application with a database, get clean data for each run, and automated tests on CI run in the same environment as locally.

mq-11:1.title: How do image, container, Dockerfile and registry differ?
mq-11:1.html:
• Dockerfile is the recipe: which base image to start from, what to install, which command to run.
  • Image is the template built from the recipe, immutable and versioned (with a tag).
  • Container is a running instance of an image. Many containers can be started from one image.
  • Registry is a store of images: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, a company's private registry.

An analogy: the Dockerfile is the recipe, the image is the frozen dish, the container is the reheated portion on the plate.

In an interview: A Dockerfile is the build recipe, an image is the built immutable template with a version, a container is a running instance of that image, and a registry is a store of images, for example Docker Hub. As many containers as you like can be started from one image.

mq-11:2.title: Which Docker commands does QA use every day?
mq-11:2.html:
For testing it is more important to be able to figure out what is already running than to build images.

docker ps                      # running containers
docker ps -a                   # all, including those that crashed
docker logs -f payments-api    # logs in real time
docker logs --since 10m api    # logs for the last 10 minutes
docker exec -it payments-db psql -U qa -d payments   # get into the database
docker exec -it api sh         # a shell inside the container
docker inspect api             # config: variables, ports, networks
docker restart api
docker pull registry.example.com/payments-api:2.15.0   # a specific version
docker images
docker stop api && docker rm api
In an interview: Every day I use docker ps to see what is running and what crashed, docker logs to find an error by time, and docker exec to get into a container or connect to the database. Inspect shows environment variables and ports, and pull with a tag lets me run a specific version of a service to reproduce a bug.

mq-11:3.title: What is Docker Compose and how do you bring up a test environment with it?
mq-11:3.html:
Compose describes several services in one YAML file and brings them up together: an application, a database, a cache, a mock of an external service. The services see each other by name in a shared network.

# compose.yml
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/payments-api:2.15.0
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      DB_URL: postgres://qa:qa@db:5432/payments
      PROVIDER_URL: http://provider-mock:9000
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: qa
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: qa
      POSTGRES_DB: payments
    volumes:
      - ./seed:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d   # SQL for test data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "qa"]
      interval: 2s
      retries: 15

  provider-mock:
    image: wiremock/wiremock:3.9.1
    volumes: ["./mocks:/home/wiremock"]

# docker compose up -d        bring up
# docker compose logs -f api  a service's logs
# docker compose down -v      stop and delete the data
In an interview: Compose describes several services in one file: in my case an API, PostgreSQL with test data and a mock of the payment provider. With one up command I bring up the whole environment, and down with the v flag resets the data completely. The healthcheck guarantees that the API starts only after the database is ready.

mq-11:4.title: How do volumes and networks work, and how do you reset test data?
mq-11:4.html:
Volumes store data outside the container: without them the database data disappears together with the container, and with them it survives a restart. For testing this cuts both ways: it is convenient, but old data may "leak" between runs.

  • docker compose down: the containers are removed, and the data in the volume remains.
  • docker compose down -v: the volumes are removed too: the next start has a clean database and the seed scripts.

Networks: in Compose services reach each other by service name (db:5432), not through localhost. From outside, from your computer, through published ports (localhost:8080).

In an interview: Volumes store data outside the container, so the database survives a restart. To start from a clean state I do compose down with the v flag, which removes the volumes and runs the seed scripts again. Inside Compose services reach each other by name, and from my computer through published ports on localhost.

mq-11:5.title: How do you run automated tests in Docker on CI?
mq-11:5.html:
Tests run in the official image with browsers already installed and a fixed version: the same environment locally and on CI, with no "I have a different Chrome".

  • Playwright: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.x.x: the image version must match the package version.
  • Cypress: cypress/included:<version> or cypress/browsers.

A typical scheme on CI: docker compose up -d brings up the application and dependencies, the tests run against it, artifacts (reports, screenshots) are saved, and at the end docker compose down -v.

# GitHub Actions
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.48.0-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright test
In an interview: I run automated tests in the official image with a fixed browser version: for Playwright it is Microsoft's image, for Cypress it is cypress included. Then the environment is the same locally and on CI. I bring up the application and its dependencies with Compose before the tests, and after the run I save the reports and remove the containers together with the data.

mq-11:6.title: What typical problems occur with Docker and how do you diagnose them?
mq-11:6.html:
SymptomCause and what to do
The container stops immediatelydocker ps -a + docker logs: a startup error, a missing environment variable, a failed connection to the database
"port is already allocated"The port is taken by another process or container: change the external port or stop the conflicting one
A service doesn't see the database at localhostInside a container localhost is the container itself; use the service name (db)
The API fails because the database isn't ready yetdepends_on without a healthcheck waits only for the container to start: add a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy
Tests see old dataA volume remained: docker compose down -v
Behaviour differs from CIThe latest tag pulled a different version: pin specific tags
In an interview: If a container crashes, I look at docker ps with the a flag and the logs: usually a missing environment variable or no connection to the database is there. Common problems are an occupied port, going to localhost inside a container instead of the service name, the API starting before the database without a healthcheck, old data in a volume, and the latest tag pulling a different version.

mq-11:7.title: How does a Docker container differ from a virtual machine?
mq-11:7.html:
ContainerVirtual machine
IsolationProcesses on the host OS's shared kernelA full guest OS with its own kernel
StartSecondsMinutes
SizeTens to hundreds of MBGigabytes
When for QAServices, databases, automated testsAnother OS: a Windows application, specific system versions
In an interview: A container is isolated processes on a shared OS kernel, so it starts in seconds and weighs little. A virtual machine has a full OS of its own, and it is heavier and slower. For services, databases and automated tests I take containers, and virtual machines when another operating system is needed.

mq-11:8.title: Docker for a test environment, and Git
mq-11:8.html:
Docker packages an application with all its dependencies into a container that works the same on any machine. For QA this solves the "it works for me" problem: tests on CI and locally run in the same environment. With docker-compose you can bring up the application, the DB and dependent services for tests with one command.

Docker also gives an isolated clean environment for every run, fixed browser versions through the official Cypress images and easy launching of parallel containers. Basic commands: docker run, docker ps, docker logs, docker-compose up.

In Git I most often work with the feature branch flow: a separate branch per task from main or develop, then a merge request with code review and passing CI. Merge combines branches, keeping all history, and creates a merge commit. Rebase moves commits on top of another branch and gives a linear history, but rewrites commits. So rebase isn't done for branches that others already work on: it breaks their history.

mq-12:0.title: What is an LLM and how does it work in simple words?
mq-12:0.html:
An LLM (large language model) is a neural network trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next fragment of text (a token). It doesn't "know" facts the way a database does, but has learned the patterns of language: which words and ideas usually go together.

An analogy: a very advanced autocomplete. You give a prompt, and the model step by step adds the most likely continuation. All it "sees" at the moment is the context window: the prompt, the conversation history and attached files. So the quality of the answer depends directly on the context you gave.

In an interview: An LLM is a neural network that learned from a huge amount of text to predict the next word. It doesn't check facts, but generates the most likely continuation based on the context I gave it. Hence the main rule of working with it: the more precise the context, the better the result, and any answer must be verified.

mq-12:1.title: How does AI help in QA's work?
mq-12:1.html:
• Requirements analysis: find ambiguities, missed scenarios, questions for the PM.
  • Test design: drafts of test cases and checklists, boundary values, negative scenarios.
  • Test data: generate JSON, CSV, sets of invalid values.
  • Bugs: structure a bug report, analyse a stack trace or a log.
  • Automation: drafts of automated test code, locators, SQL queries; Copilot in the editor.
  • Documentation: a test plan, a report, release notes from a list of tasks.

What they all have in common: AI makes a draft faster, but the decision, verification and responsibility are QA's.

In an interview: I use AI at several stages: to find gaps in requirements, to get a draft of test cases with boundary and negative scenarios, to generate test data, to analyse a log and to write automated test code faster. But it is always a draft: I review it, complete it and answer for the result.

mq-12:2.title: How do you write prompts to get decent test cases and not fluff?
mq-12:2.html:
• Context: a description of the feature, acceptance criteria, constraints, business rules.
  • Role: "You are a Senior QA testing a payment form".
  • Techniques: "apply equivalence classes and boundary values, add negative scenarios".
  • Format: a table with the columns ID, preconditions, steps, expected result, priority.
  • An example of one good case, so the model repeats the style.
  • Iterations: "what did I miss on security?", "add network failure scenarios".
Bad:
  Write test cases for a transfer.

Good:
  You are a Senior QA on a fintech product. The feature: a card-to-card transfer.
  Rules: amount 1–10,000 UAH, 2 decimal places, daily limit 20,000,
  fee 1%, minimum 5 UAH.
  Apply equivalence classes and boundary values, add negative
  scenarios, double submission and a timeout.
  Format: a table ID | Preconditions | Steps | Expected result | Priority.
  Separately list the questions about requirements that remain unclear.
In an interview: I give the model context: a description of the feature, business rules and acceptance criteria, set a role, name the test design techniques and the result format, sometimes with an example. And at the end I ask it to list separately the unclear questions about the requirements, which is often the most valuable part of the answer. Then I iterate: I ask what is missing on security or failures.

mq-12:3.title: What are hallucinations and why can't you take an AI answer as is?
mq-12:3.html:
A hallucination is when a model confidently produces something untrue: a nonexistent API method, an invented config option, a requirement that isn't in the document. The cause is that the model generates plausible text and doesn't check facts; when data is lacking, it fills the gap with the most likely variant.

What follows for QA:

  • Check generated cases against the real requirements: the model could have added its own "rules".
  • Run and review code as a colleague's code on a PR.
  • Check methods, commands and parameters against the documentation.
  • AI doesn't know your product, the history of bugs and the team's agreements, so coverage from it is never complete.
In an interview: A hallucination is when a model confidently produces something untrue, because it generates plausible text rather than checking facts. So I check everything generated against requirements and documentation, and I run and review code as a colleague's code. AI doesn't know our product and the history of bugs, so its cases are a starting point, not complete coverage.

mq-12:4.title: What data must not be passed to AI tools?
mq-12:4.html:
• Customers' personal data, real database dumps.
  • Passwords, tokens, API keys, configs with secrets.
  • The customer's code and documentation, unless the company has approved a specific tool.
  • Data covered by an NDA.

The rule: use only tools approved by the company (corporate plans where data doesn't go into training models), and anonymise everything you pass. If there is no policy, ask rather than assume.

In an interview: I don't pass personal data, secrets, or the customer's code and documentation into public AI tools unless it is approved. I work with tools the company has allowed, and I anonymise examples. And if there is no policy, I ask rather than decide myself.

mq-12:5.title: How do you test features built on LLMs (a chatbot, an assistant)?
mq-12:5.html:
The main difference is non-determinism: for the same query the answer is a little different each time, so a check "the answer equals X" doesn't work.

  • Criteria instead of exact text: the answer contains the needed facts, doesn't contain forbidden ones, has the right language and tone, and the format meets requirements.
  • A set of reference queries (an eval set) with expected quality, run after every prompt or model change.
  • Prompt injection: attempts to make the bot ignore instructions, reveal the system prompt or other users' data.
  • Hallucinations: questions the bot must answer with "I don't know" or hand over to a human.
  • Boundaries: the bot gives no advice outside its role and takes no actions without confirmation.
  • Non-functional: response time, query cost, behaviour when the model is unavailable.
In an interview: LLM responses are non-deterministic, so I check not the exact text but criteria: whether the needed facts are there, whether forbidden ones are absent, whether the format and tone are right. I have a set of reference queries that I run after every prompt or model change. Separately I test prompt injection, hallucinations, and that the bot correctly says "I don't know" or hands the question to a human.

mq-12:6.title: What are the limits of AI-generated test cases?
mq-12:6.html:
• It doesn't know the product's context: integrations, incident history, team decisions.
  • It generates many obvious cases and few deep ones: races, states, unusual data.
  • It may invent rules that aren't in the requirements.
  • It duplicates cases and doesn't prioritise by risk.
  • Quality depends directly on the quality of the requirements: bad requirements give bad cases.

So a stronger approach is to ask AI not to "write cases" but to find gaps in the requirements and in the cases already written.

In an interview: AI doesn't know the product's context and the history of bugs, generates many obvious cases and few deep ones, may invent rules and doesn't prioritise by risk. So I more often use it as a reviewer: I ask it to find gaps in the requirements and in my cases, not to write everything for me.

mq-12:7.title: Tell me how you use AI in your work.
mq-12:7.html:
This question is about your experience, so the answer must be concrete: tool → task → result → how you verified. The structure:

  1. Which tools and where: Copilot in the editor, Claude or ChatGPT for analysing requirements and documentation.
  2. A concrete task: for example, drafts of step definitions, test cases from acceptance criteria, PR review.
  3. The result, preferably with a number: faster by X, less routine.
  4. How you controlled quality: review, running, checking against requirements.
  5. The limits: what you don't pass to AI and where it doesn't help.

Don't exaggerate: the interviewer will almost always ask for details, and the answer must come from your own experience.

In an interview: Right now I work in AI-driven automation: I use Copilot in the editor for drafts of automated test code and Claude for analysing requirements, generating test cases from acceptance criteria and reviews. This noticeably reduces routine, but everything generated I review, run and check against the requirements. I don't pass customer data and secrets to AI.

mq-12:8.title: How is AI changing QA's role and will it replace testers?
mq-12:8.html:
AI takes over the routine: drafts of cases, data, code, a first analysis of logs and defect triage. QA's value shifts to what AI does poorly: understanding business context and risks, exploratory testing, critical thinking, communication with the team, and verifying AI systems themselves.

A balanced answer: AI won't replace QA, but a QA who uses AI effectively will replace one who doesn't.

In an interview: AI takes over the routine: drafts of cases, data and code, a first analysis of logs. And QA's value shifts to understanding risks and the business, exploratory testing, critical thinking and testing AI features themselves. I don't think AI will replace testers, but a tester who knows how to use it will be stronger than one who doesn't.

mq-12:9.title: AI tools in QA's work
mq-12:9.html:
For code I use AI assistants in the IDE: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code. They speed up writing automated tests, Page Objects, custom commands and refactoring. They also help to understand someone else's code and to find the cause of a test failure from a log.

Chat assistants (Claude, ChatGPT) I use for generating ideas for test cases and checklists from requirements, and for finding boundary and negative scenarios. Also for generating test data, SQL queries, JSON schemas and regular expressions. It is useful to ask AI to analyse requirements for contradictions and missed cases.

Other uses: writing bug reports and documentation, translation, self-healing locators in some platforms, analysing large logs. It is important to mention the limits too: I don't pass confidential data, tokens and users' personal data to external AI services.

mq-12:10.title: Risks of AI-generated tests and code
mq-12:10.html:
AI can generate tests that check the wrong thing or that duplicate the current behaviour, bugs included. Invented APIs, methods or library options that don't exist, or outdated syntax, are common. Generated code may contain antipatterns: fixed waits, brittle selectors, no assertions.

More risks: superficial coverage of "happy" scenarios without edge cases, tests that always pass, and leaking confidential data to an external service. Also AI doesn't know the business context unless you provide it.

I validate like this: I read and understand every generated test, check it against requirements, and verify that it fails when the functionality is broken. The code goes through the same code review, linter and CI as hand-written code. The responsibility for the result stays with me, and AI is only a tool.

mq-12:11.title: Testing a non-deterministic LLM feature
mq-12:11.html:
Since the answer is different every time, exact string comparison doesn't work, so we check the properties of the answer, not the specific text. For example: the answer contains the key information, answers the question, has the needed format, language and length, and doesn't contain forbidden topics. This is similar to a property-based approach.

A test dataset is needed: a set of typical, boundary and complex queries with the expected characteristics of answers. Each query is run several times and stability is assessed: for example, 9 out of 10 answers must be correct. The result is not "passed/failed" but a metric with a threshold.

Helper techniques: lowering temperature to 0 for reproducibility on a test environment, fixing the model and prompt version. I also check edge cases: an empty query, very long text, another language, an ambiguous question, an irrelevant query. And regression whenever the prompt or model changes is a must.

mq-12:12.title: Hallucinations
mq-12:12.html:
A hallucination is a confident, plausible answer from a model that is factually wrong or not confirmed by sources. Examples: invented facts, quotes, links, function names, numbers, or an answer that contradicts the provided context. Especially critical in RAG systems, where the model must answer only from the documents.

I detect them manually by checking facts against ground truth: comparing with documentation, the knowledge base, system data. Provocative questions about what isn't in the context are useful: the right behaviour is to say "I don't know", not to invent. I also check that links and quotes really exist.

Automated: comparison with a reference answer from a golden dataset, a faithfulness check, whether every statement of the answer is supported by the context. For this LLM-as-a-judge and frameworks like RAGAS, DeepEval or promptfoo are used. Metrics: faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision.

mq-12:13.title: Quality criteria for an LLM answer
mq-12:13.html:
The main criteria: factual correctness, relevance to the question, completeness, conformance to context, following the format and instructions. Also tone and style matching the brand, language, length, safety (no harmful, biased or toxic content). For production, latency and query cost matter too.

A golden dataset is a reference set of queries with expected answers or criteria, prepared and verified by people. Every new version of a prompt or model is run on it and the metrics are compared. It works as a regression suite for an LLM.

A rubric is a clear evaluation scale, for example 1–5 for each criterion with a description of each level. LLM-as-a-judge is when another model evaluates an answer against a rubric, which makes evaluation scalable. But the judge must be calibrated: its scores are selectively checked against human ones.

mq-12:14.title: Prompt injection and jailbreak
mq-12:14.html:
Prompt injection is an attack where an attacker inserts instructions that make the model ignore the system prompt. A direct one is in the user's message, for example "Ignore previous instructions and...". An indirect one comes through data the model reads: a web page, a document, an email, an API response.

A jailbreak is an attempt to bypass a model's safety restrictions to get forbidden content. Typical techniques: role play, hypothetical scenarios, text encoding, splitting a request into parts, another language. The goal of testing is to make sure the protections work.

How I test: a set of attack prompts from known catalogues, for example the OWASP Top 10 for LLM, checking for leaks of the system prompt and confidential data. I also check that the model doesn't perform dangerous actions through tools without permission. Automation is helped by promptfoo, Garak and other red-teaming tools.

mq-12:15.title: Automating checks of LLM answers
mq-12:15.html:
The first level is deterministic checks: JSON structure against a schema, presence of required fields, length, language, keywords, absence of forbidden words or personal data. They are fast and cheap, so they run on every commit. This can also be done in an ordinary Cypress or Playwright test through the API.

The second level is semantic checks: comparing an answer with a reference through embeddings and cosine similarity with a threshold, for example 0.8. The third is LLM-as-a-judge with a rubric, which evaluates correctness, relevance and tone. For RAG, the metrics faithfulness and context relevance are added.

Because of non-determinism each case is run several times and the percentage of successful answers is counted. In tests you can lower the temperature, but the final evaluation must be on production settings. Results are tracked over time to see regression after a prompt or model change.

mq-13:0.title: There are no requirements or they are incomplete. What do you do?
mq-13:0.html:
1. Gather what exists: the ticket, mockups, correspondence, similar features, competitors' behaviour, Swagger.
  2. Draw up a list of questions and open assumptions and go through it with the PM or an analyst.
  3. Write the agreements in the ticket: that is what the requirements are.
  4. Test based on risks and experience, marking which expectations are my assumptions.
In an interview: I gather everything there is: the ticket, mockups, correspondence, Swagger, similar features. I draw up a list of questions and my assumptions and go through it with the PM, and I record the agreements in the ticket. In parallel I test based on risks, marking where the expected result is my assumption.

mq-13:1.title: The release is tomorrow and there's no time for full testing. What do you do?
mq-13:1.html:
1. Prioritise by risk: what changed, what is most critical for the business, where things broke most often.
  2. Test in this order: the release's changes → critical scenarios (money, login) → the rest of the regression.
  3. Transparently report what was tested and what wasn't, and what the risks are.
  4. The release decision is made by the team and the business, and QA gives information for that decision.
In an interview: I prioritise by risk: first what changed in the release, then the critical scenarios, money and login, and then the rest. And I honestly report what we managed to check, what not, and what the risks are. The release decision is made by the team with the business, and my job is to give them truthful information for it.

mq-13:2.title: Users found a critical bug in production. What do you do?
mq-13:2.html:
1. Quickly reproduce and assess the scale: how many users, how much money, whether it is ongoing.
  2. Tell the team and the responsible people immediately, with all the details.
  3. Help with the decision: rollback, a feature flag, a hotfix, and test the fix.
  4. After the incident, work it out without looking for someone to blame: why the tests missed it, and add a case to the regression or automated tests.
In an interview: First I reproduce it and assess the scale, and immediately tell the team with the details. Then I help choose a solution: a rollback, turning the feature off, or a hotfix, and I test the fix. After the incident we analyse why the tests missed it, and I add that scenario to the regression so it doesn't happen again.

mq-13:3.title: How would you test a login form?
mq-13:3.html:
Positive: valid data, "remember me", login after logout.

Negative: a wrong password, a nonexistent email, empty fields, spaces, a wrong format, email case.

Security: blocking after N failed attempts, the same message for a wrong login and a wrong password (so as not to reveal which emails exist), the password masked and not in the URL, HTTPS, SQL injections and XSS in the fields, the session expiring after inactivity.

Other: Enter instead of a click, browser autofill, several tabs, "Back" after logout, localisation of errors, the mobile version.

In an interview: I split checks into positive, negative, security and usability. Besides the obvious invalid data, I always check blocking after several attempts, the same error message for login and password so as not to reveal existing accounts, session termination, and that the Back button after logout doesn't return to the personal account.

mq-13:4.title: How would you test a money transfer between cards?
mq-13:4.html:
• Validation: the card number (format, the Luhn checksum), the amount (boundaries, fractional parts, zero, negative), your own card as the recipient.
  • Business rules: sufficient funds, limits, the fee per tariff, the recipient's currency.
  • Result: the sender's and recipient's balance, the operation history, notifications, the receipt.
  • States and failures: a decline by the bank, 3-D Secure, a timeout, a dropped network.
  • Duplicates and races: a double click, "Back" and resubmission, two tabs.
  • Security: number masking, access to other people's transfers, logs without card data.
  • Data: records in the DB and in the audit log, reconciliation.
In an interview: I check field validation, including the card checksum and amount boundaries, business rules (balance, limits and fee), and the result on both accounts and in the history. Separately, failures and timeouts, double submission, card data security, and that everything is recorded correctly in the database and the audit log.

mq-13:5.title: You are the only QA on a new project. What do you do in the first 30 days?
mq-13:5.html:
Week 1: understand the product and the people: go through the product as a user, meet the PM, the dev lead and the analyst, find out what hurts: where there are the most complaints, incidents, returned tasks.

Week 2: assess the current state: what tests and documentation exist, how the release goes, which environments there are, how bugs are handled in Jira, what is already automated.

Week 3: quick wins: a smoke checklist of critical scenarios, a bug report template, taking part in grooming with acceptance criteria.

Week 4: a plan: a risk-based test strategy, priorities for regression and automation, 2–3 health metrics. Agree it with the team.

The main thing is not to break the process in the first week, but first to understand why it is the way it is.

In an interview: The first week I study the product and talk to the PM and developers to understand where it hurts most. The second I assess what already exists: tests, documentation, the release process. The third I deliver quick results: a smoke checklist of critical scenarios and taking part in grooming. And in the fourth I propose a risk-based test strategy and agree it with the team. The main thing is to understand the process first and only then change it.

mq-13:6.title: A developer says "it works for me", and the bug reproduces for you. What do you do?
mq-13:6.html:
1. Compare conditions: the environment (local vs staging), the build version, configs and feature flags, the user's data, the browser.
  2. Show, don't argue: a video, a HAR file, the exact time for searching server logs, the request ID.
  3. Reproduce together: 5 minutes on a shared call often save a day of correspondence.
  4. If the difference is in the environment, that is also a finding: a config mismatch between environments may repeat in production.
In an interview: First I look for a difference in conditions: environment, build, configs, feature flags, the user's data. I give evidence, a video, a HAR and the exact time for searching the logs, and suggest reproducing it together on a call. If the cause is a mismatch of environments, that is a separate important defect, because it may repeat in production.

mq-13:7.title: The PM wants to release with a known critical bug. What is your position?
mq-13:7.html:
The release decision belongs to the business, and QA's job is to make it a conscious one.

  1. Describe the impact clearly: how many users, which scenarios, what financial, legal or reputational consequences, the probability.
  2. Offer options: releasing without this feature (a feature flag), a workaround, a hotfix in the next few days, monitoring and a rollback plan.
  3. Record the decision in writing: who made it, with which risks and conditions.

If the bug breaks the law or data security, escalate higher rather than just agreeing.

In an interview: The release decision is made by the business, and my job is to make it a conscious one. I explain the bug's impact clearly, offer options, such as turning the feature off with a flag, a workaround, a quick hotfix with monitoring, and I record the decision in writing. But if the bug affects data security or regulatory requirements, I escalate higher.
