mq-13:8.title: Tasks arrive for testing on the last day of the sprint. How do you fix it?
mq-13:8.html:
This is a process problem, not a QA speed problem. Solutions:

  • Split stories into smaller ones, so they reach testing during the sprint.
  • Limit the number of tasks in progress (WIP), so the team finishes tasks instead of starting new ones.
  • Test earlier: test cases before development, API before UI, testing on the feature branch.
  • Developers do a basic check against a checklist before handing over.
  • Show the problem with data: time in the "Ready for QA" status, how many tasks arrive in the last two days, and bring it to the retro.
In an interview: It is a process problem, so I bring data to the retro: how many tasks arrive in the last days of the sprint. I suggest splitting stories into smaller ones, limiting the tasks in progress so they get finished, and testing earlier: cases before development, API before UI. Testing is the team's work, not a stage at the end.

mq-13:9.title: Requirements changed after you had already tested the feature. What do you do?
mq-13:9.html:
1. Record the change in the ticket: what changed, who decided, when.
  2. Assess the impact: which cases are outdated, what needs retesting, which related functions are affected.
  3. Update the test cases and automated tests.
  4. Tell the team if the change affects the testing timeline.

If this keeps happening, it is a topic for the retro: requirements must be stable at the moment a task is taken into the sprint (Definition of Ready).

In an interview: I record the change in the ticket, assess which cases are outdated and what needs retesting, update the documentation and automated tests, and tell the team if it affects the timeline. If this happens often, I raise it at the retro: requirements must be stable when a task is taken into the sprint.

mq-13:10.title: Regression takes three days, and releases are weekly. What do you do?
mq-13:10.html:
• Prioritise: split regression into levels: a critical smoke (hours), the main regression, a full one (rarely).
  • Risk-based selection: for each release, the critical scenarios plus the areas touched by changes.
  • Clean up the suite: delete duplicates and outdated cases, merge small ones.
  • Automate: first of all stable, repeatable, critical scenarios and API checks.
  • Parallelise: distribute manual regression among people, and automated tests among workers.

The goal is for the most important part of regression to take hours, not days.

In an interview: I split regression into levels: a quick critical smoke for every release, the main regression by change areas, and a full one rarely. I clean the suite of duplicates and outdated cases, and I automate stable critical scenarios and the API. The goal is for the most important part of the checks to take hours, not days.

mq-13:11.title: A flaky automated test blocks a merge, and the team wants to just turn it off. What do you do?
mq-13:11.html:
You may turn it off, but as a temporary step with accountability:

  1. Mark the test as quarantine or skip with a ticket, an owner and a deadline.
  2. Check that the scenario isn't left with no coverage at all: check it manually for the time being.
  3. Investigate the cause: the test, test data, the environment, or a real race in the product. Sometimes flakiness is a real bug.
  4. Track the number of tests in quarantine: if it grows, the suite loses value.
In an interview: I agree to turn a test off temporarily, but only with a ticket, an owner and a deadline, and in the meantime I check the scenario manually. Then I investigate the cause: the test, data, the environment or a real race in the product, because sometimes flakiness reveals a real bug. And I make sure there are not more tests in quarantine over time.

mq-13:12.title: The test environment keeps going down, and the deadline is close. What do you do?
mq-13:12.html:
• Tell the team immediately and record the downtime: it is a blocker, not QA's personal problem.
  • Test what you can: the API on another environment, bringing it up locally in Docker, requirement review and preparing cases and data.
  • Reprioritise: with limited time, critical scenarios first.
  • Transparently update the release risks: what wasn't checked because of the environment.
  • After the deadline, raise environment stability as a separate task with data on downtime.
In an interview: I tell the team immediately and record the downtime, because it is a blocker for everyone. While the environment is down, I test what I can, the API and local bring-up in Docker, and I prepare cases and data. I reprioritise to the critical scenarios and honestly update the release risks. And after the deadline I bring data on the downtime, so that environment stability becomes a separate task.

mq-13:13.title: The customer asks to skip testing to make the release. What do you do?
mq-13:13.html:
In outsourcing the decision belongs to the customer, but they must make it understanding the consequences.

  1. Don't argue "you can't do that", but offer a minimal check: a smoke of the critical scenarios in a few hours.
  2. Name the specific risks: what exactly isn't checked and what may happen.
  3. Record the decision in writing, in an email or a ticket.
  4. Offer a check right after the release and a ready rollback plan.
  5. Inform your manager or lead on the company's side.
In an interview: I don't just say "you can't do that", but offer a minimal smoke of the critical scenarios in a few hours and clearly name the risks. The decision is the customer's, but I record it in writing, suggest a check right after the release with a rollback plan, and keep my manager informed.

mq-13:14.title: During testing you found a bug unrelated to your task. What do you do?
mq-13:14.html:
File it as a separate ticket, don't stay silent and don't add it to the current task.

  • Check that there isn't already such a bug.
  • Write a full report with severity.
  • If the bug is critical, tell the team right away, not just create a ticket.
  • Note whether it blocks the current task and link the tickets.
In an interview: I check that there isn't already such a bug, and file a separate ticket with a full report instead of adding it to the current task. If it is critical, I tell the team at once. And if it blocks my task, I link the tickets and mention it at the daily.

mq-13:15.title: How do you estimate the time for testing a task?
mq-13:15.html:
I break it into components and take risks into account:

  • Requirements analysis and questions.
  • Test design: cases, data.
  • Execution: positive, negative, integrations, cross-browser.
  • Retest after fixes: I usually allow a cycle or two.
  • Regression of the affected areas, automated tests.

Coefficients: new or familiar functionality, the quality of requirements, environment stability. I check against the history of similar tasks. I give the estimate as a range and say what it depends on, and if the requirements are unclear, I first allocate time for clarifying.

In an interview: I break the work into requirements analysis, test design, execution, retests and regression, and check against the history of similar tasks. I take into account how new the functionality is and whether the environment is stable. I give the estimate as a range and explain what it depends on, and if the requirements are vague, I first allow time for clarifying them.

mq-13:16.title: How would you test exporting a statement to PDF or CSV?
mq-13:16.html:
• Data: operations for the period match the history and the database; amounts, currencies, dates; totals add up.
  • Filters: period boundaries (inclusive or not), an empty period, a very large period, the time zone.
  • Format: the CSV opens in Excel without broken characters (UTF-8 encoding, Cyrillic), separators, the decimal sign; the PDF: layout, page breaks, details.
  • Volume: thousands of operations: generation time, file size, asynchronous generation with a notification.
  • Security: only own accounts, masking of card numbers, access to the file by link.
  • CSV injection: values starting with =, +, -, @ aren't executed as formulas in Excel.
In an interview: I check that the data in the statement matches the history and the database and the totals add up, the period boundaries and time zones, the format: Cyrillic and separators in the CSV, the layout in the PDF. Separately, large volumes, access only to own accounts, card masking, and CSV injection, where a value with an equals sign is executed in Excel as a formula.

mq-13:17.title: Incomplete or contradictory requirements
mq-13:17.html:
First I analyse the requirements and record specific questions, not a general "it's unclear". I clarify with the PO, a business analyst or a developer, preferably in writing, in a ticket or Confluence, so that the decision stays documented. I show contradictions with the example of a specific scenario.

If there is no answer yet, I rely on sources of implicit requirements: the behaviour of similar functionality in the product, competitors, UX standards and common sense. I explicitly record my assumptions in test cases or comments. Questions that block work I raise at the daily.

It is best to ask such questions at the grooming or refinement stage, before development starts. This is part of the shift-left approach: a defect in requirements is cheapest to fix before any code is written.

mq-13:18.title: Testing a login form
mq-13:18.html:
Positive checks: login with valid data, session persistence, the "Remember me" option, redirect to the right page, logout. I also check login with Enter, browser autofill and working on different devices.

Negative: a wrong password, a nonexistent email, empty fields, an invalid email format, spaces at the start and end, case in the email and password. The error message must not hint which exactly is wrong, the login or the password.

Security: the password is hidden and doesn't end up in the URL or logs, transmission only over HTTPS, blocking or CAPTCHA after several failed attempts. Also SQL injections and XSS in the fields, the HttpOnly and Secure flags for cookies, session invalidation after logout. Separately, the UI, keyboard accessibility and password recovery.

sq-0:0.title: What is a relational database and what is SQL?
sq-0:0.html:
A relational database stores data in tables: each row is one record (a user, an account, a transaction), each column is its property. Tables are linked to each other with keys: a transaction knows which account it belongs to, and an account knows which user.

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to work with this data: read, add, change, delete and describe the structure. The main feature is that SQL is declarative: you describe what you want to get, and how exactly to find it is decided by the DBMS itself.

Popular DBMSs: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle. Basic SQL is the same in them, and the details differ: LIMIT versus TOP, date functions, some types. The examples in this guide are for PostgreSQL.

In an interview: A relational database stores data in tables linked to each other, and SQL is a declarative language for working with them: I describe what data I want, and the database decides how to find it. I have worked mostly with PostgreSQL, but the basic syntax is the same across different DBMSs.

sq-0:1.title: What are a primary key and a foreign key?
sq-0:1.html:
• A primary key (PRIMARY KEY) is a column that uniquely identifies a row. It is unique and can't be NULL. Usually it is id.
  • A foreign key (FOREIGN KEY) is a column that references the primary key of another table. It creates a link and doesn't let you write a reference to a nonexistent record.

In our schema accounts.user_id references users.id. An attempt to create an account for user 999, who doesn't exist, will fail with a foreign key violation error.

CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  balance  NUMERIC(14,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
In an interview: A primary key uniquely identifies a row: it is unique and never empty. A foreign key references the primary key of another table and guarantees integrity: for example, you can't create an account for a user who doesn't exist. For me as QA it is also a hint of what to test: whether the system handles such errors correctly.

sq-0:2.title: Which data types should QA know?
sq-0:2.html:
TypeWhat forWhat to watch for
INTEGER, BIGINTIntegers, IDsRange limits: INTEGER up to ~2.1 billion
NUMERIC(p,s) / DECIMALExact fractions, moneyNUMERIC(14,2): up to 14 digits, 2 after the point
REAL, DOUBLE PRECISIONApproximate fractionsThey have an error: not for money
VARCHAR(n), TEXTStringsLength: what happens with a string longer than n
BOOLEANYes / noMay also be NULL
DATE, TIMESTAMP, TIMESTAMPTZDates and timeWith or without a time zone
UUID, JSONBUnique IDs, flexible dataFormat, nested fields

A column's type directly suggests boundary values for tests: the maximum string length, the number of decimal places, the numeric range.

In an interview: Most often I deal with integers for IDs, NUMERIC for money, strings, booleans and dates with or without a time zone. A column's type is for me a source of boundary values: the maximum string length, the number of decimal places, the numeric range. If the UI allows more than the database, that is a potential bug.

sq-0:3.title: What is NULL and how does it differ from 0 and an empty string?
sq-0:3.html:
NULL means "the value is unknown or absent". It is neither zero nor an empty string:

  • 0 is a known value: the balance is zero.
  • '' is a known value: a string with nothing in it.
  • NULL is an unknown value: the balance hasn't been calculated yet, the phone isn't given.

The main property: any comparison with NULL gives neither TRUE nor FALSE, but UNKNOWN. Even NULL = NULL is not TRUE. And arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 100 + NULL = NULL.

Because of this NULL is a source of many bugs: rows "disappear" from filters, sums become empty, counters don't add up.

In an interview: NULL means that a value is unknown or absent: it is neither zero nor an empty string. Any comparison with NULL gives not "yes" and not "no", but "unknown", so rows with NULL often drop out of filters, and arithmetic with NULL gives NULL. So I always check separately how the system behaves with empty values.

sq-0:4.title: Which groups are SQL commands divided into?
sq-0:4.html:
GroupCommandsWhat they do
DQL: queriesSELECTRead data
DML: manipulationINSERT, UPDATE, DELETEChange data
DDL: definitionCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATEChange structure
DCL: accessGRANT, REVOKEManage permissions
TCL: transactionsBEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACKManage transactions

Sometimes SELECT is put under DML: both variants occur.

In an interview: SQL commands are divided into groups: SELECT for reading, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE for changing data, CREATE, ALTER and DROP for structure, GRANT and REVOKE for permissions, and BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK for transactions. As QA I write SELECT most often, and INSERT and UPDATE less often, for preparing test data, and always in a transaction.

sq-0:5.title: Why does QA need to know SQL?
sq-0:5.html:
• Verifying the result: the UI shows "Transfer successful", but does the database have the right amount, status, fee, a record in the history?
  • Test data: find a user in the needed state or create one without going through ten steps in the UI.
  • Diagnostics: is the bug in the front end, in the API or in the data itself? A database query often answers in a minute.
  • Integrity: find duplicates, "orphaned" records, impossible states.
  • Automated tests: data preparation and cleanup, checks after actions.
In an interview: SQL for me is a way to check the truth outside the interface. The UI may show "success", while the database has the wrong amount or status. I also use SQL to quickly find or create test data, to localise a bug (front end, backend or data) and to look for integrity violations such as duplicates or records without a parent.

sq-1:0.title: How is a SELECT query structured?
sq-1:0.html:
The minimal query is SELECT and FROM. The other parts are optional, but are always written in this order:

SELECT   email, country          -- which columns
FROM     users                   -- from which table
WHERE    country = 'PL'          -- row filter
GROUP BY ...                     -- grouping
HAVING   ...                     -- group filter
ORDER BY created_at DESC         -- sorting
LIMIT    10;                     -- limiting the count

-- SELECT * returns all columns: convenient for exploration,
-- but in automated tests and reports it is better to list columns explicitly
In an interview: A query starts with SELECT and a list of columns, then FROM with a table, and then, as needed, WHERE for a filter, GROUP BY and HAVING for grouping, ORDER BY for sorting and LIMIT for restriction. For quick exploration I write SELECT star, but in automated tests I list the columns explicitly, so the test doesn't depend on changes to the table's structure.

sq-1:1.title: In what order is a query actually executed?
sq-1:1.html:
The logical order differs from the order of writing:

  1. FROM and JOIN: assemble rows from the tables
  2. WHERE: filter the rows
  3. GROUP BY: group
  4. HAVING: filter the groups
  5. SELECT: compute columns and aliases
  6. DISTINCT: remove duplicates
  7. ORDER BY: sort
  8. LIMIT / OFFSET: cut off

Practical consequences: an alias from SELECT can't be used in WHERE, because at the WHERE moment it doesn't exist yet. But in ORDER BY it can, because sorting goes after SELECT. And an aggregate function can't be put in WHERE; for that there is HAVING.

-- error: the alias amount_usd doesn't exist yet at the WHERE stage
SELECT amount * 0.25 AS amount_usd FROM transactions WHERE amount_usd > 100;

-- correct: repeat the expression
SELECT amount * 0.25 AS amount_usd FROM transactions WHERE amount * 0.25 > 100;

-- and in ORDER BY the alias works
SELECT amount * 0.25 AS amount_usd FROM transactions ORDER BY amount_usd DESC;
In an interview: A query isn't executed in the order it is written: first FROM and JOIN, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and only then SELECT, ORDER BY and LIMIT. That is why an alias from SELECT can't be used in WHERE, but can in ORDER BY, and why aggregates are filtered with HAVING and not with WHERE.

sq-1:2.title: Which operators are used in WHERE?
sq-1:2.html:
• Comparison: =, <> or !=, >, <, >=, <=.
  • Logical: AND, OR, NOT.
  • Sets and ranges: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL.

The trap is precedence: AND is evaluated before OR. Without parentheses a query may return something quite different.

-- intended: failed transactions of type deposit or withdrawal
-- in fact: (deposit) OR (withdrawal AND failed)
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE type = 'deposit' OR type = 'withdrawal' AND status = 'failed';

-- correct
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE (type = 'deposit' OR type = 'withdrawal') AND status = 'failed';
In an interview: In WHERE I use comparison operators, the logical AND, OR, NOT, as well as IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL. The main trap is precedence: AND is evaluated before OR, so when combining them I always put parentheses, so that the query does exactly what I intended.

sq-1:3.title: How do IN, BETWEEN and LIKE work?
sq-1:3.html:
• IN: the value is in a list: status IN ('pending', 'failed').
  • BETWEEN: a range inclusive of both boundaries: amount BETWEEN 100 AND 500 is >= 100 AND <= 500.
  • LIKE: pattern search: % is any number of characters, _ is exactly one. In PostgreSQL ILIKE ignores case.

The BETWEEN trap with dates: created_at BETWEEN '2026-09-01' AND '2026-09-30' for a column with time will cut off the whole day of 30 September after 00:00. A half-open range is more reliable.

-- reliable for TIMESTAMP: including the 1st, without 1 October
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01';

-- all gmail addresses, case-insensitively
SELECT email FROM users WHERE email ILIKE '%@gmail.com';
In an interview: IN checks membership in a list, BETWEEN a range inclusive of both boundaries, and LIKE searches by a pattern, where the percent sign is any number of characters and the underscore is one character. With dates I don't use BETWEEN: if the column has a time, the last day gets cut off. Instead I write "greater than or equal to the start and less than the next day".

sq-1:4.title: How do you find rows where the value is NULL?
sq-1:4.html:
Only through IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. The condition = NULL gives UNKNOWN for every row, so the query will return zero rows with no error at all. This is especially treacherous: it seems that there is simply no data.

The second trap: WHERE status <> 'failed' won't return rows where status is NULL. If they are needed, the condition must be supplemented.

SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone IS NULL;       -- correct
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = NULL;        -- always 0 rows

-- everything except failed, including NULL
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE status <> 'failed' OR status IS NULL;

-- or in PostgreSQL
SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'failed';
In an interview: I look for empty values only through IS NULL, because a comparison "equals NULL" always gives "unknown" and returns zero rows without an error. And I remember the reverse trap: a "not equal" condition also skips rows with NULL, so if they are needed, I add OR IS NULL.

sq-1:5.title: What does DISTINCT do?
sq-1:5.html:
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result. Uniqueness is counted by the whole combination of the selected columns, not by the first one.

SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users;              -- a list of countries
SELECT DISTINCT currency, status FROM accounts;   -- unique pairs
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM accounts;    -- how many users have an account
In an interview: DISTINCT removes duplicates from the result, with uniqueness counted by the whole combination of columns. I use it to see the set of possible values, for example all the statuses in a table: it is a quick way to notice an unexpected value that isn't described in the documentation.

sq-1:6.title: How do ORDER BY and LIMIT work?
sq-1:6.html:
• ORDER BY col ASC is ascending (the default), DESC is descending. You can sort by several columns.
  • LIMIT n returns n rows, OFFSET k skips k. In SQL Server, instead of LIMIT there is TOP n or OFFSET … FETCH.

Two traps:

  • LIMIT without ORDER BY returns arbitrary rows. Without ORDER BY the order is not guaranteed anywhere: a test for "the first record" will be unstable.
  • NULL in sorting: in PostgreSQL NULL is considered greater than all values: at the end for ASC and at the start for DESC. In MySQL it is the other way round. Explicitly: NULLS LAST.
-- the 10 latest transactions; id as a second key makes the order stable
SELECT * FROM transactions
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;
In an interview: ORDER BY sorts in ascending or descending order, and LIMIT restricts the number of rows. Without ORDER BY the order isn't guaranteed, so LIMIT without sorting gives random rows and unstable tests. For stability I add a second sort key, for example id, and I remember that different DBMSs place NULL differently when sorting.

sq-2:0.title: What aggregate functions are there?
sq-2:0.html:
An aggregate function reduces many rows to one value:

  • COUNT: the count
  • SUM: the sum
  • AVG: the average
  • MIN, MAX: the minimum and maximum (work with dates and strings too)
SELECT COUNT(*)    AS total,
       SUM(amount) AS volume,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_amount,
       MAX(created_at) AS last_tx
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'completed';
In an interview: Aggregate functions reduce many rows to one value: COUNT counts the number, SUM the total, AVG the average, MIN and MAX the extreme values, and not only for numbers but also for dates. For example, MAX of the creation date quickly shows when the last transaction was.

sq-2:1.title: How do COUNT(*), COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col) differ?
sq-2:1.html:
• COUNT(*) is the number of rows, including those with NULL.
  • COUNT(phone) is the number of rows where phone is not NULL.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is the number of unique non-empty values.

If a table has 100 users and 30 without a phone: COUNT(*) = 100, COUNT(phone) = 70. The difference between them is a quick way to count empty values.

SELECT COUNT(*)                AS users_total,
       COUNT(phone)            AS with_phone,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(phone) AS without_phone
FROM users;
In an interview: COUNT star counts all rows, COUNT of a column only those where the value is not NULL, and COUNT DISTINCT the number of unique non-empty values. The difference between the first two immediately shows how many records have an empty field, and I often use this to check data completeness after a migration.

sq-2:2.title: How does GROUP BY work?
sq-2:2.html:
GROUP BY splits rows into groups with equal values and computes an aggregate for each group separately.

The rule: every column in SELECT must be either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function. Otherwise it is unclear which of the group's many values to show, and the database will return an error.

-- the number and volume of transactions by type and status
SELECT type, status, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(amount) AS volume
FROM transactions
GROUP BY type, status
ORDER BY type, status;

-- error: email is neither in GROUP BY nor in an aggregate
SELECT country, email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY country;
In an interview: GROUP BY splits rows into groups with equal values and computes an aggregate for each group. The rule is simple: every column in SELECT must be either in GROUP BY or in an aggregate function. I often group by status to see the distribution of data and notice anomalies, for example an unexpectedly large number of failed.

sq-2:3.title: How does WHERE differ from HAVING?
sq-2:3.html:
• WHERE filters rows before grouping. Aggregates can't be used in it.
  • HAVING filters groups after grouping, by the results of aggregates.

If a condition can go into WHERE, it goes there: fewer rows go into grouping, and the query is faster.

-- users who have more than 3 failed transactions in September
SELECT a.user_id, COUNT(*) AS failed_cnt
FROM transactions t
JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
WHERE t.status = 'failed'                      -- row filter
  AND t.created_at >= '2026-09-01'
  AND t.created_at <  '2026-10-01'
GROUP BY a.user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;                           -- group filter
In an interview: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, and HAVING filters ready groups by the results of aggregates. So a condition like "the count is more than three" can only be written in HAVING. And everything that can be filtered before grouping I put in WHERE, so the query processes less data.

sq-2:4.title: How do aggregates behave with NULL? What is COALESCE?
sq-2:4.html:
• SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX ignore NULL. AVG of (100, NULL, 200) is 150, not 100.
  • An aggregate over an empty set of rows returns NULL, not 0. The exception is COUNT, which returns 0.

COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first value that is not NULL. It is used to substitute default values.

-- the sum of deposits of a user without transactions is NULL, not 0
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 999;          -- NULL
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 999; -- 0
In an interview: Aggregate functions ignore NULL, so the average is computed only over filled values. And a sum over an empty set of rows returns not zero but NULL, and if the code doesn't expect that, an empty field or an error will appear on screen. To turn NULL into a default value I use COALESCE.

sq-2:5.title: How do you use CASE WHEN and conditional aggregation?
sq-2:5.html:
CASE is conditional logic in a query, the equivalent of if/else. It is especially useful together with aggregates: you can compute several indicators in one pass.

SELECT
  type,
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed,        -- PostgreSQL
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS completed_volume,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') / COUNT(*), 1) AS failed_pct
FROM transactions
GROUP BY type;

-- amount categories
SELECT id,
  CASE WHEN amount < 100  THEN 'small'
       WHEN amount < 1000 THEN 'medium'
       ELSE 'large' END AS bucket
FROM transactions;
In an interview: CASE WHEN is conditional logic in a query, like if-else. It is most useful to combine it with aggregates: in one query I can compute the total count, the number of failed ones and their percentage for each transaction type. Note the 100.0: without the fractional part, integer division would give zero.

sq-2:6.title: WHERE vs HAVING and grouping
sq-2:6.html:
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, so aggregate functions can't be used in it. HAVING filters the already formed groups after GROUP BY and works with aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG. The order of execution: FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

A query: the number of orders per user, only where more than 5:

SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS orders_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY orders_count DESC;

In a SELECT with GROUP BY you may list only grouping fields and aggregates. If you also need the user's name, I add a JOIN with users and group by id and name. A filter such as "only paid orders" I put in WHERE, so it works before grouping and is more efficient.

sq-3:0.title: What is a JOIN and why is it needed?
sq-3:0.html:
Data is spread across different tables so as not to be duplicated: an email is stored once in users, not in every transaction. JOIN connects tables by a condition, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key, and lets you get the full picture in one query.

-- transactions with the owner's email
SELECT t.id, t.amount, t.status, u.email
FROM transactions t
JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
JOIN users    u ON u.id = a.user_id;
In an interview: JOIN connects tables by a condition, usually by a foreign key. Data is stored in different tables so as not to be duplicated, and JOIN brings it together: for example, a transaction, an account and the owner's email in one query.

sq-3:1.title: How does INNER JOIN work?
sq-3:1.html:
It returns only the rows for which a match was found in both tables. Rows without a match disappear from the result. The word INNER can be omitted: JOIN is inner by default.

A consequence for QA: if an INNER JOIN result "lacks" records, maybe they have no match, and that itself may be a data bug.

-- only users who have at least one account
SELECT u.email, a.currency, a.balance
FROM users u
INNER JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id;
In an interview: INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have a match in both tables, and the rest disappear. So if after a JOIN there are fewer records than expected, I check whether some records have no match: it may be a problem in the data.

sq-3:2.title: How does LEFT JOIN work?
sq-3:2.html:
It returns all rows from the left table, and from the right only those that found a match. If there is no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL.

-- all users, even without accounts
SELECT u.email, a.id AS account_id, a.balance
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id;

-- result:
-- anna@test.com | 10 | 500.00
-- ivan@test.com | 11 | 0.00
-- olha@test.com | NULL | NULL     <- no account
In an interview: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, and from the right only those that have a match, otherwise NULL. I use it when it is important not to lose records: for example, to show all users, including those who don't have an account yet.

sq-3:3.title: What are RIGHT, FULL OUTER and CROSS JOIN?
sq-3:3.html:
• RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT: all rows from the right table. In practice it is almost always replaced with LEFT by swapping the tables, which is more readable.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN is all rows from both tables; where there is no match, NULL. Useful for reconciling two data sets. MySQL doesn't have it: it is emulated with a UNION of two LEFT JOINs.
  • CROSS JOIN is every row with every row (a Cartesian product). 1000 × 1000 = a million rows. Sometimes useful for generating combinations of test data.
-- reconciliation: our transactions against the provider's statement
SELECT o.id AS our_id, p.external_id AS provider_id
FROM transactions o
FULL OUTER JOIN provider_report p ON p.external_id = o.external_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL OR p.external_id IS NULL;   -- present on one side only
In an interview: RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT, and it is usually replaced with LEFT by swapping the tables. FULL OUTER JOIN returns everything from both sides, and it is ideal for reconciling two data sets, for example our transactions with a provider's statement. CROSS JOIN gives all combinations of rows, so you have to be careful with it.

sq-3:4.title: How do you find records that have no match in another table?
sq-3:4.html:
The classic technique is an anti-join: a LEFT JOIN and a condition that the right table's key IS NULL. The alternative is NOT EXISTS.

For QA this is one of the most useful queries: "orphaned" records are a frequent sign of a bug.

-- users without a single account
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id
WHERE a.id IS NULL;

-- the same through NOT EXISTS
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.user_id = u.id);
In an interview: I look for records without a match through a LEFT JOIN with the condition that the right table's key IS NULL, or through NOT EXISTS. This is one of my main queries for integrity checks: for example, users without an account after registration, or transactions without an account, mean a process broke off somewhere in the middle.

sq-3:5.title: What is the difference between a condition in ON and in WHERE with a LEFT JOIN?
sq-3:5.html:
• A condition in ON affects which rows of the right table are joined. All rows of the left one remain.
  • A condition in WHERE filters the ready result. Rows without a match have NULL, and the condition a.status = 'active' gives UNKNOWN for them, so they disappear. The LEFT JOIN quietly turns into an INNER one.
-- all users + their active accounts (if any)
SELECT u.email, a.id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id AND a.status = 'active';

-- a trap: users without an active account will disappear
SELECT u.email, a.id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id
WHERE a.status = 'active';
In an interview: With a LEFT JOIN, a condition on the right table in ON only limits what is joined, and all the left rows remain. And the same condition in WHERE discards the rows where the right side is NULL, and the LEFT JOIN effectively becomes an INNER. It is a subtle mistake: the query works without errors, but returns less data than needed.

sq-3:6.title: Why did the row count grow after a JOIN and the sum double?
sq-3:6.html:
If the join is "one to many", each row on the "one" side is repeated as many times as it has matches. That is normal, but aggregates over columns of the "one" side become wrong after such a JOIN.

Example: a user has 2 accounts and 5 transactions. A JOIN users → accounts → transactions gives 5 rows, and SUM(a.balance) will count each account's balance several times.

How to avoid it: aggregate before the JOIN in a subquery or CTE, or count from the table of the right level.

-- wrong: the account balance is multiplied by the number of its transactions
SELECT u.id, SUM(a.balance), COUNT(t.id)
FROM users u
JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.id
GROUP BY u.id;

-- right: aggregate the transactions separately, then join
WITH tx AS (
  SELECT account_id, COUNT(*) AS tx_cnt FROM transactions GROUP BY account_id
)
SELECT u.id, SUM(a.balance) AS total_balance, COALESCE(SUM(tx.tx_cnt), 0) AS tx_cnt
FROM users u
JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN tx ON tx.account_id = a.id
GROUP BY u.id;
In an interview: In a one-to-many join the row on the "one" side is duplicated for each pair, and aggregates over its columns get doubled. So when I count sums across several levels, user, accounts, transactions, I first aggregate the child table in a subquery and then join. And as QA I use this trap as a hint: if a report shows doubled sums, the first thing I check is the JOIN.

sq-3:7.title: What is a self join?
sq-3:7.html:
Joining a table with itself when rows reference other rows of the same table. The classic is an employee and their manager in one employees table. Different aliases are required.

SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id;
In an interview: A self join is joining a table with itself, when a row references another row of the same table, like an employee referencing a manager. The table is included twice with different aliases. A LEFT JOIN is needed here so as not to lose a top-level executive who has no manager.

sq-3:8.title: Types of JOIN and users without orders
sq-3:8.html:
INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows of the left table and the matches from the right, and where there is no match, NULL. RIGHT JOIN does the same the other way round, FULL JOIN returns all rows from both tables.

CROSS JOIN gives a Cartesian product, every row with every row. SELF JOIN is joining a table with itself, for example an employee and their manager in the same table. The join condition is set with ON.

Users without orders is a classic task for a LEFT JOIN with a NULL check:

SELECT u.id, u.name
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

The alternative is WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id). The NOT IN variant is dangerous: if the subquery has a NULL, it won't return a single row.

sq-4:0.title: What is a subquery and where can it be used?
sq-4:0.html:
A subquery is a query inside another query, in parentheses.

  • Scalar: returns one value, can be compared: WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) …).
  • In WHERE with IN / EXISTS: a membership or existence check.
  • In FROM: a temporary table, with an alias required.
  • Correlated: references the outer query and is logically executed for each of its rows.
-- transactions larger than the average
SELECT id, amount FROM transactions
WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM transactions);

-- correlated: each account's largest transaction
SELECT t.* FROM transactions t
WHERE t.amount = (SELECT MAX(t2.amount)
                  FROM transactions t2
                  WHERE t2.account_id = t.account_id);
In an interview: A subquery is a query in parentheses inside another query. It can return one value for comparison, a list for IN, a temporary table in FROM, or be correlated, referencing the outer query and being executed for each of its rows. For example, finding transactions larger than the average is easiest with a scalar subquery.

sq-4:1.title: How does IN differ from EXISTS?
sq-4:1.html:
• IN compares a value with a list returned by a subquery.
  • EXISTS only checks whether the subquery returns at least one row, and can stop at the first one found.

For positive checks modern optimisers often execute both variants the same way. The real difference is in handling NULL in the negative form: NOT EXISTS behaves predictably, and NOT IN doesn't (see the next question).

-- users who have at least one failed transaction
SELECT u.email FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
  JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.id
  WHERE a.user_id = u.id AND t.status = 'failed'
);
In an interview: IN compares a value with a list from a subquery, and EXISTS only checks whether there is at least one row and can stop at the first. In the positive form modern databases often execute them the same way, so the main difference is in negation: NOT EXISTS is safe, and NOT IN breaks if the subquery contains NULL.

sq-4:2.title: Why can NOT IN return zero rows?
sq-4:2.html:
If the subquery in NOT IN returns at least one NULL, the condition becomes UNKNOWN for every row, and the result is empty. With no error at all.

The logic: 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means 5 <> 1 AND 5 <> 2 AND 5 <> NULL. The last is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition is not TRUE.

The solution: NOT EXISTS, an anti-join through LEFT JOIN, or explicitly filter out NULL in the subquery.

-- if at least one account.user_id = NULL, it returns 0 rows
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM accounts);

-- safe
SELECT * FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.user_id = u.id);
In an interview: If the subquery in NOT IN returns at least one NULL, the comparison with it gives "unknown", and the whole query returns zero rows without an error. So to find missing records I use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN with a NULL check. Such a bug is easy to miss: the query looks right and just finds nothing.

sq-4:3.title: What is a CTE (WITH) and why is it needed?
sq-4:3.html:
A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named temporary result declared with WITH before the main query. The same as a subquery in FROM, but with a name.

  • Readability: a complex query is split into clear steps from top to bottom.
  • Reuse: one CTE can be referenced several times.
  • Recursion: WITH RECURSIVE walks hierarchies, for example a category tree or subordination.
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT a.user_id, SUM(t.amount) AS deposits
  FROM transactions t
  JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
  WHERE t.type = 'deposit' AND t.status = 'completed'
    AND t.created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND t.created_at < '2026-10-01'
  GROUP BY a.user_id
)
SELECT u.email, m.deposits
FROM monthly m
JOIN users u ON u.id = m.user_id
WHERE m.deposits > 10000
ORDER BY m.deposits DESC;
In an interview: A CTE is a named intermediate result declared with WITH. It makes a complex query readable: I break it into steps, each with a name, and can refer to a step several times. There is also a recursive variant for hierarchies, for example a category tree.

sq-4:4.title: How does UNION differ from UNION ALL? What are INTERSECT and EXCEPT?
sq-4:4.html:
• UNION combines the results of two queries and removes duplicates, so it is slower.
  • UNION ALL combines everything as is, with duplicates. If duplicates can't occur or are needed, take it.
  • INTERSECT: the rows present in both results.
  • EXCEPT: the rows from the first that aren't in the second (in Oracle it is MINUS).

The condition: the same number of columns and compatible types.

-- emails that are in the old system but missing in the new one after migration
SELECT email FROM legacy_users
EXCEPT
SELECT email FROM users;
In an interview: UNION combines results and removes duplicates, UNION ALL doesn't remove them, so it is faster. INTERSECT gives the common rows, and EXCEPT the rows of the first query that aren't in the second. EXCEPT is very handy for checking migrations: with one query I see which records didn't get transferred.

sq-5:0.title: How do you add data with INSERT?
sq-5:0.html:
List the columns explicitly, then the query won't break if new ones are added to the table. You can insert several rows at once. In PostgreSQL RETURNING immediately returns the created values, for example a generated id.

INSERT INTO users (email, name, country)
VALUES ('qa_1@test.com', 'QA One', 'PL'),
       ('qa_2@test.com', 'QA Two', 'UA')
RETURNING id, email;

-- inserting the result of another query
INSERT INTO accounts (user_id, currency, balance)
SELECT id, 'PLN', 0 FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'qa_%@test.com';
In an interview: INSERT adds rows; I always list the columns explicitly so the query doesn't break from changes in the table, and I can insert several rows at once. In PostgreSQL RETURNING immediately returns the generated id, which is handy for preparing test data: I created a user and at once have their id for the next steps.

sq-5:1.title: How do you run UPDATE and DELETE safely?
sq-5:1.html:
The main rule: UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE change the whole table. A habit that saves you:

  1. First write a SELECT with the same WHERE and look at which rows and how many will be changed.
  2. Open a transaction.
  3. Run the change and check the number of changed rows.
  4. COMMIT if all is as expected, ROLLBACK if not.
SELECT id, status FROM accounts WHERE user_id = 42;   -- 1. what we will touch

BEGIN;                                                -- 2.
UPDATE accounts SET status = 'blocked' WHERE user_id = 42;
-- UPDATE 2   <- we expected 2 accounts                 3.
COMMIT;                                               -- 4. or ROLLBACK;
In an interview: UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE change the whole table, so I have an iron habit: first a SELECT with the same WHERE to see which rows I'll touch, then the change in a transaction, a check of the number of changed rows and only then COMMIT. If the number is wrong, ROLLBACK.

sq-5:2.title: How do DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP differ?
sq-5:2.html:
DELETETRUNCATEDROP
What it removesRows (can use WHERE)All rowsThe whole table with its structure
WHEREYesNoNo
SpeedSlow, row by rowFastFast
Row triggersFireNoNo
RollbackIn a transaction, yesDepends on the DBMS: yes in PostgreSQL, no in MySQLDepends on the DBMS
The id counterNot resetMySQL resets it; PostgreSQL only with RESTART IDENTITYDisappears with the table
In an interview: DELETE removes rows by a condition, works row by row, fires triggers and rolls back in a transaction. TRUNCATE quickly removes all rows without a condition, and whether it can be rolled back depends on the DBMS. DROP removes the table together with its structure. For cleaning up test data I use DELETE with a precise filter, and TRUNCATE only on my own local environment.

sq-5:3.title: What is a transaction and how does QA use it?
sq-5:3.html:
A transaction is a group of operations that are executed as a whole: either all or none. A transfer is a debit from one account and a credit to another; if the second one failed, the first must also roll back.

  • BEGIN: start
  • COMMIT: save the changes
  • ROLLBACK: cancel everything from the start of the transaction

How QA uses it: to change data manually in a safe way (there is a way back); to prepare a state for verification and roll back afterwards; to test that the application doesn't leave "half-finished" operations on failure.

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 10;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 11;
-- I check that both balances are correct
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (10, 11);
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK if something is wrong
In an interview: A transaction is a group of operations executed as a whole: either all or none. A classic example is a transfer: the debit and the credit must go through together. As QA I use transactions to change data safely with the ability to roll back, and I test that the application doesn't leave half-finished operations if a failure happens in the middle.

sq-5:4.title: What is ACID?
sq-5:4.html:
• Atomicity: a transaction is executed completely or not at all.
  • Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another without violating constraints: keys, CHECK, uniqueness.
  • Isolation: parallel transactions don't see each other's intermediate states (the degree depends on the isolation level).
  • Durability: after COMMIT the data won't disappear even on a server failure.
In an interview: ACID is four guarantees of transactions. Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the database moves between valid states without violating constraints. Isolation: parallel transactions don't see each other's intermediate states. Durability: what was committed with COMMIT won't disappear even on a failure. Using a transfer as the example: money can't be debited without being credited, and two parallel transfers can't both spend the same balance.

sq-5:5.title: What are isolation levels and which concurrency problems do they solve?
sq-5:5.html:
Anomalies that arise when transactions work at the same time:

  • Dirty read: reading uncommitted changes of another transaction, which are then rolled back.
  • Non-repeatable read: reading the same row again within a transaction gives a different value.
  • Phantom read: a repeated query with the same filter returns new rows.
  • Lost update: two transactions read a balance of 100, both subtract 80 and write 20. One debit got "lost".

The levels from weaker to stronger: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable. By default PostgreSQL uses Read Committed, and MySQL InnoDB uses Repeatable Read.

Protection against a lost update: an atomic UPDATE … SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE balance >= 80, row locking with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or a higher isolation level.

BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 10 FOR UPDATE;  -- locks the row
-- a second transaction with FOR UPDATE will wait here
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = 10;
COMMIT;
In an interview: When transactions run at the same time, anomalies occur: a dirty read of uncommitted data, a non-repeatable read, phantom rows and a lost update. Isolation levels, from Read Uncommitted to Serializable, protect against them to different degrees; in PostgreSQL the default is Read Committed. As QA I test this with parallel requests: for example, two simultaneous debits from one account must not produce a negative balance.

sq-5:6.title: How do you safely change data on a shared test environment?
sq-5:6.html:
• Work only with your own data: mark it with a marker (an email prefix qa_, a tag, a separate tenant) and filter by it.
  • First SELECT, then the change in a transaction, a check of the row count.
  • Don't touch data that colleagues or automated tests depend on; if you have to, warn in the team channel.
  • Keep preparation and cleanup scripts so that they can be repeated.
  • Never make changes in production. Production access is read-only and only if allowed.
In an interview: On a shared environment I change only my own data, marked with a marker, for example a prefix in the email, and filter by it. First a SELECT, then the change in a transaction with a check of the row count. I keep the preparation and cleanup scripts so they can be repeated, and I warn the team if I touch shared data.

sq-5:7.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP and caution
sq-5:7.html:
DELETE removes rows by a WHERE condition, writes each operation to the log, fires triggers and can be rolled back in a transaction. TRUNCATE quickly empties the whole table without conditions and usually resets the autoincrement counter. DROP removes the table itself together with its structure, indexes and data.

On a shared environment one mistake affects the whole team: a DELETE or UPDATE without WHERE changes all rows. So first I write a SELECT with the same condition and check which rows exactly will be changed. I delete only my own test data, preferably marked with a prefix or a separate account.

Transactions help: BEGIN, then the change, checking the result and ROLLBACK if something is wrong, or COMMIT if all is right. It is worth remembering that in PostgreSQL TRUNCATE can be rolled back in a transaction, but in MySQL it can't, because there it is a DDL command with an implicit COMMIT. In production I change nothing without approval and a backup.

sq-6:0.title: What constraints are there and how do you test them?
sq-6:0.html:
• PRIMARY KEY: a unique row identifier.
  • FOREIGN KEY: a reference must point to an existing record.
  • NOT NULL: the value is required.
  • UNIQUE: no repeats, for example email.
  • CHECK: an arbitrary condition, for example balance >= 0.
  • DEFAULT: the value if none was passed.

For QA constraints are a ready list of negative cases: what does the application do when the database rejects a record? The message must be clear to the user, not a "500 Internal Server Error" with the database's error text.

ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT balance_non_negative CHECK (balance >= 0);
ALTER TABLE users    ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email);

-- test: registration with an already existing email through the UI/API
-- expected: 409 or a clear message, not 500
In an interview: The main constraints are primary and foreign keys, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and default values. For me they are ready negative cases: I check how the application reacts when the database rejects a record, for example registration with an existing email must give a clear message, not a five hundred error with text from the database.

sq-6:1.title: What happens to child records when a parent is deleted?
sq-6:1.html:
It is determined by the foreign key's ON DELETE option:

  • RESTRICT / NO ACTION (the default): the parent can't be deleted while child records exist.
  • CASCADE: child records are deleted together with the parent.
  • SET NULL: the reference in the children becomes NULL.

What to test: deleting a user with accounts: an error, a cascade or a "soft delete"? Was history that must be kept removed by a cascade?

In an interview: This is determined by the foreign key's setting: RESTRICT forbids deletion while child records exist, CASCADE deletes them together with the parent, and SET NULL nulls the reference. I check that the behaviour matches the requirements: for example, that deleting a user won't destroy by cascade the transaction history that must be kept by law.

sq-6:2.title: What is an index and why is it needed?
sq-6:2.html:
An index is a separate data structure (most often a B-tree) that lets you find rows without scanning the whole table. An analogy is a subject index in a book.

  • Pros: fast search, JOIN and sorting by the indexed columns.
  • Cons: takes space and slows down INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, because the index also has to be updated.

A primary key and UNIQUE automatically create an index. Foreign keys in PostgreSQL don't, and they are often indexed manually.

For QA: if a search or a filter in the UI is slow on large data, one of the first hypotheses is a missing index.

CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_account_created
  ON transactions (account_id, created_at);
In an interview: An index is a separate structure, like a pointer in a book, that lets you find rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds up search and JOIN, but takes space and slows down writes. As QA I mention indexes when a filter or a report is slow on a large amount of data, and then together with a developer we look at the query plan.

sq-6:3.title: What is EXPLAIN and how do you use it?
sq-6:3.html:
EXPLAIN shows the query's execution plan: how the database is going to look for data. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also actually runs the query and shows the real time and row counts.

  • Seq Scan: a scan of the whole table. On a large table with a selective filter it is suspicious.
  • Index Scan / Index Only Scan: search through an index.
  • A big difference between the expected and actual number of rows means stale statistics.

Careful: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an UPDATE or DELETE will really change data: run it only in a transaction with ROLLBACK.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 10 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01';

-- Index Scan using idx_transactions_account_created on transactions
--   (actual time=0.03..0.21 rows=48 loops=1)
In an interview: EXPLAIN shows the query's execution plan, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs it and shows the actual time. I look at whether an index is used or a full table scan happens. In a bug report about a slow page this lets me give the developer specifics, not just "it's slow". And I remember that ANALYZE on an UPDATE really changes the data.

sq-6:4.title: What are normalisation and denormalisation?
sq-6:4.html:
Normalisation is designing tables so that each fact is stored once. In simple words about the first three normal forms:

  • 1NF: one value in a cell, no comma-separated lists.
  • 2NF: each non-key column depends on the whole key, not on part of it.
  • 3NF: non-key columns don't depend on each other: the user's email isn't repeated in every transaction.

Denormalisation is deliberate duplication for read speed, for example storing an account's balance separately rather than computing it from transactions every time.

For QA denormalisation means a risk of getting out of sync: duplicated data must be checked for consistency.

In an interview: Normalisation is designing tables so that each fact is stored in one place, without duplication. Denormalisation is deliberate duplication for speed, for example a separately stored balance instead of constantly computing it from transactions. For me as QA every such duplication is a risk of falling out of sync, so I check that the copies of data match.

sq-6:5.title: How do you test database migrations?
sq-6:5.html:
A migration is a script that changes the schema or the data: adds a column, renames, moves data. What to check:

  • Counts: the number of rows before and after is the same (or changed as expected).
  • Values: selectively and with aggregates: sums and counts by status match.
  • New columns: how old records were filled: NULL, the default, a computed value?
  • Constraints: the new NOT NULL and UNIQUE didn't fail on existing data.
  • Application: works with old data after the migration; old records open and can be edited.
  • Rollback: if there is a down migration, does it restore the state without loss.
  • Time: how long the migration takes on a volume close to production and whether it locks the table.
-- before and after the migration: identical checksums
SELECT status, COUNT(*), SUM(amount)
FROM transactions
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
In an interview: For migrations I compare the state before and after: the row count and checksums by groups must match. I check how the new columns were filled for old records, whether the new constraints failed, whether the application works with the old data and whether the rollback is correct. And separately, how long the migration takes on a large volume of data, because it may lock the table in production.

sq-7:0.title: What are window functions and how do they differ from GROUP BY?
sq-7:0.html:
A window function computes a value over a group of related rows (a "window"), but, unlike GROUP BY, doesn't collapse the rows: every row stays in the result and gets an additional column.

The syntax: function() OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …).

  • PARTITION BY: how to split into groups (like GROUP BY, but without collapsing).
  • ORDER BY: the order inside the group (for ranks and running totals).
-- each transaction + the total for its account alongside
SELECT id, account_id, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id) AS account_total
FROM transactions;
In an interview: A window function computes a value over a group of rows, but, unlike GROUP BY, doesn't collapse them: every row stays and gets an extra column. PARTITION BY sets the groups, and ORDER BY the order inside. That way I can, for example, show each transaction and next to it the total amount for its account in one query.

sq-7:1.title: How do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ?
sq-7:1.html:
All three number rows in the ORDER BY order. The difference is in equal values:

SalaryROW_NUMBERRANKDENSE_RANK
9000111
8000222
8000322
7000443
  • ROW_NUMBER: always unique numbers; among equal ones the order is arbitrary.
  • RANK: equal ones get an equal rank, then a gap.
  • DENSE_RANK: an equal rank without gaps.
SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
FROM employees;
In an interview: All three number rows by the sort order, and the difference is in equal values. ROW_NUMBER always gives unique numbers, RANK gives equal values an equal rank with a gap after them, and DENSE_RANK has no gap. So for "the second highest salary" taking ties into account I use DENSE_RANK, and for deduplication ROW_NUMBER.

sq-7:2.title: How do you find the top N records in each group?
sq-7:2.html:
Number the rows inside each group with a window function, and then filter by the number. You can't filter a window function directly in WHERE: it is computed later, so a CTE or a subquery is needed.

-- the 3 largest transactions of each account
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, account_id, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn
  FROM transactions
  WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT account_id, id, amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY account_id, rn;
In an interview: I number the rows inside each group with ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY and a sort, and then in the outer query I take the numbers from one to N. A window function can't be filtered directly in WHERE, because it is computed after it, so a CTE or a subquery is needed.

sq-7:3.title: What do LAG and LEAD do?
sq-7:3.html:
LAG(col) returns the value from the previous row in the window, LEAD(col) from the next one. Useful for comparison with the previous state: the difference between events, intervals, status changes.

-- the interval between consecutive transactions of an account
SELECT account_id, id, created_at,
       created_at - LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at) AS gap
FROM transactions;

-- suspicious: several identical transactions less than 5 seconds apart (double submission?)
WITH g AS (
  SELECT id, account_id, amount, created_at,
         LAG(amount)     OVER w AS prev_amount,
         LAG(created_at) OVER w AS prev_at
  FROM transactions
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at)
)
SELECT * FROM g
WHERE amount = prev_amount AND created_at - prev_at < INTERVAL '5 seconds';
In an interview: LAG returns the value from the previous row in the window, LEAD from the next. I use them to compare events with previous ones: for example, to find identical transactions from one account a few seconds apart, which is a typical sign of double submission.

sq-7:4.title: How do you compute a running total?
sq-7:4.html:
SUM() OVER (… ORDER BY …) adds values from the first row of the window up to the current one. This is how the balance at each moment is reconstructed from the transaction history.

SELECT account_id, id, created_at, type, amount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END)
         OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at, id) AS running_balance
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'completed'
ORDER BY account_id, created_at, id;
In an interview: A running total is computed by SUM with OVER and ORDER BY: everything before is added to each row within the group. That is how I reconstruct an account's balance at each moment from the transaction history and can find the point where it became negative or diverged from the expected.

sq-8:0.title: How do you verify in the database the result of an action in the UI?
sq-8:0.html:
Example: a user topped up an account with 500 PLN. What I check:

  1. The record is created: a new transaction with the right amount, type, currency, account.
  2. The status matches the stage: pending → completed, not stuck.
  3. Side effects: the balance changed by exactly the amount, a fee record was created if there is one.
  4. Nothing extra: there is no duplicate, other people's accounts didn't change.
  5. Service fields: created_at in the right time zone, an audit record, who performed the action.
-- the account's latest transaction
SELECT id, type, amount, status, created_at
FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 10
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- how many identical transactions in the last minute (a duplicate?)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 10 AND amount = 500 AND type = 'deposit'
  AND created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '1 minute';
In an interview: After an action in the UI I check in the database that the record was created with the right data and status, that the side effects happened (the balance changed, the fee was charged) and that there is nothing extra: a duplicate or changes in other people's records. Separately I look at service fields, such as a date in the right time zone.

sq-8:1.title: How do you find anomalies and data integrity violations?
sq-8:1.html:
A set of queries worth having at hand:

  • Orphaned records: children without a parent (an anti-join).
  • Duplicates where they can't be (GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT > 1).
  • Impossible values: negative amounts, dates in the future, unknown statuses.
  • Impossible combinations: a blocked account with new transactions, a completed transaction without a completion date.
  • Stuck states: pending for longer than a reasonable time.
-- statuses that aren't in the documentation
SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM transactions GROUP BY status;

-- negative balances
SELECT id, user_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE balance < 0;

-- transactions "stuck" in pending for more than an hour
SELECT id, account_id, amount, created_at FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour';

-- transactions on blocked accounts after the block
SELECT t.id, a.id AS account_id
FROM transactions t JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
WHERE a.status = 'blocked' AND t.created_at > a.blocked_at;
In an interview: I keep a set of integrity queries: orphaned records through an anti-join, duplicates through GROUP BY with HAVING, impossible values like a negative balance, impossible combinations like transactions on a blocked account, and operations stuck in pending. Such checks often find bugs that aren't visible from the UI.

sq-8:2.title: What should you pay attention to when working with dates and time zones?
sq-8:2.html:
• TIMESTAMP stores time without a zone, TIMESTAMPTZ a point in time (in PostgreSQL it is stored in UTC and shown in the session's zone).
  • The UI shows local time, the database often UTC. A difference of 1–2 hours in reconciliation isn't necessarily a bug, but you need to know what is where.
  • Day boundaries: "transactions for 30 September" is >= '2026-09-30' AND < '2026-10-01', not = '2026-09-30'.
  • Day boundaries in different zones: an operation at 23:30 in Warsaw is already the next day in UTC+3. "Per day" reports may diverge.
  • The daylight saving change: an hour that repeats or disappears.
SHOW timezone;                                     -- the session's zone
SELECT NOW(), NOW() AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Warsaw';

-- transactions for the day in Warsaw time
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-30 00:00:00+02'
  AND created_at <  '2026-10-01 00:00:00+02';
In an interview: With dates I always find out in which zone time is stored in the database and in which it is shown in the UI: a difference of an hour or two is often not a bug but different zones. I write day ranges as "from the start of the day inclusive to the next day exclusive". And separately I test day boundaries and the daylight saving change, because reports and limits often break there.

sq-8:3.title: How do you store money correctly and what bugs are there?
sq-8:3.html:
FLOAT and DOUBLE store numbers in binary form with an error: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. For money this is unacceptable: cents get "lost" when summing thousands of operations.

The right way: NUMERIC(p, s) or an integer in minimal units (cents).

What to test:

  • Amounts with cents: 0.01, 0.10, 99.99, 100.005.
  • Rounding rules for fees and conversion: to which place, in which direction.
  • Does the sum of the rounded parts equal the rounded sum? (splitting 100 into three parts).
  • Currencies with different numbers of decimal places: JPY has none, some have three.
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8;          -- 0.30000000000000004
SELECT 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric;        -- 0.3

SELECT ROUND(2.675::numeric, 2);           -- 2.68
SELECT ROUND(2.675::float8::numeric, 2);   -- may give 2.67 because of the float error
In an interview: Money must not be stored in FLOAT, because it has a binary error: zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three, and over thousands of operations cents get lost. The right way is NUMERIC or integer minor units. As QA I test amounts with cents, the rounding rules of fees, and whether the sum of the parts matches the total.

sq-8:4.title: How do you prepare and clean up test data with SQL?
sq-8:4.html:
• A marker: all test records are marked: an email prefix, a tag, a separate tenant. Then cleanup is a DELETE by the marker, with no risk of touching someone else's data.
  • RETURNING: get the id of the created record and use it further.
  • Idempotency: the script can be run again: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING or clean up old data first.
  • Order: create from parents to children, delete the other way, so as not to fail on foreign keys.
  • Bulk data: generate_series for load and pagination tests.
-- 1000 transactions for checking pagination
INSERT INTO transactions (account_id, type, amount, status, created_at)
SELECT 10, 'deposit', (random() * 1000)::numeric(14,2), 'completed',
       NOW() - (g || ' minutes')::interval
FROM generate_series(1, 1000) AS g;

-- cleanup: from children to parents
DELETE FROM transactions WHERE account_id IN
  (SELECT a.id FROM accounts a JOIN users u ON u.id = a.user_id
   WHERE u.email LIKE 'qa_auto_%@test.com');
DELETE FROM accounts WHERE user_id IN
  (SELECT id FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'qa_auto_%@test.com');
DELETE FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'qa_auto_%@test.com';
In an interview: I mark all test data with a marker, for example a prefix in the email, so I can later clean up only my own. I make scripts idempotent, create records from parents to children and delete in the reverse order because of foreign keys. For checking pagination or large volumes I generate data with generate_series.

sq-8:5.title: What is SQL injection and how do you test for it?
sq-8:5.html:
SQL injection is when user input is inserted into a query as part of the code, not as data. Then a specially chosen string changes the query's logic: bypasses authorisation, reads other people's data, drops tables.

-- vulnerable code builds the query as a string:
--   "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + input + "'"
-- input:  ' OR '1'='1
-- we get: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1'   -> all users

-- defence: a parameterised query, input is always only data
--   SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1
In an interview: SQL injection is when user input gets into a query as code, and a special string, for example with a quote and a "one equals one" condition, changes the query's logic. The defence is parameterised queries. As QA I check search fields, filters and API parameters with basic strings with quotes and comments: I expect them to be handled as plain text, with no database errors in the response.

sq-8:6.title: How do you check that a balance matches the transaction history?
sq-8:6.html:
This is a reconciliation of denormalised data: the stored balance must equal the sum of all completed money movements on the account. The query returns only accounts with a discrepancy; normally the result is empty.

SELECT a.id, a.balance,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN t.type = 'deposit' THEN t.amount ELSE -t.amount END), 0) AS calculated
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN transactions t
       ON t.account_id = a.id AND t.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY a.id, a.balance
HAVING a.balance <> COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN t.type = 'deposit' THEN t.amount ELSE -t.amount END), 0);
In an interview: I compute the sum of all completed transactions of each account with the direction taken into account and compare with the stored balance, and the query returns only discrepancies, normally it is empty. The details matter here: a LEFT JOIN so as not to lose accounts without transactions, the status condition in ON, not in WHERE, and COALESCE, because the sum of an empty set is NULL.

sq-8:7.title: How do you use SQL in automated tests?
sq-8:7.html:
• Cypress: browser code can't connect to the database directly, so the query is executed in Node through cy.task (for example with the pg library).
  • Playwright: tests run in Node anyway, so a database client is connected directly, conveniently through a fixture.

Rules: a separate database user for tests with minimal rights; credentials in environment variables; tests don't depend on data created by other tests; data is cleaned up by the marker.

// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import { Client } from 'pg';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('task', {
        async dbQuery({ sql, params }: { sql: string; params?: unknown[] }) {
          const client = new Client({ connectionString: config.env.DB_URL });
          await client.connect();
          try {
            const res = await client.query(sql, params);
            return res.rows;
          } finally {
            await client.end();
          }
        },
      });
    },
  },
});

// in the test
cy.task('dbQuery', {
  sql: 'SELECT status FROM transactions WHERE id = $1',
  params: [txId],
}).then((rows: any) => expect(rows[0].status).to.eq('completed'));
In an interview: In Cypress browser code has no access to the database, so I run the query in the Node process through cy.task with the pg library and parameterised queries. In Playwright I connect to the database directly, conveniently through a fixture. For tests I use a separate database user with minimal rights, keep credentials in environment variables, and clean data up by the marker.

sq-8:8.title: API validation through the DB
sq-8:8.html:
After a creation request I take the ID from the API response and do a SELECT by that ID in the relevant table. I check that the record exists and all fields match what was sent. I also check the fields the server fills in: created\_at, the default status, the author.

For an update I compare the state before and after: only the expected fields changed, and updated\_at was updated. For a delete I check whether the record was physically removed or it is a soft delete with a deleted\_at flag. It is important to check related tables too: for example, whether order items were created and the product's stock decreased.

I also check that data is stored in the right format: the password is hashed, dates are in UTC, amounts have the right precision. In automated tests such checks are done through a Node.js task cy.task with a DB client or a separate API helper. It is desirable to have read-only access to the DB on the test environment.

sq-9:0.title: Task: find the second highest salary.
sq-9:0.html:
The first clarification worth stating: "if two people have the maximum salary, is the second highest the same amount or the next one?" Usually the next unique amount is meant.

-- variant 1: a subquery, returns NULL if there is no second
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_max
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

-- variant 2: DISTINCT + OFFSET
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

-- variant 3: DENSE_RANK, easy to generalise to the Nth
WITH r AS (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr
  FROM employees
)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM r WHERE dr = 2;
In an interview: First I clarify whether to take repeats of the maximum salary into account. The simplest solution is the maximum salary among those smaller than the overall maximum. For the Nth highest DENSE_RANK is more convenient. And the variant with LIMIT and OFFSET without DISTINCT gives a wrong answer if the maximum salary repeats.

sq-9:1.title: Task: find duplicated emails.
sq-9:1.html:
Group by email and keep the groups with more than one row. Case and spaces should be taken into account: Anna@test.com and anna@test.com may also be a duplicate.

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- taking case and spaces into account
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email_norm, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM users
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
In an interview: I group by email and keep the groups with a count greater than one through HAVING. And as QA I also normalise the values with LOWER and TRIM, because duplicates that differ in case or a space are a typical bug when the uniqueness check on the backend compares strings literally.

sq-9:2.title: Task: find users who have no accounts at all.
sq-9:2.html:
An anti-join or NOT EXISTS. It is worth mentioning why not NOT IN.

SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.user_id = u.id
WHERE a.id IS NULL;
In an interview: I do a LEFT JOIN of users with accounts and take those whose account key is NULL. The alternative is NOT EXISTS. And I don't use NOT IN here: if a NULL turns up in the subquery, it returns zero rows.

sq-9:3.title: Task: the top 3 users by the sum of completed deposits.
sq-9:3.html:
Three tables, a filter, grouping, sorting and limiting. It is worth saying what to do with equal sums in third place.

SELECT u.id, u.email, SUM(t.amount) AS total_deposits
FROM users u
JOIN accounts a     ON a.user_id = u.id
JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.id
WHERE t.type = 'deposit' AND t.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email
ORDER BY total_deposits DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- if with equal sums you need to show everyone: RANK() and rnk <= 3
In an interview: I join users, accounts and transactions, filter completed deposits in WHERE, group by user, sort by the sum and take three. I clarify what to do with equal sums at the boundary: LIMIT will cut arbitrarily, and if everyone with equal sums must be shown, I use RANK.

sq-9:4.title: Task: the number and sum of transactions by month.
sq-9:4.html:
Grouping by a date truncated to the month. DATE_TRUNC is PostgreSQL; in MySQL you use DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m').

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS month,
       COUNT(*)    AS tx_count,
       SUM(amount) AS volume
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;
In an interview: I truncate the date to the month with DATE_TRUNC, group by it and count the number and the sum. It is worth remembering that months without transactions won't get into the result: if they are needed with zeros, you have to generate a list of months with generate_series and join with a LEFT JOIN.

sq-9:5.title: Task: employees who earn more than their manager.
sq-9:5.html:
A classic self join.

SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
In an interview: This is a self join: I join the employees table with itself, where the manager is another row by manager_id, and compare salaries. An INNER JOIN fits here, because employees without a manager can't earn more than them anyway.

sq-9:6.title: Task: remove duplicates, leaving one record each.
sq-9:6.html:
Number the rows in each group of duplicates and delete all except the first. Before the DELETE: a SELECT of the same rows and a transaction, without fail.

BEGIN;

-- what will be deleted: all except the oldest record of each email
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(email) ORDER BY created_at, id) AS rn
  FROM users
)
SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1;

-- deletion
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(email) ORDER BY created_at, id) AS rn
  FROM users
)
