DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1);

COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK
In an interview: I number the rows in each group of duplicates with ROW_NUMBER and PARTITION BY and delete everything with a number greater than one, keeping the oldest record. First I run a SELECT of those same rows, and I do everything in a transaction. And I clarify whether the duplicates have child records, otherwise foreign keys won't let the delete happen or the related data will vanish through a cascade.

sq-9:7.title: Task: the percentage of failed transactions for each type.
sq-9:7.html:
Conditional aggregation and care with integer division.

SELECT type,
       COUNT(*) AS total,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') / COUNT(*), 2) AS failed_pct
FROM transactions
GROUP BY type
ORDER BY failed_pct DESC;

-- without FILTER (MySQL, SQL Server):
-- SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
In an interview: I group by type and count the total and the number of failed ones through FILTER or SUM with CASE, and then divide. I multiply by 100.0, not by 100, because integer division in PostgreSQL discards the fractional part, and instead of 3.5 percent you'd get zero.

sq-9:8.title: Task: the employee with the highest salary in each department.
sq-9:8.html:
You need not only the maximum value but also the name, so a simple GROUP BY is not enough. The solution is a window function or a JOIN with an aggregate.

-- a window function: RANK will show everyone if several people share the maximum
WITH r AS (
  SELECT name, department, salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
)
SELECT department, name, salary FROM r WHERE rnk = 1;

-- without window functions
SELECT e.department, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN (SELECT department, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
      FROM employees GROUP BY department) m
  ON m.department = e.department AND m.max_salary = e.salary;
In an interview: GROUP BY with MAX gives only the amount, not the name, so I use the window function RANK partitioned by department and take rank one, so I see everyone if several people share the maximum. An alternative without window functions is to join the table with a subquery that computes the maximum per department.

sq-9:9.title: Finding duplicate emails
sq-9:9.html:
I look for duplicates by grouping by the field and filtering groups with more than one record:

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

If duplicates may differ in case or spaces, I group by LOWER(TRIM(email)). To see the duplicate records themselves with all their fields, I use this query as a subquery in WHERE email IN (...).

The second way is the window function ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id), where everything with a number above 1 is a duplicate. For QA a found duplicate often means a bug: a missing UNIQUE constraint in the DB or a validation problem with parallel requests.

api-cs:0.title: Client and server: who is responsible for what
api-cs:0.html:
The client asks, and the server decides and responds. The client is a browser, a mobile application or Postman. The server holds the business logic and access to the database; the client never goes into the database directly.

The path of one request when a user pressed "Transfer" in a banking application:

  1. DNS turns the domain into the server's IP address.
  2. A TCP connection and TLS encryption (HTTPS) are established.
  3. The client sends an HTTP request: POST /api/transfers with a token and a JSON body.
  4. A load balancer or an API Gateway passes the request to one of the server instances.
  5. The server checks authorisation, validates the data and runs the business logic: whether there are enough funds, whether limits are exceeded.
  6. The server reads and writes to the database within a transaction.
  7. The server returns a response: status 201, headers, JSON with the transfer id.
  8. The client shows the result to the user.

For a tester it is important that each step can have its own problem: DNS or a certificate on the test environment, a balancer that leads to an old instance, business logic or a transaction that wrote half the data. When I understand this path, it is easier for me to localise a bug and describe it correctly in a report.

In an interview: The client sends an HTTP request, the server checks authorisation, validates the data, runs the business logic, works with the database in a transaction and returns a response with a status. The client doesn't go to the database directly, everything goes through the API.

api-cs:1.title: Three ideas that get asked in interviews
api-cs:1.html:
HTTP is stateless. Each request is independent, and the server doesn't remember the previous one. So a token or a cookie is passed in every request. For tests this means any request can be reproduced separately if it has all the needed headers.

Validation on the client is convenience, on the server it is security. A UI form can be bypassed by sending a request directly from Postman or curl. If the server trusts only the front end, you can pass a negative amount or someone else's id. That is exactly why the API is tested separately from the UI, not only through the interface.

Where to look for a bug. The logic is simple:

  • A wrong request in DevTools: a front-end bug.
  • A right request but a wrong response: a backend bug.
  • A right response but wrong display: the front end again.

I use this algorithm every day: I open the Network tab, find the needed request and see at which stage the data became wrong. That way a bug goes to the right team right away.

In an interview: HTTP is stateless, so authorisation goes in every request. Server-side validation is mandatory, because the client can be bypassed, and that is the main reason to test the API separately from the UI.

api-cs:2.title: REST and alternatives
api-cs:2.html:
REST is a style of building an API where data are resources at URLs (/users/42), and actions on them are set with HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT and PATCH change, DELETE removes. REST is stateless, data is usually passed in JSON, and the result is described with a status code.

Alternatives worth knowing:

  • GraphQL: one endpoint, and the client itself describes which fields it needs.
  • SOAP: XML and a strict contract (WSDL), often found in old banking systems.
  • WebSocket: a persistent two-way connection, for example for quotes or a real-time chat.

For QA the choice of style changes the approach to testing. In REST I check methods, status codes and resources. In GraphQL the status is often 200 even on an error, and you must check the errors array in the body. In SOAP conformance to the XML schema matters, and in WebSocket the order and delivery of messages.

In an interview: REST is an API style where data are resources at URLs and actions are set with HTTP methods; it is stateless and usually works with JSON. If a project is on GraphQL or SOAP, I change my approach to checks, but the principles are the same: contract, validation, authorisation.

api-anatomy:0.title: What a request and a response consist of
api-anatomy:0.html:
A request = a method + a URL + headers + a body. A response = a status code + headers + a body.

POST https://api.bank.test/v1/accounts/42/transfers?dryRun=false
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c-...

{ "toAccount": "UA21...", "amount": 150.00, "currency": "UAH" }

Here all the parts are visible: the POST method, the base URL with the API version, the path to the resource with the path parameter 42, the query parameter dryRun, three headers and a JSON body. Each of these parts is a separate source of test cases, so when analysing a new endpoint I break down the request exactly like this, piece by piece.

Path vs query. The path points to a specific resource (/users/42), the query filters or configures the output (/users?status=active&page=2). The rule is simple: if without the parameter the resource loses meaning, it is path; if it is an output option, it is query.

In an interview: A request consists of a method, a URL, headers and a body, and a response of a status code, headers and a body. A path parameter identifies a resource, and a query parameter filters, sorts or paginates the output.

api-anatomy:1.title: What to check in each part
api-anatomy:1.html:
This table is a ready plan of negative and positive cases for any endpoint.

PartExampleWhat to check
Base URLhttps://api.bank.test/v1Move into the variable {{baseUrl}}
Path/accounts/42/transfersSomeone else's or a nonexistent id gives 403 or 404
Path param42An invalid type (abc) gives 400
Query param?dryRun=falseFilters, pagination, sorting
HeadersAuthorization, Content-Type, AcceptWithout a token 401; a wrong Content-Type 415
BodyJSON with fieldsRequired fields, types, boundaries
Status201 CreatedThe code matches the documentation
Response headersContent-Type, LocationContent type, cache, CORS
Response body{ "id": "tr_91", "status": "pending" }Structure, types, values, no extra sensitive fields
Time180 msWithin the SLA

Note the Location in a creation response: it often holds the URL of the new resource, and it is convenient to use for the next GET. And checking for "no extra sensitive fields" is not a formality: if a response has a password hash or a full card number, that is already a security defect, even when everything else is right.

In an interview: I go through a request part by part: the URL and path parameters, the query, headers, body, and in the response the status, headers, body and time. Each part has its own negative cases, for example an invalid id type gives 400, and a wrong Content-Type gives 415.

api-methods:0.title: HTTP methods, idempotency, PUT vs PATCH
api-methods:0.html:
The main methods: GET retrieves a resource, POST creates, PUT replaces completely, PATCH changes partially, DELETE removes. HEAD also returns only headers, and OPTIONS returns the allowed methods, which CORS preflight uses. Safe methods don't change the server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.

An idempotent method is one where several identical requests give the same server state as one. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST isn't: two POSTs create two records. The response may differ, for example a repeated DELETE returns 404 instead of 204.

PUT sends the full representation of a resource, and fields absent from the body may be reset. PATCH sends only the fields that change. PATCH isn't guaranteed to be idempotent, for example the operation "increase the counter by 1". This is worth checking in tests: a repeated PUT must not create duplicates.

api-methods:1.title: The methods table
api-methods:1.html:
An idempotent method is one where a repeated identical request doesn't change the server state beyond the first. A safe one is one that doesn't change data at all.

MethodWhat forBodyIdempotentTypical success code
GETRetrieve a resource or a listNoYes (and safe)200
POSTCreate a resource or perform an actionYesNo201
PUTReplace a resource completelyYesYes200 or 204
PATCHChange individual fieldsYesNot guaranteed200
DELETERemove a resourceUsually noYes204 or 200
HEADLike GET but only headersNoYes200
OPTIONSWhich methods are allowed; CORS preflightNoYes204

Idempotency concerns the server state, not the response. A repeated DELETE may return 404 instead of 204, but the resource is deleted all the same, so the method remains idempotent. HEAD is useful when you need to check that a resource exists or a file's size without downloading the body.

In an interview: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS are idempotent, POST isn't, and PATCH is not guaranteed. Safe methods, like GET and HEAD, don't change data at all.

api-methods:2.title: PUT vs PATCH and Idempotency-Key in fintech
api-methods:2.html:
PUT vs PATCH. PUT sends the whole object, and a field you didn't pass may become empty. PATCH changes only the passed fields. This is a ready test case: do a PUT without one field and check through GET what happened to it. If the field was wiped and the documentation says PUT is a full replacement, the behaviour is correct; if the API behaves like PATCH, it is a deviation from the contract.

Fintech. POST is non-idempotent, so pressing "Pay" again or repeating a request after a network timeout may debit money twice. The protection is the Idempotency-Key header: the client generates a unique key, the server remembers it and on a repeat returns the same result without creating a second payment.

How I test it:

  1. Send POST /transfers with the key K1, get 201 and the transfer id.
  2. Send the same request with the same K1.
  3. Check that the response contains the same id, and that in the database or history there is one transaction.
  4. Send a different body with the same K1 and check that the server returns an error (often 409 or 422), not quietly executing a new payment.
In an interview: PUT replaces a resource entirely, PATCH changes only the passed fields, and I check this with a GET after a PUT without one field. For payments POST is protected by Idempotency-Key, and I test that a repeat with the same key doesn't create a second transaction.

api-status:0.title: 401 vs 403, 400 vs 422, 500 vs 503
api-status:0.html:
401 Unauthorized means the client isn't authenticated: there is no token, or it is invalid or expired. 403 Forbidden means the client is authenticated but has no rights to the resource, for example an ordinary user going to an admin endpoint. In short: 401 is "who are you?", 403 is "I know who you are, but you may not".

400 Bad Request means the request is syntactically incorrect: broken JSON, a wrong data type, a missing required parameter. 422 Unprocessable Entity means the request is syntactically correct but fails business validation, for example the email is already taken or the end date is before the start date. Many APIs use 400 for both cases, so it is worth checking against the contract.

500 Internal Server Error is an unexpected error on the server, most often a bug in the code, and for a tester it is always a reason to file a defect. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily unavailable: overload, maintenance, a dependency not responding. Often 503 comes with a Retry-After header.

api-status:1.title: Groups and a table of codes
api-status:1.html:
The first digit is the group: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

CodeMeaningWhen to expect
200 OKSuccess with a bodyGET, a successful PUT or PATCH
201 CreatedThe resource was createdPOST
204 No ContentSuccess without a bodyDELETE
301 / 302RedirectionA changed URL, a redirect to login
304 Not ModifiedData hasn't changed, take it from cacheCaching
400 Bad RequestAn invalid requestBroken JSON, a missing required field
401 UnauthorizedNot authenticatedNo token or an expired one
403 ForbiddenKnown who, but no rightsAn ordinary user goes to the admin area
404 Not FoundNo such resourceA nonexistent id
405 Method Not AllowedThe method isn't supportedDELETE on an endpoint that doesn't have it
409 ConflictA state conflictA duplicate email, a parallel change
415 Unsupported Media TypeAn unsupported body formatA wrong Content-Type
422 Unprocessable EntitySyntax OK, a business rule violatedAn amount greater than the balance
429 Too Many RequestsThe request limit was exceededRate limiting
500 Internal Server ErrorAn unhandled server errorAlways a bug
502 / 503 / 504A gateway problem, the service unavailable, a timeoutA crash or an overload
In an interview: I go by the first digit: 2xx is success, 4xx means the client sent something wrong, 5xx is a problem on the server. I check the specific code against the documentation, because teams use, for example, 400 and 422 differently.

api-status:2.title: The most popular traps
api-status:2.html:
401 vs 403 is the most popular question: 401 is "who are you?", 403 is "I know who you are, but you may not". That is, 401 is an authentication problem (no token, it is expired or corrupted), 403 is an authorisation one (the user has no role or rights for this resource).

A bug or not. Invalid input must give a 4xx with a clear message. A 500 for bad input is a bug, even if "an error did come back": 500 means the server didn't handle the situation and an exception was thrown somewhere. Likewise a 200 with { "error": "..." } in the body is a bug: clients, monitoring and automated tests go by the status and will consider such a request successful.

A few more points I pay attention to:

  • A 201 on creation should come with the new resource's id in the body or a URL in the Location header.
  • A 204 must not have a body; if there is one, the client may ignore it.
  • A 404 for someone else's resource instead of 403 is normal practice: that way the API doesn't reveal that the resource exists.
  • The error body must not contain a stack trace, an SQL query or internal paths.
In an interview: 401 is not authenticated, 403 is authenticated but without rights. A 500 in response to invalid data is always a bug, as is a 200 with an error in the body.

api-postman:0.title: Collections, environments and variables
api-postman:0.html:
A collection is a set of requests for one API, laid out in folders (for example Auth, Accounts, Transfers). At the collection and folder level you can set shared authorisation, variables and scripts, which requests inherit. This is the main reason to structure it right: the token and baseUrl are configured once, not in every request.

An environment is a set of variables for a specific test environment: dev, stage, prod. One collection, three environments: you switch the environment with one dropdown in the top right corner.

A variable is inserted with double curly braces in the URL, headers and body:

{{baseUrl}}/accounts/{{accountId}}

Built-in dynamic variables generate data: {{$guid}}, {{$timestamp}}, {{$randomEmail}}, {{$randomInt}}. They are convenient when each run must create a unique user or a unique key, so as not to catch 409 on duplicates.

In an interview: I keep requests in a collection with folders by resource, and set authorisation and shared variables at the collection level. I separate environments through Postman environments, so the same collection runs on dev and stage without changes.

api-postman:1.title: Variable scopes and secrets
api-postman:1.html:
Variable scopes go from wide to narrow. If names match, the narrow one wins.

ScopeWhere it appliesTypical useIn a script
GlobalThe whole workspaceRarely; better avoidedpm.globals
CollectionOne collectionThe API version, constant settingspm.collectionVariables
EnvironmentThe active environmentbaseUrl, test logins, a tokenpm.environment
DataOne Runner iterationA row from CSV or JSONpm.iterationData
LocalOne request or runTemporary valuespm.variables

pm.variables.get('x') reads the value taking priority into account: from the scope that won. So if the variable baseUrl exists both in the collection and in the environment, the environment's value goes into the request.

Initial vs current value. The initial value is synced with the team through the shared workspace. The current one lives only locally with you, and it is the one substituted into requests. Keep tokens and passwords only in the current value or mark the variable with the secret type, otherwise they end up in shared access or in an exported file.

In an interview: The variable scopes are Global, Collection, Environment, Data and Local; with equal names the narrower wins. I keep secrets only in the current value or as secret, so they don't end up in the shared workspace or an export.

api-auth:0.title: JWT and testing tokens
api-auth:0.html:
A JWT consists of three parts separated by dots: a header (the algorithm and type), a payload (claims: user data, roles, issue and expiry time) and a signature. Each part is encoded in Base64URL, so the payload can be read by anyone: it isn't encrypted. The signature guarantees the token wasn't altered, and the server checks it with a secret or a public key.

Key claims: exp is the expiry time, iat is the issue time, sub is the user identifier. The token is passed in the header Authorization: Bearer <token>. There is usually a short-lived access token and a longer refresh token for getting a new one.

Tests: an expired token must return 401, for which I take an old token or a test environment with a short lifetime. A forged token: I change the role in the payload without re-signing, and the server must reject it because of the invalid signature. I also check the algorithm none, a token from another environment, an empty and a truncated token, as well as token invalidation after logout and a password change.

api-auth:1.title: Authorisation types in Postman
api-auth:1.html:
Authorisation is set once at the collection level, and in requests you put Inherit auth from parent. For public endpoints, for example login, No Auth.

TypeWhat it looks like in a request
Bearer TokenAuthorization: Bearer <token>: the most common, the token is usually a JWT
Basic AuthAuthorization: Basic base64(login:password): this is encoding, not encryption
API KeyA header (x-api-key: ...) or a query parameter
OAuth 2.0Postman itself goes through the flow and gets an access token
CookieA session cookie after login; managed through the Cookies tab

An important nuance about Basic: base64 is decoded in a second, so without HTTPS the login and password are effectively transmitted in plain text. An API Key in a query parameter is also risky, because the URL ends up in server and proxy logs.

In an interview: Most often it is a Bearer token, usually a JWT, which I set at the collection level, and requests inherit the authorisation. I also know Basic, API Key, OAuth 2.0 and cookie sessions, and I remember that Basic is encoding, not encryption.

api-auth:2.title: The token automatically and what to check
api-auth:2.html:
The token automatically. In the post-response script of the POST /auth/login request save the token into a variable, and in the collection specify Bearer {{token}}:

pm.test('Login 200', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
const { accessToken } = pm.response.json();
pm.environment.set('token', accessToken);

Now it is enough to run the login once, and all the collection's requests pick up the fresh token. For Runner and Newman the login is put as the first request in the collection, or the token is obtained through pm.sendRequest in the collection's pre-request script.

What to check:

  • Without a token: 401.
  • A corrupted and an expired token: 401.
  • A token after logout: 401.
  • Another user's token against someone else's resource: 403 or 404, but never data.

The last one is IDOR, one of the most dangerous bugs in fintech. To check it I need two test users: I create a resource under the first and then access it with the second's token. If the response has someone else's account or transfer, it is a critical defect.

In an interview: I save the token after login with pm.environment.set and use {{token}} at the collection level. Then I check 401 without a token, with an expired and a corrupted one and after logout, as well as IDOR: access to someone else's resource with another user's token.

api-scripts:0.title: Postman: variables, scripts, chaining
api-scripts:0.html:
Variable scopes from wider to narrower: global, collection, environment, data and local. The narrower one overrides the wider, so a variable of the same name from the environment will override a global one. Environments let you run the same collection on dev, stage and prod by simply switching the environment.

A pre-request script runs before the request: generating unique data, getting a token, computing a signature or a timestamp. A post-response script (formerly the Tests tab) runs after the response: checks through pm.test and pm.expect, for example the status, fields and response time. Scripts can be set at the request, folder and collection level.

Chaining is passing data between requests: after creating a user I save their ID with pm.environment.set('userId', json.id). Following requests use {{userId}}. A collection is run through the Collection Runner with CSV or JSON for data-driven tests, or through Newman on CI.

api-scripts:1.title: Pre-request, post-response and basic checks
api-scripts:1.html:
A pre-request script runs before the request is sent (prepare data, a token), post-response runs after (check the response, save values). The order: the collection's script, then the folder's, then the request's. The language is JavaScript, and assertions are Chai through pm.expect.

A basic set of checks:

pm.test('Status 201', () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));
pm.test('Response time < 800 ms', () => {
  pm.expect(pm.response.responseTime).to.be.below(800);
});
pm.test('JSON content type', () => {
  pm.response.to.have.header('Content-Type');
  pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('Content-Type')).to.include('application/json');
});
const body = pm.response.json();
pm.test('Body fields', () => {
  pm.expect(body).to.have.property('id');
  pm.expect(body.status).to.eql('pending');
  pm.expect(body.amount).to.be.a('number').and.eql(150);
  pm.expect(body).to.not.have.property('cardNumber'); // sensitive data isn't returned
});

Each pm.test is a separate line in the report, so it is better to have several small tests with clear names than one big one. Then the Runner report immediately shows what exactly broke.

In an interview: Pre-request prepares data and the token, post-response checks the response and saves values. I check the status, time, Content-Type, key fields and the absence of sensitive data, each check in a separate pm.test.

api-scripts:2.title: Schema validation and a chain of requests
api-scripts:2.html:
Schema validation checks the whole structure: required fields, types, allowed values.

const schema = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['id', 'status', 'amount', 'currency'],
  properties: {
    id: { type: 'string' },
    status: { enum: ['pending', 'completed', 'failed'] },
    amount: { type: 'number', exclusiveMinimum: 0 },
    currency: { type: 'string', pattern: '^[A-Z]{3}$' }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
};
pm.test('Schema is valid', () => pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(schema));

additionalProperties: false catches the situation where the backend suddenly started returning a new field, for example an internal identifier. It is both protection against data leakage and a signal of an undocumented contract change.

A request chain is passing data from one request to the next:

// post-response in POST /accounts
pm.environment.set('accountId', pm.response.json().id);
// the next request: GET {{baseUrl}}/accounts/{{accountId}}
In an interview: A schema checks the whole response structure in one test, and additionalProperties: false catches extra fields. I pass data between requests through variables: I save the id in post-response and use {{accountId}} in the next request.

api-scripts:3.title: Useful commands and a strong test
api-scripts:3.html:
Useful commands:

  • pm.sendRequest(...) sends a helper request from a script, for example to get a token in pre-request.
  • pm.execution.setNextRequest('Name') changes the order in the Runner; null stops the run. In old collections you encounter postman.setNextRequest.
  • pm.environment.unset('token') cleans up a variable after yourself.
  • console.log(...) prints to the Postman Console (at the bottom of the window): there you see the raw request and response, it is the main debugging tool.

The Postman Console is especially useful when a variable wasn't substituted: it shows the final URL and headers, and it is immediately clear whether the request went with {{token}} literally or with the real value.

A weak test vs a strong one. Checking only status 200 will miss an empty or wrong array. The minimum is the status, the schema and key values. For a write, also the following GET, to make sure the data was really saved. For example, after PATCH /accounts/42 with a new name I do GET /accounts/42 and check that only the name field changed and the rest stayed as it was.

In an interview: A test that checks only 200 guarantees almost nothing. I check the status, the schema and key values, and after a write I do a GET to confirm the change was saved.

api-runner:0.title: Collection Runner and data-driven tests
api-runner:0.html:
The Collection Runner runs a whole collection or folder sequentially, with the chosen environment, number of iterations and a delay between requests. The result is a pass/fail table for each pm.test.

Data-driven. In the Runner you attach a CSV or JSON file: one row is one iteration, and the columns become variables. Convenient for boundary values and negative cases:

amount,currency,expectedStatus
150,UAH,201
0,UAH,400
-10,UAH,400
1000000000,UAH,422
150,XXX,400

In the request body: {{amount}} and {{currency}}, and in the test:

pm.test(`amount=${pm.iterationData.get('amount')}`, () => {
  pm.response.to.have.status(Number(pm.iterationData.get('expectedStatus')));
});

The test name contains the value from the iteration, so the report shows at which row it failed. Number(...) is needed because values from CSV arrive as strings. That way one request covers five cases, and new boundaries are added as a row in the file without changing scripts.

In an interview: The Collection Runner runs a collection with an environment and iterations. For data-driven runs I attach a CSV or JSON where each row is an iteration with input data and the expected status, and that is how I cover boundary and negative values.

api-runner:1.title: Newman and CI
api-runner:1.html:
Newman is a CLI runner of collections without a UI, for CI. The collection and environment are exported to JSON and put in the repository:

npm i -g newman newman-reporter-htmlextra
newman run bank-api.postman_collection.json \
  -e stage.postman_environment.json \
  -d transfers.csv \
  --env-var "password=$API_PASSWORD" \
  -r cli,htmlextra,junit

If at least one test fails, Newman exits with a non-zero code, and the CI job turns red. The JUnit report is picked up by Jenkins, GitLab and GitHub Actions. Secrets are passed through --env-var from the CI secrets, not stored in the environment file.

An alternative from Postman itself is the Postman CLI (postman collection run), which works with collections from the cloud workspace.

The HTML report from htmlextra is convenient to save as a job artifact: when something fails at night, the raw requests and responses are visible without rerunning.

In an interview: On CI I run the collection through newman run with an exported environment and a JUnit reporter, and pass secrets through --env-var. A failed test gives a non-zero exit code, and the pipeline turns red.

api-runner:2.title: Postman's limits
api-runner:2.html:
A large set of API tests with logic, data factories and git review is easier to maintain in code: Playwright request, Cypress cy.request, RestAssured. Postman is strong for exploring an API, quick checks and shared documentation with developers.

The reasons regression is moved into code:

  • A JSON collection reads poorly in a diff, and reviewing script changes is inconvenient.
  • It is hard to reuse logic: helpers, test data factories, shared fixtures.
  • In code, API tests live next to UI tests, with the same CI, reporting and types.
  • In API tests in TypeScript you can type responses and catch contract changes at compile time.

At the same time I don't reject Postman: when a new endpoint arrives, I first explore it in Postman, and then move stable scenarios into automated tests. Importing OpenAPI into Postman also saves time at the start.

In an interview: Postman is for exploration and quick checks, and a large regression suite I keep in code, for example on Playwright request, next to the UI tests and with git review. That makes it easier to reuse logic and maintain the tests.

api-checklist:0.title: What to check when testing an endpoint
api-checklist:0.html:
The basics: the status code, the response structure against a schema, the types and values of fields, headers (Content-Type, caching, CORS) and response time. For POST, PUT and DELETE I check the side effect: through GET or a DB query. I also check conformance to the Swagger documentation.

Negative cases: missing required fields, wrong data types, empty strings and null, boundary values of length and numbers, extra fields. Also a nonexistent ID (404), an invalid ID format, a wrong method (405), a wrong Content-Type (415). Errors must return clear messages without stack traces and internal details.

Security and more: a request without a token and with an expired token, access to someone else's resource by changing the ID (IDOR), SQL injections in parameters. Then pagination, sorting and filters, idempotency, parallel requests and rate limiting.

api-checklist:1.title: Positive and negative cases
api-checklist:1.html:
Go through this list for every new endpoint; in an interview, recite the same list in answer to "how would you test this API".

Positive

  • A valid request gives the right status, schema and field values.
  • The record was really saved: check through GET or SQL.
  • Only the required fields, and all fields together.
  • Pagination, filters, sorting; an empty result is [], not an error.
  • Response time within the SLA.

Negative

  • Without a required field, with null, an empty string.
  • A wrong type: a string instead of a number, an array instead of an object.
  • Boundary values: 0, minimum, maximum, maximum + 1, long strings.
  • Invalid JSON and a wrong Content-Type.
  • A nonexistent id gives 404; an unsupported method 405.
  • A duplicate of a unique value gives 409.
  • In all cases a 4xx with a clear message, without a stack trace and without a 500.

There are usually more negative cases than positive ones, and they are what find most validation bugs.

In an interview: First the positive cases: status, schema, values and a check of saving through GET or SQL. Then the negative ones: missing fields, wrong types, boundaries, invalid JSON, a nonexistent id and duplicates, and everywhere I expect a 4xx with a decent message, not a 500.

api-checklist:2.title: Security and fintech
api-checklist:2.html:
Security and access

  • Without a token, with an expired and a corrupted token: 401.
  • A role without rights: 403.
  • Someone else's id in the URL: no one else's data (IDOR).
  • The response has no passwords, full card numbers or internal fields.
  • SQL injection and special characters in string fields don't break the request.
  • Rate limiting: 429 after the limit.

Fintech

  • Amounts are exact decimals: 0.1 + 0.2, rounding, cents.
  • A negative amount, zero, an amount above the balance or limit.
  • A repeat with the same Idempotency-Key: no double debit.
  • Currency: ISO 4217 codes, an unsupported currency.
  • The balances of sender and recipient after a transfer add up; on an error nothing is partly debited.
  • Dates and time zones: the ISO 8601 format, operations near midnight.

The point about 0.1 + 0.2 is a reminder that in JavaScript it gives 0.30000000000000004. If the backend or front end calculates money in float, cents sooner or later "drift", so amounts must be stored in decimal types or in minor units (cents).

In an interview: For security I check 401 and 403, IDOR, the absence of sensitive data, injections and rate limiting. In fintech I add amount precision, payment idempotency, ISO 4217 currencies, balance consistency and time zones.

api-faq:0.title: Basics, methods and statuses
api-faq:0.html:
An answer in two sentences is exactly what an interviewer expects for a basic question. Then the conversation will go deeper by itself.

QuestionShort answer
How does client-server architecture work?The client sends an HTTP request, the server checks authorisation, runs the logic, works with the database and returns a response with a status. HTTP is stateless, so the token goes in every request.
What is REST?An API style where data are resources at URLs, and actions are set by HTTP methods. Stateless, usually JSON.
PUT vs PATCH?PUT replaces a resource entirely and is idempotent. PATCH changes individual fields.
What is idempotency?A repeated identical request doesn't change the state beyond the first. GET, PUT, DELETE: yes; POST: no, so payments have an Idempotency-Key.
401 vs 403?401: not authenticated. 403: authenticated, but without rights.
400 vs 422?400: the request is incorrect in form. 422: the form is fine, but a business rule is violated.
The server returned 500 for invalid data. Is that a bug?Yes. Invalid input must give a 4xx with an explanation; 500 means an unhandled exception.
In an interview: Short answers are the basics, but after them it is worth giving an example from a project, for example how I caught a 500 on invalid input or checked an Idempotency-Key. An example shows experience better than a definition.

api-faq:1.title: Postman and automation
api-faq:1.html:
QuestionShort answer
Variable scopes in Postman?Global, Collection, Environment, Data, Local; with equal names the narrower scope wins.
How do you pass data between requests?In post-response save a value with pm.environment.set, and in the next request use {{name}}.
Pre-request vs post-response?Pre-request is preparation before sending (data, a token). Post-response is checks and saving values after the response.
How do you run a collection on CI?Export the collection and environment, run newman run with a JUnit reporter; secrets through --env-var.
What do you check in a response besides the status?The schema, field types and values, headers, response time, the absence of sensitive data and that the change was really saved.
Postman or code for API automation?Postman is for exploration and quick checks. A large regression suite goes in code next to UI tests, with git review.

These questions often follow one another: from variables to chaining, from chaining to the Runner, from the Runner to CI. So it is useful to have one story in your head: how I build a collection, how I pass the token and ids between requests, how I run a data-driven set and how it gets into the pipeline.

In an interview: I talk about Postman as a chain: variables and environments, scripts and chaining, the Runner with data, Newman on CI. And to the question "Postman or code" I answer that for regression I choose code and keep Postman for exploration.

api-design:0.title: Pagination: offset vs cursor
api-design:0.html:
A list isn't returned whole: thousands of records in one response kill both the server and the client. There are two main approaches.

Offset pagination: GET /transactions?limit=20&offset=40 or ?page=3&size=20. Simple to implement and you can jump to any page. The downsides: on large offsets the database still walks through the skipped rows, and if a new record was added between requests, items "shift": one appears twice and another disappears.

Cursor pagination: GET /transactions?limit=20&cursor=eyJpZCI6MTAyNH0. The server returns a nextCursor that points to the last received item, and the next page starts after it. It is stable on insertions and fast, but you can't jump to page 50.

What I check:

  • Boundaries: limit=0, negative, above the maximum, non-numeric.
  • The last page: an empty array or a missing nextCursor, not an error.
  • No duplicates and gaps when walking through all pages; the sum of items equals total, if it is given.
  • Stable sorting: without a unique key in the sort, the order between pages may float.
  • A corrupted or someone else's cursor gives 400, not 500.
In an interview: Offset is simple and lets you jump to any page, but it is slow at large offsets and skips or duplicates records on insertions. Cursor is stable and fast, and I check both variants at the boundaries, the last page and the absence of duplicates.

api-design:1.title: Filtering, sorting and versioning
api-design:1.html:
Filtering and sorting usually go in the query: GET /transactions?status=completed&from=2026-01-01&sort=-createdAt. A minus before the field often means descending, but that is a convention of a specific API, so I check the documentation. I check a combination of several filters, a filter with no results (must be []), an unknown sort or filter field (400 or ignored, but documented), case and special characters in values, and date boundaries inclusive or exclusive.

Versioning is needed to change an API without breaking existing clients. Common variants:

  • In the path: /v1/accounts, /v2/accounts: the most visible and the easiest to test.
  • In a header: for example a custom Api-Version: 2 or a version in Accept.
  • In the query: ?version=2: found less often.

For QA versioning means old versions must also be regressed while they are supported. Mobile applications are especially sensitive: a user may not update the app for months, and the old client keeps going to v1. I also check that a deprecated version returns a deprecation warning if the team agreed so, and that a request without a version behaves as documented.

In an interview: I test filters and sorting in combinations, with an empty result and with unknown fields. If an API is versioned, I regress the old version too, because real clients, especially mobile ones, are still on it.

api-design:2.title: GraphQL: basics and testing
api-design:2.html:
GraphQL is one endpoint (usually POST /graphql), and in the request the client describes exactly which fields it wants. A query reads data, a mutation changes it, a subscription subscribes to events. The structure is described in a schema with types.

{
  "query": "query($id: ID!) { account(id: $id) { id balance currency } }",
  "variables": { "id": "42" }
}

What is different from REST:

  • The status is often 200 even on an error; errors lie in the errors array in the body. So checking only the status in GraphQL gives almost nothing.
  • A response may be partial: part of data is there, and some fields are null with an error in errors.
  • Authorisation must be checked at the level of fields and nested objects, not only the endpoint: access to account is allowed, but isn't someone else's owner returned through a nested field.
  • Deeply nested queries and large batches can bring a server down, so I check depth and complexity limits.
  • Introspection in production is often turned off, so as not to reveal the schema.
In an interview: GraphQL has one endpoint, and the client picks the fields itself. I check not the status but data and errors, authorisation at the field level and the limits on query depth.

api-headers:0.title: Key headers
api-headers:0.html:
Headers are metadata of a request and a response, and many bugs live in them that aren't visible in the body.

HeaderWhereWhat for
Content-TypeRequest and responseThe body format, for example application/json
AcceptRequestWhich format the client wants to receive
AuthorizationRequestA token or credentials
LocationResponseThe URL of the created resource or a redirect
Cache-ControlResponseCaching rules
ETagResponseThe resource version for the cache and concurrent changes
Retry-AfterResponseWhen a request can be repeated after 429 or 503
Set-CookieResponseSet a cookie with security attributes

Typical checks: the response's Content-Type matches the real content; for Accept: application/xml, if the API doesn't support it, the server returns 406, not JSON silently; the session cookie's Set-Cookie has HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite; the response has no headers that reveal the server or framework version.

In an interview: I check not only the body but also headers: Content-Type, Location after creation, caching rules and cookie security attributes. Errors in headers often break clients or create security problems.

api-headers:1.title: ETag, 304 and Cache-Control
api-headers:1.html:
ETag is an identifier of a resource's version. The server returns ETag: "v7". Next time the client sends If-None-Match: "v7": if the resource hasn't changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified without a body, and the client takes the data from the cache. If it changed, 200 with a new body and a new ETag.

GET /accounts/42
If-None-Match: "v7"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "v7"

ETag also protects against lost updates: the client sends a PUT with If-Match: "v7", and if someone has already changed the resource, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed.

Cache-Control: no-cache vs no-store is a classic trap:

  • no-cache: it may be stored, but before use its freshness must be validated with the server (through ETag or a date).
  • no-store: don't store at all, neither in the browser nor in intermediate caches.
  • max-age=60: consider the response fresh for 60 seconds; private: only in the user's browser, not in shared caches.

For personal and financial data I expect no-store or at least private, otherwise one user's balance may end up in a CDN cache and be served to another.

Test cases: after the resource changes, the ETag changes; an old ETag in If-None-Match gives 200, not 304; responses with personal data aren't cached by shared caches.

In an interview: ETag is a resource's version: with If-None-Match the server returns 304 if nothing changed. no-cache means "validate before use" and no-store means "don't store at all", and for financial data I expect exactly no-store.

api-headers:2.title: CORS and preflight
api-headers:2.html:
CORS is a browser mechanism that allows or forbids JavaScript on one origin (scheme + domain + port) to read responses from another. Important: it is a restriction of the browser specifically. Postman, curl and server-side clients don't apply CORS, so "it works in Postman but not in the browser" is a typical sign of a CORS problem.

For "non-simple" requests, for example with Content-Type: application/json, an Authorization header or the PUT and DELETE methods, the browser first sends a preflight, an OPTIONS request:

OPTIONS /api/transfers
Origin: https://app.bank.test
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type

The server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers. If something is missing, the browser won't send the main request, and a CORS error appears in the Console.

What I check:

  • The allowed front-end origin gets the right headers, and a foreign one doesn't.
  • There is no Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with passing cookies or tokens: the browser blocks that anyway, and reflecting any Origin back in the response is a security hole.
  • The preflight returns 2xx and doesn't require authorisation.
In an interview: CORS is browser protection, so it isn't visible in Postman. For non-simple requests the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS, and I check that the server allows only trusted origins and the right methods and headers.

api-security:0.title: OWASP API Top 10: access and authentication
api-security:0.html:
The OWASP API Security Top 10 is a list of the most common API risks. QA doesn't have to be a pentester, but everyone should do the basic checks from it.

BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization), a.k.a. IDOR, is first on the list. A user changes the id in the URL or body and gets someone else's object: GET /accounts/43 with the token of the owner of account 42. The check: two test users, the first one's resource is requested with the second's token, and we expect 403 or 404. I check all methods, not only GET: someone else's account can also be changed and deleted.

Broken Function Level Authorization: an ordinary user calls an admin function, for example DELETE /admin/users/5, because the front end just hides the button and the server doesn't check the role.

Broken Authentication: weak spots in login and tokens:

  • There is no limit on login attempts, and a password can be guessed.
  • A token isn't invalidated after logout or a password change.
  • A token is passed in the URL and ends up in logs.
  • Changing a password or email without re-confirmation.
In an interview: The most important thing in API security is BOLA, or IDOR: I check access to someone else's resource with another user's token for all methods. I also check admin functions under an ordinary role and the handling of tokens: logout, the login attempt limit, invalidation after a password change.

api-security:1.title: Excessive data, mass assignment, injections, rate limiting
api-security:1.html:
Excessive data exposure: the API returns more than the UI shows, hoping the front end will filter it. A profile response may include a password hash, internal flags, a full card number. I check the raw JSON, not the screen, and use a schema with additionalProperties: false.

Mass assignment: the server binds the whole request body to a model. A user adds "role": "admin" or "balance": 1000000 to PATCH /users/me, and it is saved. The test: send fields that the client has no right to change and check through GET that they didn't change.

{ "name": "Ivan", "role": "admin", "isVerified": true }

Injection: SQL, NoSQL or command injection through parameters. I basically check quotes, ' OR 1=1--, special characters and very long strings in fields and the query: the response must be a 4xx or a correct result, with no 500 and no SQL error in the body.

Rate limiting (in the current list, unrestricted resource consumption): without limits an API can be DDoSed or SMS codes can be brute-forced. I check that after the limit a 429 with Retry-After arrives, and that the limit applies per user or IP, not only per endpoint. Separately, page and file sizes: limit=100000 must not bring the service down.

In an interview: I look at the raw JSON for extra sensitive fields, try mass assignment by adding role or balance to the body, and basic injections in string fields. I also check rate limiting: after the limit there must be a 429, not endless attempts.

api-security:2.title: JWT traps
api-security:2.html:
I already know the structure of a JWT and the basic token tests; here are the typical vulnerabilities asked about at the senior level.

  • The none algorithm. An attacker sets "alg": "none" in the header and removes the signature. A server that trusts the alg field will accept such a token. Expected: 401.
  • Swapping RS256 for HS256. A server with an asymmetric key accepts a token signed symmetrically with its own public key. A correct implementation hard-codes the expected algorithm.
  • A weak HS256 secret. A short secret can be brute-forced offline, and then any payload can be signed.
  • Sensitive data in the payload. The payload is only encoded, so an email, phone or account number is visible to everyone.
  • No check of exp, aud, iss. A token from another service or environment must not be accepted.
  • Inability to revoke a token. A JWT is stateless, so after logout or blocking a user the access token lives until exp. The protection is a short access token lifetime, refresh token rotation and a denylist for critical cases.

For tests I decode the token (the payload is readable without a key), change the role or sub and send it without re-signing, and I also check a token from stage on dev.

In an interview: Besides an expired and a corrupted token, I check alg: none, a token from another environment and sensitive data in the payload. I also ask how the team revokes tokens, because a JWT is stateless and after logout lives until exp.

api-contracts:0.title: Swagger/OpenAPI in testing
api-contracts:0.html:
OpenAPI is a specification for describing REST APIs, and Swagger is a set of tools around it, including the interactive Swagger UI. The specification describes endpoints, methods, parameters, request and response schemas, response codes and authorisation. For QA it is the main source of requirements for the API.

Through Swagger UI you can quickly execute a request right from the browser, authorise and see the real response. The specification can be imported into Postman to automatically get a collection of all the requests. I also take schemas from it for validating responses in automated tests.

During testing I check whether the API's real behaviour matches the documentation: field types, whether required, error codes. Discrepancies are either a bug in the code or a bug in the documentation, and both are worth filing. Contract testing is built on the specification, and API clients are generated from it.

api-contracts:1.title: OpenAPI as a source of tests
api-contracts:1.html:
An OpenAPI specification describes endpoints, parameters, body schemas, response codes and authorisation. For me it is not only documentation but raw material for automated tests.

How I use it in practice:

  • I take schemas from components/schemas and validate responses in automated tests with them, instead of rewriting the structure by hand.
  • I generate TypeScript types from the specification (for example, openapi-typescript), and a contract change breaks the compilation of tests.
  • I run a specification linter in CI to catch incomplete descriptions: missing error codes, fields without a type.
  • I compare the specification between versions to see changes that break clients.

Typical discrepancies I find: a field marked as required but null arrives; 400 is documented, but in reality it is 422; there is no description of errors in the specification at all; an enum in the documentation doesn't match the real values.

Transfer:
  type: object
  required: [id, status, amount]
  properties:
    id: { type: string }
    status: { type: string, enum: [pending, completed, failed] }
    amount: { type: number }
In an interview: OpenAPI for me is the source of truth and raw material for tests: from the schemas I validate responses and generate types. Any discrepancy between the specification and real behaviour I file as a bug, either in the code or in the documentation.

api-contracts:2.title: Schema validation in code: ajv and zod
api-contracts:2.html:
In Postman a schema is checked by jsonSchema, and in TypeScript automated tests ajv (a JSON Schema validator) or zod (schemas right in TypeScript with type inference) are usually used.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { z } from 'zod';

const Transfer = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  status: z.enum(['pending', 'completed', 'failed']),
  amount: z.number().positive(),
  currency: z.string().regex(/^[A-Z]{3}$/),
}).strict();

test('create transfer matches contract', async ({ request }) => {
  const res = await request.post('/v1/transfers', {
    data: { toAccount: 'UA21', amount: 150, currency: 'UAH' },
  });
  expect(res.status()).toBe(201);
  const parsed = Transfer.safeParse(await res.json());
  expect(parsed.success, JSON.stringify(parsed.error?.issues)).toBe(true);
});

.strict() in zod works like additionalProperties: false: an extra field fails the test. The choice of tool is simple: if schemas already exist in OpenAPI or JSON Schema, I take ajv and don't duplicate them; if there are no schemas, zod is more convenient, because it gives both the check and the type at once.

In an interview: In code I validate responses with ajv if there are ready JSON schemas from OpenAPI, or with zod if I describe the contract myself in TypeScript. Strict mode catches extra fields, and the error message immediately shows which field didn't match.

api-contracts:3.title: Consumer-driven contracts and breaking changes
api-contracts:3.html:
Contract testing checks that two services understand each other, without bringing up the whole system. In the consumer-driven contracts approach (the Pact tool) the consumer, for example a front end or another microservice, describes in a test which requests it makes and which fields it expects. A contract is generated from this, it is published to the Pact Broker, and the provider in its own CI verifies that the real API fulfils this contract.

Advantages: fast, isolated, and the provider learns that it broke a specific consumer before deployment. Pact checks only what the consumer really uses, so it isn't a replacement for the provider's functional tests.

Breaking vs non-breaking changes:

ChangeType
Add a new optional field to a responseNon-breaking
Add a new endpointNon-breaking
Add an optional parameter to a requestNon-breaking
Remove or rename a response fieldBreaking
Change a field's type, for example a number to a stringBreaking
Make an optional request field requiredBreaking
Change the status code or the error formatBreaking

A nuance: a new value in an enum is formally an "addition", but may break a client that handles only known values.

In an interview: In consumer-driven contracts the consumer records its expectations in a contract through Pact, and the provider verifies it in its own CI before deployment. Adding fields usually doesn't break clients, while removing, renaming or changing a type is a breaking change that needs a new API version.

api-perf:0.title: Kinds of load tests and percentiles
api-perf:0.html:
TypeWhat we doWhat we look for
LoadThe expected working load for a long timeWhether we hold the SLA under normal conditions
StressGradually raise the load above normalThe breaking point and how the system degrades
SpikeA sudden jump, for example 10 times in a minuteWhether it withstands the spike and recovers
SoakA moderate load for many hoursMemory leaks, connection pool exhaustion

Tools: k6, JMeter, Gatling, Locust.

Why not the average. An average time of 200 ms may hide that every twentieth request takes 5 seconds. So percentiles are used: p95 means 95% of requests are faster than this value, p99 means 99%. An SLA is usually worded like this: "p95 < 500 ms at 200 RPS, errors under 0.1%". The p99 tail often hurts the most, because one page makes dozens of requests, and someone almost always hits a slow one.

It is important to test on an environment close to production with realistic data: on an empty database everything is fast.

In an interview: Load checks the expected load, stress looks for the limit, spike a sudden burst, and soak stability over a long time. I evaluate p95 and p99, not the average, because the average hides the slow tail.

api-perf:1.title: Timeouts, retries and idempotency keys
api-perf:1.html:
Timeouts. Every call to another service must have a timeout, otherwise one hung service holds threads and connections, and everything falls down. I test that with a slow dependency the client gets a controlled error (often a 504 from the gateway) in a predictable time and doesn't hang for a minute.

Retries with backoff. Only temporary errors may be repeated: a timeout, 429, 502, 503, 504. On 400 or 422 a retry is pointless: the result won't change. Retries are done with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) and jitter, a random offset, so that thousands of clients don't hit the server at once. The number of attempts is limited.

Idempotency keys. Retrying a non-idempotent POST is dangerous: a timeout doesn't mean the request wasn't executed, maybe only the response was lost. So the client generates an Idempotency-Key once per operation and passes it in all repeats, and the server returns the stored result instead of a second payment.

A fintech test case: emulate a response timeout (for example through a proxy or a mock of the dependency), wait for the client's retry and check in the database that there is one transfer.

In an interview: I check that calls have timeouts, and that retries happen only on temporary errors with exponential backoff and jitter. For payments every retry goes with the same Idempotency-Key, and I check that there is one transaction in the database.

api-perf:2.title: 429, 503, Retry-After and the circuit breaker
api-perf:2.html:
429 Too Many Requests means the client exceeded a limit. 503 Service Unavailable means the service temporarily can't process the request: overload, a deploy, a dependency is down. Both may have the Retry-After header: the number of seconds or a date after which it is worth repeating:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30

A correct client respects Retry-After and doesn't retry earlier. What I check: the limit fires at the right threshold; the header is present and has a valid value; after the pause requests go through again; the client (our front end or service) shows a clear message instead of spinning a loader forever.

A circuit breaker is a fuse between services. If a dependency fails again and again, the breaker "opens" (the open state), and calls to it immediately return an error or a fallback without waiting for the timeout. After some time it lets a few trial requests through (half-open): if they succeed, it closes again (closed). This stops the failure of one service from bringing down the whole system in a cascade.

For QA these are resilience scenarios: turn off or slow down a dependency and check that the main service responds quickly with a controlled error or a fallback, and that after the dependency recovers everything returns to normal without manual intervention.

In an interview: On 429 and 503 I check for Retry-After and that the client respects it. A circuit breaker, after a series of failures, stops going to the dependency and quickly returns an error or a fallback, and I test this by turning off the dependency and checking recovery.

sd-approach:0.title: What exactly is assessed in QA System Design
sd-approach:0.html:
System Design for Senior QA Automation consists of two different parts. The first part is designing a test system. You are asked to design a framework, a CI pipeline, a test data strategy or a testing strategy for microservices. The second part is understanding the backend. You are shown a diagram "client, load balancer, services, cache, DB, queue" and asked what could break here and how you would test it.

The interviewer doesn't expect a perfect architecture. They look at four things:

  • whether you ask clarifying questions instead of starting to draw at once;
  • whether you think about scale: the number of tests, teams, environments, run time;
  • whether you see the trade-offs and can explain why you chose one thing over another;
  • whether you can measure the result: metrics, pipeline SLAs, the flaky level.

A typical Middle candidate's mistake: starting with a tool. "Let's take Playwright and Allure" is not design, it is picking a library. A Senior starts with the problem: who the framework's users are, how many tests, what time constraints, what the business risks are.

For fintech add risks that the interviewer will definitely appreciate: money can't be debited twice, a balance can't go negative without permission, every operation must be traceable. If you naturally mention idempotency and audit, it is a strong signal.

In an interview: I understand System Design for QA as two things: how to build a scalable test system and how to test a distributed system while understanding its architecture. I always start with requirements and constraints, not tools, and finish with the metrics by which we will know the solution works.

sd-approach:1.title: Answer structure: requirements, layers, solution, trade-offs, metrics
sd-approach:1.html:
To avoid getting lost over 40-60 minutes, stick to one scheme. It works both for a test framework and for a backend task.

  1. Requirements. Functional: what the system must do. Non-functional: how many tests, in what time, how many teams, which environments, which integrations. Clarify the numbers out loud.
  2. Layers. Break the system into blocks: for a framework these are tests, business steps, page objects and API clients, fixtures, config, reporting. For a backend these are the client, LB, services, storages, queues.
  3. Solution. For each layer say what exactly you do and why.
  4. Trade-offs. What you pay for the solution: speed versus isolation, infrastructure cost versus feedback time, data realism versus stability.
  5. Metrics. How you will know the solution worked: pipeline time, flaky rate, time to feedback on a PR, the number of bugs that reached production.
Requirements -> Layers -> Solution -> Trade-offs -> Metrics
  |          |         |           |            |
numbers    blocks    why so    what we pay   how we measure

A useful habit: after each block, briefly summarise and ask the interviewer whether to go deeper. That way you manage time and show that you can work with stakeholders.

In an interview: I answer by a scheme: first I clarify requirements and numbers, then break the system into layers, propose a solution for each, talk through the trade-offs and finish with success metrics. This keeps me from jumping into tool details before the problem is understood.

sd-approach:2.title: Which questions to clarify at the start
sd-approach:2.html:
The first 5 minutes are the most important. Good clarifying questions immediately show your level. Here is a set worth having in your head.

For a test system:

  • How many tests are there now and how many in a year? Which types: unit, API, e2e?
  • What is the time target: feedback on a PR in 10 minutes or a nightly run?
  • How many teams write tests? One repository or several?
  • Which environments exist: local, ephemeral per PR, staging?
  • Which external dependencies: a payment provider, KYC, bank APIs?
  • What is the budget for CI infrastructure?

For a backend task:

  • What is the load: RPS, peak hours, growth?
  • What matters more: consistency or availability? For an account balance the answer is usually consistency.
  • What delivery guarantees does the queue have: at-least-once or something else?
  • Are there regulator requirements: audit, data retention, PCI DSS?

You don't need to ask all the questions. Choose the 4-6 most important, write down the answers and refer to them later. If the interviewer says "decide yourself", state your assumptions out loud: "Let's assume 2000 e2e tests, an average test of 20 seconds, a target of 15 minutes".

In an interview: I start with questions about scale, the time target, environments and external dependencies. If there are no numbers, I state assumptions out loud myself, so that all the calculations afterwards are transparent.

sd-framework:0.title: Test framework layers
sd-framework:0.html:
A scalable framework is not a folder with tests but several layers with clear boundaries. Each layer knows only about the layer beneath it.

tests/            - scenarios: what we check (Given/When/Then)
steps/ or flows/  - business steps: createUser, makeTransfer
pages/ + api/     - Page Objects and typed API clients
fixtures/         - lifecycle: login, data, clients
config/           - environments, secrets, timeouts
reporting/        - reporters, artifacts, notifications

Why layers. A test must read like a business scenario: "a user with a balance of 100 transfers 30". The details of locators and HTTP requests are hidden below. When the UI changes, you fix one Page Object, not 200 tests.

Separately about API clients. In a fintech project most preconditions must be created through the API, not the UI: create a user, pass KYC, top up an account. This is many times faster and more stable. We leave the UI only for what the test itself verifies.

Fixtures in Playwright are the main composition mechanism. With test.extend you describe what a test receives ready: an authorised page, an API client, a user with a balance. A fixture itself cleans up after the test.

type Fixtures = { api: BankApi; funded: User };

export const test = base.extend<Fixtures>({
  api: async ({ request }, use) => {
    await use(new BankApi(request));
  },
  funded: async ({ api }, use) => {
    const user = await api.createUser();
    await api.deposit(user.accountId, 100);
    await use(user);
    await api.deleteUser(user.id);
  },
});
In an interview: I build a framework in layers: tests describe the business scenario, steps and Page Objects hide the details, and fixtures manage data and the lifecycle. I create preconditions through the API, and use the UI only for what I really verify.

sd-framework:1.title: Task: 2000 e2e tests must finish in 15 minutes
sd-framework:1.html:
A classic task. We break it down by the scheme.

Requirements and calculation

We clarify: an average test of 20 seconds, a target of 15 minutes for the whole suite, a run on every merge into main. We calculate: 2000 x 20 s = 40,000 s, which is about 667 minutes sequentially. We leave 3 minutes for starting containers, installing browsers and merging reports, so the tests themselves get 12 minutes. 667 / 12 = about 56 parallel slots. We take it with a margin: 8 machines (shards) of 8 workers each = 64 slots.

The solution

  • Test isolation: each test creates its own data, with no dependencies between tests. Otherwise parallelism is impossible.
  • Parallelism: fullyParallel: true, sharding through --shard=i/8, reports in blob format and merging through merge-reports.
  • Preconditions through the API, login through a saved storageState.
  • A ready image with browsers and dependencies, so as not to spend minutes on installation.
  • Reviewing the pyramid: some of the 2000 e2e tests can be moved to the API level. That often gives more than new machines.

Trade-offs

More machines mean higher CI cost and more load on the test environment. 64 parallel sessions may "bring down" staging, so the environment must be scaled too, or each shard given its own.

Metrics

Pipeline time p50 and p95, flaky rate, shard imbalance (the longest shard against the average), the cost of one run.

In an interview: First I calculate: 2000 tests of 20 seconds each is about 11 hours sequentially, so about 60 parallel slots are needed. Then I ensure data isolation, sharding with blob reports, a ready Docker image, and in parallel I review the pyramid, because moving part of the tests to the API is often cheaper than buying machines.

sd-framework:2.title: Configuration, environments and secrets
sd-framework:2.html:
One framework must run locally, on a PR environment and on staging without changing code. So config is a separate layer.

Principles:

  • All environment variables are read in one place and validated at startup. If BASE_URL isn't set, the run fails immediately, not on the 300th test.
  • Secrets (API keys, test users' passwords) only from the CI secret store or a vault, never in the repository.
  • Timeouts are set centrally in playwright.config.ts, not scattered across tests.
  • Projects in Playwright separate runs: api, chromium, mobile, smoke. You can run separate sets through --project.
export default defineConfig({
  fullyParallel: true,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 8 : undefined,
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
  use: {
    baseURL: env.BASE_URL,
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/ },
    { name: 'chromium', dependencies: ['setup'] },
  ],
});

The setup project with a dependency is the standard way to log in once and save a storageState that all tests then use.

A separate question is several teams. If 5 teams write tests, the shared core (clients, fixtures, config) is worth moving into an internal package with versioning, and the tests kept next to the teams' services. Then the core evolves centrally, and the teams don't block each other.

In an interview: I keep config as a separate layer: one place to read env with validation, secrets only from CI, timeouts centralised. For several teams I move the framework core into a separate versioned package.

sd-data:0.title: Test data strategies
sd-data:0.html:
Test data is the most frequent cause of unstable and slow tests. There are several approaches, and a Senior must explain when to use which.

ApproachProsCons
Static data in the DBSimple, fastConflicts in parallel runs, data gets "spoiled"
Generating through the API in the testIsolation, realisticSlower, depends on the API
A seed script or a DB snapshotA fast environment startMust be maintained together with the schema
Factories plus direct DB writesVery fastBypasses business logic, can create an impossible state

The basic rule: each test creates its own data and doesn't rely on data from other tests. Only reference data that nobody changes can be shared: currencies, countries, tariffs.

For fintech there is a nuance: creating a "ready" user often requires KYC, phone verification, opening an account. Test hooks help here: an internal endpoint, available only in test environments, that creates a verified user with one request. This must be agreed with development and closed off from production.

Data must be unique: an email with testInfo.workerIndex and a random suffix, unique account numbers. No real personal data and no real cards: only the provider's test cards.

In an interview: My principle is that each test creates the needed data itself through the API or test hooks and doesn't depend on other tests. I leave only immutable reference data shared, and I don't use real personal data in tests at all.

sd-data:1.title: Task: test data for parallel runs
sd-data:1.html:
The condition: 64 parallel workers, a shared staging, tests of transfers between accounts. The tests periodically fail because the balance isn't what was expected.

Why it fails

Two tests use one user, "test_user_1". Test A transfers 30, and test B at that moment checks the balance of 100 and gets 70. This is a classic shared state conflict.

The solution

  1. Unique data per test. A fixture creates a new user and account before the test.
  2. A pool of accounts per worker, if creation is expensive. The worker with index N takes accounts from pool N. A worker-scoped fixture in Playwright creates them once per worker.
  3. A run prefix. All entities carry a run label, for example run_8f2c_w3_. That makes it easy to find and clean up garbage after the run.
  4. Relative checks, not absolute, if the state is shared: remember the balance before the action and compare the difference.
export const test = base.extend<{}, { account: Account }>({
  account: [async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
    const acc = await createAccount(`run_${RUN_ID}_w${workerInfo.workerIndex}`);
    await use(acc);
    await closeAccount(acc.id);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

Trade-offs

Fresh data for every test gives maximum isolation, but loads the API and the database grows. A pool per worker is faster, but tests within a worker must clean up their state.

Metrics

The number of failures caused by data, the volume of garbage in the DB after a run, the time spent preparing data in a test.

In an interview: I remove shared state: each test or each worker gets its own accounts with a run label. If creation is expensive, I use a worker-scoped fixture, and after the run I clean the data by prefix.

sd-data:2.title: Environments: local, ephemeral, staging
sd-data:2.html:
A test system is not only the test code but also the environments where they run.

Local (docker compose)        -> a fast test development loop
Ephemeral env per PR          -> isolated verification of a change
Shared staging                -> integration with real dependencies
Production (smoke, synthetic) -> a check after release

An ephemeral environment is an environment brought up for every PR (for example a namespace in Kubernetes) and destroyed after the merge. The plus: no conflicts between teams, clean data. The minus: cost and spin-up time, and it is hard to bring up all 40 microservices.

The compromise: bring up only the changed service and its closest dependencies, and take the rest from the shared staging or replace them with stubs.

External dependencies. A payment provider, a KYC service and bank APIs often have a sandbox with limitations: rate limits, instability, the inability to reproduce certain errors. So for most tests I put in a stub at the HTTP level (WireMock or similar) with controllable responses: success, refusal, timeout, a duplicate callback. I keep the real sandbox for a small set of integration tests that run separately and don't block the PR.

In an interview: I separate environments by purpose: local for development, ephemeral per PR for isolation, staging for integration and smoke in production. External payment services I mostly replace with controllable stubs, to reproduce errors and timeouts, and I use the real sandbox in a separate small set.

sd-ci:0.title: Tests in the pipeline: stages and quality gates
sd-ci:0.html:
A good pipeline gives fast feedback with cheap tests and runs expensive tests when it makes sense.

PR:      lint + typecheck -> unit -> API -> e2e smoke (5-10 min)
main:    full API + full e2e (up to 15 min)
nightly: cross-browser, long scenarios, performance
release: smoke on staging -> deploy -> smoke in production

A quality gate is a rule that blocks a merge or a deploy. Examples: all unit and API tests are green, the e2e smoke is green, coverage of changed files didn't drop. Important: a gate must be reliable. If the smoke is flaky, teams will start ignoring it, and the gate loses its meaning.

What to run on a PR. The full suite on every PR is often too expensive. Options:

  • A smoke set tagged @smoke through --grep.
  • Tests related to changed files: Playwright has --only-changed, which takes changes relative to a git branch. It works for tests that import the changed modules, so for a backend change it won't help.
  • Rerunning only the failed: --last-failed locally.

For fintech I always include the critical money scenarios in the PR set: a transfer, a top-up, a refusal on insufficient balance. Their cost of error is the highest.

In an interview: I build the pipeline in layers: on a PR fast checks and smoke, on main the full set, at night long and cross-browser tests, after the deploy smoke in production. A gate blocks a merge only with stable tests, otherwise the team stops trusting it.

sd-ci:1.title: Workers and shards: how parallelisation works
sd-ci:1.html:
Playwright has two levels of parallelism.

  • Workers are processes on one machine. Each worker has its own browser. The number is limited by the machine's CPU and memory.
  • Shards split the test suite between several machines through --shard=1/4, --shard=2/4 and so on.
strategy:
  matrix:
    shard: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
steps:
  - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/8
  - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
    with:
      name: blob-${{ matrix.shard }}
      path: blob-report

After all the shards a separate job downloads all the blob reports and calls npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports. That gives you one HTML report.

Important nuances:

  • By default Playwright parallelises files, and tests inside a file run sequentially. With fullyParallel: true individual tests are parallelised, and the shards are balanced better.
  • If one file has 200 tests and the others have 5 each, without fullyParallel one shard will be much longer.
  • The number of workers on a machine must not exceed its resources. 8 browsers on 2 vCPUs will give timeouts and flakiness.
  • Tests with mode: 'serial' aren't parallelised inside the group. They should be minimised.

The efficiency metric: the difference between the longest and the average shard. If the longest shard is 14 minutes and the average is 6, you pay for idle time.

In an interview: I use two levels: workers on a machine and shards between machines, with fullyParallel for an even distribution and blob reports that I merge in a separate job. I choose the number of workers to fit the machine's resources, because overloading immediately gives flakiness.

sd-ci:2.title: Feedback speed and cost
sd-ci:2.html:
