A Senior must talk not only about speed but also about money and where the real bottleneck is.

Where pipeline time comes from:

  • Runner start and dependency installation. The solution: caching node_modules, a ready Docker image with browsers.
  • Data preparation and login. The solution: the API instead of the UI, storageState.
  • Slow tests. The solution: find the top 20 longest and rewrite them or move them to the API.
  • Waiting for the environment. The solution: a health check before starting, not sleep.

When to add machines and when not. If tests run into the shared staging (the DB, a rate limit), adding shards won't speed up the run but will increase timeouts. First you must find the bottleneck.

Another optimisation is fail fast. The maxFailures option stops the run after N failures. On a PR this saves minutes when something basic is broken, for example login.

Cost. Roughly calculate: 8 machines for 15 minutes on every merge, 50 merges a day. That is already noticeable money. So nightly for rare scenarios and smoke on a PR is not laziness but economy.

In an interview: Before adding machines I look for the bottleneck: dependency installation, login through the UI, the slowest tests or an overloaded environment. Parallelism helps only when the environment can withstand the load.

sd-flaky:0.title: Where flaky tests come from
sd-flaky:0.html:
A flaky test is one that, on the same code, sometimes passes and sometimes fails. The main harm is not in one failure but in the team ceasing to trust the results.

The main causes, from the most frequent:

  1. Synchronisation. A test checks the state before the UI or backend updated it. Manual waitForTimeout instead of waiting for a condition.
  2. Shared data. Parallel tests change one account.
  3. Order dependence. A test works only after another test.
  4. An asynchronous backend. A transfer is processed through a queue, and the test checks the balance immediately.
  5. An unstable environment. An overloaded staging, slow external sandboxes, the network.
  6. Time and dates. A test fails at midnight, on the last day of the month or in a different time zone.
  7. Animations and unstable locators. Dependence on CSS classes or the order of elements.

How to tell a product bug from a flaky test. We look at the trace: if the UI really showed a wrong amount, that may be a race condition in the product, and it is a bug, not "flaky". Some flaky tests actually catch real concurrency problems. So "just add a retry" is dangerous.

In Playwright most synchronisation problems are solved by web-first assertions: await expect(locator).toHaveText('70.00') waits and rechecks until the timeout. For the backend there is expect.poll.

In an interview: The most frequent causes of flakiness are synchronisation, shared data, order dependence and an asynchronous backend. Before calling a test flaky, I look at the trace, because sometimes an unstable test catches a real race condition in the product.

sd-flaky:1.title: The process of fighting flakiness: detect, isolate, fix
sd-flaky:1.html:
One engineer fixing tests doesn't scale. A process is needed.

Detection -> Quarantine -> Analysis -> Fix -> Return

Detection. We collect the history of each test's results between runs. A test that passed after a retry is marked flaky by Playwright. If a test has several such results in a week, it is a candidate. Additionally the suite can be run once a night with --repeat-each=5 to find unstable tests before they bother the teams.

Quarantine. An unstable test is taken out of the blocking gate: the tag @quarantine, a separate non-blocking job. A ticket with an owner and a deadline is always created for it. Without an owner, quarantine turns into a graveyard.

Analysis. Trace, video, backend logs by correlation id. We classify the cause: the test, the data, the environment or the product.

Fix and return. After a fix the test is run many times (for example --repeat-each=20) and only then returned to the gate.

Rules I would set:

  • A quarantine limit, for example 2 weeks. After that the test is either fixed or deleted.
  • The flaky rate as a team metric, visible on the dashboard.
  • A new test is run several times before merge.
In an interview: I build a process: automatic detection from history, quarantine with an owner and a deadline, analysis through trace and logs, and return to the gate only after many stable runs. The key is that every flaky test has an owner, otherwise quarantine grows forever.

sd-flaky:2.title: Retries: when they help and when they hurt
sd-flaky:2.html:
Retries in Playwright are configured through retries in the config. A test that failed and passed on a repeat gets the flaky status.

When a retry is useful:

  • As temporary protection against infrastructure failures on CI.
  • For collecting diagnostics: trace: 'on-first-retry' records a trace exactly when a test failed.
  • As a source of data for detecting flakiness.

When a retry hurts:

  • When it hides a product bug. A race condition in a money debit may show up in 1 run out of 10. A retry will make the pipeline green, and the bug goes to production.
  • When retries are large (3-5). Run time grows, and real stability doesn't improve.
  • When a step-level retry repeats a non-idempotent action. A repeated transfer POST may create a second transfer.

The difference between a test retry and waiting for a condition. Waiting is a normal part of a test: expect.poll waits until the transfer status becomes COMPLETED. A test retry is restarting the whole test from scratch. The first is correct synchronisation, the second is a backup mechanism.

await expect.poll(async () => {
  const res = await api.getTransfer(id);
  return res.status;
}, { timeout: 15_000, intervals: [500, 1000, 2000] }).toBe('COMPLETED');
In an interview: On CI I set at most 1-2 retries and always track tests that pass only on a repeat. A retry is insurance and a source of diagnostics, not a solution: in fintech it can hide a race condition in debiting money.

sd-report:0.title: A report that helps find the cause
sd-report:0.html:
A report must answer three questions: what failed, why and whether it failed before. A list of green and red tests is the minimum, not the goal.

What a report must have for every failure:

  • The assertion message and the stack.
  • The Playwright trace: steps, DOM snapshots, network requests, console.
  • A screenshot and video (as needed, because they take space).
  • The requests' correlation ids, to find backend logs.
  • The environment, build version, shard number.

Reporting levels:

  1. The Playwright HTML report is for an engineer analysing a failure.
  2. History and trends (Allure or your own results DB) are for finding flaky and slow tests.
  3. A chat notification: briefly, how many failed, a link to the report, who authored the commit.
  4. A dashboard for the team and management: stability, pipeline time, the trend.

A mistake I often see: a notification for every failure in a general channel. A week later everyone ignores the channel. It is better to send it to the PR author or the area's owner, and only failures on main to the general channel.

Separately keep raw results (JSON or JUnit XML). Then you can build your own analytics without being tied to one reporting tool.

In an interview: I set up a report so that it answers what failed, why and whether it failed before: a trace, a correlation id, the test's history. Notifications go specifically to the change's author, because a general noisy channel quickly stops being read.

sd-report:1.title: Test system metrics
sd-report:1.html:
What isn't measured isn't improved. Here are the metrics I would show on a dashboard.

MetricWhat it showsBenchmark
Pipeline time p50 and p95Feedback speedA PR under 10-15 min
Flaky rateThe share of tests that passed only with a retryUnder 1-2 percent
Pass rate on mainThe health of the main branchClose to 100 percent
Escaped defectsBugs found in productionA downward trend
Failure analysis timeHow much time goes into analysisA downward trend
Run costMoney on CIUnder control

Why p95 and not the average. An average time of 10 minutes may hide that every fifth run takes 25 minutes because of a slow shard. Developers feel exactly the tail.

Escaped defects are the most honest quality metric. Analyse every production bug: could a test have caught it, at which level, why it didn't. That gives concrete actions, not an abstract "increase coverage".

Careful with code coverage. High coverage doesn't guarantee quality checks. A test without meaningful assertions also gives coverage. For e2e, coverage of business scenarios or risks is more useful: are all payment methods, currencies and transfer statuses covered.

In an interview: I look at the p95 of pipeline time, flaky rate, pass rate on main and escaped defects. What gives me the most is analysing production bugs: for each I ask at which level a test should have caught it, and I turn exactly that into a plan.

sd-report:2.title: Observability and testing
sd-report:2.html:
Observability is the ability to understand a system's state from its external signals: logs, metrics, traces. For QA it is a way to find the cause of a failure in a distributed system, not only in the browser.

A correlation id (or trace id) is an identifier that passes through all the services within one request. A test can pass its own header and then use it to find logs in all services.

test('transfer completes', async ({ request }, testInfo) => {
  const corrId = `e2e-${testInfo.testId}-${Date.now()}`;
  const res = await request.post('/api/transfers', {
    headers: { 'X-Correlation-Id': corrId },
    data: { from: 'acc_1', to: 'acc_2', amount: 30 },
  });
  testInfo.annotations.push({ type: 'correlationId', description: corrId });
  expect(res.status()).toBe(201);
});

The header's name depends on the project: it may be X-Request-Id or the standard traceparent from W3C Trace Context.

How else QA uses observability:

  • Checks not only the API response but also that an event reached the queue and the audit log.
  • After a deploy looks at error and latency metrics as part of the release check.
  • Synthetic monitoring is a small set of scenarios that regularly go to production (for example login and viewing the balance on a test account) and alert on failure.
In an interview: I pass a correlation id from the test and store it in the report, to find the logs of all services for a specific failure within a minute. After a release I use metrics and synthetic checks in production as a continuation of testing.

sd-backend:0.title: Client-server and the load balancer
sd-backend:0.html:
The basic diagram you must be able to draw and explain:

Client -> DNS -> Load Balancer -> [App 1, App 2, App 3] -> Cache
                                         |                 |
                                         +------> DB <-----+
                                         +------> Queue -> Workers

A load balancer distributes requests between several instances of a service. Algorithms: round robin, least connections, a hash of the IP or a key. An LB also does health checks and stops sending traffic to an unhealthy instance.

A stateless service doesn't keep the client's state in memory. The session lives in a token or in a shared store. Then any instance can handle any request, and the service scales easily.

Sticky sessions bind a client to one instance. This is simpler for stateful logic, but when the instance fails the session is lost, and the load is distributed worse.

What QA tests here:

  • A scenario where one instance fails in the middle of a flow: does the user continue working.
  • Consecutive requests land on different instances: is there no in-memory state that gets "lost". A typical bug: the first request created a payment draft in the memory of instance 1, and the second landed on instance 2 and got 404.
  • A rolling deploy: during an update some instances have the new version and some the old. Are they compatible with each other.
  • LB timeouts: a long request (a report, an export) may be cut off at the LB before the service responds.
In an interview: A load balancer distributes traffic and removes unhealthy instances, and the services behind it must be stateless. I separately test an instance failing in the middle of a scenario and mixed versions during a rolling deploy, because bugs often hide there.

sd-backend:1.title: Cache: where it stands and what breaks in it
sd-backend:1.html:
A cache keeps frequently read data in fast storage (for example Redis), so as not to go to the DB every time.

The main patterns:

  • Cache-aside: the service looks in the cache, and if it isn't there, reads from the DB and puts it in the cache. The most common.
  • Write-through: a write goes to the cache and the DB at once.
  • TTL: an entry in the cache lives for a limited time and then disappears.

The hardest part is invalidation. When data changed in the DB, the cache may still return the old value. For a product catalogue, 30 seconds of a stale price is often acceptable. For an account balance, it isn't.

What can break and what to test:

  1. Stale data. After a transfer the balance in the UI is old, because it is read from the cache. The test: change the data and check that a read returns the new value within the promised time.
  2. A wrong cache key. The key doesn't take the user or currency into account, and one user sees another's data. That is already a security incident.
  3. Cache stampede. A popular key expired, and thousands of requests go to the DB at once. Checked with a load test.
  4. The cache is unavailable. The service must work more slowly, but work, not fail.

For tests a cache creates one more problem: a test reads data that another test or a previous run put into the cache. So in test environments it is useful to have a way to reset the cache, or short TTLs.

In an interview: A cache speeds up reads, but gives a risk of stale data, so I first ask what delay is acceptable for each type of data. Separately I check the cache keys, because a mistake in a key may show a user someone else's data, and the service's behaviour when the cache is unavailable.

sd-backend:2.title: The database: indexes, replication, sharding
sd-backend:2.html:
An index is a structure that lets you quickly find rows without a full table scan. An index speeds up reads, but slows down writes and takes space. For QA this matters in two places: slow queries on large volumes of data (on staging with 1000 rows everything is fast, in production with 50 million it isn't) and unique indexes as protection against duplicates.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_transfers_idem
  ON transfers (client_id, idempotency_key);

Such an index guarantees at the DB level that the same transfer request won't be written twice.

Replication means copies of the DB. The primary accepts writes, and replicas serve reads. Replication is usually asynchronous, so there is replication lag: just-written data may not be on the replica yet. A typical bug: a user created a transfer, the history page reads from a replica, and the transfer isn't there yet. What to test: reading right after a write, and behaviour under an artificial replication delay.

Sharding is distributing data between several DBs by a key, for example by user_id. Each shard stores part of the data. The difficulties: queries across several shards, transactions between shards (a transfer between users on different shards), rebalancing. For testing it is important to have data on different shards, not only on one.

Transactions and isolation. A transfer is a debit and a credit that must happen together. Concurrent transfers from one account may produce a negative balance if there is no locking or the right isolation level. This is checked with parallel requests in a test.

In an interview: Indexes speed up reads and can guarantee uniqueness, replication gives read scale but creates replication lag, and sharding distributes data by a key and complicates operations across shards. As QA I test reading after a write, transfers between shards and concurrent debits from one account.

sd-backend:3.title: Message queues and delivery guarantees
sd-backend:3.html:
A queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) decouples services: a producer puts a message in, and a consumer processes it later. This gives resilience to peaks and independence of services, but makes the system asynchronous.

Delivery guarantees:

  • At-most-once: a message may be lost, but won't be duplicated.
  • At-least-once: a message won't be lost, but may arrive twice. The most common variant.
  • Exactly-once: hard to achieve across a whole system. In practice you do at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer.

From at-least-once follows the main rule: the consumer must be idempotent. If the message "credit 30 to the account" arrives twice, the money must be credited once. Usually a consumer stores the ids of processed messages and skips duplicates.

Other concepts:

  • DLQ (dead letter queue): where messages go that couldn't be processed after N attempts. They can't just be ignored: in fintech this is money stuck in limbo.
  • Order. In Kafka order is guaranteed only within a partition. If events of one account go to different partitions, a "debit" may be processed before a "top-up".
  • Consumer lag: how many messages are waiting to be processed. A metric for monitoring and for tests under load.

What to test: a duplicate message, a message out of order, a consumer failing in the middle of processing, a poison message that must go to the DLQ and not block the queue.

In an interview: In most systems the queue gives at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent. I test duplicates, order violations, a consumer failing in the middle of processing, and I check that invalid messages go to the DLQ and don't hang.

sd-micro:0.title: A microservices testing strategy
sd-micro:0.html:
In a monolith an e2e test covers everything at once. In microservices there are 30 services, each team deploys independently, and a full e2e on every change becomes slow and unstable. So the strategy is different.

              e2e (few, critical paths)
         contract tests (between services)
    component tests (a service in isolation, dependencies are stubs)
  integration (a service + its DB, queue)
unit (many)

A component test tests one service through its API, with a real DB in a container (Testcontainers), while neighbouring services are replaced by stubs. Fast, stable, runs in the service's CI.

A contract test checks that a producer and a consumer understand the API the same way. The consumer-driven approach (Pact): the consumer describes which requests it makes and which responses it expects, and the producer in its own CI verifies that it fulfils these contracts. That way a breaking API change is caught before deployment, without a shared environment.

E2E is left for a few critical business flows: registration, top-up, transfer, withdrawal. There must not be hundreds of them.

What else is important:

  • Testing asynchronous contracts: the format of events in a queue is also a contract.
  • Backward compatibility: a new service must accept the old format until all consumers have updated.
  • Each team owns its service's tests. The QA architect sets standards and shared tools.
In an interview: For microservices I shift the main weight to component and contract tests, which run in each service's CI without a shared environment. I leave E2E only for a few critical money flows, because hundreds of e2e tests through 30 services would be slow and unstable.

sd-micro:1.title: Task: how to test a transfer system with a queue
sd-micro:1.html:
The condition: a user creates a transfer through the API. Transfer Service writes the transfer with the status PENDING and publishes an event to the queue. Ledger Service debits and credits the funds, then publishes an event, and the status becomes COMPLETED. Notification Service sends a push.

Client -> Transfer API -> DB (PENDING) -> Queue -> Ledger -> Queue -> Transfer (COMPLETED)
                                                       \-> Notification

Requirements and risks

Money must not be debited twice or lost. A balance doesn't go negative. Every transfer reaches a final status: COMPLETED or FAILED. A repeated client request doesn't create a second transfer.

Test layers

  1. Unit: fee calculation, amount validation, status transitions.
  2. Component Transfer Service: the API plus a real DB, the queue as a stub or a container. We check that the event is published in the right format.
  3. Component Ledger: we feed an event into the queue and check the ledger records. A duplicate event gives one debit.
  4. Contract: the event format between Transfer and Ledger.
  5. E2E: create a transfer through the API, wait for COMPLETED with expect.poll, check both balances.

Negative scenarios

  • Insufficient funds: status FAILED, the balance didn't change.
  • A repeated POST with the same idempotency key: the same transfer.
  • Ledger failed mid-processing: after a restart the transfer completes once.
  • An invalid event goes to the DLQ, and there is an alert.
  • 20 parallel transfers from one account for an amount greater than the balance: none gives a minus.

Metrics

The number of transfers "stuck" in PENDING longer than N minutes, DLQ sizes, consumer lag, discrepancies in balance reconciliation.

In an interview: I break the system into layers: unit for logic, component for each service with a real DB, contract for the event format and a few e2e tests that wait for the final status. The main focus is negative scenarios: duplicates, a consumer failing, parallel debits and transfers stuck in PENDING.

sd-micro:2.title: Eventual consistency and sagas in tests
sd-micro:2.html:
Eventual consistency means that after a change, data in different parts of the system becomes consistent not at once but after some time. The balance in Ledger has already changed, and the history service hasn't yet.

How to test:

  • Don't check immediately after the action. Wait for the final state with polling and a timeout: expect.poll or expect(...).toPass().
  • The timeout must match the SLA. If the business promises an update within 5 seconds, a test with a 60-second timeout will miss a degradation.
  • No fixed sleep: it is either too short (flaky) or too long (slow).

A saga is a way to perform a business operation across several services without a distributed transaction. Each step has a compensating action. For example an e-commerce order: reserve the item, debit the payment, create the delivery. If creating the delivery failed, refund the money and release the reservation.

What to test in a saga:

  • A failure at each step and the right compensation.
  • A failure of the compensation itself: is there a retry and an alert.
  • Repeated delivery of events at each step.
  • The final state: there are no "half-finished" operations where money is debited and the item isn't reserved.
await expect(async () => {
  const order = await api.getOrder(orderId);
  expect(order.status).toBe('CANCELLED');
  expect(order.refundStatus).toBe('REFUNDED');
}).toPass({ timeout: 10_000 });
In an interview: In an asynchronous system I check the final state through polling with a timeout that matches the SLA, not through sleep. For sagas I test a failure at each step and that the compensation returns the system to a consistent state, for example the money is refunded if the order is cancelled.

sd-scale:0.title: Vertical and horizontal scaling
sd-scale:0.html:
Vertical scaling is a bigger machine: more CPU, more memory. Simple, no code changes, but there is a ceiling and a single point of failure.

Horizontal scaling is more instances behind a load balancer. Almost no ceiling and more resilient to failures, but it requires stateless services, shared storage for state and complicates the system.

Autoscaling adds instances by a metric: CPU, the number of requests, queue length. Important nuances: a new instance doesn't start instantly, and the DB often scales worse than services.

What QA tests in the context of scaling:

  • A load test: behaviour under the expected load: p95 and p99 latency, error rate.
  • A stress test: where and how the system breaks: whether it degrades gradually or fails completely.
  • A spike test: a sudden peak, for example a sale or a salary payout at 9:00. Does autoscaling keep up.
  • A soak test: several hours of load to find memory and connection leaks.

Tools: k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust. The choice of tool is less important than a realistic load profile and an environment close to production.

A typical mistake: running load on staging with an empty database. Queries that are fast on 1000 rows become slow on 50 million. A realistic data volume is needed.

In an interview: Horizontal scaling requires stateless services and gives resilience, while vertical is simpler but has a ceiling. As QA I check scaling with load, stress, spike and soak tests with a realistic data volume and look at p95, p99 and the error rate.

sd-scale:1.title: Idempotency, retries and rate limiting
sd-scale:1.html:
Idempotency means a repeated call of an operation gives the same result as the first. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent by the HTTP specification, and POST isn't. For payments POST is made idempotent too through an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key and passes it in a header. The server remembers the result by the key and on a repeat returns the same result without creating a new payment.

Why: the network is unreliable. The client sent a transfer, the response got lost, the client repeated. Without a key, a double debit.

Test cases for an idempotency key:

  • A repeat with the same key and the same body: the same transfer, one debit.
  • The same key with a different body: an error, not silent ignoring.
  • Two parallel requests with one key: one transfer.
  • A repeat after the key's retention period has expired: behaviour per the specification.

Retries with exponential backoff and jitter. The client repeats a request with a growing pause (1, 2, 4 seconds) and a random offset, so that thousands of clients don't repeat at the same time. Only idempotent operations may be repeated.

Rate limiting restricts the number of requests from a client over time, for example 100 requests per minute. Exceeding it gets a 429 Too Many Requests response, often with a Retry-After header. Algorithms: token bucket, sliding window. What to test: the limit boundary, the window reset, limits for different clients are independent, the client reacts to 429 correctly.

In an interview: For payments I always test an idempotency key: a repeat, parallel requests with one key and the same key with a different body. Separately I check rate limiting at the limit boundary and that the client handles 429 correctly with backoff, rather than repeating the request instantly.

sd-scale:2.title: CAP and reliability at a basic level
sd-scale:2.html:
The CAP theorem says: during a network partition (P) a distributed system must choose between consistency (C) and availability (A). Partitions do happen in a real network, so the choice is in fact between C and A at the moment of a failure.

  • CP: better to refuse an operation than to return inconsistent data. Example: debiting an account. A failure is better than a double debit.
  • AP: better to respond even if the data is slightly stale. Example: a product catalogue, the number of likes, recommendations.

The practical conclusion for QA: you need to know which behaviour is chosen for each function and test exactly that. If the balance is CP, then when the ledger is unavailable the API must return an error, not an old balance from the cache.

Reliability patterns worth knowing:

  • A timeout on every call to another service. Without a timeout one slow service blocks all threads.
  • A circuit breaker: after a series of errors it stops calling a dependency for a while and immediately returns a fallback or an error.
  • Graceful degradation: if the recommendations service is unavailable, the payment page still works.
  • A bulkhead: isolation of resources, so that the failure of one function doesn't take all the connections.

How to test this: chaos testing and fault injection. Delay a dependency's responses, kill an instance, break the DB connection, and check that the system behaves as intended. It is worth starting on staging and with controlled experiments.

In an interview: In practice CAP means a choice between consistency and availability during a network failure: for a balance I expect CP, for a catalogue AP is acceptable. I test this behaviour through fault injection: delays, failing dependencies, and I check timeouts, the circuit breaker and degradation of non-critical functions.

pt-pom:0.title: What problem Page Object solves
pt-pom:0.html:
Without Page Object, locators and UI actions are scattered across all the tests. The data-testid of the login button changed, and you fix 40 files. Tests read as a set of clicks, not as a business scenario.

A Page Object (POM) encapsulates a page or a screen: locators and actions live in one class, and a test calls methods with business names. The main benefits:

  • One point of change. A locator changed, you fix one line.
  • Readability. await loginPage.login(user) instead of three fill and click.
  • Reuse. The same actions aren't copied between tests.

Playwright has an important feature: a Locator is lazy. It doesn't look for an element at the moment of creation, only at an action or a check. So locators can be safely created in the constructor as readonly fields, even if the page isn't open yet.

It is important to understand that POM is not "a class for every URL". The boundaries of a Page Object are defined by meaning: a logical screen, a modal window, a complex form. If a page is huge, it is split into components (the next section).

In an interview: A Page Object encapsulates a page's locators and actions in one class, so when the UI changes I fix one place, and tests read as business scenarios. In Playwright locators are lazy, so I declare them in the constructor as readonly fields.

pt-pom:1.title: A minimal Page Object in Playwright
pt-pom:1.html:
import { type Page, type Locator, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export class LoginPage {
  readonly email: Locator;
  readonly password: Locator;
  readonly submit: Locator;
  readonly error: Locator;

  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {
    this.email = page.getByLabel('Email');
    this.password = page.getByLabel('Password');
    this.submit = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' });
    this.error = page.getByRole('alert');
  }

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('/login');
  }

  async login(email: string, password: string) {
    await this.email.fill(email);
    await this.password.fill(password);
    await this.submit.click();
  }
}

The test:

test('shows error for wrong password', async ({ page }) => {
  const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
  await loginPage.goto();
  await loginPage.login('user@test.com', 'wrong');
  await expect(loginPage.error).toHaveText('Invalid credentials');
});

Key points: page comes from outside through the constructor (not a global variable), methods are async and return a Promise, locators are public so a test can make web-first checks with expect(locator). Methods describe the user's intent (login), not the mechanics (clickSubmitButton). If an action leads to another page, the method may return a new Page Object, but in Playwright this isn't mandatory, because the page is the same.

In an interview: My Page Object gets page in the constructor, keeps locators as readonly fields and has async methods with business names. I leave locators accessible, so as to make checks through expect(locator) in the test.

pt-pom:2.title: Assertions in a Page Object, god objects and inheritance
pt-pom:2.html:
Assertions inside a Page Object

A classic discussion. Martin Fowler advises keeping assertions in tests: a Page Object describes a page, and the test decides what to check. A compromise approach, popular in Playwright: state-waiting methods are allowed, for example expectLoaded() with await expect(this.heading).toBeVisible(), because this is synchronisation, not a business check. But verifyOrderTotalIs100() in a Page Object hides the test's purpose and is poorly reusable.

A God Page Object

A class of 1500 lines with all the application's elements. Signs: dozens of unrelated methods, constant merge conflicts, nobody knows what is in there. The cure: split into pages and components (header, table, modal).

Inheritance chains

BasePage -> AuthenticatedPage -> AdminPage -> AdminUsersPage. A year later a change in BasePage breaks everything, and to understand a method you have to go through 4 files. A better option: a minimal or no base class, and shared parts through composition (readonly header = new Header(page)).

Other mistakes

  • Methods return a boolean instead of giving the test a locator (isVisible() doesn't wait, unlike expect().toBeVisible()).
  • page.waitForTimeout() in methods instead of auto-waiting.
  • A Page Object creates test data or goes to the API: that is a different responsibility.
In an interview: I keep business assertions in tests, and in a Page Object I allow only page state waits like expectLoaded. I split large pages into components, and instead of deep inheritance hierarchies I use composition.

pt-comp:0.title: Page Component: what it is and why
pt-comp:0.html:
A real UI consists of repeating blocks: a header, navigation, a table with pagination, a date picker, a modal window. They appear on many pages. If you describe them in every Page Object you get duplication, and if in BasePage, a god object.

A Page Component is a class that describes one UI block and receives not page but the block's root locator. All inner locators are built from the root, so a component can be used several times on one page.

export class DataTable {
  constructor(private readonly root: Locator) {}

  rows() {
    return this.root.getByRole('row');
  }

  rowByText(text: string) {
    return this.rows().filter({ hasText: text });
  }

  async sortBy(column: string) {
    await this.root.getByRole('columnheader', { name: column }).click();
  }
}

Now on a page with two tables (active and archived payments) two instances are created with different roots. Locators in Playwright are chainable, so scoping from the root works naturally and without complex CSS selectors.

In an interview: I move repeating UI blocks into a Page Component that takes a root Locator. That way one table or modal component works on any page and even several times on one.

pt-comp:1.title: Composition instead of inheritance
pt-comp:1.html:
The principle "has-a instead of is-a". A page doesn't inherit a header, it has a header.

export class PaymentsPage {
  readonly header: Header;
  readonly active: DataTable;
  readonly archived: DataTable;

  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {
    this.header = new Header(page.getByRole('banner'));
    this.active = new DataTable(page.getByTestId('active-payments'));
    this.archived = new DataTable(page.getByTestId('archived-payments'));
  }

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('/payments');
  }
}
await paymentsPage.header.openProfileMenu();
await expect(paymentsPage.active.rowByText('INV-42')).toBeVisible();

Advantages over inheritance:

  • A page takes only the components that are really on it.
  • Changing a component doesn't drag the whole hierarchy with it.
  • Components are easy to combine (a modal may contain the same table).

When NOT to: a small block with one element doesn't need a separate class, that is unnecessary abstraction. Also don't make a component "for growth" if the block is on only one page and is unlikely to repeat.

A typical interview mistake: saying "I have a BasePage with a header, footer and menu, and all pages inherit from it". The interviewer will ask what to do with a login page that has no header, and the hierarchy starts to crack.

In an interview: I prefer composition: a page has component fields rather than inheriting them. A base class, if there is one, is very thin, for example only page and goto.

pt-fixtures:0.title: Fixtures: DI built into Playwright Test
pt-fixtures:0.html:
Dependency Injection means that an object doesn't create its dependencies itself but receives them from outside. In Playwright Test this is implemented through fixtures: a test declares in its arguments what it needs, and the runner creates, passes in and then cleans up.

page, context, browser, request are built-in fixtures. Your own are added through test.extend:

import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { LoginPage } from './pages/login-page';
import { PaymentsPage } from './pages/payments-page';

type Pages = { loginPage: LoginPage; paymentsPage: PaymentsPage };

export const test = base.extend<Pages>({
  loginPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(new LoginPage(page));
  },
  paymentsPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(new PaymentsPage(page));
  },
});
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
test('archived payment visible', async ({ paymentsPage }) => {
  await paymentsPage.goto();
  await expect(paymentsPage.archived.rowByText('INV-1')).toBeVisible();
});

Key properties: fixtures are lazy (created only if a test requested them), can depend on other fixtures, the code before use is setup, after use is teardown, and the teardown runs even if the test failed. Several sets of fixtures from different modules can be combined with mergeTests.

In an interview: Fixtures in Playwright are built-in DI: a test asks for a dependency in its arguments, and the runner creates and cleans it up. I register Page Objects and API clients as fixtures, so there is no new or manual cleanup in tests.

pt-fixtures:1.title: Scope, auto and setup/teardown
pt-fixtures:1.html:
A fixture may have scope test (the default, new for every test) or worker (one per worker process, living between that worker's tests).

type WorkerFx = { apiToken: string };
type TestFx = { account: Account };

export const test = base.extend<TestFx, WorkerFx>({
  apiToken: [async ({}, use) => {
    const token = await fetchServiceToken();
    await use(token);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  account: async ({ request, apiToken }, use) => {
    const acc = await createAccount(request, apiToken);
    await use(acc);
    await deleteAccount(request, apiToken, acc.id);
  },
});

Rules asked about in interviews:

  • A worker fixture can't depend on a test fixture (for example on page), because it lives longer.
  • Worker fixtures suit expensive and immutable resources: a token, a DB connection, a test user per worker.
  • { auto: true } runs a fixture for every test, even if it wasn't requested. It fits logging and collecting console errors. Don't abuse it, because it is hidden magic.
  • The teardown order is the reverse of setup.

When NOT to: turn a fixture into a scenario with a dozen steps. A fixture prepares the environment, and the scenario itself must be visible in the test.

In an interview: I make expensive immutable resources worker fixtures, and everything a test can change test fixtures with cleanup after use. I use auto fixtures only for cross-cutting things like logging.

pt-fixtures:2.title: Fixtures or a base test class
pt-fixtures:2.html:
In the Java/Selenium world the standard is a BaseTest with @BeforeEach, where the driver and all pages are created. Candidates often carry this into Playwright, and that is a mistake.

Why fixtures are better:

  • Laziness. A base class creates everything for all tests. A fixture is created only for a test that needs it.
  • Isolation. Each test gets its own instances, and there are no shared class fields that can be accidentally changed.
  • Guaranteed teardown even when a test fails.
  • Composition. Fixtures combine through extend and mergeTests, whereas a base class can be inherited only once.
  • Typing. TypeScript knows the types of all the fixtures in the arguments.

beforeEach also has its place: for a simple step specific to one file (opening the needed page). But if the same beforeEach is copied into 10 files, it is a candidate for a fixture.

A typical mistake: declaring let loginPage: LoginPage at the describe level and filling it in beforeEach. This works, but a module variable easily becomes shared state, and TypeScript doesn't guarantee it is initialised.

In an interview: In Playwright I don't make a BaseTest, because fixtures give lazy creation, isolation, guaranteed cleanup and composition. I leave beforeEach for simple local steps within one file.

pt-builder:0.title: Test Data Builder: the problem and the solution
pt-builder:0.html:
Test objects in fintech are large: a payment has an amount, a currency, accounts, a status, dates, metadata. If each test assembles such an object by hand, you get noise, and when a required field is added all the tests break.

A Test Data Builder creates an object with valid default values and lets you change only what matters for a specific test.

export class PaymentBuilder {
  private data: Payment = {
    amount: 100,
    currency: 'EUR',
    status: 'pending',
    from: 'UA001',
    to: 'UA002',
  };

  withAmount(amount: number) { this.data.amount = amount; return this; }
  withCurrency(c: Currency) { this.data.currency = c; return this; }
  failed() { this.data.status = 'failed'; return this; }

  build(): Payment {
    return { ...this.data };
  }
}
const payment = new PaymentBuilder().withAmount(0).failed().build();

The test immediately shows what matters in it: a zero amount and the status failed. The other fields are simply valid. The methods return this, so a fluent chain works. Named methods like failed() express the domain language better than withStatus('failed').

build() returns a copy, so that a repeated call doesn't hand out the same mutable object.

In an interview: A builder gives a valid object by default, and the test changes only the fields that matter for the scenario. That way the test reads better, and I add a new required field in one place.

pt-builder:1.title: A Builder with faker, determinism and when a Builder is unnecessary
pt-builder:1.html:
Defaults are often generated through @faker-js/faker to avoid conflicts on unique fields in parallel runs:

import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';

export class UserBuilder {
  private data: NewUser = {
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    firstName: faker.person.firstName(),
    password: 'Str0ng!Pass',
  };

  withEmail(email: string) { this.data.email = email; return this; }
  build() { return { ...this.data }; }
}

Pitfalls:

  • Non-reproducibility. A test failed on a specific name with an apostrophe, and on a rerun the data is different. The solution: log the generated data or use faker.seed() for reproduction.
  • Randomness in values the check depends on. If a test checks an amount, the amount must be set explicitly, not taken from faker.
  • Defaults at the class field level are generated when an instance is created, so each new UserBuilder() gives a new user. If you move a default into a static constant, all tests get the same email.

When a Builder is NOT needed: an object with 2-3 fields. Then a function with Partial is enough: makeUser({ email }). In TypeScript object spread does much of what a Builder is needed for in Java. In an interview exactly this awareness sounds good, not "I make builders everywhere".

In an interview: For unique fields I use faker, but the values a test verifies I set explicitly, and I log the generated data so a failure can be reproduced. For simple objects I get by with a factory function with Partial, because a Builder is unnecessary there.

pt-factory:0.title: A test data factory
pt-factory:0.html:
A Factory encapsulates creating an object. In TypeScript tests the most popular variant is a simple function with defaults and a Partial override:

export function createCard(overrides: Partial<Card> = {}): Card {
  return {
    number: '4111111111111111',
    holder: 'TEST USER',
    expiry: '12/30',
    cvv: '123',
    ...overrides,
  };
}

const expired = createCard({ expiry: '01/20' });

This is shorter than a Builder and fully typed: TypeScript won't let you pass a field that isn't in Card.

The second popular form is a factory that not only builds an object but also creates the entity in the system through the API:

export async function createAccountViaApi(
  request: APIRequestContext,
  overrides: Partial<NewAccount> = {},
) {
  const res = await request.post('/api/accounts', {
    data: { currency: 'EUR', ...overrides },
  });
  expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  return (await res.json()) as Account;
}

Such a function is conveniently wrapped in a fixture, to add cleanup after use.

A nuance with spread: overrides with a field set to undefined will overwrite the default with undefined. For nested objects spread is shallow, so nested overrides must be merged separately.

In an interview: For data I most often make factory functions with defaults and a Partial override, which is short and type-safe. Factories that create entities through the API I wrap in fixtures, so cleanup is guaranteed.

pt-factory:1.title: Factory vs Builder and a Page Objects factory
pt-factory:1.html:
How they differ:

CriterionFactoryBuilder
Callone functiona chain of methods
Objectsimple or mediumcomplex, many variations
Domain languagethrough parametersthrough methods like failed()
Amount of codeminimalmore boilerplate

In practice they are combined: a Builder may use a defaults factory inside.

Another use is a Page Objects factory, so as not to write new in every test. For example an App class with the getters loginPage, paymentsPage. But in Playwright this role is usually better played by fixtures: they are lazy and already integrated with the runner. A separate page factory makes sense when pages must be created dynamically inside a test (for example, after opening a new tab you got a new page).

When a factory is NOT needed: if the object is used in one test and its fields are the essence of the check. Then an explicit literal in the test reads better (DAMP).

A typical mistake: a factory that returns the same constant object, and a test mutates it. The next test gets spoiled data. A factory must always return a new object.

In an interview: A factory is one function for simple variations, and a Builder is a fluent API for complex objects with a domain language. A Page Objects factory in Playwright I usually replace with fixtures.

pt-facade:0.title: Facade and business steps
pt-facade:0.html:
A Facade gives a simple interface to a complex subsystem. In tests it is a "steps" layer that combines several Page Objects and API calls into one business action: "make a transfer", "pass KYC".

export class TransferSteps {
  constructor(
    private readonly accounts: AccountsPage,
    private readonly transfer: TransferPage,
  ) {}

  async sendMoney(from: string, to: string, amount: number) {
    return test.step(`send ${amount} from ${from} to ${to}`, async () => {
      await this.accounts.open(from);
      await this.accounts.clickTransfer();
      await this.transfer.fill(to, amount);
      await this.transfer.confirm();
    });
  }
}

test.step groups actions in the report and trace, so a failure is seen as "send 100 from A to B", not as a click without context. test.step returns the callback's value. The option { box: true } shows the place of the error at the step's call line, not inside.

When NOT to: hide in a Facade what the test verifies. If a test is about validation of the transfer form, it must work with TransferPage directly. A Facade is needed for preconditions and repeated end-to-end paths.

A typical mistake: layers Test -> Steps -> Actions -> Pages -> Components, where each layer just forwards the call. That is not abstraction but indirection, which is hard to debug.

In an interview: My Facade is a steps class that combines several pages into one business action, wrapped in test.step for the report. I use it for preconditions, and what the test verifies I leave visible in the test itself.

pt-facade:1.title: App Actions: preconditions without the UI
pt-facade:1.html:
App Actions (a term popularised by Cypress) means preparing state through the API, the DB or the application itself, not by clicking the UI. For example, login through the UI in every test is slow and brittle, though the test is about something quite different.

Playwright has several mechanisms for this:

  • storageState. A setup project logs in once and saves cookies and localStorage to a file, and other projects pick it up through use: { storageState }.
  • The request fixture for creating data through the API before a test.
  • page.route for replacing backend responses.
// auth.setup.ts
import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';

setup('authenticate', async ({ request }) => {
  await request.post('/api/login', {
    data: { email: 'qa@test.com', password: process.env.QA_PASS },
  });
  await request.storageState({ path: '.auth/user.json' });
});

In the config this setup is declared as a separate project, and the main project lists it in dependencies and uses storageState: '.auth/user.json'.

When NOT to: for the login test itself, because there the UI is exactly what is being verified. You also need at least a few E2E tests that go through the key path fully through the UI.

In an interview: I prepare preconditions through the API and storageState, not through the UI, because it is many times faster and more stable. Through the UI I go only through what the test really verifies, plus a few end-to-end smoke scenarios.

pt-strategy:0.title: Strategy: varying behaviour behind a shared interface
pt-strategy:0.html:
Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, with the choice made at runtime. In a test framework typical examples are: different ways of logging in (UI, API, SSO), different payment methods, data generation for different regions.

interface LoginStrategy {
  login(page: Page, user: User): Promise<void>;
}

class UiLogin implements LoginStrategy {
  async login(page: Page, user: User) {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(user.email);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(user.password);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  }
}

class ApiLogin implements LoginStrategy {
  async login(page: Page, user: User) {
    const res = await page.request.post('/api/login', { data: user });
    expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  }
}

page.request shares cookies with the page's context, so after an API login the page is already authenticated (if the session is kept in cookies, not in localStorage).

The choice of strategy can be made through a fixture option set by test.use or a project in the config. Then the test doesn't know how exactly the login happened.

The advantage over if/else or switch: a new way is added with a new class, without changes in tests and in existing strategies (Open/Closed).

In an interview: I use Strategy when there are several interchangeable ways to do the same thing, for example login through the UI or the API. The test works with the interface, and the concrete implementation is chosen through a fixture option.

pt-strategy:1.title: Fixture options as Strategy and when the pattern is unnecessary
pt-strategy:1.html:
Playwright Test has a ready mechanism for choosing behaviour: option fixtures. The value is set in projects or through test.use.

type Opts = { loginMode: 'ui' | 'api' };

export const test = base.extend<Opts & { loggedIn: void }>({
  loginMode: ['api', { option: true }],
  loggedIn: async ({ page, loginMode }, use) => {
    const strategy = loginMode === 'ui' ? new UiLogin() : new ApiLogin();
    await strategy.login(page, defaultUser);
    await use();
  },
});
test.describe('login flow', () => {
  test.use({ loginMode: 'ui' });
  // ...
});

This is a combination of Strategy and DI: the test depends on loggedIn, and the concrete strategy is substituted by configuration.

When Strategy is NOT needed:

  • There are only two variants and no new ones are expected. A simple if in a fixture is more honest than an interface and three classes.
  • The difference between the "strategies" is one parameter. Then it is enough to pass a parameter.
  • For different browsers and devices. Playwright itself already does this through projects and devices, so you don't need to write your own browser strategy.

A typical interview mistake: calling any switch a Strategy. Strategy is about polymorphism: different implementations of one contract that can be swapped independently.

In an interview: In Playwright I implement Strategy through an option fixture: the value comes from projects or test.use, and the fixture picks the implementation. If there are two variants and there won't be more, I get by with a simple if.

pt-singleton:0.title: Singleton in Node and the Playwright worker model
pt-singleton:0.html:
A Singleton guarantees a single instance of a class and a global access point. In TypeScript it is often made not as a class with static getInstance(), but simply as an export of an object from a module, because a module is cached and executed once per process.

The key Playwright nuance: tests run in parallel in several worker processes (separate Node processes). Each worker loads modules anew. So:

  • A singleton is "one instance per worker", not for the whole run.
  • State written in one worker isn't visible in another.
  • Code in globalSetup runs in a separate process, so the variables it filled aren't visible to tests. Data must be passed through a file, environment variables or storageState.
// db.ts - a "singleton"
let pool: Pool | undefined;
export function getDb() {
  pool ??= new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DB_URL });
  return pool;
}

With workers: 4 there will be 4 pools. That is fine, but someone has to close them, and an ordinary module has no teardown hook. It is even worse with mutable state: a currentUser in a global module that tests change. The order of tests in a worker isn't guaranteed after a retry, and a test failure and a worker restart resets the state.

In an interview: In Playwright each worker is a separate Node process, so a module-level singleton lives separately in each worker, and shared state between them is impossible. So I don't keep mutable global state, and I make expensive resources worker fixtures.

pt-singleton:1.title: The alternative: a worker fixture instead of a Singleton
pt-singleton:1.html:
Everything candidates make a Singleton for (a DB connection, an API client, config) is better done in Playwright as a worker fixture. It gives the same "one instance per worker", but with a managed lifecycle.

export const test = base.extend<{}, { db: Pool }>({
  db: [async ({}, use) => {
    const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DB_URL });
    await use(pool);
    await pool.end();
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

What we get:

  • An explicit dependency: it is visible which tests use the DB.
  • Guaranteed closing of the resource.
  • Easy to replace in a separate file through a new extend.

Unique data per worker can be built from workerInfo.workerIndex or test.info().parallelIndex. parallelIndex lies in the range from 0 to workers - 1 and is preserved when a worker restarts, so it is convenient to use for a pool of pre-created test accounts.

When a Singleton is acceptable: an immutable config read once from env. There is no state there that can be spoiled.

A typical mistake: "I made a Singleton for the browser so as not to open it in every test". Playwright already reuses browser at the worker level, and test isolation is given by a new context. A custom singleton browser breaks isolation and parallelism.

In an interview: Instead of a Singleton I make worker fixtures: the same one instance per worker, but with an explicit dependency and a guaranteed teardown. I leave Singleton only for immutable config.

pt-screenplay:0.title: What Screenplay is
pt-screenplay:0.html:
Screenplay (formerly the Journey pattern) is an alternative to Page Object built around actors, not pages. A popular implementation for TypeScript and Playwright is Serenity/JS.

The main concepts:

  • Actor: who acts (for example, "Olena, a bank customer").
  • Ability: what an actor can do: drive a browser, call an API.
  • Task: a business task composed of other tasks and interactions ("Transfer money").
  • Interaction: a low-level action (a click, typing).
  • Question: what an actor can learn about the system (text, state), used in checks.

A test looks like a description of behaviour: an actor performs tasks and asks questions.

await actorCalled('Olena').attemptsTo(
  Navigate.to('/transfers'),
  TransferMoney.of(100).to('UA002'),
  Ensure.that(Text.of(Balance.label()), equals('900.00 EUR')),
);

The idea is that Tasks are small and independent, easy to combine, and each follows the single responsibility principle. A Page Object, on the contrary, often grows, because it gathers everything on the page.

In an interview: Screenplay models a test through actors, their abilities, tasks and questions to the system, not through pages. In the TS world it is implemented by Serenity/JS, and it scales well to large domain scenarios with several roles.

pt-screenplay:1.title: Screenplay vs POM: when not to
pt-screenplay:1.html:
A realistic assessment that is expected at a senior interview:

CriterionPOM + fixturesScreenplay
Learning curvelowhigh
Prevalence in Playwrightthe standardniche
Several roles in a scenarioby handnatural
Amount of codelessmore small classes

Screenplay is justified when many actors interact in one scenario (a customer, an operator, an admin), the domain is complex and tests are written as living documentation.

When NOT to:

  • The team is small or of mixed levels, and the learning curve becomes a bottleneck.
  • A medium-sized project where POM with components and fixtures already covers the needs.
  • You want a "trendy" framework without a real problem it solves.

Playwright fixtures and a Steps layer already give most of the benefits: DI, business steps, reporting through test.step. So for most Playwright projects the standard is POM.

A typical mistake: claiming that Screenplay is "better than POM" without context, or on the contrary dismissing it without knowing the idea. A right answer shows the trade-off.

In an interview: I know Screenplay and understand its advantages for complex domains with several roles, but for most Playwright projects I choose POM with components and fixtures, because the learning curve is lower and the team writes tests faster.

pt-principles:0.title: SOLID in a test framework
pt-principles:0.html:
SOLID is applicable to test code, but with an adjustment for the goal: tests must be simple and readable.

  • S, Single Responsibility. A Page Object describes the UI, a factory creates data, an API client goes to the API, a test verifies. A Page Object that also creates a user through the DB violates SRP.
  • O, Open/Closed. A new login method is added by a new strategy, not by editing a switch in ten places.
  • L, Liskov. If AdminPage extends BasePage, then everywhere BasePage is expected, AdminPage must work correctly. Deep page hierarchies often violate this.
  • I, Interface Segregation. Don't make one ApiClient of 200 methods. Better PaymentsApi, UsersApi.
  • D, Dependency Inversion. A test depends on an abstraction (the loggedIn fixture), not on a specific way of logging in. In Playwright fixtures implement this naturally.

The main caveat: SOLID in tests is not an end in itself. An interface with one implementation and three layers of abstraction for a 5-line test makes the code worse.

In an interview: The most important for me in tests are SRP and Dependency Inversion: each class does one thing, and tests get dependencies through fixtures. The rest I apply when there is real variability, not for the sake of a template.

pt-principles:1.title: DRY vs DAMP and KISS
pt-principles:1.html:
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) says remove duplication. DAMP (Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases) says a test must read on its own, even at the cost of repetition.

In tests you have to balance:

  • DRY for infrastructure: locators, steps, fixtures, factories.
  • DAMP for the test itself: input data and expectations must be visible in the test body.

Bad (too DRY):

test('limit', async ({ transferPage }) => {
  await runScenario(transferPage, SCENARIOS[3]);
});

To understand what is being checked, you have to open two files. Better:

test('blocks transfer above daily limit', async ({ transferPage }) => {
  await transferPage.fill('UA002', 50_001);
  await transferPage.confirm();
  await expect(transferPage.error).toHaveText('Daily limit exceeded');
});

KISS (Keep It Simple) and YAGNI: don't build an abstraction "for the future". Three tests with the same two lines aren't yet a reason for a new layer. Logic in tests (if, loops with conditions) is also a signal: a test must be linear.

Parameterisation through a for loop over an array of cases with test() inside is fine, if each case has a clear name.

In an interview: I apply DRY to infrastructure, and write tests in the DAMP style, so that data and expectations are visible without jumping into other files. I add an abstraction when duplication has become a real problem, not in advance.

pt-principles:2.title: Typical antipatterns in frameworks
pt-principles:2.html:
A list worth knowing and being able to explain:

  • A God Page Object and a God Helper: a 2000-line utils.ts where everything is dumped.
  • Deep inheritance of pages and tests instead of composition.
  • Shared mutable state between tests: module variables, test order as a dependency. In Playwright tests must be isolated, because they run in parallel and may be restarted.
  • Hard waits with waitForTimeout instead of web-first assertions and auto-waiting.
  • Assertions with no purpose in helpers: a helper silently checks ten things, and it is unclear what failed.
  • Wrappers over wrappers: your own click() that calls locator.click() with no added value. It hides API options and gets in the way of the trace.
  • Logic in tests: if (await el.isVisible()) makes a test non-deterministic.
  • Test data constants that tests mutate.
  • Abstraction for growth: Screenplay, interfaces and factories for 20 tests.

How to talk about this in an interview: don't just list them, give an example from experience and what was done. For example: "We had a BasePage with 60 methods, we moved the header and tables into components, and reworked login to storageState. The run time went down, and there were fewer conflicts in PRs."

In an interview: The most frequent antipatterns I have seen are god objects, deep inheritance, shared state between tests and hard timeouts. I fixed them with components, fixtures, isolated data and web-first assertions.
